lessons.briefing:
# 00 — Hello, Dojo (ASP.NET Core)

Welcome to the .NET track. Everything you have written so far in this dojo has
been a function that someone called. From here on, the caller is the network:
you write endpoints, and something outside your process decides when to run
them, with what input, and what to do with what comes back. That shift is the
whole subject of this track, and it starts with the smallest possible version
of it — one route, one handler, one HTTP response.

There is a running ASP.NET Core application in this repository. It is real: it
has a `Program.cs`, an `appsettings.json`, a dependency-injection container and
a middleware pipeline, and `dotnet run` would serve it on a port. You will
never run it on a port, though, because the gate does something better. It
boots the *same* application in memory, wires an `HttpClient` straight into its
pipeline, and makes real requests through real routing and real model binding —
with no socket, no port, no flaky "is the server up yet" sleep. Your gate is an
integration test, and integration tests that fast are the reason .NET teams
write so many of them.

The second thing to get straight is where things live, because this track
splits a lesson across three places and the split is not arbitrary. Your *code*
lives in the web application, `src/Api/`, one folder per lesson — because
that's where the compiler and the web host need it. The *lesson* — this README,
the theory, the hints — lives under `lessons/00_hello_dojo/`. The *gate* lives
in `tests/Gates/`, which is exactly where tests live in every .NET repository
you will ever join.

So: **you edit files under `src/Api/`. You read files under `lessons/`. You
never edit `tests/Gates/`** — though you should absolutely read it, and it is
quoted verbatim at the bottom of this page.

## The loop

For this lesson the map is:

```
tracks/dotnet/
├── src/Api/
│   ├── Program.cs                     the composition root (you rarely touch it)
│   ├── LessonModules.cs               how a lesson's endpoints get wired up
│   └── L00_HelloDojo/                 <- YOU EDIT THESE
│       ├── Ex1.cs                        namespace DotnetDojo.Api.L00_HelloDojo
│       ├── Ex2.cs
│       └── Ex3.cs
├── tests/Gates/L00_HelloDojoTests.cs   <- the gate (read it, never edit it)
└── lessons/00_hello_dojo/             <- this README, reading.md, hints
```

The commands you will live in:

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo        # grade the whole lesson
uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex2    # grade just one exercise
uv run dojo hint dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex2    # stuck? reveal the next tier
uv run dojo read dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex2    # the theory behind it
uv run dojo status dotnet                    # the progress dashboard
uv run dojo next dotnet                      # what should I do now?
```

`dotnet` also answers to `net`, so `uv run dojo test net 00 ex2` is the same
command with less typing.

Before you write a single line, run the gate and watch it fail:

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo
```

Three red tests. Each one made a real HTTP request, got a **500**, and printed
the response body — which is the `NotImplementedException` your stub threw,
because in the Development environment ASP.NET Core turns an unhandled
exception into a 500 whose body is the exception itself. That is the correct
state of a fresh checkout, and it is worth noticing that it is *not* a compiler
error: every stub in this course compiles, so a half-finished exercise never
breaks the lesson next to it.

## Concept — a route, a handler, a result

Here is a complete ASP.NET Core endpoint:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/hello", () => TypedResults.Ok(new { message = "hi" }));
```

Read it in three pieces, because each piece is a different job.

`MapGet("/hello", …)` is **routing**: it says that a `GET` whose path is
`/hello` should be handled here. There is a `MapPost`, a `MapPut`, a
`MapDelete` and a `MapPatch` too, and the HTTP method is part of the route —
`GET /hello` and `POST /hello` are two different endpoints that can live in two
different methods.

The lambda is the **handler**. ASP.NET Core calls it when the route matches,
and — this is the part that surprises people coming from Express or Flask — it
looks at your handler's *parameters* and fills them in for you. That is model
binding, and you will meet it in ex2 and ex3.

`TypedResults.Ok(value)` is the **result**: an object that knows how to write
itself onto the response. `Ok` means status 200 and serialise `value` as JSON.
There are siblings for every status code you care about — `TypedResults.NotFound()`,
`TypedResults.BadRequest()`, `TypedResults.NoContent()`, `TypedResults.Created(uri, value)` —
and you will use all of them in lesson 01. Returning a *result object* rather
than writing bytes to the response yourself is what keeps a handler testable:
it is a value you could inspect, not a side effect you have to observe.

In this course, handlers are written as named methods and passed to `MapGet`
as a method group, like this:

```csharp
public class Ex0 : IEndpointMapper
{
    public void MapEndpoints(IEndpointRouteBuilder app)
    {
        app.MapGet("/l00/example", Example);
    }

    private static IResult Example() => TypedResults.Ok(new { ok = true });
}
```

Two reasons. A named method has a signature you can read, which matters when
we start injecting services into it. And a lambda whose body is nothing but
`throw` has no return type for the compiler to infer, so the stubs would not
even build — which tells you something useful about how much of minimal-API
magic is really just C# overload resolution.

The `IEndpointMapper` wrapper is this course's own convention, not
ASP.NET Core's. `Program.cs` never grows a route per lesson; instead it asks
`LessonModules` to find every class in the assembly that implements
`IEndpointMapper` and call it. So the moment you write a mapper class, its
routes exist. Read `src/Api/LessonModules.cs` once — it is about forty lines
and there is nothing clever in it.

## Exercise 1 — your first endpoint

Edit `src/Api/L00_HelloDojo/Ex1.cs`. The route is already mapped; implement
`Ping` so that `GET /l00/ping` answers **200** with this JSON body:

```json
{"status":"ok","lesson":"00_hello_dojo"}
```

The file already declares `public record PingResponse(string Status, string Lesson)`
for you — return an `Ok` of one of those. Note that the C# properties are
`Status` and `Lesson` in PascalCase while the JSON comes out `status` and
`lesson` in camelCase; ASP.NET Core's JSON defaults do that conversion, and
you do not have to ask for it.

Every route in this track starts with the lesson's own prefix — `/l00/…` here,
`/l01/…` next lesson — so that lesson 07's `/orders` can never collide with
lesson 05's.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — read the query string, and say no

Edit `src/Api/L00_HelloDojo/Ex2.cs`. Implement `Echo` so that
`GET /l00/echo?message=hi` answers **200** with:

```json
{"message":"hi","length":2}
```

`length` is the number of characters in the message, so `?message=dojo` gives
`4`.

The handler signature is `Echo(string? message)`, and that parameter is already
bound to the `message` query-string value for you — the name matches, the type
is simple, so ASP.NET Core reads it out of the query. It is `string?` because
the caller might not send one at all.

When the message is missing, empty, or nothing but whitespace, answer **400
Bad Request** with no body. That is the honest status code: the request was
malformed, and the caller — not your server — is the one that has to change.
Returning a 200 with an empty string would be lying, and letting the handler
throw would be a 500, which blames you for their mistake.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — read a JSON request body

Edit `src/Api/L00_HelloDojo/Ex3.cs`. Implement `Greet` so that
`POST /l00/greetings` with the body `{"name":"Ada"}` answers **200** with:

```json
{"greeting":"Hello, Ada!"}
```

A whitespace-only or missing name is a **400**, exactly as in ex2.

The handler takes a `GreetingRequest request` — a complex type, so ASP.NET Core
binds it from the JSON request body rather than the query string. That rule is
worth memorising now: *simple types come from the route and query string,
complex types come from the body.* Nothing in the code says "read the body";
the parameter's type said it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex3
```

# Reading - dotnet/00_hello_dojo

The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole course.
This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the problems you
just solved. Read it **after** you attempt a problem, whether the gate went
green or red.

## Notes

**What actually happened when you ran the gate.** `dojo test dotnet` shells out
to `dotnet test`, which compiles `src/Api` into `Api.dll`, compiles
`tests/Gates` into `Gates.dll` (which references the first), and hands the test
assembly to xUnit. Then `DojoWebFactory` — a `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` —
runs your `Program.cs` for real, all the way to a built `WebApplication`, but
swaps the network transport for an in-memory one. `factory.CreateClient()`
returns an `HttpClient` whose message handler is that transport. No port is
opened, nothing is listening, and yet routing, model binding, dependency
injection, middleware and JSON serialisation all run exactly as they would in
production. That is why this course can grade a web application as
deterministically as it grades a pure function.

**Minimal APIs versus controllers.** What you wrote today is a *minimal API*:
routes declared with `MapGet`/`MapPost` and handlers that are plain methods.
The older MVC style puts handlers on a `Controller` class with `[HttpGet]`
attributes, discovered by convention. Both sit on the same routing, binding and
filter machinery, and both are fully supported; minimal APIs start smaller and
have less ceremony, controllers organise a large surface into classes and give
you model-validation attributes for free. Interviewers like asking which you
prefer — the answer they are listening for is that you know they share a
foundation, not that one is "modern" and the other "legacy".

**`Results` versus `TypedResults`.** `Results.Ok(x)` returns `IResult`;
`TypedResults.Ok(x)` returns the concrete `Ok<T>`, which still *is* an
`IResult`. The concrete type buys you two things: the compiler can check that
you returned what your signature promised, and ASP.NET Core can describe your
endpoint in OpenAPI without running it. Prefer `TypedResults` in new code. When
a handler can return more than one shape, `Results<Ok<Widget>, NotFound>` as
the return type keeps both benefits — you will use that in lesson 01.

**Async, everywhere, on purpose.** Every gate method here is
`async Task` and every call is awaited. That is not test ceremony: a web server
handles thousands of concurrent requests on a small pool of threads, and it can
only do that if a request that is waiting on a database or an HTTP call gives
its thread back. Blocking on `.Result` or `.Wait()` inside a handler takes that
thread out of circulation and, under load, is how a .NET service deadlocks
itself. "Async all the way down" is the phrase, and it is one of the most
common interview questions on this stack.

## ex1 - a route, a handler, a result

The smallest interesting thing in this exercise is that you never wrote any
JSON. You returned a `PingResponse` record and something turned it into
`{"status":"ok","lesson":"00_hello_dojo"}` — that something is
`System.Text.Json`, configured by ASP.NET Core with what it calls *web
defaults*: camelCase property names, case-insensitive reading, and numbers
written as numbers. The casing conversion is why the C# property `Status`
arrives at the client as `status`, and why the gate can read it back into a
record whose property is `Status` again.

The other thing worth noticing is that `Ping` returns `IResult` rather than a
`PingResponse`. You *could* have returned the record directly — ASP.NET Core
would serialise it and use 200 — but then the status code would be an
assumption rather than a decision, and there would be nowhere to put the 400
you needed one exercise later. Returning a result object means the status code
is part of the value your handler produces.

## ex2 - model binding, and the 400 that means "your fault"

`Echo(string? message)` reads from the query string because of a rule you can
state in one sentence: parameters of *simple* types (string, int, Guid,
DateTime, anything with a `TryParse`) are looked for in the route template
first and the query string second, while *complex* types come from the request
body. Nothing annotated anything. If you ever need to override that guess the
attributes exist — `[FromQuery]`, `[FromRoute]`, `[FromBody]`, `[FromHeader]`,
`[FromServices]` — and being explicit is not a sin, but knowing the default is
what lets you read other people's handlers.

The 400 is the part with real content. Four hundred means *the request was
wrong*; five hundred means *the server was wrong*. If your handler throws on a
missing query parameter, you have told the caller "my fault, try again later"
when the truth was "your fault, fix the request" — and every retry policy,
alert and error budget downstream of you now behaves incorrectly. Deciding
which side of that line a failure falls on is a judgement your framework cannot
make for you, and lesson 08 turns it into a policy.

`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` rather than `== null` is the small half of the
lesson: `?message=` sends an empty string, and `?message=%20` sends a space.
Both are "no message" to a human and neither is null.

## ex3 - the body, and where DTOs come from

Binding a JSON body into a record is one line of nothing — declare the
parameter, get the object — and that is exactly why it deserves a warning. The
type you bind is a *contract with the outside world*. It gets versioned by
clients you do not control, it can carry properties an attacker chose, and it
should never be the same type you persist. Lesson 07 makes that split explicit
under the name DTOs versus entities; today just notice that `GreetingRequest`
exists only to describe what arrives, and `GreetingResponse` exists only to
describe what leaves.

`request.Name` is `string?` for a reason: JSON is not the C# type system. A
client can send `{}`, or `{"name":null}`, or `{"name":123}`, and the first two
give you a null `Name` with no complaint at all. Nullable reference types are
telling you the truth here — the value really might be missing — and the
`IsNullOrWhiteSpace` check is not defensive programming, it is the validation
that turns an untrusted payload into a value your code can rely on.

## Further reading

- [Minimal APIs overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/overview) — the whole surface you will use for the next ten lessons, in one page.
- [Parameter binding in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding) — the exact rules for what comes from the route, the query, the body and the container.
- [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses) — `Results` versus `TypedResults`, and the full catalogue of result helpers.
- [Integration tests in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests) — `WebApplicationFactory`, which is the machinery behind every gate in this track.
- [The `dotnet test` command](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-test) — including `--filter`, which is how one exercise gets graded on its own.

```csharp
using System.Net;
using System.Net.Http.Json;

namespace DotnetDojo.Gates;

public class L00_HelloDojoTests(DojoWebFactory factory) : IClassFixture<DojoWebFactory>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex1_PingReportsThatTheApiIsUp()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/l00/ping");

        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, response,
            "GET /l00/ping must answer 200 OK. A 500 here means the handler still throws; "
                + "a 404 means the route was never mapped - reread README ex1.");

        var body = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<PingDto>();
        Teach.Equal("ok", body?.Status,
            "The JSON body needs a \"status\" property whose value is exactly \"ok\".");
        Teach.Equal("00_hello_dojo", body?.Lesson,
            "The JSON body needs a \"lesson\" property whose value is exactly \"00_hello_dojo\".");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex2_EchoReadsTheQueryStringAndRejectsAnEmptyOne()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var ok = await client.GetAsync("/l00/echo?message=hi");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, ok,
            "GET /l00/echo?message=hi must answer 200 OK - reread README ex2.");

        var body = await ok.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<EchoDto>();
        Teach.Equal("hi", body?.Message,
            "Echo the message back unchanged: the value came from the query string, "
                + "so it must not be hard-coded.");
        Teach.Equal(2, body?.Length,
            "\"length\" is the number of characters in the message - \"hi\" is 2.");

        var longer = await client.GetAsync("/l00/echo?message=dojo");
        var longerBody = await longer.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<EchoDto>();
        Teach.Equal(4, longerBody?.Length,
            "\"dojo\" is 4 characters. A hard-coded 2 passes the first check and fails this one.");

        var missing = await client.GetAsync("/l00/echo");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest, missing,
            "GET /l00/echo with no message at all is the caller's mistake, so it is a 400, "
                + "not a 200 with an empty string and not a 500.");

        var blank = await client.GetAsync("/l00/echo?message=%20%20");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest, blank,
            "A message of two spaces is blank too. Check for whitespace, not just for null.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex3_GreetingsReadsTheJsonRequestBody()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var ok = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/l00/greetings", new { name = "Ada" });
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, ok,
            "POST /l00/greetings with {\"name\":\"Ada\"} must answer 200 OK - reread README ex3.");

        var body = await ok.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<GreetingDto>();
        Teach.Equal("Hello, Ada!", body?.Greeting,
            "The body needs a \"greeting\" property equal to \"Hello, Ada!\" - comma, "
                + "exclamation mark and all.");

        var other = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/l00/greetings", new { name = "Grace" });
        var otherBody = await other.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<GreetingDto>();
        Teach.Equal("Hello, Grace!", otherBody?.Greeting,
            "The name has to come out of the request body, not be hard-coded.");

        var blank = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/l00/greetings", new { name = "   " });
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest, blank,
            "A whitespace-only name is not a name: answer 400.");
    }

    private sealed record PingDto(string? Status, string? Lesson);

    private sealed record EchoDto(string? Message, int? Length);

    private sealed record GreetingDto(string? Greeting);
}
```

In plain English: `factory.CreateClient()` boots the whole application in
memory and hands you an `HttpClient` plugged into its pipeline, so every
`GetAsync` below is a genuine request through routing, model binding and your
handler. `Teach.Status` asserts a status code and, when it does not match,
prints the body — which is where the real message usually is.
`Teach.Equal(expected, actual, why)` behaves like xUnit's `Assert.Equal` but
leads with the sentence telling you what to reread. Both live in
`tests/Gates/Teach.cs`; there is nothing clever in there.

Note the naming: the class is `L00_HelloDojoTests` and each method starts
`Ex1_`, `Ex2_`, `Ex3_`. That is how `uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex2`
becomes a `dotnet test --filter` expression, and it is the convention every
lesson in this track follows.

Notice too what the gate never does: it does not reach into the container to
check that you registered something, and it does not call your handler methods
directly. It asks the same questions a client would ask — what status, what
headers, what body — which is why passing it means the endpoint really works,
not that it satisfied a test.

## The teaching point

The habit this lesson builds is **predicting the failure**. You ran the gate
before writing anything, so you know what red looks like; every red run from
here is a comparison, not a surprise. And you already know the three shapes of
red in this track: a 404 means the route never got mapped, a 500 means your
handler blew up, and a 200 with the wrong body means your logic is wrong. Those
three tell you where to look before you have read a single line of the diff.

The other habit is choosing the status code deliberately. You wrote a 400 twice
today, in both cases because the *caller* got it wrong. Most bugs in real APIs
are not crashes; they are a service that answers 200 to a request it did not
understand, and a client that carries on as if everything is fine.

Next: **01_routing_endpoints**, where routes get parameters, groups and every
result type you will need for a real resource.

# Reading - dotnet/00_hello_dojo

The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole course.
This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the problems you
just solved. Read it **after** you attempt a problem, whether the gate went
green or red.

## Notes

**What actually happened when you ran the gate.** `dojo test dotnet` shells out
to `dotnet test`, which compiles `src/Api` into `Api.dll`, compiles
`tests/Gates` into `Gates.dll` (which references the first), and hands the test
assembly to xUnit. Then `DojoWebFactory` — a `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` —
runs your `Program.cs` for real, all the way to a built `WebApplication`, but
swaps the network transport for an in-memory one. `factory.CreateClient()`
returns an `HttpClient` whose message handler is that transport. No port is
opened, nothing is listening, and yet routing, model binding, dependency
injection, middleware and JSON serialisation all run exactly as they would in
production. That is why this course can grade a web application as
deterministically as it grades a pure function.

**Minimal APIs versus controllers.** What you wrote today is a *minimal API*:
routes declared with `MapGet`/`MapPost` and handlers that are plain methods.
The older MVC style puts handlers on a `Controller` class with `[HttpGet]`
attributes, discovered by convention. Both sit on the same routing, binding and
filter machinery, and both are fully supported; minimal APIs start smaller and
have less ceremony, controllers organise a large surface into classes and give
you model-validation attributes for free. Interviewers like asking which you
prefer — the answer they are listening for is that you know they share a
foundation, not that one is "modern" and the other "legacy".

**`Results` versus `TypedResults`.** `Results.Ok(x)` returns `IResult`;
`TypedResults.Ok(x)` returns the concrete `Ok<T>`, which still *is* an
`IResult`. The concrete type buys you two things: the compiler can check that
you returned what your signature promised, and ASP.NET Core can describe your
endpoint in OpenAPI without running it. Prefer `TypedResults` in new code. When
a handler can return more than one shape, `Results<Ok<Widget>, NotFound>` as
the return type keeps both benefits — you will use that in lesson 01.

**Async, everywhere, on purpose.** Every gate method here is
`async Task` and every call is awaited. That is not test ceremony: a web server
handles thousands of concurrent requests on a small pool of threads, and it can
only do that if a request that is waiting on a database or an HTTP call gives
its thread back. Blocking on `.Result` or `.Wait()` inside a handler takes that
thread out of circulation and, under load, is how a .NET service deadlocks
itself. "Async all the way down" is the phrase, and it is one of the most
common interview questions on this stack.

## ex1 - a route, a handler, a result

The smallest interesting thing in this exercise is that you never wrote any
JSON. You returned a `PingResponse` record and something turned it into
`{"status":"ok","lesson":"00_hello_dojo"}` — that something is
`System.Text.Json`, configured by ASP.NET Core with what it calls *web
defaults*: camelCase property names, case-insensitive reading, and numbers
written as numbers. The casing conversion is why the C# property `Status`
arrives at the client as `status`, and why the gate can read it back into a
record whose property is `Status` again.

The other thing worth noticing is that `Ping` returns `IResult` rather than a
`PingResponse`. You *could* have returned the record directly — ASP.NET Core
would serialise it and use 200 — but then the status code would be an
assumption rather than a decision, and there would be nowhere to put the 400
you needed one exercise later. Returning a result object means the status code
is part of the value your handler produces.

## ex2 - model binding, and the 400 that means "your fault"

`Echo(string? message)` reads from the query string because of a rule you can
state in one sentence: parameters of *simple* types (string, int, Guid,
DateTime, anything with a `TryParse`) are looked for in the route template
first and the query string second, while *complex* types come from the request
body. Nothing annotated anything. If you ever need to override that guess the
attributes exist — `[FromQuery]`, `[FromRoute]`, `[FromBody]`, `[FromHeader]`,
`[FromServices]` — and being explicit is not a sin, but knowing the default is
what lets you read other people's handlers.

The 400 is the part with real content. Four hundred means *the request was
wrong*; five hundred means *the server was wrong*. If your handler throws on a
missing query parameter, you have told the caller "my fault, try again later"
when the truth was "your fault, fix the request" — and every retry policy,
alert and error budget downstream of you now behaves incorrectly. Deciding
which side of that line a failure falls on is a judgement your framework cannot
make for you, and lesson 08 turns it into a policy.

`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` rather than `== null` is the small half of the
lesson: `?message=` sends an empty string, and `?message=%20` sends a space.
Both are "no message" to a human and neither is null.

## ex3 - the body, and where DTOs come from

Binding a JSON body into a record is one line of nothing — declare the
parameter, get the object — and that is exactly why it deserves a warning. The
type you bind is a *contract with the outside world*. It gets versioned by
clients you do not control, it can carry properties an attacker chose, and it
should never be the same type you persist. Lesson 07 makes that split explicit
under the name DTOs versus entities; today just notice that `GreetingRequest`
exists only to describe what arrives, and `GreetingResponse` exists only to
describe what leaves.

`request.Name` is `string?` for a reason: JSON is not the C# type system. A
client can send `{}`, or `{"name":null}`, or `{"name":123}`, and the first two
give you a null `Name` with no complaint at all. Nullable reference types are
telling you the truth here — the value really might be missing — and the
`IsNullOrWhiteSpace` check is not defensive programming, it is the validation
that turns an untrusted payload into a value your code can rely on.

## Further reading

- [Minimal APIs overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/overview) — the whole surface you will use for the next ten lessons, in one page.
- [Parameter binding in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding) — the exact rules for what comes from the route, the query, the body and the container.
- [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses) — `Results` versus `TypedResults`, and the full catalogue of result helpers.
- [Integration tests in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests) — `WebApplicationFactory`, which is the machinery behind every gate in this track.
- [The `dotnet test` command](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-test) — including `--filter`, which is how one exercise gets graded on its own.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — your first endpoint

Edit `src/Api/L00_HelloDojo/Ex1.cs`. The route is already mapped; implement
`Ping` so that `GET /l00/ping` answers **200** with this JSON body:

```json
{"status":"ok","lesson":"00_hello_dojo"}
```

The file already declares `public record PingResponse(string Status, string Lesson)`
for you — return an `Ok` of one of those. Note that the C# properties are
`Status` and `Lesson` in PascalCase while the JSON comes out `status` and
`lesson` in camelCase; ASP.NET Core's JSON defaults do that conversion, and
you do not have to ask for it.

Every route in this track starts with the lesson's own prefix — `/l00/…` here,
`/l01/…` next lesson — so that lesson 07's `/orders` can never collide with
lesson 05's.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The route is already mapped for you; the only thing missing is what `Ping`
gives back. Two decisions are hiding in one line: which status code, and which
value gets serialised into the body.

The file already declares the record you need. Scroll to the bottom of
`Ex1.cs`.

## Hint 2

Replace the `throw` with a `return` of a result object. The helper for "200 and
here is the JSON" is `TypedResults.Ok(value)`, and `value` is a
`new PingResponse(...)` built from the two strings the gate is looking for.

Because the body is a single expression, you can keep the expression-bodied
form (`=>`) rather than adding braces.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
private static IResult Ping() =>
    TypedResults.Ok(new PingResponse(/* status */, /* lesson */));
```

The two strings are exactly the ones in the README's JSON block, including the
underscores in the lesson slug. Do not convert anything to camelCase yourself —
the serialiser does that on the way out.

## Exercise 2 — read the query string, and say no

Edit `src/Api/L00_HelloDojo/Ex2.cs`. Implement `Echo` so that
`GET /l00/echo?message=hi` answers **200** with:

```json
{"message":"hi","length":2}
```

`length` is the number of characters in the message, so `?message=dojo` gives
`4`.

The handler signature is `Echo(string? message)`, and that parameter is already
bound to the `message` query-string value for you — the name matches, the type
is simple, so ASP.NET Core reads it out of the query. It is `string?` because
the caller might not send one at all.

When the message is missing, empty, or nothing but whitespace, answer **400
Bad Request** with no body. That is the honest status code: the request was
malformed, and the caller — not your server — is the one that has to change.
Returning a 200 with an empty string would be lying, and letting the handler
throw would be a 500, which blames you for their mistake.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 00_hello_dojo ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — read a JSON request body

Edit `src/Api/L00_HelloDojo/Ex3.cs`. Implement `Greet` so that
`POST /l00/greetings` with the body `{"name":"Ada"}` answers **200** with:

```json
{"greeting":"Hello, Ada!"}
```

The handler takes a `GreetingRequest request` — a complex type, so ASP.NET Core
binds it from the JSON request body rather than the query string. That rule is
worth memorising now: *simple types come from the route and query string,
complex types come from the body.* Nothing in the code says "read the body";
the parameter's type said it.

## Hint 1

Structurally this is ex2 again: validate, return 400 if the input is not
usable, otherwise return 200 with a record. The only new thing is where the
value comes from.

`GreetingRequest` is a complex type, so ASP.NET Core has already read the JSON
body and handed you the object. There is nothing to parse — reach into the
parameter.

## Hint 2

`request.Name` is `string?`, so the same null-or-whitespace guard from ex2
applies before you use it.

For the greeting itself, C# string interpolation (`$"..."`) is the readable
way to build `"Hello, Ada!"` from a name. Watch the punctuation: comma after
"Hello", exclamation mark at the end, no trailing space.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
private static IResult Greet(GreetingRequest request)
{
    if (/* the same guard as ex2, on request.Name */)
    {
        return TypedResults.BadRequest();
    }

    return TypedResults.Ok(new GreetingResponse($"Hello, {/* … */}!"));
}
```

The `$` prefix is the part people forget: without it you would return the
literal characters `{request.Name}` and the gate would show them to you.

lessons.briefing:
# 01 — Routing and endpoints

Lesson 00's three endpoints were three separate facts: a path, a handler, a
response. A real API is not a bag of facts, it is a *resource* — a set of
routes that share a prefix, a shape and a vocabulary, so that a client who has
learned `GET /orders/3` can guess `POST /orders` without reading your docs.
This lesson is about the machinery that makes that possible, and about the part
nobody teaches: choosing the status code that tells the truth.

The dataset is five orders and three products, sitting in a static list in
`src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Catalog.cs`. Read it before you start — every
expected value in this lesson comes from that file, and there is no database in
the way yet:

```
Id  Customer  Status      TotalCents
1   Ada       shipped     4200
2   Grace     pending     1999
3   Ada       shipped     15000
4   Linus     cancelled   800
5   Grace     shipped     2500
```

## Concept — the route template, the constraint, and the result

A route template is a pattern with holes in it:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/l01/example/{id:int}", Example);

private static IResult Example(int id) => TypedResults.Ok(new { youAsked = id });
```

`{id:int}` declares a **route parameter** named `id` with an `int`
**constraint**. Two things follow from that, and both matter.

First, the parameter arrives in your handler already parsed. You wrote
`int id`, not `string id` plus a `TryParse` — routing matched the name and the
type did the rest.

Second, and less obvious: a request to `/l01/example/banana` does not reach
your handler at all. The constraint is part of *matching*, so there is simply
no route for that URL, and routing answers **404**. That surprises people who
expect a 400. Think of it this way: a constraint says "this route is only for
integers", not "this route validates integers". `{id:int:min(1)}`,
`{code:guid}`, `{slug:alpha}` and `{name:length(1,50)}` all work the same way,
and you use them in the challenge.

Routes that share a prefix go in a **group**:

```csharp
var group = app.MapGroup("/l01/example/widgets");
group.MapGet("", ListWidgets);            // GET /l01/example/widgets
group.MapGet("/{id:int}", GetWidget);     // GET /l01/example/widgets/3
group.MapPost("", CreateWidget);          // POST /l01/example/widgets
```

Note `""` for the group's own root: the group already contributed the prefix,
so the child pattern adds nothing. Groups are not only tidiness — anything you
attach to the group (authorisation, filters, OpenAPI metadata) applies to every
endpoint inside it, which is how lesson 09 secures a whole resource in one
line.

Finally, the results. You met `Ok` and `BadRequest` in lesson 00; here is the
rest of the working vocabulary:

| helper | status | when |
|---|---|---|
| `TypedResults.Ok(value)` | 200 | here is what you asked for |
| `TypedResults.Created(uri, value)` | 201 | I made something; it lives at `uri` |
| `TypedResults.NoContent()` | 204 | done, and there is nothing to say |
| `TypedResults.BadRequest()` | 400 | *your* request was malformed |
| `TypedResults.NotFound()` | 404 | no such thing |
| `TypedResults.Conflict()` | 409 | the request is fine, the current state forbids it |

A handler that can return more than one of these can say so in its signature:

```csharp
private static Results<Ok<Widget>, NotFound> GetWidget(int id) =>
    Store.Find(id) is { } widget ? TypedResults.Ok(widget) : TypedResults.NotFound();
```

`Results<A, B>` is a union type. The compiler now checks that you only return
one of the two shapes you promised, and ASP.NET Core can describe both in
OpenAPI without running your code. `IResult` on its own gives up both benefits;
use it when a handler really has four or five outcomes and the union stops
being readable — as it does in this lesson's challenge.

## Exercise 1 — a route parameter, and an honest 404

Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Ex1.cs`. Implement `GetOrder` so that
`GET /l01/orders/{id}` answers **200** with the matching order from
`Catalog.Orders`, and **404** when no order has that id.

The JSON body is the `Order` record as-is:
`{"id":3,"customer":"Ada","status":"shipped","totalCents":15000}`.

Leave the `{id:int}` constraint on the route template — the gate checks that
`/l01/orders/banana` gives a 404 from routing rather than a 500 from your code.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 01_routing_endpoints ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a route group

Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Ex2.cs`. Nothing is mapped in that file yet,
so both of its routes currently 404. Create a group for `/l01/customers` and
map two endpoints onto it:

- `GET /l01/customers` → **200** with every distinct customer name in
  `Catalog.Orders`, sorted A–Z: `["Ada","Grace","Linus"]`. Ada has two orders
  and must appear once.
- `GET /l01/customers/{name}/orders` → **200** with that customer's orders, id
  ascending. A name nobody has ordered under is **404**, not an empty list —
  the customer does not exist, and saying "here are Zoe's zero orders" invents
  a Zoe.

Both handlers are already declared for you; you write the two mapping lines and
the two bodies.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 01_routing_endpoints ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — 201, and where the new thing lives

Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Ex3.cs`. Implement `CreateOrder` so that
`POST /l01/orders` with a body of `{"customer":"Ada","totalCents":500}` answers:

- **201 Created**
- a `Location` header of `/l01/orders/6`
- a body that is the new order: id 6, the customer from the request, status
  `"pending"`, and the requested `totalCents`

`Catalog.NextOrderId` gives you 6. Nothing is persisted — this lesson has no
store, and lesson 07 fixes that — so a second POST also produces 6, which is
fine.

A blank customer, or a `totalCents` that is not positive, is **400**.

The status the client sends, if any, is ignored: a new order is always
`"pending"`. Letting a caller choose the initial state of a resource is one of
the most common holes in a young API.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 01_routing_endpoints ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — optional query parameters and a typed union

Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Ex4.cs`. Implement `SearchOrders` behind
`GET /l01/orders`, with two optional query parameters:

- `status` filters to orders with that status. Valid values are the three in
  `Catalog.Statuses`.
- `sort` is either `id` (the default) or `total`, meaning `totalCents`
  ascending.

So `/l01/orders` returns all five, id ascending; `?status=shipped` returns 1, 3
and 5; `?status=shipped&sort=total` returns 5, 1, 3. Filter first, then sort.

An unknown `status` or `sort` value is **400**, and the body must name the
value you rejected — `unknown status 'banana'` is enough. The signature is
already a `Results<Ok<List<Order>>, BadRequest<string>>`, so the compiler will
hold you to exactly those two outcomes.

Both parameters are `string?`. `null` means "the client did not send it", which
is a different thing from "the client sent something I do not understand" —
one is the default, the other is a 400.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 01_routing_endpoints ex4
```

## Challenge — four status codes, one decision

Honest difficulty note: the code is short; getting the *order of the checks*
right is the whole problem.

Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Challenge.cs`. Implement `ChangeStatus`
behind `PUT /l01/orders/{id:int:min(1)}/status`, with a body of
`{"status":"shipped"}`:

- no order with that id → **404**
- a status that is not in `Catalog.Statuses` → **400**
- the order is currently `"cancelled"` → **409 Conflict**
- otherwise → **204 No Content**, with no body at all

409 is the code most APIs never learn. It means: I understood you, the resource
is there, and the *current state* makes this impossible. A cancelled order
cannot be shipped, and answering 400 would tell the client to fix their
request, which they cannot — there is nothing wrong with it.

Note also what the route constraint is doing: `min(1)` means `/l01/orders/0/status`
matches no route and gets a 404 without your handler running.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 01_routing_endpoints challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this lesson; the spaced-review scheduler
brings it back days later. Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Review1.cs` and
implement the two product endpoints — `GET /l01/review/products` (all
products, cheapest first) and `GET /l01/review/products/{sku}` (200 or 404).
Same ideas, different data.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/01_routing_endpoints

Routing is the part of ASP.NET Core that decides *which of your methods runs*,
and it does a surprising amount of work before your code sees a request. This
page is about that work, and about the status codes you spent the lesson
choosing.

## Notes

**Two-phase routing.** ASP.NET Core matches in two steps. `UseRouting` (added
for you by `WebApplication`) looks at the incoming path and method, walks a
prebuilt tree of every route template in the app, and selects an `Endpoint` —
or none. Everything after that point in the pipeline can *see* which endpoint
was selected, which is how authorisation knows whether the target needs a
token before your handler runs. Then `UseEndpoints`, at the very end, actually
executes it. That gap between "we know where this is going" and "we go there"
is where middleware does its most useful work, and lesson 03 lives in it.

**Route constraints are matching, not validation.** `{id:int}` says the
template only matches when that segment parses as an integer. A request that
fails a constraint has not been rejected; it has simply not matched, and if no
other route matches either you get a 404. This is why `/l01/orders/banana` was
a 404 and not a 400 — and why constraints are a poor place to express business
rules. `{id:int:min(1)}` is fine because it is still a statement about the
shape of the URL. "Only ids belonging to this customer" is not, and belongs in
your handler where you can answer 403.

**Ambiguity and precedence.** Templates are scored, not tried in order:
literal segments beat parameters, and constrained parameters beat unconstrained
ones. So `/l01/orders/count` and `/l01/orders/{id:int}` can coexist and the
literal wins for `/l01/orders/count`. When two routes are genuinely equally
specific, the app throws an `AmbiguousMatchException` on that request rather
than picking silently — a loud failure you will meet the first time you map
`{id}` twice.

**PUT versus POST, and idempotency.** POST is not idempotent: send it twice,
get two orders. PUT is defined to be idempotent — sending the same PUT ten
times must leave the resource in the same state as sending it once — which is
why PUT usually takes the *whole* new representation and why the challenge's
PUT returns 204 rather than a body. This is one of the most common interview
questions on REST, and the interesting follow-up is "so how do you make a
create idempotent?" (an `Idempotency-Key` header the server remembers, or
letting the client choose the id and using PUT).

**204 is not 200 with an empty body.** A 204 tells the client, at the protocol
level, that there is no content and none is coming; it must not have a message
body at all. A 200 with a zero-length body says "here is your representation,
and it is empty", which is a different claim. Small distinction, but caches,
proxies and generated clients act on it.

## ex1 - the parameter, the constraint and the 404

The whole exercise is three lines, and the interesting one is the last:
returning `TypedResults.NotFound()` instead of `TypedResults.Ok(null)`. The
temptation to return 200-with-null is strong because it makes the handler's
type simpler, and it is always wrong. A 404 is a *fact about the world* — this
identifier names nothing — that the client can act on: stop retrying, show an
empty state, remove the stale link. A 200 with null forces every caller to
re-derive that fact from the body, and half of them will forget.

The other thing worth internalising is the difference between the two failures
the gate checks. `/l01/orders/99` reaches your handler, which decides there is
no such order: your 404. `/l01/orders/banana` never reaches your handler:
routing's 404. Same status, two entirely different code paths, and knowing
which one you are looking at is the difference between a five-minute and a
fifty-minute debugging session.

## ex2 - groups, and the shape of a resource

`MapGroup` looks like string concatenation and is not. A `RouteGroupBuilder` is
a real object that carries *conventions* down to its children: call
`group.RequireAuthorization()` and every endpoint in the group needs a token;
call `group.AddEndpointFilter<ValidationFilter>()` and every endpoint gets
validated. That is why grouping by resource rather than by verb is the
convention — the things you want to apply in bulk (auth, rate limits,
versioning, OpenAPI tags) are almost always per-resource.

The design decision hiding in this exercise is the 404 for an unknown
customer. A defensible alternative exists: if `/l01/customers/{name}/orders` is
read as "the collection of orders filtered by name", an unknown name is just an
empty collection, and 200 with `[]` is correct. The rule that settles it is
whether the URL names a *sub-resource of an entity that must exist*. Here it
does — there is no Zoe — so 404. If the route were `/l01/orders?customer=Zoe`,
the empty list would be right, because the collection exists and the filter
matched nothing. Being able to argue both sides of this is worth more in an
interview than knowing one answer.

## ex3 - 201, Location, and who chooses the initial state

Three separate ideas got compressed into one small handler.

The **201** says a resource came into existence. The **Location header** says
where, and it is not optional in spirit even though nothing enforces it: a
client that just created something needs a URL to fetch, update or delete it,
and if you do not give one it has to guess from your docs. In a real app you
would build that URL from the route name rather than a string literal —
`TypedResults.CreatedAtRoute("GetOrder", new { id })` — so that changing the
route template does not silently break every `Location` you emit.

The third idea is the one that becomes a security bug: **the client does not
choose the initial state.** You ignored any `status` in the request body and
wrote `"pending"` yourself. The general form of this rule is called
*mass assignment* — if you bind a request body straight onto your domain object
and save it, a caller can set `IsAdmin`, `Balance` or `Status` just by adding a
field to their JSON. Lesson 07 gives it its proper treatment (DTOs in, entities
out) and lesson 09 gates it. The habit starts here: enumerate the fields you
accept, do not accept the object.

## ex4 - optional parameters, and the difference between absent and wrong

`string? status` has three states and the exercise turns on all three: absent
(null, so no filter), valid, and present-but-nonsense. Collapsing the first and
third — treating an unknown status as "no filter" — produces the worst possible
API, one that answers 200 with plausible data to a request that made no sense.
Collapsing them the other way, and 400-ing on absence, breaks every caller who
wanted everything.

`Results<Ok<List<Order>>, BadRequest<string>>` is doing real work here, not
decoration. The compiler now refuses a `TypedResults.NotFound()` in this
method, because you did not promise one; and tooling can generate an OpenAPI
document that lists both a 200 and a 400 with their body types, from the
signature alone, without executing anything. The cost is that the signature
gets long, which is a fair trade at two outcomes and a bad one at five — the
challenge, with four, is written against plain `IResult` for exactly that
reason. Knowing where that line is, and being able to say why, is the answer
interviewers are listening for when they ask about `IResult` versus

# Reading - dotnet/01_routing_endpoints

Routing is the part of ASP.NET Core that decides *which of your methods runs*,
and it does a surprising amount of work before your code sees a request. This
page is about that work, and about the status codes you spent the lesson
choosing.

## Notes

**Two-phase routing.** ASP.NET Core matches in two steps. `UseRouting` (added
for you by `WebApplication`) looks at the incoming path and method, walks a
prebuilt tree of every route template in the app, and selects an `Endpoint` —
or none. Everything after that point in the pipeline can *see* which endpoint
was selected, which is how authorisation knows whether the target needs a
token before your handler runs. Then `UseEndpoints`, at the very end, actually
executes it. That gap between "we know where this is going" and "we go there"
is where middleware does its most useful work, and lesson 03 lives in it.

**Route constraints are matching, not validation.** `{id:int}` says the
template only matches when that segment parses as an integer. A request that
fails a constraint has not been rejected; it has simply not matched, and if no
other route matches either you get a 404. This is why `/l01/orders/banana` was
a 404 and not a 400 — and why constraints are a poor place to express business
rules. `{id:int:min(1)}` is fine because it is still a statement about the
shape of the URL. "Only ids belonging to this customer" is not, and belongs in
your handler where you can answer 403.

**Ambiguity and precedence.** Templates are scored, not tried in order:
literal segments beat parameters, and constrained parameters beat unconstrained
ones. So `/l01/orders/count` and `/l01/orders/{id:int}` can coexist and the
literal wins for `/l01/orders/count`. When two routes are genuinely equally
specific, the app throws an `AmbiguousMatchException` on that request rather
than picking silently — a loud failure you will meet the first time you map
`{id}` twice.

**PUT versus POST, and idempotency.** POST is not idempotent: send it twice,
get two orders. PUT is defined to be idempotent — sending the same PUT ten
times must leave the resource in the same state as sending it once — which is
why PUT usually takes the *whole* new representation and why the challenge's
PUT returns 204 rather than a body. This is one of the most common interview
questions on REST, and the interesting follow-up is "so how do you make a
create idempotent?" (an `Idempotency-Key` header the server remembers, or
letting the client choose the id and using PUT).

**204 is not 200 with an empty body.** A 204 tells the client, at the protocol
level, that there is no content and none is coming; it must not have a message
body at all. A 200 with a zero-length body says "here is your representation,
and it is empty", which is a different claim. Small distinction, but caches,
proxies and generated clients act on it.

## ex1 - the parameter, the constraint and the 404

The whole exercise is three lines, and the interesting one is the last:
returning `TypedResults.NotFound()` instead of `TypedResults.Ok(null)`. The
temptation to return 200-with-null is strong because it makes the handler's
type simpler, and it is always wrong. A 404 is a *fact about the world* — this
identifier names nothing — that the client can act on: stop retrying, show an
empty state, remove the stale link. A 200 with null forces every caller to
re-derive that fact from the body, and half of them will forget.

The other thing worth internalising is the difference between the two failures
the gate checks. `/l01/orders/99` reaches your handler, which decides there is
no such order: your 404. `/l01/orders/banana` never reaches your handler:
routing's 404. Same status, two entirely different code paths, and knowing
which one you are looking at is the difference between a five-minute and a
fifty-minute debugging session.

## ex2 - groups, and the shape of a resource

`MapGroup` looks like string concatenation and is not. A `RouteGroupBuilder` is
a real object that carries *conventions* down to its children: call
`group.RequireAuthorization()` and every endpoint in the group needs a token;
call `group.AddEndpointFilter<ValidationFilter>()` and every endpoint gets
validated. That is why grouping by resource rather than by verb is the
convention — the things you want to apply in bulk (auth, rate limits,
versioning, OpenAPI tags) are almost always per-resource.

The design decision hiding in this exercise is the 404 for an unknown
customer. A defensible alternative exists: if `/l01/customers/{name}/orders` is
read as "the collection of orders filtered by name", an unknown name is just an
empty collection, and 200 with `[]` is correct. The rule that settles it is
whether the URL names a *sub-resource of an entity that must exist*. Here it
does — there is no Zoe — so 404. If the route were `/l01/orders?customer=Zoe`,
the empty list would be right, because the collection exists and the filter
matched nothing. Being able to argue both sides of this is worth more in an
interview than knowing one answer.

where, and it is not optional in spirit even though nothing enforces it: a
client that just created something needs a URL to fetch, update or delete it,
and if you do not give one it has to guess from your docs. In a real app you
would build that URL from the route name rather than a string literal —
`TypedResults.CreatedAtRoute("GetOrder", new { id })` — so that changing the
route template does not silently break every `Location` you emit.

The third idea is the one that becomes a security bug: **the client does not
choose the initial state.** You ignored any `status` in the request body and
wrote `"pending"` yourself. The general form of this rule is called
*mass assignment* — if you bind a request body straight onto your domain object
and save it, a caller can set `IsAdmin`, `Balance` or `Status` just by adding a
field to their JSON. Lesson 07 gives it its proper treatment (DTOs in, entities
out) and lesson 09 gates it. The habit starts here: enumerate the fields you
accept, do not accept the object.

(null, so no filter), valid, and present-but-nonsense. Collapsing the first and
third — treating an unknown status as "no filter" — produces the worst possible

## Challenge — four status codes, one decision

Honest difficulty note: the code is short; getting the *order of the checks*
right is the whole problem.

Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Challenge.cs`. Implement `ChangeStatus`
behind `PUT /l01/orders/{id:int:min(1)}/status`, with a body of
`{"status":"shipped"}`:

- no order with that id → **404**
- a status that is not in `Catalog.Statuses` → **400**
- the order is currently `"cancelled"` → **409 Conflict**
- otherwise → **204 No Content**, with no body at all

409 is the code most APIs never learn. It means: I understood you, the resource
is there, and the *current state* makes this impossible. A cancelled order
cannot be shipped, and answering 400 would tell the client to fix their
request, which they cannot — there is nothing wrong with it.

Note also what the route constraint is doing: `min(1)` means `/l01/orders/0/status`
matches no route and gets a 404 without your handler running.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 01_routing_endpoints challenge
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Catalog.Orders` is an ordinary `IReadOnlyList<Order>`, so this is a LINQ
problem wearing a web-framework hat: find the one element whose `Id` matches,
then decide what to return when there isn't one.

The route already parsed the id into an `int` for you. You do not need to touch
the template.

## Hint 2

`FirstOrDefault` returns `null` when nothing matches, which is exactly the
signal you need for the 404. `First` would throw, and a thrown exception is a
500 — the wrong answer to "there is no order 99".

Two results, one expression: a conditional (`cond ? a : b`) whose branches are
`TypedResults.NotFound()` and `TypedResults.Ok(order)` is legal here because
both convert to the declared `IResult`.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
private static IResult GetOrder(int id)
{
    var order = Catalog.Orders.FirstOrDefault(/* which one? */);
    return order is null ? /* … */ : /* … */;
}
```

Return the `order` object itself; the serialiser turns the record into
`{"id":…,"customer":…,"status":…,"totalCents":…}` with no help from you.

## Hint 1

`Catalog.Orders` is an ordinary `IReadOnlyList<Order>`, so this is a LINQ
problem wearing a web-framework hat: find the one element whose `Id` matches,
then decide what to return when there isn't one.

The route already parsed the id into an `int` for you. You do not need to touch
the template.

## Hint 2

`FirstOrDefault` returns `null` when nothing matches, which is exactly the
signal you need for the 404. `First` would throw, and a thrown exception is a
500 — the wrong answer to "there is no order 99".

Two results, one expression: a conditional (`cond ? a : b`) whose branches are
`TypedResults.NotFound()` and `TypedResults.Ok(order)` is legal here because
both convert to the declared `IResult`.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
private static IResult GetOrder(int id)
{
    var order = Catalog.Orders.FirstOrDefault(/* which one? */);
    return order is null ? /* … */ : /* … */;
}
```

Return the `order` object itself; the serialiser turns the record into
`{"id":…,"customer":…,"status":…,"totalCents":…}` with no help from you.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — a route group

Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Ex2.cs`. Nothing is mapped in that file yet,
so both of its routes currently 404. Create a group for `/l01/customers` and
map two endpoints onto it:

- `GET /l01/customers` → **200** with every distinct customer name in
  `Catalog.Orders`, sorted A–Z: `["Ada","Grace","Linus"]`. Ada has two orders
  and must appear once.
- `GET /l01/customers/{name}/orders` → **200** with that customer's orders, id
  ascending. A name nobody has ordered under is **404**, not an empty list —
  the customer does not exist, and saying "here are Zoe's zero orders" invents
  a Zoe.

Both handlers are already declared for you; you write the two mapping lines and
the two bodies.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 01_routing_endpoints ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two jobs. First, `MapEndpoints` is empty — until you map something, both routes
are 404s, which is what the gate is telling you. Second, the two handlers need
bodies.

Start with the mapping, run the gate, and watch the failure change from 404 to
500. A moving failure is progress.

## Hint 2

`app.MapGroup("/l01/customers")` gives you a builder. Map the list handler on
the group's own root — the pattern for that is the empty string, because the
group already supplied the prefix — and the second one on `"/{name}/orders"`.

For `ListCustomers`, the pipeline is: take every order's customer, remove
duplicates, sort. LINQ has one method for each of those three words.

For `OrdersFor`, filter by name and order by id — then decide what "nobody has
that name" means. The gate says 404, so you need to look at the result before
you return it.

## Hint 3

The mapping is:

```csharp
var customers = app.MapGroup("/l01/customers");
customers.MapGet("", ListCustomers);
customers.MapGet("/{name}/orders", OrdersFor);
```

`ListCustomers` is one LINQ chain ending in `.ToList()`, wrapped in
`TypedResults.Ok(...)`. Use `StringComparer.Ordinal` in `OrderBy` if you want
the sort to be independent of the machine's locale.

`OrdersFor` materialises the filtered list first, then returns
`TypedResults.NotFound()` when `orders.Count == 0`. Note it is the *empty
result*, not a missing customer record, that tells you the customer does not
exist — there is no customer table in this lesson.

## Exercise 4 — optional query parameters and a typed union

Edit `src/Api/L01_RoutingEndpoints/Ex4.cs`. Implement `SearchOrders` behind
`GET /l01/orders`, with two optional query parameters:

- `status` filters to orders with that status. Valid values are the three in
  `Catalog.Statuses`.
- `sort` is either `id` (the default) or `total`, meaning `totalCents`
  ascending.

So `/l01/orders` returns all five, id ascending; `?status=shipped` returns 1, 3
and 5; `?status=shipped&sort=total` returns 5, 1, 3. Filter first, then sort.

An unknown `status` or `sort` value is **400**, and the body must name the
value you rejected — `unknown status 'banana'` is enough. The signature is
already a `Results<Ok<List<Order>>, BadRequest<string>>`, so the compiler will
hold you to exactly those two outcomes.

Both parameters are `string?`. `null` means "the client did not send it", which
is a different thing from "the client sent something I do not understand" —
one is the default, the other is a 400.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 01_routing_endpoints ex4
```

## Hint 1

Each parameter has three cases and you must treat them differently: `null`
means "not sent, do nothing", a known value means "apply it", and anything else
means 400. Write the two rejections at the top and the query underneath.

Careful with the order of operations in the query itself — the gate checks that
`?status=shipped&sort=total` returns three orders and not five.

## Hint 2

`Catalog.Statuses` is the list of legal status values, so `Contains` answers
the first validation question. The legal `sort` values are only `"id"` and
`"total"`, and there is no constant for them.

For the query, start from `Catalog.Orders.AsEnumerable()` and keep reassigning
the variable: apply `Where` only when there is a filter, then apply exactly one
`OrderBy` at the end. Both branches of that sort must exist — `id` is the
default, not the absence of sorting.

The return type is a union, so `return TypedResults.BadRequest("...")` and
`return TypedResults.Ok(list)` both convert automatically; nothing else will.

## Hint 3

The shape is:

```csharp
if (status is not null && !Catalog.Statuses.Contains(status))
{
    return TypedResults.BadRequest($"unknown status '{status}'");
}
// … the same idea for sort …

var query = Catalog.Orders.AsEnumerable();
if (status is not null)
{
    query = query.Where(/* … */);
}

query = sort == "total" ? query.OrderBy(/* … */) : query.OrderBy(/* … */);
return TypedResults.Ok(query.ToList());
```

The 400 body has to contain the offending value, which is why the message is
interpolated rather than a constant string.

lessons.briefing:
# 02 — Dependency injection and lifetimes

Every handler you have written so far reached out and took what it needed:
`Catalog.Orders`, a static list, right there in the same assembly. That works
exactly until the data lives in a database, or behind an HTTP call, or has to
be a fake in a test — at which point a static reference is a hard-wired
decision your handler is no longer allowed to change.

Dependency injection turns that around. Your handler declares what it needs as
a *parameter*, and something else — the container — decides which
implementation to hand over and how long that object should live. You have
already used it without noticing: the gate boots your app, and ASP.NET Core
builds an `IServiceProvider` before the first request. This lesson is about
putting your own things in it.

And it is really about the second half of that sentence: **how long**. Getting
the type right is easy; getting the *lifetime* right is where .NET services
break in ways that only show up under concurrency, on the second request, in
production, on a Friday. Every exercise below is graded by making two requests
and comparing what came back, because that is the only honest way to see a
lifetime.

## Concept — three lifetimes, and the scope

Registration happens in a class implementing `IServiceRegistrar`, which this
course's `LessonModules` calls before the container is built:

```csharp
public class ExampleServices : IServiceRegistrar
{
    public void Register(IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration configuration)
    {
        services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();
        services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();
        services.AddTransient<IEmailBuilder, EmailBuilder>();
    }
}
```

Read `AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>()` as: *when someone asks
for `IOrderRepository`, give them a `SqlOrderRepository`, and reuse the same one
for everything in the current scope.* The first type is what callers depend on;
the second is what actually gets built.

The three lifetimes differ only in when the container builds a new object:

| lifetime | a new instance… | use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `AddSingleton` | once, for the life of the application | caches, configuration, counters, anything expensive and stateless-per-request |
| `AddScoped` | once per scope — in a web app, once per **request** | database contexts, unit of work, the current user, anything that belongs to "this request" |
| `AddTransient` | every single time it is resolved | cheap, stateless helpers |

The word doing the work is **scope**. ASP.NET Core creates one
`IServiceScope` per HTTP request, resolves your handler's parameters from it,
and disposes it when the response is finished. So "scoped" means "one per
request" *because* the framework happens to open a scope per request — the
container itself knows nothing about HTTP. That distinction matters the first
time you resolve services from a background job, where nobody opens a scope for
you and you have to do it yourself with `IServiceScopeFactory`.

Once a service is registered, a minimal API handler gets it by declaring a
parameter:

```csharp
private static IResult Example(IClock clock) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(new { now = clock.UtcNow });
```

ASP.NET Core sees a parameter whose type is a registered service and resolves
it instead of trying to bind it from the request. That is why an unregistered
interface produces `Unable to resolve service for type 'IClock'` at request
time — and why one of the failures in this lesson is a 500 rather than a wrong
value.

### The rule you have to know

**A service may depend on things that live at least as long as it does, never
on things that live less.** A singleton holding a scoped object keeps that
object alive forever, long after its request has ended — one request's data,
served to everybody. That bug has a name, *captive dependency*, and it is the
challenge below.

.NET tries to protect you: in the Development environment the container
validates on build and refuses to start an app whose singleton takes a scoped
constructor parameter. What it cannot see through is a singleton that captures
a **transient** — perfectly legal to build, just as wrong at runtime — or one
that resolves a scoped service out of a `IServiceProvider` it was handed. So
the validator is a seatbelt, not a substitute for knowing the rule.

## Exercise 1 — singleton and transient, told apart

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Ex1.cs`. Two things to do.

Implement `GetTicket` so that `GET /l02/ticket` answers **200** with
`{"ticket": …, "first": …, "second": …}` — the `ITicketSource`'s `Ticket`, and
the `Value` of each of the two `IIdGenerator` parameters.

Then fix the registrations, which are both currently `AddTransient`, so that:

- every request sees the **same** `ticket`, and
- the two `IIdGenerator` parameters *within one request* see **different**
  values.

Two parameters of the same type is not a typo. The container is asked twice,
and what you get back the second time is the whole definition of a lifetime.

```

```

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Ex2.cs`. Implement `GetScope` to answer
**200** with `{"first": …, "second": …}` from its two `IRequestScope`
parameters, then choose the registration that makes both of these true at once:

- within one request, `first` and `second` are the **same** value
- across two requests, they are **different**

Exactly one of the three lifetimes can do that, and neither of the two you used
in ex1 is it.

```

```

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Ex3.cs`. `ICorrelation` is an id that
identifies one request; `IAuditTrail` is a log that outlives all of them. Both

back. Then fix both lifetimes so that:

- the first request reports `seen: 1`, the second reports `seen: 2`
- the two requests report **different** correlation ids

pair — a per-request value written into an application-wide store — is the
single most common shape in a real service, and it needs one of each lifetime.

```

```

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Ex4.cs`. Three classes implement

register it, and every caller picks it up without being edited.


## Challenge — the captive dependency

Honest difficulty note: the fix is a handful of lines, but it requires changing
an interface, which people are strangely reluctant to do.

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Challenge.cs`. `Dispatcher` is a
singleton — it counts every dispatch the application has ever made — and it
