lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/02_dependency_injection

Dependency injection is two ideas wearing one name: *inversion of control*
(your class declares what it needs instead of constructing it) and a
*container* (something that knows how to build the graph). ASP.NET Core ships
with a container, wires it into everything, and asks you for exactly one
decision per registration — the lifetime. This page is mostly about that
decision.

## Notes

**What the container actually stores.** `IServiceCollection` is a list of
`ServiceDescriptor`s, and each one is a triple: the service type you ask for,
how to build it (a concrete type, a factory delegate, or an already-built
instance), and a lifetime. `builder.Build()` freezes that list into an
`IServiceProvider`, which compiles resolution plans for the graph. Two
consequences that catch people out: registering the same service type twice
does not replace anything — the *last* registration wins for a single
`GetService<T>` call, while `GetServices<T>` returns all of them in
registration order — and nothing is built at registration time, so a typo in a
factory delegate is a runtime failure.

**Scopes are not requests; requests happen to open scopes.**
`IServiceProvider.CreateScope()` makes a scope. ASP.NET Core calls it once per
HTTP request and disposes it when the response completes. Nothing else does.
In a `BackgroundService`, a message-queue consumer or a startup task, there is
no ambient scope, so injecting a scoped service into a singleton hosted service
is a genuine error — the fix is to inject `IServiceScopeFactory`, call
`CreateScope()` for each unit of work, and resolve inside it. That is one of
the highest-value things you can know about this container.

**Disposal is ownership.** The container disposes what it *created*, when the
scope that created it ends: scoped and transient services resolved from a
request scope are disposed with the request, singletons at application
shutdown. It does *not* dispose an instance you registered yourself with
`AddSingleton(new Thing())` — you gave it an object, so you kept the ownership.
And a transient `IDisposable` resolved from the root provider is held until the
application exits, which is a slow, real memory leak: transient plus disposable
plus long-lived scope is a combination to be suspicious of.

**Constructor injection is the norm; the alternatives are not.** Prefer
constructor parameters, because they make dependencies visible in the type and
impossible to forget. `[FromServices]` on a handler parameter (or just the bare
parameter, as in this lesson) is the minimal-API equivalent. Reaching for
`IServiceProvider` and calling `GetRequiredService` yourself — the *service
locator* pattern — hides the dependency from every caller and every test, and
is worth avoiding except in the handful of places (factories, background
scopes) where it is genuinely the only option.

**Keyed services, if you need to choose at runtime.** Since .NET 8,
`AddKeyedSingleton<IPaymentGateway, StripeGateway>("stripe")` plus
`[FromKeyedServices("stripe")]` lets several implementations of one interface
coexist and be picked by name. Useful and worth knowing exists; the
`IEnumerable<T>` approach from ex4 is still the right answer when you want
*all* of them rather than *one*.

## ex1 - a lifetime is only visible over time

The reason this exercise makes two requests is that a lifetime has no
observable meaning inside one. Ask the container for a service once, and
singleton, scoped and transient all give you an object; the difference only
exists in what happens *the next time you ask*, and where the boundary between
"times" falls.

The two `IIdGenerator` parameters are the sharpest version of that.
`GetTicket(ITicketSource, IIdGenerator, IIdGenerator)` resolves three services,
and the last two are the same service type resolved twice within one scope.
Transient hands back two objects; scoped or singleton would hand back one
object twice. If you ever want to know what a registration really is, that
one-line experiment answers it faster than reading the registration.

The classic mistake in the other direction is making everything transient
"to be safe". Transient is not safer; it is just more allocation, and it
silently breaks anything that was supposed to accumulate — a cache that is
rebuilt per resolution is not a cache, and a counter that resets is not a
counter.

## ex2 - what a scope is for

Scoped is the lifetime that has no equivalent in a console application, and it
exists because request handling has a natural unit of work. Everything touching
one request — the database context and its transaction, the identity of the
caller, a correlation id, an accumulated list of domain events — should be one
object for that request and gone afterwards. `AddScoped` is how you say that.

The two failure modes the gate checks are the two directions you can get it
wrong, and they fail differently. Transient is the *silent* one: your code
works, nothing throws, and then two components that both "have the repository"
turn out to have two repositories with two transactions and two change
trackers, and a save in one is invisible to the other. Singleton is the *loud*
one, eventually: shared mutable state across concurrent requests, which under
load produces data belonging to one user appearing in another user's response.
If you only remember one thing from this lesson, make it that second sentence.

## ex3 - one of each, which is what real code looks like

Almost every service you write is a mixture. The interesting shape here is a
short-lived value flowing into a long-lived collaborator: the correlation id
belongs to the request, the audit trail belongs to the application, and the
handler is the thing that has both and puts one into the other.

Note what `AuditTrail` had to do to be a singleton: lock. Every request in the
process is inside a singleton at the same time, so any mutable state in it is
shared mutable state, and the ordinary `List<T>` is not thread-safe — concurrent
`Add` calls can corrupt its internal array or throw. `lock`,
`Interlocked`, a `Concurrent*` collection or immutability are the four ways
out. "Singletons must be thread-safe" is one of those sentences that sounds
like trivia until the first time a production service returns nonsense under
load.

The other half of the pair is that `Correlation` needs *no* thread safety at
all, because a scoped object is only ever touched by the one request that owns
it. Lifetime and concurrency are the same conversation.

## ex4 - registering the same interface many times

`services.AddScoped<IOrderRule, PositiveTotalRule>()` three times over, with
three implementations, gives the container three descriptors for one service
type. Ask for `IOrderRule` and you get the last one registered; ask for
`IEnumerable<IOrderRule>` and you get all three, in registration order. That
second behaviour is the foundation of every plug-in point in ASP.NET Core
itself — validators, model binder providers, authentication handlers,
`IHostedService`s are all resolved as collections.

The design pattern it enables is worth naming: this is the open/closed
principle with a container behind it. Adding a fourth rule means writing a
class and registering it; no existing file changes, no `switch` grows a case,
and the endpoint does not know how many rules exist. Compare it with the
alternative — an `if` per rule inside the handler — and notice what got better:
each rule is independently testable, and the *order* of the rules stopped being
encoded in the shape of the code.

The sort in the endpoint is not decoration. Registration order is deterministic
but it is not *meaningful*, and letting it leak into your response makes your
API's contract depend on the order of lines in a file nobody reading the API
can see.

## challenge - the captive dependency, and how to fix it without breaking the singleton

The bug is entirely in one constructor parameter. `Dispatcher` is registered as
a singleton, so the container builds it exactly once, at the first request that
needs it, and to build it, it must resolve an `IRequestToken` — once. That
token is now a field on an object that will live until the process exits, and
every request for the rest of the application's life gets told about a request
that finished long ago.

The two wrong fixes are worth naming because both are common.

*Make the dispatcher scoped.* This makes the token correct and destroys the
thing the dispatcher was for — the count restarts at 1 every request, because
the counter is now per-request state. The gate checks `handled` precisely to
catch this. In real code the equivalent is downgrading a cache or a connection
pool to scoped to silence a validation error, quietly turning an optimisation
into overhead.

*Resolve the token inside the singleton from a captured `IServiceProvider`.*
This looks like it decouples things and does not: resolving a scoped service
from the root provider either throws (`Cannot resolve scoped service … from
root provider`, which is what .NET's scope validation is for) or, with
validation off, hands you a root-scoped instance that is captive in exactly the
same way.

The fix that works is the boring one: **pass it in**. `Dispatch(IRequestToken
token)` lets a singleton operate on per-request data without ever holding it.
Generalised: when a long-lived component needs short-lived data, that data is an
argument, not a field. The same reasoning is why `HttpContext` is not injectable
into your services and why `IHttpContextAccessor` — which is the "hold it
anyway" escape hatch, backed by an `AsyncLocal` — is a smell more often than it
is a solution.

Worth knowing for interviews: the scoped-into-singleton form of this bug is
caught at startup in Development because `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` turns on
`ValidateScopes` and `ValidateOnBuild`. The transient-into-singleton form, which
is what you just fixed, is *not* caught, because it is legal by the rules the
validator checks. "Why didn't the validator catch it?" is the classic follow-up
question.

## review1 - when does a scope end?

`disposedBefore` reading 0, 1, 2 across three requests is a direct measurement
of the request scope's lifetime. The container created the unit of work when
the handler asked for it, kept it for the rest of that request, and called
`Dispose()` on it when the response finished — after your handler returned,
which is why the count you observe is always the number of *previous* requests
rather than the current one.

Registered as a singleton, `Dispose()` is called exactly once, at application
shutdown, so the count stays 0 for the entire life of the app. That is not a
crash and not a wrong number in the usual sense; it is a connection that is
never returned to the pool, a transaction that is never committed, a file
handle that is never closed. Resource leaks caused by a lifetime that is too
long are the second-most-common DI bug after captive dependencies, and they
never show up in a test that makes one request.

## Further reading

- [Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/dependency-injection) — the framework view, including how the request scope is created.
- [Dependency injection guidelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection-guidelines) — captive dependencies, disposal ownership and the anti-patterns, straight from the docs.
- [Service lifetimes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection#service-lifetimes) — singleton, scoped and transient with the rules for combining them.
- [Keyed services](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection#keyed-services) — choosing between several implementations of one interface by name.
- [Use scoped services in a BackgroundService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/scoped-service) — the `IServiceScopeFactory` pattern for code that lives outside a request.

```csharp
        var b = await (await client.GetAsync("/l02/ticket")).Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<TicketDto>();

        Teach.True(a!.Ticket != Guid.Empty,
            "\"ticket\" is missing from the response body. Return the ITicketSource's Ticket.");

        Teach.Equal(a.Ticket, b!.Ticket,
            "Two separate requests saw two different tickets, so ITicketSource is being "
                + "built again every time. One value shared by the whole application is a "
                + "singleton.");

        Teach.True(a.First != a.Second,
            "Both IIdGenerator parameters in ONE request came back with the same value, so "
                + "the container is reusing an instance. A fresh object per resolution is "
                + "transient.");

        Teach.True(a.First != b.First,
            "The two requests got the same generated id. Transient means a new instance "
                + "every time anyone asks - across requests as well as within one.");
    }

    public async Task Ex2_ScopedIsOnePerRequestAndNotOnePerApplication()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var first = await client.GetAsync("/l02/scope");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, first,
            "GET /l02/scope must answer 200 - reread README ex2.");

        var a = await first.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<ScopeDto>();
        var b = await (await client.GetAsync("/l02/scope")).Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<ScopeDto>();

                + "handed back two different objects. That is transient behaviour; a request "
                + "scope has to be one instance for the whole request.");

        Teach.True(a.First != b!.First,
            "Two different requests shared one IRequestScope, which is singleton behaviour. "
                + "A scope ends when the request ends.");
    }

        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, first,

        var b = await (await client.GetAsync("/l02/audit")).Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<AuditDto>();

                + "so Record must give back 1. If you got 0, you are not calling Record; if "

                + "the whole application. A value that identifies one request has to be born "

    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var first = await client.GetAsync("/l02/dispatch");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, first,
            "GET /l02/dispatch must answer 200 - reread README challenge.");

        var a = await first.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<DispatchDto>();
        var b = await (await client.GetAsync("/l02/dispatch")).Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<DispatchDto>();

            "The dispatcher counts every dispatch the application has made, so the first "
                + "one is 1.");
        Teach.Equal(2, b!.Handled,
            "The count went back to 1, so the dispatcher is being rebuilt per request. It "
                + "is meant to be a singleton - fixing the captive dependency must not mean "
                + "making the singleton scoped.");

            "Both requests were dispatched under the same token. The dispatcher captured one "
                + "IRequestToken when it was constructed and has been holding it ever since - "
                + "that is a captive dependency.");

                + "handler. The dispatcher must work on the token belonging to the request "
                + "it is handling, and the request's token must be one object for the whole "
                + "request.");

    public async Task Review1_AScopedServiceIsDisposedWhenTheRequestEnds()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var first = await client.GetAsync("/l02/review/unit-of-work");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, first,
            "GET /l02/review/unit-of-work must answer 200 - reread README review.");

        var a = await first.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<UnitOfWorkDto>();
        var b = await (await client.GetAsync("/l02/review/unit-of-work")).Content
            .ReadFromJsonAsync<UnitOfWorkDto>();
        var c = await (await client.GetAsync("/l02/review/unit-of-work")).Content
            .ReadFromJsonAsync<UnitOfWorkDto>();

        Teach.Equal(0, a!.DisposedBefore,
            "Nothing has been disposed before the very first request.");
        Teach.Equal(1, b!.DisposedBefore,
            "By the second request, the first request's unit of work should have been "
                + "disposed. A count stuck at 0 means the container never owned a "
                + "per-request instance to dispose.");
        Teach.Equal(2, c!.DisposedBefore,
            "One disposal per finished request - the container disposes what it created "
                + "when the scope it created it in ends.");

        Teach.True(a.Id != b.Id,
            "Every request should get its own unit of work; these two shared one.");
    }

    private static async Task<string> Violations(HttpResponseMessage response)
    {
        var body = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<RuleDto>();
        return string.Join(",", body?.Violations ?? []);
    }

    private sealed record TicketDto(Guid Ticket, Guid First, Guid Second);

    private sealed record ScopeDto(Guid First, Guid Second);

    private sealed record AuditDto(Guid CorrelationId, int Seen);

    private sealed record RuleDto(List<string>? Violations);

    private sealed record DispatchDto(Guid Token, Guid Echo, int Handled);

    private sealed record UnitOfWorkDto(Guid Id, int DisposedBefore);
}
```

In plain English: every test here makes **two** requests and compares. That is
deliberate — a lifetime is invisible in a single request, and almost every
real-world lifetime bug is a "works on my machine, wrong on the second call"
bug. Note also that nothing reaches into the container to inspect a
registration. The gate only knows what a client can see, which means passing it
means the behaviour is right, not that the registration looks right.

## The teaching point

Ask "how long should this live?" every time you register something, and answer
it with a sentence about *ownership* rather than performance. A database
context belongs to one request because a transaction does. A cache belongs to
the application because the whole point is that it outlives requests. A
`StringBuilder`-shaped helper belongs to nobody, so make it transient and stop
thinking about it.

Two rules of thumb worth carrying: **singletons must be thread-safe**, because
every request will be inside them at once — `AuditTrail` locks for exactly that
reason. And **a longer-lived service must never hold a shorter-lived one**, but
it may happily *receive* one as an argument. Almost every captive dependency in
the wild is fixed by moving a constructor parameter into a method signature.

Next: **03_middleware**, where you find out what runs before your handler, in
what order, and what happens when one of them decides not to call the next.

# Reading - dotnet/02_dependency_injection

Dependency injection is two ideas wearing one name: *inversion of control*
(your class declares what it needs instead of constructing it) and a
*container* (something that knows how to build the graph). ASP.NET Core ships
with a container, wires it into everything, and asks you for exactly one
decision per registration — the lifetime. This page is mostly about that
decision.

## Notes

**What the container actually stores.** `IServiceCollection` is a list of
`ServiceDescriptor`s, and each one is a triple: the service type you ask for,
how to build it (a concrete type, a factory delegate, or an already-built
instance), and a lifetime. `builder.Build()` freezes that list into an
`IServiceProvider`, which compiles resolution plans for the graph. Two
consequences that catch people out: registering the same service type twice
does not replace anything — the *last* registration wins for a single
`GetService<T>` call, while `GetServices<T>` returns all of them in
registration order — and nothing is built at registration time, so a typo in a
factory delegate is a runtime failure.

**Scopes are not requests; requests happen to open scopes.**
`IServiceProvider.CreateScope()` makes a scope. ASP.NET Core calls it once per
HTTP request and disposes it when the response completes. Nothing else does.
In a `BackgroundService`, a message-queue consumer or a startup task, there is
no ambient scope, so injecting a scoped service into a singleton hosted service
is a genuine error — the fix is to inject `IServiceScopeFactory`, call
`CreateScope()` for each unit of work, and resolve inside it. That is one of
the highest-value things you can know about this container.

**Disposal is ownership.** The container disposes what it *created*, when the
scope that created it ends: scoped and transient services resolved from a
request scope are disposed with the request, singletons at application
shutdown. It does *not* dispose an instance you registered yourself with
`AddSingleton(new Thing())` — you gave it an object, so you kept the ownership.
And a transient `IDisposable` resolved from the root provider is held until the
application exits, which is a slow, real memory leak: transient plus disposable
plus long-lived scope is a combination to be suspicious of.

**Constructor injection is the norm; the alternatives are not.** Prefer
constructor parameters, because they make dependencies visible in the type and
impossible to forget. `[FromServices]` on a handler parameter (or just the bare
parameter, as in this lesson) is the minimal-API equivalent. Reaching for
`IServiceProvider` and calling `GetRequiredService` yourself — the *service
locator* pattern — hides the dependency from every caller and every test, and
is worth avoiding except in the handful of places (factories, background
scopes) where it is genuinely the only option.

**Keyed services, if you need to choose at runtime.** Since .NET 8,
`AddKeyedSingleton<IPaymentGateway, StripeGateway>("stripe")` plus
`[FromKeyedServices("stripe")]` lets several implementations of one interface
coexist and be picked by name. Useful and worth knowing exists; the
`IEnumerable<T>` approach from ex4 is still the right answer when you want
*all* of them rather than *one*.

## ex1 - a lifetime is only visible over time

The reason this exercise makes two requests is that a lifetime has no
observable meaning inside one. Ask the container for a service once, and
singleton, scoped and transient all give you an object; the difference only
exists in what happens *the next time you ask*, and where the boundary between
"times" falls.

The two `IIdGenerator` parameters are the sharpest version of that.
`GetTicket(ITicketSource, IIdGenerator, IIdGenerator)` resolves three services,
and the last two are the same service type resolved twice within one scope.
Transient hands back two objects; scoped or singleton would hand back one
object twice. If you ever want to know what a registration really is, that
one-line experiment answers it faster than reading the registration.

The classic mistake in the other direction is making everything transient
"to be safe". Transient is not safer; it is just more allocation, and it
silently breaks anything that was supposed to accumulate — a cache that is
rebuilt per resolution is not a cache, and a counter that resets is not a
counter.

## ex2 - what a scope is for

Scoped is the lifetime that has no equivalent in a console application, and it
exists because request handling has a natural unit of work. Everything touching
one request — the database context and its transaction, the identity of the
caller, a correlation id, an accumulated list of domain events — should be one
object for that request and gone afterwards. `AddScoped` is how you say that.

The two failure modes the gate checks are the two directions you can get it
wrong, and they fail differently. Transient is the *silent* one: your code
works, nothing throws, and then two components that both "have the repository"
turn out to have two repositories with two transactions and two change
trackers, and a save in one is invisible to the other. Singleton is the *loud*
one, eventually: shared mutable state across concurrent requests, which under
load produces data belonging to one user appearing in another user's response.
If you only remember one thing from this lesson, make it that second sentence.

## ex3 - one of each, which is what real code looks like

Almost every service you write is a mixture. The interesting shape here is a
short-lived value flowing into a long-lived collaborator: the correlation id
belongs to the request, the audit trail belongs to the application, and the
handler is the thing that has both and puts one into the other.

Note what `AuditTrail` had to do to be a singleton: lock. Every request in the
process is inside a singleton at the same time, so any mutable state in it is
shared mutable state, and the ordinary `List<T>` is not thread-safe — concurrent
`Add` calls can corrupt its internal array or throw. `lock`,
`Interlocked`, a `Concurrent*` collection or immutability are the four ways
out. "Singletons must be thread-safe" is one of those sentences that sounds
like trivia until the first time a production service returns nonsense under
load.

The other half of the pair is that `Correlation` needs *no* thread safety at
all, because a scoped object is only ever touched by the one request that owns
it. Lifetime and concurrency are the same conversation.

## ex4 - registering the same interface many times

`services.AddScoped<IOrderRule, PositiveTotalRule>()` three times over, with
three implementations, gives the container three descriptors for one service
type. Ask for `IOrderRule` and you get the last one registered; ask for
`IEnumerable<IOrderRule>` and you get all three, in registration order. That
second behaviour is the foundation of every plug-in point in ASP.NET Core
itself — validators, model binder providers, authentication handlers,
`IHostedService`s are all resolved as collections.

The design pattern it enables is worth naming: this is the open/closed
principle with a container behind it. Adding a fourth rule means writing a
class and registering it; no existing file changes, no `switch` grows a case,
and the endpoint does not know how many rules exist. Compare it with the
alternative — an `if` per rule inside the handler — and notice what got better:
each rule is independently testable, and the *order* of the rules stopped being
encoded in the shape of the code.

The sort in the endpoint is not decoration. Registration order is deterministic
but it is not *meaningful*, and letting it leak into your response makes your
API's contract depend on the order of lines in a file nobody reading the API
can see.

## challenge - the captive dependency, and how to fix it without breaking the singleton

The bug is entirely in one constructor parameter. `Dispatcher` is registered as
a singleton, so the container builds it exactly once, at the first request that
needs it, and to build it, it must resolve an `IRequestToken` — once. That
token is now a field on an object that will live until the process exits, and
every request for the rest of the application's life gets told about a request
that finished long ago.

The two wrong fixes are worth naming because both are common.

*Make the dispatcher scoped.* This makes the token correct and destroys the
thing the dispatcher was for — the count restarts at 1 every request, because
the counter is now per-request state. The gate checks `handled` precisely to
catch this. In real code the equivalent is downgrading a cache or a connection
pool to scoped to silence a validation error, quietly turning an optimisation
into overhead.

*Resolve the token inside the singleton from a captured `IServiceProvider`.*
This looks like it decouples things and does not: resolving a scoped service
from the root provider either throws (`Cannot resolve scoped service … from
root provider`, which is what .NET's scope validation is for) or, with
validation off, hands you a root-scoped instance that is captive in exactly the
same way.

The fix that works is the boring one: **pass it in**. `Dispatch(IRequestToken
token)` lets a singleton operate on per-request data without ever holding it.
Generalised: when a long-lived component needs short-lived data, that data is an
argument, not a field. The same reasoning is why `HttpContext` is not injectable
into your services and why `IHttpContextAccessor` — which is the "hold it
anyway" escape hatch, backed by an `AsyncLocal` — is a smell more often than it
is a solution.

Worth knowing for interviews: the scoped-into-singleton form of this bug is
caught at startup in Development because `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` turns on
`ValidateScopes` and `ValidateOnBuild`. The transient-into-singleton form, which
is what you just fixed, is *not* caught, because it is legal by the rules the
validator checks. "Why didn't the validator catch it?" is the classic follow-up
question.

## review1 - when does a scope end?

`disposedBefore` reading 0, 1, 2 across three requests is a direct measurement
of the request scope's lifetime. The container created the unit of work when
the handler asked for it, kept it for the rest of that request, and called
`Dispose()` on it when the response finished — after your handler returned,
which is why the count you observe is always the number of *previous* requests
rather than the current one.

Registered as a singleton, `Dispose()` is called exactly once, at application
shutdown, so the count stays 0 for the entire life of the app. That is not a
crash and not a wrong number in the usual sense; it is a connection that is
never returned to the pool, a transaction that is never committed, a file
handle that is never closed. Resource leaks caused by a lifetime that is too
long are the second-most-common DI bug after captive dependencies, and they
never show up in a test that makes one request.

- [Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/dependency-injection) — the framework view, including how the request scope is created.
- [Dependency injection guidelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection-guidelines) — captive dependencies, disposal ownership and the anti-patterns, straight from the docs.
- [Service lifetimes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection#service-lifetimes) — singleton, scoped and transient with the rules for combining them.
- [Keyed services](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection#keyed-services) — choosing between several implementations of one interface by name.
- [Use scoped services in a BackgroundService](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/scoped-service) — the `IServiceScopeFactory` pattern for code that lives outside a request.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the captive dependency

Honest difficulty note: the fix is a handful of lines, but it requires changing
an interface, which people are strangely reluctant to do.

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Challenge.cs`. `Dispatcher` is a
singleton — it counts every dispatch the application has ever made — and it
takes an `IRequestToken` in its constructor so it can report which request it
is working on. That constructor parameter is the bug: the container builds the
singleton once, hands it one token, and that token is now the answer forever.

Make `GET /l02/dispatch` answer **200** with
`{"token": …, "echo": …, "handled": …}` such that:

- `handled` counts across requests: 1, then 2 — the dispatcher stays a
  singleton, so "make it scoped" is not the fix
- `token` is **different** on every request
- `token` equals `echo`, the token the container gave the handler — and the
  handler asks for `IRequestToken` twice, so the request's token must be one
  object for the whole request

The move is to stop *holding* the short-lived thing and start *receiving* it:
a singleton can be handed per-request data as a method argument all day long.
You are allowed — expected — to change `IDispatcher`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 02_dependency_injection challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Find the exact line where the bug lives before changing anything. `Dispatcher`
is a singleton, so the container calls its constructor once, ever. Whatever
that constructor is handed is kept for the lifetime of the process.

Now ask the question that unlocks it: does the dispatcher need to *hold* a
token, or does it need to *be told* one?

## Hint 2

The dispatcher must stay a singleton — the gate checks that `handled` counts
1, 2 across requests, so downgrading it to scoped trades one bug for another.

That leaves changing how the token reaches it. A method parameter is allowed to
be short-lived even when the object it is called on is not, so move the
`IRequestToken` from the constructor into the method. You will need `Dispatch`
to give back both the token it used and the new count — a small record, or a
tuple, does that.

Then look at the registration for `IRequestToken`: the handler asks for it
twice and the gate insists both asks give the same object.

## Hint 3

The pieces:

```csharp
public interface IDispatcher
{
    Dispatched Dispatch(IRequestToken token);
}

public sealed class Dispatcher : IDispatcher
{
    private int _handled;

    public Dispatched Dispatch(IRequestToken token) =>
        new(token.Value, Interlocked.Increment(ref _handled));
}
```

…with a `public record Dispatched(Guid Token, int Handled);` next to them. The
handler then calls `dispatcher.Dispatch(token)` and builds its response from
the result plus `echo.Value`. One registration still needs its lifetime
changed — the one that has to be a single object per request.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Find the exact line where the bug lives before changing anything. `Dispatcher`
is a singleton, so the container calls its constructor once, ever. Whatever
that constructor is handed is kept for the lifetime of the process.

Now ask the question that unlocks it: does the dispatcher need to *hold* a
token, or does it need to *be told* one?

## Hint 2

The dispatcher must stay a singleton — the gate checks that `handled` counts
1, 2 across requests, so downgrading it to scoped trades one bug for another.

That leaves changing how the token reaches it. A method parameter is allowed to
be short-lived even when the object it is called on is not, so move the
`IRequestToken` from the constructor into the method. You will need `Dispatch`
to give back both the token it used and the new count — a small record, or a
tuple, does that.

Then look at the registration for `IRequestToken`: the handler asks for it
twice and the gate insists both asks give the same object.

## Hint 3

The pieces:

```csharp
public interface IDispatcher
{
    Dispatched Dispatch(IRequestToken token);
}

public sealed class Dispatcher : IDispatcher
{
    private int _handled;

    public Dispatched Dispatch(IRequestToken token) =>
        new(token.Value, Interlocked.Increment(ref _handled));
}
```

…with a `public record Dispatched(Guid Token, int Handled);` next to them. The
handler then calls `dispatcher.Dispatch(token)` and builds its response from
the result plus `echo.Value`. One registration still needs its lifetime
changed — the one that has to be a single object per request.

## Exercise 1 — singleton and transient, told apart

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Ex1.cs`. Two things to do.

Implement `GetTicket` so that `GET /l02/ticket` answers **200** with
`{"ticket": …, "first": …, "second": …}` — the `ITicketSource`'s `Ticket`, and
the `Value` of each of the two `IIdGenerator` parameters.

Then fix the registrations, which are both currently `AddTransient`, so that:

- every request sees the **same** `ticket`, and
- the two `IIdGenerator` parameters *within one request* see **different**
  values.

Two parameters of the same type is not a typo. The container is asked twice,
and what you get back the second time is the whole definition of a lifetime.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 02_dependency_injection ex1
```

## Hint 1

Two separate jobs, and it is worth doing them in order. First make the endpoint
return the three values — that is three property reads and a `TypedResults.Ok`.
Run the gate; now the failures are about *values*, not about a 500.

Then read those failures. Two of them are about the same value appearing twice,
one is about two values that should differ.

## Hint 2

Translate each gate message into a sentence about time:

- "every request sees the same ticket" — how many of these should exist for the
  whole application?
- "two parameters in one request differ" — how many should exist per *ask*?

The registration methods are `AddSingleton`, `AddScoped` and `AddTransient`,
and only two of the three are needed here.

## Hint 3

The endpoint is:

```csharp
private static IResult GetTicket(ITicketSource source, IIdGenerator first, IIdGenerator second) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(new TicketResponse(source.Ticket, first.Value, second.Value));
```

For the registrations: `ITicketSource` is one object for the life of the
application, and `IIdGenerator` is a new object every time anyone resolves it.
Leave one of the two `AddTransient` lines exactly as it is.

## Exercise 3 — two lifetimes, working together

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Ex3.cs`. `ICorrelation` is an id that
identifies one request; `IAuditTrail` is a log that outlives all of them. Both
registrations are currently wrong, in opposite directions.

id in the trail and answers **200** with
`{"correlationId": …, "seen": …}`, where `seen` is the number `Record` gave you
back. Then fix both lifetimes so that:

- the first request reports `seen: 1`, the second reports `seen: 2`
- the two requests report **different** correlation ids

`AuditTrail` is given code and is already thread-safe; do not change it. This
pair — a per-request value written into an application-wide store — is the
single most common shape in a real service, and it needs one of each lifetime.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 02_dependency_injection ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the two interfaces and ask, for each one, *who owns this?*

`ICorrelation` is described as "an id that identifies one request while it is
being handled". `IAuditTrail` is "a log that outlives every request". Those two
sentences are the two registrations; the current file has them the wrong way
round.

## Hint 2

The endpoint has to call `Record` and use what it gives back — it returns the
running total, so you do not need to count anything yourself. That means the
handler body is two statements, not one expression.

Do not change `AuditTrail`. It already locks, because a singleton is touched by
every request at once.

## Hint 3

```csharp
private static IResult Audit(ICorrelation correlation, IAuditTrail trail)
{
    int seen = trail.Record(correlation.Id);
    return TypedResults.Ok(new AuditResponse(correlation.Id, seen));
}
```

For the registrations: swap the two lifetimes. The one that is currently
`AddSingleton` should be per-request, and the one that is currently `AddScoped`
should be application-wide. If `seen` comes back as 1 twice, you changed only
one of them.

## Hint 1

Read the two interfaces and ask, for each one, *who owns this?*

`ICorrelation` is described as "an id that identifies one request while it is
being handled". `IAuditTrail` is "a log that outlives every request". Those two
sentences are the two registrations; the current file has them the wrong way
round.

## Hint 2

The endpoint has to call `Record` and use what it gives back — it returns the
running total, so you do not need to count anything yourself. That means the
handler body is two statements, not one expression.

Do not change `AuditTrail`. It already locks, because a singleton is touched by
every request at once.

## Hint 3

```csharp
private static IResult Audit(ICorrelation correlation, IAuditTrail trail)
{
    int seen = trail.Record(correlation.Id);
    return TypedResults.Ok(new AuditResponse(correlation.Id, seen));
}
```

For the registrations: swap the two lifetimes. The one that is currently
`AddSingleton` should be per-request, and the one that is currently `AddScoped`
should be application-wide. If `seen` comes back as 1 twice, you changed only
one of them.

## Exercise 4 — many implementations of one interface

Edit `src/Api/L02_DependencyInjection/Ex4.cs`. Three classes implement
`IOrderRule`; only one of them is registered. Register the other two, then
implement `CheckRules` so that `GET /l02/rules?totalCents=…` answers **200**
with `{"violations": [ … ]}` — the `Name` of every rule the total does *not*
satisfy, sorted A–Z.

So `?totalCents=0` gives `["PositiveTotalRule"]`, `?totalCents=99999` gives
`["MaximumTotalRule","WholeCurrencyRule"]`, and `?totalCents=2500` gives `[]`.

Registering the same interface more than once is not an error and does not
overwrite anything. `IEnumerable<IOrderRule>` gets you all of them, in
registration order — which is why the endpoint sorts, so the answer does not
depend on the order you happened to type. This is how validation pipelines,
notification channels and export formats are normally built: add a class,
register it, and every caller picks it up without being edited.

## Hint 1

The endpoint is one line: return the unit of work's `Id` and the log's current
`Count`, wrapped in `UnitOfWorkResponse`.

The interesting part is that you never call `Dispose` yourself. Something else
does — and the question this exercise asks is *when*.

## Hint 2

The container disposes the `IDisposable` objects it created, at the moment the
scope that created them ends. So for the count to go up once per finished
request, the unit of work has to be something the container builds once per
request.

It is currently registered as a singleton, which is disposed exactly once — at
application shutdown, long after these three requests.

## Hint 3

```csharp
services.AddScoped<IUnitOfWork, UnitOfWork>();
```

and

```csharp
private static IResult GetUnitOfWork(IUnitOfWork work, IDisposalLog log) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(new UnitOfWorkResponse(work.Id, log.Count));
```

Note why the first request reports 0 and not 1: its own unit of work is still
alive while the response is being written, and is disposed after your handler
returns.

## Hint 1

The endpoint is one line: return the unit of work's `Id` and the log's current
`Count`, wrapped in `UnitOfWorkResponse`.

The interesting part is that you never call `Dispose` yourself. Something else
does — and the question this exercise asks is *when*.

## Hint 2

The container disposes the `IDisposable` objects it created, at the moment the
scope that created them ends. So for the count to go up once per finished
request, the unit of work has to be something the container builds once per
request.

It is currently registered as a singleton, which is disposed exactly once — at
application shutdown, long after these three requests.

## Hint 3

```csharp
services.AddScoped<IUnitOfWork, UnitOfWork>();
```

and

```csharp
private static IResult GetUnitOfWork(IUnitOfWork work, IDisposalLog log) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(new UnitOfWorkResponse(work.Id, log.Count));
```

Note why the first request reports 0 and not 1: its own unit of work is still
alive while the response is being written, and is disposed after your handler
returns.
