# 03 — Middleware and the pipeline

Your handler is never the first thing to see a request. By the time
`GetOrder(int id)` runs, something has already parsed the HTTP message, matched
a route, decided whether the caller is allowed in, possibly rejected them, and
started a stopwatch. That "something" is the **middleware pipeline**, and it is
the single most distinctive idea in ASP.NET Core: not a list of hooks, but a
chain of components, each one wrapped around the next.

The picture that makes it click is an onion, and it is worth drawing once:

```
request  ──▶ correlation ──▶ timing ──▶ auth ──▶ [ your handler ]
response ◀── correlation ◀── timing ◀── auth ◀───────┘
```

Every middleware gets the request on the way in *and* the response on the way
out. The order you add them is the order they see the request, and the exact
reverse of the order they see the response. That single fact explains almost
every "why doesn't my middleware work" question ever asked.

In this lesson you build small pipelines and mount them at routes, so you can
see the order rather than take it on trust.

## Concept — `next`, and the three ways to add something

A middleware is any class with this shape. There is no interface to implement
and no attribute to apply; ASP.NET Core finds `InvokeAsync` by convention:

```csharp
public class ExampleMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        // on the way in - the request has not been handled yet
        context.Response.Headers["X-Example"] = "before";

        await next(context);          // run everything downstream

        // on the way out - the handler has finished
        Console.WriteLine(context.Response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

`next` is the rest of the pipeline, compressed into one delegate. Three things
you can do with it, and they are the whole vocabulary:

- **Call it.** Your middleware is a pass-through that decorates the request or
  inspects the response.
- **Don't call it.** The request stops here and whatever you wrote onto the
  response is the answer. This is **short-circuiting**: how a 401, a cached
  response, or a rate-limit rejection is produced.
- **Call it conditionally**, or call it and then change your mind about the
  status code — with the important caveat below.

The caveat: **once the response has started, headers are frozen.** ASP.NET Core
writes the status line and headers the moment the first byte of the body is
flushed, so a middleware that tries to set a header *after* `await next(...)`
usually finds it has no effect, or throws. Set headers on the way in; read
status codes on the way out.

Three methods put middleware into a pipeline, and knowing which is which is a
guaranteed interview question:

| method | what it does |
|---|---|
| `app.Use(...)` / `app.UseMiddleware<T>()` | adds a link in the chain; it may call `next` |
| `app.Run(...)` | adds a **terminal** — it has no `next` and always ends the request |
| `app.Map("/x", branch)` | splits the pipeline: `/x` goes down a separate chain and never comes back |
| `app.UseWhen(pred, branch)` | splits on a predicate, and the branch **rejoins** the main pipeline if it does not terminate |

`Run` at the end of a chain is not decoration — a pipeline with no terminal
just 404s.

### How this lesson mounts a pipeline

Normally you would add middleware to `Program.cs` with `app.UseWhatever()`. In
this course `Program.cs` stays a composition root, so each exercise builds its
own little pipeline and mounts it at a route:

```csharp
var pipeline = app.CreateApplicationBuilder();   // a fresh, empty chain
pipeline.UseMiddleware<ExampleMiddleware>();
pipeline.Run(context => context.Response.WriteAsync("done"));

app.Map("/l03/example", pipeline.Build());       // mount it
```

`CreateApplicationBuilder()` gives you the same `IApplicationBuilder` that
`Program.cs` uses, and `Build()` turns the chain into a single
`RequestDelegate`. Everything you learn here is the same API you would use at
the top of a real application; only the mounting differs.

One more piece you will need: a middleware can take *per-request* services as
extra parameters on `InvokeAsync`, even though its constructor runs only once:

```csharp
public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, IStatusLog log) { … }
```

The constructor is called once when the pipeline is built, so anything injected
there is effectively a singleton — putting a scoped service in a middleware
constructor is the captive dependency from lesson 02, wearing a hat.
`InvokeAsync` parameters are resolved from the request's scope, which is where
scoped services belong.

## Exercise 1 — your first middleware

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex1.cs`. Implement `StampMiddleware.InvokeAsync`
so that `GET /l03/stamp`:

- comes back with the response header `X-Dojo-Stamp: l03`, and
- still has the body `handler`, written by the terminal that sits after you

Two lines. The second one is the one people forget: if you do not call `next`,
the request stops at your middleware and the body is empty.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the order is the design

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex2.cs`, and only the `Configure` method. Three
marker middlewares are given; each one stamps the trace on the way in and again
on the way out. Add all three so that `GET /l03/order` returns exactly:

```
correlation>,timing>,auth>,handler,auth<,timing<,correlation<
```

The order is not arbitrary, and the reasoning is what to take away.
Correlation goes outermost so that *every* log line, including the timing
numbers and any authentication failure, can be tied to one request. Timing goes
next, so the time you report includes the cost of authenticating — otherwise
your dashboards will show a fast API while users wait. Auth goes last, closest
to the handler, because it is the final gate before your code runs.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — short-circuiting

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex3.cs`. Implement `ApiKeyMiddleware.InvokeAsync`
so that a request to `/l03/secure` only reaches the handler when the header
`X-Api-Key` is exactly `dojo-key`. Anything else — a missing header, a wrong
value — gets **401** and goes no further.

The middleware downstream of yours sets `X-Reached-Handler: yes`, and the gate
checks that the header is *absent* on your 401. That is the real test of a
short-circuit: it is not enough to set the status code, you have to stop the
request. `context.Response.StatusCode = 401;` followed by `await next(context)`
is the classic broken version — it sets a status the handler will then overwrite
while doing all the work you meant to prevent.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — `Use`, `UseWhen` and `Run`

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex4.cs`, method `Configure`. Build a pipeline,
mounted under `/l03/branch/`, that:

- adds `X-Branch-Seen: all` to **every** response under that prefix
- answers with the body `admin` for any path under `/l03/branch/admin`
- answers with the body `default` for everything else

Three pieces, one of each kind: a `Use` for the shared header, a `UseWhen`
whose predicate looks at `context.Request.Path`, and a `Run` for the fallback.
`HttpRequest.Path` has a `StartsWithSegments` method that compares whole path
segments — worth preferring over `StartsWith`, which would also match
`/l03/branch/administrators`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex4
```

## Challenge — a pipeline that is only correct in one order

Honest difficulty note: two small middlewares plus three lines of ordering.
Every wrong order still compiles and still returns plausible answers, which is
exactly what makes pipeline bugs expensive.

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Challenge.cs`. `CorrelationIdMiddleware` is given.
Implement the other two and arrange all three in `Configure` so that
`/l03/challenge/…`:

- always answers with an `X-Correlation-Id` header — **including on rejections**
  — echoing the client's value when one was sent
- answers **401** when `X-Api-Key` is not `dojo-key`
- answers **403** for paths under `/l03/challenge/admin` when the caller has a
  valid key but no `X-Role: admin` header
- answers **200 ok** otherwise

The 401-must-still-be-correlated requirement is what pins the order down. A
correlation id that only appears on successful responses is worse than none: the
requests you most need to trace are the ones that failed.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this lesson; the scheduler brings it back
later. Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Review1.cs`: implement
`StatusRecorderMiddleware` so it records the status code each request ended
with, and order it against the given `TeapotMiddleware` (which short-circuits
with **418** for paths ending in `/teapot`) so that the recorder sees both a
418 and a 200. The question underneath: *which side of a short-circuit do you
have to be on to observe it?*
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/03_middleware

The pipeline is where ASP.NET Core stops looking like a routing library and
starts looking like a web server you can reason about. Everything
cross-cutting — authentication, HTTPS, compression, CORS, exception handling,
tracing — is a middleware, which means all of it obeys the same three rules you
just used.

## Notes

**What `next` actually is.** `IApplicationBuilder.Build()` walks your list of
middleware factories *backwards*, starting from a terminal delegate (a 404
handler if you never added a `Run`), and wraps each one around what it has so
far. The result is a single `RequestDelegate` — one function from `HttpContext`
to `Task` — with your whole chain closed over inside it. There is no list being
iterated at request time and no framework loop dispatching to hooks; the
composition happened once at startup. That is why the order of your
registration lines is the order of execution, and why it cannot change at
runtime.

**Two ways to write one.** The inline form, `app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{ … })`, is right for three lines. The class form — a constructor taking
`RequestDelegate next` plus an `InvokeAsync(HttpContext)` method, added with
`UseMiddleware<T>()` — is right for anything with dependencies or tests. There
is also `IMiddleware`, an actual interface, which is resolved from DI *per
request* and so can hold scoped dependencies as fields; it needs to be
registered in the container itself, which is the trade. Convention-based
classes are the common case by a wide margin.

**Middleware constructors run once.** `UseMiddleware<T>` builds one instance
when the pipeline is built and reuses it for every request, so its constructor
parameters come from the *root* provider and behave as singletons. Put a scoped
service there and you have a captive dependency; in Development you will get an
outright error the first time it runs. The supported route is extra parameters
on `InvokeAsync`, which are resolved from the request scope. Same rule as
lesson 02, new disguise.

**The response has a point of no return.** Status code and headers are buffered
until the first body byte is written or the response is explicitly started;
after that, `HasStarted` is true and mutating headers throws. This is why the
"handle the exception and turn it into a nice 500" pattern in lesson 08 has to
sit *outside* everything that writes, and why a middleware that wants to add a
header based on the outcome uses `context.Response.OnStarting(callback)` —
a hook that fires at the last possible moment before the headers go out.

**`Map` versus `UseWhen`.** `Map` splits the pipeline permanently: the branch
handles the request and never returns to the main chain, and it also strips the
matched prefix off `Request.Path` into `Request.PathBase`. `UseWhen` runs the
branch and, if the branch does not terminate, control comes back and continues
down the main pipeline. `MapWhen` is the predicate-based version of `Map` — a
split that does not rejoin. Choosing wrongly gives you either a shared terminal
you did not want or a branch that mysteriously falls through.

**Middleware versus endpoint filters.** Since .NET 7 there is a second, smaller
extension point: `AddEndpointFilter` runs around a *single endpoint's handler*,
after routing and model binding, and it sees the bound arguments. Validation
belongs there far more naturally than in middleware, which only has raw
`HttpContext`. Rule of thumb: if it applies to every request and needs no
knowledge of the endpoint, it is middleware; if it applies to some endpoints and
wants their arguments, it is a filter.

## ex1 - the two lines, and which order they go in

Setting the header before `await next(context)` is not stylistic. The terminal
handler writes the body, which starts the response, which freezes the headers —
so a `X-Dojo-Stamp` assignment placed after the await is a line that either
silently does nothing or throws `InvalidOperationException`. Anything you want
to *send* goes on the way in; anything you want to *observe* goes on the way
out.

The second half is `next` itself. A middleware that forgets to call it is not
broken in an obvious way: it returns a 200 with an empty body, because the
status code defaults to 200 and nothing ever wrote anything. That is the same
failure mode as an accidental short-circuit, and it is why the gate checks the
body as well as the header.

Note the primary constructor: `StampMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)` captures
`next` as a field without you declaring one. `UseMiddleware<T>` supplies that
argument itself; any *other* constructor parameters are resolved from the
container.

## ex2 - why that order, in a real system

The trace is a picture of nesting. `correlation>` appears first and
`correlation<` last, so everything else happened *inside* the correlation
middleware — which is exactly the property you want from something whose job is
to tag all the work belonging to one request.

The ordering argument generalises. Ask, for each pair: *does the outer one need
to see what the inner one did, or make something available to it?*

- Correlation must be outermost because logging, timing and the failure path
  all want the id. If it were innermost, an authentication rejection would be
  logged with no id and you could not join it to anything.
- Timing wraps auth because the user's experience includes the time spent
  validating a token, calling an identity provider, or hitting a cache miss. A
  timer that starts after auth reports a number nobody outside the process can
  reproduce.
- Auth is innermost because it is the last gate; anything after it can assume a
  caller.

Real `Program.cs` files have a canonical order for the same reason, and it is
worth having seen it: exception handler, HSTS, HTTPS redirection, static files,
routing, CORS, authentication, authorisation, endpoints. Every adjacent pair in
that list has an argument like the ones above behind it. The most commonly
botched pair is CORS-before-auth: put them the other way round and a browser
preflight gets rejected with a 401 that has no CORS headers on it, so the
browser reports a CORS error and you spend an afternoon looking in the wrong
place.

## ex3 - what a short-circuit really is

Short-circuiting is defined by omission: you *do not* call `next`. Everything
else — setting a status code, writing a body — is just what you happen to do
before returning.

The broken version the gate is designed to catch looks reasonable:

```csharp
if (!Valid(context)) { context.Response.StatusCode = 401; }
await next(context);            // ← the bug
```

The status is set, and then the handler runs anyway, does the work, and writes
a 200 over the top. The request you meant to reject has now hit your database.
Checking that a *downstream* marker header is absent is the only way to prove
from outside that the pipeline really stopped — a fact worth remembering when
you write tests for your own auth middleware.

One more detail: `return Task.CompletedTask` versus `return;` in an `async`
method are the same thing here. The reference is not `async` at all, because it
never awaits anything on the rejection path, and returning the task from `next`
directly avoids an unnecessary state machine. That is a micro-optimisation, but
it is idiomatic in framework-level code and you will see it everywhere.

## ex4 - Use, Run, Map, UseWhen

Four names, one distinction repeated twice. `Use` continues, `Run` terminates.
`UseWhen` continues after the branch, `Map`/`MapWhen` do not.

The `Use` middleware that adds `X-Branch-Seen` runs for both paths because it
sits above the split. Move it inside the `UseWhen` and only admin requests get
it; move it after the `Run` and nothing gets it, because the terminal already
ended the request — a middleware registered after a terminal is dead code, and
nothing warns you.

`StartsWithSegments` over `StartsWith` is the small but real lesson.
`Request.Path` is a `PathString`, a type that exists specifically to make
segment-aware comparisons the easy ones: `StartsWithSegments("/admin")` matches
`/admin` and `/admin/users` but not `/administrators`. Path-prefix checks
written with plain string methods are a recurring source of authorisation
bypasses.

## challenge - order as a security property

The requirement that pins everything down is "the 401 must still carry a
correlation id". It forces correlation above the key check, and once you see
why, you have the general rule: **anything that must be true of every response,
including the ones you reject, has to be added before the thing that rejects.**
The same argument governs CORS headers on error responses and rate-limit
headers on 429s.

The admin check being inside a `UseWhen` is the second half. Put it in the main
chain and it applies everywhere, so ordinary endpoints start demanding a role
they never needed — a failure that is *safe* (nobody gets extra access) but
completely breaks the API. The opposite mistake, putting the key check inside
the branch, is the dangerous one: unauthenticated callers sail through
everything except `/admin`.

401 versus 403 is the third: 401 means "I do not know who you are, authenticate
and try again"; 403 means "I know exactly who you are and the answer is no". A
403 with a `WWW-Authenticate` header, or a 401 for a logged-in user who lacks a
role, both tell the client to do something that cannot help.

## review1 - which side of the short-circuit are you on?

`TeapotMiddleware` never calls `next` for `/teapot`, so nothing below it in the
chain runs. A recorder placed below therefore records nothing at all — the
request it most wanted to record is exactly the one it cannot see. Placed
above, it awaits `next`, control returns as soon as the teapot middleware
returns, and `context.Response.StatusCode` is already 418.

This is the shape of every observability middleware in existence: logging,
metrics, tracing and exception handling all have to be outside the things they
observe, which is why the canonical `Program.cs` order starts with them. It is
also the reason "add logging" is not a thing you can bolt on at the bottom of a
pipeline later.

Note that the recorder reads `Response.StatusCode` *after* the await and takes
its scoped dependency as an `InvokeAsync` parameter rather than a constructor
one. Both details are load-bearing, and both come straight from lesson 02.

## Further reading

- [ASP.NET Core Middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/) — the pipeline model, `Use`/`Run`/`Map`, and the diagram this lesson's onion is based on.
- [Write custom ASP.NET Core middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/write) — the convention-based class, `IMiddleware`, and per-request dependencies.
- [Middleware order](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/#middleware-order) — the canonical `Program.cs` ordering and why each step sits where it does.
- [Request and response operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-response) — `HasStarted`, `OnStarting`, and what happens once the response is on the wire.
- [Filters versus middleware in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/min-api-filters) — endpoint filters, and when to reach for them instead.
lessons.fullReadme:
# 03 — Middleware and the pipeline

Your handler is never the first thing to see a request. By the time
`GetOrder(int id)` runs, something has already parsed the HTTP message, matched
a route, decided whether the caller is allowed in, possibly rejected them, and
started a stopwatch. That "something" is the **middleware pipeline**, and it is
the single most distinctive idea in ASP.NET Core: not a list of hooks, but a
chain of components, each one wrapped around the next.

The picture that makes it click is an onion, and it is worth drawing once:

```
request  ──▶ correlation ──▶ timing ──▶ auth ──▶ [ your handler ]
response ◀── correlation ◀── timing ◀── auth ◀───────┘
```

Every middleware gets the request on the way in *and* the response on the way
out. The order you add them is the order they see the request, and the exact
reverse of the order they see the response. That single fact explains almost
every "why doesn't my middleware work" question ever asked.

In this lesson you build small pipelines and mount them at routes, so you can
see the order rather than take it on trust.

## Concept — `next`, and the three ways to add something

A middleware is any class with this shape. There is no interface to implement
and no attribute to apply; ASP.NET Core finds `InvokeAsync` by convention:

```csharp
public class ExampleMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
{
    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        // on the way in - the request has not been handled yet
        context.Response.Headers["X-Example"] = "before";

        await next(context);          // run everything downstream

        // on the way out - the handler has finished
        Console.WriteLine(context.Response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

`next` is the rest of the pipeline, compressed into one delegate. Three things
you can do with it, and they are the whole vocabulary:

- **Call it.** Your middleware is a pass-through that decorates the request or
  inspects the response.
- **Don't call it.** The request stops here and whatever you wrote onto the
  response is the answer. This is **short-circuiting**: how a 401, a cached
  response, or a rate-limit rejection is produced.
- **Call it conditionally**, or call it and then change your mind about the
  status code — with the important caveat below.

The caveat: **once the response has started, headers are frozen.** ASP.NET Core
writes the status line and headers the moment the first byte of the body is
flushed, so a middleware that tries to set a header *after* `await next(...)`
usually finds it has no effect, or throws. Set headers on the way in; read
status codes on the way out.

Three methods put middleware into a pipeline, and knowing which is which is a
guaranteed interview question:

| method | what it does |
|---|---|
| `app.Use(...)` / `app.UseMiddleware<T>()` | adds a link in the chain; it may call `next` |
| `app.Run(...)` | adds a **terminal** — it has no `next` and always ends the request |
| `app.Map("/x", branch)` | splits the pipeline: `/x` goes down a separate chain and never comes back |
| `app.UseWhen(pred, branch)` | splits on a predicate, and the branch **rejoins** the main pipeline if it does not terminate |

`Run` at the end of a chain is not decoration — a pipeline with no terminal
just 404s.

### How this lesson mounts a pipeline

Normally you would add middleware to `Program.cs` with `app.UseWhatever()`. In
this course `Program.cs` stays a composition root, so each exercise builds its
own little pipeline and mounts it at a route:

```csharp
var pipeline = app.CreateApplicationBuilder();   // a fresh, empty chain
pipeline.UseMiddleware<ExampleMiddleware>();
pipeline.Run(context => context.Response.WriteAsync("done"));

app.Map("/l03/example", pipeline.Build());       // mount it
```

`CreateApplicationBuilder()` gives you the same `IApplicationBuilder` that
`Program.cs` uses, and `Build()` turns the chain into a single
`RequestDelegate`. Everything you learn here is the same API you would use at
the top of a real application; only the mounting differs.

One more piece you will need: a middleware can take *per-request* services as
extra parameters on `InvokeAsync`, even though its constructor runs only once:

```csharp
public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, IStatusLog log) { … }
```

The constructor is called once when the pipeline is built, so anything injected
there is effectively a singleton — putting a scoped service in a middleware
constructor is the captive dependency from lesson 02, wearing a hat.
`InvokeAsync` parameters are resolved from the request's scope, which is where
scoped services belong.

## Exercise 1 — your first middleware

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex1.cs`. Implement `StampMiddleware.InvokeAsync`
so that `GET /l03/stamp`:

- comes back with the response header `X-Dojo-Stamp: l03`, and
- still has the body `handler`, written by the terminal that sits after you

Two lines. The second one is the one people forget: if you do not call `next`,
the request stops at your middleware and the body is empty.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the order is the design

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex2.cs`, and only the `Configure` method. Three
marker middlewares are given; each one stamps the trace on the way in and again
on the way out. Add all three so that `GET /l03/order` returns exactly:

```
correlation>,timing>,auth>,handler,auth<,timing<,correlation<
```

The order is not arbitrary, and the reasoning is what to take away.
Correlation goes outermost so that *every* log line, including the timing
numbers and any authentication failure, can be tied to one request. Timing goes
next, so the time you report includes the cost of authenticating — otherwise
your dashboards will show a fast API while users wait. Auth goes last, closest
to the handler, because it is the final gate before your code runs.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — short-circuiting

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex3.cs`. Implement `ApiKeyMiddleware.InvokeAsync`
so that a request to `/l03/secure` only reaches the handler when the header
`X-Api-Key` is exactly `dojo-key`. Anything else — a missing header, a wrong
value — gets **401** and goes no further.

The middleware downstream of yours sets `X-Reached-Handler: yes`, and the gate
checks that the header is *absent* on your 401. That is the real test of a
short-circuit: it is not enough to set the status code, you have to stop the
request. `context.Response.StatusCode = 401;` followed by `await next(context)`
is the classic broken version — it sets a status the handler will then overwrite
while doing all the work you meant to prevent.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — `Use`, `UseWhen` and `Run`

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex4.cs`, method `Configure`. Build a pipeline,
mounted under `/l03/branch/`, that:

- adds `X-Branch-Seen: all` to **every** response under that prefix
- answers with the body `admin` for any path under `/l03/branch/admin`
- answers with the body `default` for everything else

Three pieces, one of each kind: a `Use` for the shared header, a `UseWhen`
whose predicate looks at `context.Request.Path`, and a `Run` for the fallback.
`HttpRequest.Path` has a `StartsWithSegments` method that compares whole path
segments — worth preferring over `StartsWith`, which would also match
`/l03/branch/administrators`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex4
```

## Challenge — a pipeline that is only correct in one order

Honest difficulty note: two small middlewares plus three lines of ordering.
Every wrong order still compiles and still returns plausible answers, which is
exactly what makes pipeline bugs expensive.

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Challenge.cs`. `CorrelationIdMiddleware` is given.
Implement the other two and arrange all three in `Configure` so that
`/l03/challenge/…`:

- always answers with an `X-Correlation-Id` header — **including on rejections**
  — echoing the client's value when one was sent
- answers **401** when `X-Api-Key` is not `dojo-key`
- answers **403** for paths under `/l03/challenge/admin` when the caller has a
  valid key but no `X-Role: admin` header
- answers **200 ok** otherwise

The 401-must-still-be-correlated requirement is what pins the order down. A
correlation id that only appears on successful responses is worse than none: the
requests you most need to trace are the ones that failed.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this lesson; the scheduler brings it back
later. Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Review1.cs`: implement
`StatusRecorderMiddleware` so it records the status code each request ended
with, and order it against the given `TeapotMiddleware` (which short-circuits
with **418** for paths ending in `/teapot`) so that the recorder sees both a
418 and a 200. The question underneath: *which side of a short-circuit do you
have to be on to observe it?*

## The gate

This is the entire gate class, `tests/Gates/L03_MiddlewareTests.cs`:

```csharp
using System.Net;
using System.Net.Http.Json;

namespace DotnetDojo.Gates;

public class L03_MiddlewareTests(DojoWebFactory factory) : IClassFixture<DojoWebFactory>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex1_TheStampMiddlewareAddsAHeaderAndLetsTheRequestThrough()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/l03/stamp");

        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, response,
            "GET /l03/stamp must answer 200. A 500 means StampMiddleware still throws - "
                + "reread README ex1.");

        Teach.Equal("l03", Header(response, "X-Dojo-Stamp"),
            "The middleware has to add the response header X-Dojo-Stamp with the value "
                + "\"l03\", and it has to add it BEFORE awaiting next - once the handler has "
                + "written the response, headers can no longer be changed.");

        Teach.Equal("handler", await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
            "The body should still be \"handler\", which is what the terminal handler writes. "
                + "An empty body means your middleware never called next, so nothing "
                + "downstream ran.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex2_ThePipelineIsAnOnionAndTheOrderIsVisible()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/l03/order");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, response,
            "GET /l03/order must answer 200 - reread README ex2.");

        Teach.Equal(
            "correlation>,timing>,auth>,handler,auth<,timing<,correlation<",
            await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
            "That trace is the shape of your pipeline. Read it as a nesting: everything "
                + "between correlation> and correlation< happened inside the correlation "
                + "middleware. The first middleware you add is the outermost one, and the "
                + "order on the way out is the reverse of the order on the way in.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex3_TheKeyCheckStopsTheRequestDead()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var anonymous = await client.GetAsync("/l03/secure");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, anonymous,
            "No X-Api-Key header at all must be 401 - reread README ex3.");
        Teach.Equal("", Header(anonymous, "X-Reached-Handler"),
            "Short-circuiting means NOT calling next. The middleware downstream of yours "
                + "still ran and set X-Reached-Handler, so the request carried on past your "
                + "401 - you set the status code and then awaited next anyway.");
        Teach.Equal("", await anonymous.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
            "The secret was written to the body of a 401. Return without calling next.");

        var wrong = await client.SendAsync(WithKey("nope"));
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, wrong,
            "A present-but-wrong key is still a 401.");

        var allowed = await client.SendAsync(WithKey("dojo-key"));
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, allowed,
            "With the right key the request must reach the handler: 200.");
        Teach.Equal("yes", Header(allowed, "X-Reached-Handler"),
            "The rest of the pipeline has to run when the key is valid - call next.");
        Teach.Equal("secret", await allowed.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
            "…and the terminal handler's body comes back.");

        static HttpRequestMessage WithKey(string key)
        {
            var message = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Get, "/l03/secure");
            message.Headers.Add("X-Api-Key", key);
            return message;
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex4_UseRunsForEveryoneAndTheBranchOnlyForSome()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var admin = await client.GetAsync("/l03/branch/admin/reports");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, admin,
            "GET /l03/branch/admin/reports must answer 200 - reread README ex4.");
        Teach.Equal("admin", await admin.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
            "Anything under /l03/branch/admin is handled by the branch, which answers "
                + "\"admin\".");
        Teach.Equal("all", Header(admin, "X-Branch-Seen"),
            "The Use middleware runs for every request, branch or not, because it was added "
                + "before the branch. If this header is missing you added it inside the "
                + "branch or after the terminal.");

        var other = await client.GetAsync("/l03/branch/orders");
        Teach.Equal("default", await other.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
            "/l03/branch/orders is not under /admin, so it falls through to the terminal "
                + "Run, which answers \"default\". Getting \"admin\" here means the branch "
                + "predicate matches everything.");
        Teach.Equal("all", Header(other, "X-Branch-Seen"),
            "The shared middleware runs on this path too.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Challenge_EveryResponseIsCorrelatedEvenTheRejections()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var anonymous = await client.GetAsync("/l03/challenge/reports");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, anonymous,
            "No API key is a 401 - reread README challenge.");
        Teach.True(Header(anonymous, "X-Correlation-Id").Length > 0,
            "A 401 with no correlation id is an incident nobody can trace. The correlation "
                + "middleware has to run BEFORE the thing that might reject the request, so "
                + "add it first.");

        var tagged = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Get, "/l03/challenge/reports");
        tagged.Headers.Add("X-Correlation-Id", "trace-me");
        var taggedResponse = await client.SendAsync(tagged);
        Teach.Equal("trace-me", Header(taggedResponse, "X-Correlation-Id"),
            "A correlation id the client supplied must be echoed, not replaced - that is how "
                + "a request is followed across services.");

        var forbidden = await client.SendAsync(Keyed("/l03/challenge/admin/tools", role: null));
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Forbidden, forbidden,
            "A valid key with no admin role, on an admin path, is 403: authenticated but not "
                + "allowed. 401 would mean 'I do not know who you are', which is false here.");

        var admin = await client.SendAsync(Keyed("/l03/challenge/admin/tools", role: "admin"));
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, admin,
            "Right key, right role: 200.");
        Teach.Equal("ok", await admin.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
            "…and the terminal handler runs.");

        var ordinary = await client.SendAsync(Keyed("/l03/challenge/reports", role: null));
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, ordinary,
            "/l03/challenge/reports is not an admin path, so a valid key is enough. Getting "
                + "403 here means the admin check is not inside a branch - it is running for "
                + "every path.");

        static HttpRequestMessage Keyed(string path, string? role)
        {
            var message = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Get, path);
            message.Headers.Add("X-Api-Key", "dojo-key");
            if (role is not null)
            {
                message.Headers.Add("X-Role", role);
            }

            return message;
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Review1_TheOutermostMiddlewareSeesTheFinalStatusCode()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var teapot = await client.GetAsync("/l03/review/pipeline/teapot");
        await Teach.Status((HttpStatusCode)418, teapot,
            "Given code refuses to brew coffee with 418. If this is a 500, "
                + "StatusRecorderMiddleware still throws - reread README review.");

        Teach.Equal(418, await LastStatus(client),
            "The recorder never saw the 418, because the middleware that produced it "
                + "short-circuited first. Whatever wants to observe a response has to be "
                + "OUTSIDE the thing that produces it.");

        await client.GetAsync("/l03/review/pipeline/tea");
        Teach.Equal(200, await LastStatus(client),
            "A request that reaches the terminal handler ends as a 200, and the recorder "
                + "should have seen that too.");
    }

    private static async Task<int> LastStatus(HttpClient client)
    {
        var body = await client.GetFromJsonAsync<LastStatusDto>("/l03/review/last-status");
        return body?.Status ?? -1;
    }

    private static string Header(HttpResponseMessage response, string name) =>
        response.Headers.TryGetValues(name, out var values) ? string.Join(",", values) : "";

    private sealed record LastStatusDto(int Status);
}
```

In plain English: every assertion here is about something a client can see — a
header, a status code, a body — because the pipeline has no other observable
surface. ex2 reads the whole shape of the onion out of one string. ex3 proves a
short-circuit by checking that a *downstream* header is missing. The challenge
proves ordering by checking that a rejection still carries the header added by
the middleware above it.

## The teaching point

When a middleware "doesn't work", there are only ever four causes, and you can
now name all of them: it was added in the wrong order; it did not call `next`
when it should have; it called `next` when it should not have; or it tried to
touch headers after the response had already started.

The deeper habit is thinking about *where a concern belongs*. Anything that
must apply to every request regardless of route — correlation ids, timing,
compression, HTTPS redirection, exception handling — is middleware. Anything
that only applies to some endpoints is either a branch, a group convention, or
an endpoint filter. Getting that split right is most of what separates a
codebase where cross-cutting concerns are one file each from one where they are
copy-pasted into forty handlers.

Next: **04_configuration_options**, where the values your middleware and
services need stop being constants in the source and start coming from
configuration.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **03 — Middleware and the pipeline**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `challenge` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex1` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex2` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex3` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex4` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `review1` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `challenge` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex1` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex2` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex3` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

## 100 retrieval prompts — 03 — Middleware and the pipeline

This is the expanded practice bank for this lesson overview: ten retrieval lenses at
each of ten spaced stages. Do one stage per scheduled session. Record an
answer before checking notes; recognition is not retrieval.

### Stage 1 — Cold recall (now)

Answer from memory before opening any course file.
1. **Contract · `challenge`:** For 03 — Middleware and the pipeline, state the exact inputs, outputs, side effects, and success condition.
2. **Mechanism · `ex1`:** For 03 — Middleware and the pipeline, trace the language or runtime mechanism that produces the result.
3. **Construction · `ex2`:** For 03 — Middleware and the pipeline, build the smallest correct example and justify every token or operation.

# Reading - dotnet/03_middleware

The pipeline is where ASP.NET Core stops looking like a routing library and
starts looking like a web server you can reason about. Everything
cross-cutting — authentication, HTTPS, compression, CORS, exception handling,
tracing — is a middleware, which means all of it obeys the same three rules you
just used.

## Notes

**What `next` actually is.** `IApplicationBuilder.Build()` walks your list of
middleware factories *backwards*, starting from a terminal delegate (a 404
handler if you never added a `Run`), and wraps each one around what it has so
far. The result is a single `RequestDelegate` — one function from `HttpContext`
to `Task` — with your whole chain closed over inside it. There is no list being
iterated at request time and no framework loop dispatching to hooks; the
composition happened once at startup. That is why the order of your
registration lines is the order of execution, and why it cannot change at
runtime.

**Two ways to write one.** The inline form, `app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{ … })`, is right for three lines. The class form — a constructor taking
`RequestDelegate next` plus an `InvokeAsync(HttpContext)` method, added with
`UseMiddleware<T>()` — is right for anything with dependencies or tests. There
is also `IMiddleware`, an actual interface, which is resolved from DI *per
request* and so can hold scoped dependencies as fields; it needs to be
registered in the container itself, which is the trade. Convention-based
classes are the common case by a wide margin.

**Middleware constructors run once.** `UseMiddleware<T>` builds one instance
when the pipeline is built and reuses it for every request, so its constructor
parameters come from the *root* provider and behave as singletons. Put a scoped
service there and you have a captive dependency; in Development you will get an
outright error the first time it runs. The supported route is extra parameters
on `InvokeAsync`, which are resolved from the request scope. Same rule as
lesson 02, new disguise.

**The response has a point of no return.** Status code and headers are buffered
until the first body byte is written or the response is explicitly started;
after that, `HasStarted` is true and mutating headers throws. This is why the
"handle the exception and turn it into a nice 500" pattern in lesson 08 has to
sit *outside* everything that writes, and why a middleware that wants to add a
header based on the outcome uses `context.Response.OnStarting(callback)` —
a hook that fires at the last possible moment before the headers go out.

**`Map` versus `UseWhen`.** `Map` splits the pipeline permanently: the branch
handles the request and never returns to the main chain, and it also strips the
matched prefix off `Request.Path` into `Request.PathBase`. `UseWhen` runs the
branch and, if the branch does not terminate, control comes back and continues
down the main pipeline. `MapWhen` is the predicate-based version of `Map` — a
split that does not rejoin. Choosing wrongly gives you either a shared terminal
you did not want or a branch that mysteriously falls through.

**Middleware versus endpoint filters.** Since .NET 7 there is a second, smaller
extension point: `AddEndpointFilter` runs around a *single endpoint's handler*,
after routing and model binding, and it sees the bound arguments. Validation
belongs there far more naturally than in middleware, which only has raw
`HttpContext`. Rule of thumb: if it applies to every request and needs no
knowledge of the endpoint, it is middleware; if it applies to some endpoints and
wants their arguments, it is a filter.

## ex1 - the two lines, and which order they go in

Setting the header before `await next(context)` is not stylistic. The terminal
handler writes the body, which starts the response, which freezes the headers —
so a `X-Dojo-Stamp` assignment placed after the await is a line that either
silently does nothing or throws `InvalidOperationException`. Anything you want
to *send* goes on the way in; anything you want to *observe* goes on the way
out.

The second half is `next` itself. A middleware that forgets to call it is not
broken in an obvious way: it returns a 200 with an empty body, because the
status code defaults to 200 and nothing ever wrote anything. That is the same
failure mode as an accidental short-circuit, and it is why the gate checks the
body as well as the header.

Note the primary constructor: `StampMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)` captures
`next` as a field without you declaring one. `UseMiddleware<T>` supplies that
argument itself; any *other* constructor parameters are resolved from the
container.

## ex2 - why that order, in a real system

The trace is a picture of nesting. `correlation>` appears first and
`correlation<` last, so everything else happened *inside* the correlation
middleware — which is exactly the property you want from something whose job is
to tag all the work belonging to one request.

The ordering argument generalises. Ask, for each pair: *does the outer one need
to see what the inner one did, or make something available to it?*

- Correlation must be outermost because logging, timing and the failure path
  all want the id. If it were innermost, an authentication rejection would be
  logged with no id and you could not join it to anything.
- Timing wraps auth because the user's experience includes the time spent
  validating a token, calling an identity provider, or hitting a cache miss. A
  timer that starts after auth reports a number nobody outside the process can
  reproduce.
- Auth is innermost because it is the last gate; anything after it can assume a
  caller.

Real `Program.cs` files have a canonical order for the same reason, and it is
worth having seen it: exception handler, HSTS, HTTPS redirection, static files,
routing, CORS, authentication, authorisation, endpoints. Every adjacent pair in
that list has an argument like the ones above behind it. The most commonly
botched pair is CORS-before-auth: put them the other way round and a browser
preflight gets rejected with a 401 that has no CORS headers on it, so the
browser reports a CORS error and you spend an afternoon looking in the wrong
place.

## ex3 - what a short-circuit really is

Short-circuiting is defined by omission: you *do not* call `next`. Everything
else — setting a status code, writing a body — is just what you happen to do
before returning.

The broken version the gate is designed to catch looks reasonable:

```csharp
if (!Valid(context)) { context.Response.StatusCode = 401; }
await next(context);            // ← the bug
```

The status is set, and then the handler runs anyway, does the work, and writes
a 200 over the top. The request you meant to reject has now hit your database.
Checking that a *downstream* marker header is absent is the only way to prove
from outside that the pipeline really stopped — a fact worth remembering when
you write tests for your own auth middleware.

One more detail: `return Task.CompletedTask` versus `return;` in an `async`
method are the same thing here. The reference is not `async` at all, because it
never awaits anything on the rejection path, and returning the task from `next`
directly avoids an unnecessary state machine. That is a micro-optimisation, but
it is idiomatic in framework-level code and you will see it everywhere.

## ex4 - Use, Run, Map, UseWhen

Four names, one distinction repeated twice. `Use` continues, `Run` terminates.
`UseWhen` continues after the branch, `Map`/`MapWhen` do not.

The `Use` middleware that adds `X-Branch-Seen` runs for both paths because it
sits above the split. Move it inside the `UseWhen` and only admin requests get
it; move it after the `Run` and nothing gets it, because the terminal already
ended the request — a middleware registered after a terminal is dead code, and
nothing warns you.

`StartsWithSegments` over `StartsWith` is the small but real lesson.
`Request.Path` is a `PathString`, a type that exists specifically to make
segment-aware comparisons the easy ones: `StartsWithSegments("/admin")` matches
`/admin` and `/admin/users` but not `/administrators`. Path-prefix checks
written with plain string methods are a recurring source of authorisation
bypasses.

## challenge - order as a security property

The requirement that pins everything down is "the 401 must still carry a
correlation id". It forces correlation above the key check, and once you see
why, you have the general rule: **anything that must be true of every response,
including the ones you reject, has to be added before the thing that rejects.**
The same argument governs CORS headers on error responses and rate-limit
headers on 429s.

The admin check being inside a `UseWhen` is the second half. Put it in the main
chain and it applies everywhere, so ordinary endpoints start demanding a role
they never needed — a failure that is *safe* (nobody gets extra access) but
completely breaks the API. The opposite mistake, putting the key check inside
the branch, is the dangerous one: unauthenticated callers sail through
everything except `/admin`.

401 versus 403 is the third: 401 means "I do not know who you are, authenticate
and try again"; 403 means "I know exactly who you are and the answer is no". A
403 with a `WWW-Authenticate` header, or a 401 for a logged-in user who lacks a
role, both tell the client to do something that cannot help.

## review1 - which side of the short-circuit are you on?

`TeapotMiddleware` never calls `next` for `/teapot`, so nothing below it in the
chain runs. A recorder placed below therefore records nothing at all — the
request it most wanted to record is exactly the one it cannot see. Placed
above, it awaits `next`, control returns as soon as the teapot middleware
returns, and `context.Response.StatusCode` is already 418.

This is the shape of every observability middleware in existence: logging,
metrics, tracing and exception handling all have to be outside the things they
observe, which is why the canonical `Program.cs` order starts with them. It is
also the reason "add logging" is not a thing you can bolt on at the bottom of a
pipeline later.

Note that the recorder reads `Response.StatusCode` *after* the await and takes
its scoped dependency as an `InvokeAsync` parameter rather than a constructor
one. Both details are load-bearing, and both come straight from lesson 02.

## Further reading

- [ASP.NET Core Middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/) — the pipeline model, `Use`/`Run`/`Map`, and the diagram this lesson's onion is based on.
- [Write custom ASP.NET Core middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/write) — the convention-based class, `IMiddleware`, and per-request dependencies.
- [Middleware order](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/#middleware-order) — the canonical `Program.cs` ordering and why each step sits where it does.
- [Request and response operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-response) — `HasStarted`, `OnStarting`, and what happens once the response is on the wire.
- [Filters versus middleware in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/min-api-filters) — endpoint filters, and when to reach for them instead.

## Challenge — a pipeline that is only correct in one order

Honest difficulty note: two small middlewares plus three lines of ordering.
Every wrong order still compiles and still returns plausible answers, which is
exactly what makes pipeline bugs expensive.

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Challenge.cs`. `CorrelationIdMiddleware` is given.
Implement the other two and arrange all three in `Configure` so that
`/l03/challenge/…`:

- always answers with an `X-Correlation-Id` header — **including on rejections**
  — echoing the client's value when one was sent
- answers **401** when `X-Api-Key` is not `dojo-key`
- answers **403** for paths under `/l03/challenge/admin` when the caller has a
  valid key but no `X-Role: admin` header
- answers **200 ok** otherwise

The 401-must-still-be-correlated requirement is what pins the order down. A
correlation id that only appears on successful responses is worse than none: the
requests you most need to trace are the ones that failed.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do the two middlewares first — both are the ex3 pattern with a different header
and a different status code — and get them compiling. Then spend your thinking
on `Configure`.

For the order, start from the requirement that is hardest to satisfy: the 401
must still carry a correlation id. Only one arrangement makes that true.

## Hint 2

If the correlation middleware runs *after* the key check, a rejected request
never reaches it, so no header. Therefore correlation goes first.

The admin check must not apply to every path — `/l03/challenge/reports` with a
valid key has to be a 200 — so it belongs inside a `UseWhen` whose predicate
matches `/l03/challenge/admin`.

That leaves the key check, which must apply everywhere, and must be inside
correlation.

## Hint 3

```csharp
pipeline.UseMiddleware<CorrelationIdMiddleware>();
pipeline.UseMiddleware</* the one that answers 401 */>();
pipeline.UseWhen(
    context => context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/l03/challenge/admin"),
    admin => admin.UseMiddleware</* the one that answers 403 */>());
```

Both of your middlewares follow ex3's shape exactly: compare a request header,
and on failure set `context.Response.StatusCode` and return
`Task.CompletedTask` without calling `next`. The 403 constant is
`StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden`.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — your first middleware

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex1.cs`. Implement `StampMiddleware.InvokeAsync`
so that `GET /l03/stamp`:

- comes back with the response header `X-Dojo-Stamp: l03`, and
- still has the body `handler`, written by the terminal that sits after you

Two lines. The second one is the one people forget: if you do not call `next`,
the request stops at your middleware and the body is empty.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two statements, and the order between them is the lesson. One of them puts a
header on the response; the other lets the rest of the pipeline run.

Ask yourself which one has to happen first, and what would be true of the
response if you did them the other way round.

## Hint 2

`context.Response.Headers["Name"] = "value"` sets a response header. It only
works while the response has not started — and the terminal handler starts it
by writing a body — so this line goes *before* you hand control on.

Handing control on means calling the `next` delegate with the context. The
method returns a `Task`; you can `return next(context);` without making the
method `async` at all.

## Hint 1

Two statements, and the order between them is the lesson. One of them puts a
header on the response; the other lets the rest of the pipeline run.

Ask yourself which one has to happen first, and what would be true of the
response if you did them the other way round.

`context.Response.Headers["Name"] = "value"` sets a response header. It only
works while the response has not started — and the terminal handler starts it
by writing a body — so this line goes *before* you hand control on.

Handing control on means calling the `next` delegate with the context. The
method returns a `Task`; you can `return next(context);` without making the
method `async` at all.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the order is the design

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex2.cs`, and only the `Configure` method. Three
marker middlewares are given; each one stamps the trace on the way in and again
on the way out. Add all three so that `GET /l03/order` returns exactly:

```
correlation>,timing>,auth>,handler,auth<,timing<,correlation<
```

The order is not arbitrary, and the reasoning is what to take away.
Correlation goes outermost so that *every* log line, including the timing
numbers and any authentication failure, can be tied to one request. Timing goes
next, so the time you report includes the cost of authenticating — otherwise
your dashboards will show a fast API while users wait. Auth goes last, closest
to the handler, because it is the final gate before your code runs.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — short-circuiting

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex3.cs`. Implement `ApiKeyMiddleware.InvokeAsync`
so that a request to `/l03/secure` only reaches the handler when the header
`X-Api-Key` is exactly `dojo-key`. Anything else — a missing header, a wrong
value — gets **401** and goes no further.

The middleware downstream of yours sets `X-Reached-Handler: yes`, and the gate
checks that the header is *absent* on your 401. That is the real test of a
short-circuit: it is not enough to set the status code, you have to stop the
request. `context.Response.StatusCode = 401;` followed by `await next(context)`
is the classic broken version — it sets a status the handler will then overwrite
while doing all the work you meant to prevent.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two paths through this method. One of them calls `next`; the other must not.

The constants you need are already on the class: `HeaderName` and `ValidKey`.
A request header is read with `context.Request.Headers[name]`, which gives you
a `StringValues` — `.FirstOrDefault()` turns it into a `string?` that is null
when the header is absent, which conveniently handles "missing" and "wrong" the
same way.

## Hint 2

On the rejection path you need to do exactly two things: set
`context.Response.StatusCode` to 401, and return *without* calling `next`.
`StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized` is the named constant.

Returning from a non-async method that promises a `Task` means returning
`Task.CompletedTask`.

Do not write a body. The gate checks that the 401 has an empty one.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    if (context.Request.Headers[HeaderName].FirstOrDefault() != ValidKey)
    {
        context.Response.StatusCode = /* … */;
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    return next(context);
}
```

If the gate says `X-Reached-Handler` was present on your 401, the `return` is
missing and control fell through to the `next` call underneath.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — `Use`, `UseWhen` and `Run`

Edit `src/Api/L03_Middleware/Ex4.cs`, method `Configure`. Build a pipeline,
mounted under `/l03/branch/`, that:

- adds `X-Branch-Seen: all` to **every** response under that prefix
- answers with the body `admin` for any path under `/l03/branch/admin`
- answers with the body `default` for everything else

Three pieces, one of each kind: a `Use` for the shared header, a `UseWhen`
whose predicate looks at `context.Request.Path`, and a `Run` for the fallback.
`HttpRequest.Path` has a `StartsWithSegments` method that compares whole path
segments — worth preferring over `StartsWith`, which would also match
`/l03/branch/administrators`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 03_middleware ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces, in this order: something that runs for everyone, something that
runs only for the admin paths, and something that catches whatever is left.

The last one is a terminal. The middle one is a branch. The first one is an
ordinary link in the chain — and it has to be first, or the branch will
terminate before it gets a turn.

## Hint 2

- `pipeline.Use(async (context, next) => { …; await next(context); })` for the
  shared header.
- `pipeline.UseWhen(predicate, branch => { … })` for the split. The predicate
  takes an `HttpContext` and returns a `bool`; use
  `context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/l03/branch/admin")`.
- `pipeline.Run(context => context.Response.WriteAsync("default"))` at the end.

Inside the branch you also want a terminal, because a branch that falls through
would carry on to the main pipeline's `Run` and answer `"default"`.

## Hint 3

```csharp
pipeline.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Response.Headers[/* … */] = /* … */;
    await next(context);
});

pipeline.UseWhen(
    context => context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments(/* … */),
    admin => admin.Run(context => context.Response.WriteAsync("admin")));

pipeline.Run(/* … */);
```

Note that the path in the predicate is the *full* request path — this pipeline
is mounted on a route, not with `Map`, so nothing has been stripped off the
front.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces, in this order: something that runs for everyone, something that
runs only for the admin paths, and something that catches whatever is left.

The last one is a terminal. The middle one is a branch. The first one is an
ordinary link in the chain — and it has to be first, or the branch will
terminate before it gets a turn.

## Hint 2

- `pipeline.Use(async (context, next) => { …; await next(context); })` for the
  shared header.
- `pipeline.UseWhen(predicate, branch => { … })` for the split. The predicate
  takes an `HttpContext` and returns a `bool`; use
  `context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/l03/branch/admin")`.
- `pipeline.Run(context => context.Response.WriteAsync("default"))` at the end.

Inside the branch you also want a terminal, because a branch that falls through
would carry on to the main pipeline's `Run` and answer `"default"`.

## Hint 3

```csharp
pipeline.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Response.Headers[/* … */] = /* … */;
    await next(context);
});

pipeline.UseWhen(
    context => context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments(/* … */),
    admin => admin.Run(context => context.Response.WriteAsync("admin")));

pipeline.Run(/* … */);
```

Note that the path in the predicate is the *full* request path — this pipeline
is mounted on a route, not with `Map`, so nothing has been stripped off the
front.

## Hint 1

Two things to decide. What does the recorder do — and there is only one moment
in a middleware at which the final status code is knowable. And where does it
sit relative to a middleware that sometimes refuses to call `next`.

## Hint 2

`context.Response.StatusCode` is only final after the rest of the pipeline has
finished, so the recorder awaits `next` first and records afterwards. That
makes it a genuinely `async` method.

`IStatusLog` is a singleton and arrives as a second parameter of `InvokeAsync`,
resolved per request — it must not be a constructor parameter.

```csharp
public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context, IStatusLog log)
{
    await next(context);
    log.Record(/* … */);
}
```

and in `Configure`, the two `UseMiddleware` lines swap places. If the gate says
the recorder never saw the 418, you left the teapot on the outside.

# 04 — Configuration and the options pattern

Look back at what you have hard-coded so far: `"dojo-key"` as an API key, a
page size that does not exist yet, a rate limit you have not written. Every one
of those is a value that will need to differ between your laptop, the staging
environment and production — and every one of them is currently a string
literal that only a redeploy can change.

Configuration is ASP.NET Core's answer, and it is a nicer answer than "read an
environment variable". The framework builds one `IConfiguration` out of a
*stack* of sources — JSON files, environment-specific JSON files, user secrets,
environment variables, command-line arguments — where later sources override
earlier ones by key. Your code asks for a value; it never asks where the value
came from. That is what lets the same binary run in three environments without
a single `if (production)` in it.

On top of that sits the **options pattern**: instead of reading loose strings
out of a dictionary all over your codebase, you bind a section once into a
class, and everything downstream injects the class.

## Concept — the stack, the section, the class

`WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args)` sets up these sources, in this order:

```
appsettings.json
appsettings.{Environment}.json      ← Development / Staging / Production
user secrets                        ← Development only, stored outside the repo
environment variables               ← e.g. Dojo__Catalog__PageSize=50
command-line arguments              ← --Dojo:Catalog:PageSize=50
```

**Later wins.** That single rule is the whole design: a value in
`appsettings.json` is a default, and anything further down the stack overrides
it for one environment, one machine, or one run. Note the double underscore in
the environment-variable form — many shells will not accept a colon in a
variable name, so `__` is the portable spelling of the `:` separator.

Configuration itself is flat. Even though `appsettings.json` looks like a tree,
what the providers produce is a dictionary of colon-separated paths:

```
Dojo:Catalog:Title      = "Dojo Catalog"
Dojo:Catalog:PageSize   = "25"
Dojo:Catalog:Currency   = "EUR"
```

Every value is a **string** — `PageSize` is `"25"`, not `25` — because an
environment variable cannot be an integer. Conversion happens when you bind.

You can read a value directly:

```csharp
string? title = configuration["Dojo:Catalog:Title"];
```

…and for one-off reads at startup that is fine. For anything a service depends
on, bind a section to a class instead:

```csharp
public class ExampleOptions
{
    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
    public int PageSize { get; set; } = 20;      // ← a default
}

// in IServiceRegistrar.Register:
services.Configure<ExampleOptions>(configuration.GetSection("Dojo:Example"));

// anywhere else:
private static IResult Handler(IOptions<ExampleOptions> options) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(options.Value.PageSize);
```

Binding is by **property name matching the key**, and it only writes properties
it finds keys for. Everything else keeps whatever the class's initialiser gave
it — which is how "sensible default, overridable in configuration" works, and
why your options classes should have real defaults rather than relying on
`0` and `null`.

Three interfaces deliver options, and the difference is a favourite interview
question:

| interface | lifetime | reads configuration |
|---|---|---|
| `IOptions<T>` | singleton | once, on first use — never again |
| `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` | scoped | once per request |
| `IOptionsMonitor<T>` | singleton | live, with a change callback, and `Get(name)` for named options |

`IOptions<T>` is the right default. Reach for `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` when a
value should be able to change without a restart, and `IOptionsMonitor<T>` when
a singleton needs the current value, or when you have several *named*
configurations of one class — the challenge.

## Exercise 1 — bind a section

Open `src/Api/appsettings.json` and read the `Dojo` section; every expected
value in this lesson comes from there.

Edit `src/Api/L04_ConfigurationOptions/Ex1.cs`. Register `CatalogOptions`
against the `Dojo:Catalog` section, and implement `GetCatalogOptions` so that
`GET /l04/catalog-options` answers **200** with the bound values:

```json
{"title":"Dojo Catalog","pageSize":25,"currency":"EUR"}
```

The class is already written. Notice that `PageSize` is an `int` while the
configuration value is the string `"25"` — the binder does that conversion, and
it will throw a clear exception at startup if it cannot.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 04_configuration_options ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — defaults, and what a partial section leaves alone

Edit `src/Api/L04_ConfigurationOptions/Ex2.cs`. The `Dojo:Reports` section
contains exactly one key, `MaxRows`. Give `ReportOptions` these defaults —
`MaxRows = 100`, `Format = "csv"`, `IncludeHeaders = true` — bind the class to
the section, and implement `GetReportOptions`.

The result should be `maxRows` **500** (configuration wins), `format` **"csv"**
and `includeHeaders` **true** (your defaults survive, because configuration says
nothing about them).

This is the property that makes the options pattern pleasant to live with: your
class is the complete specification of what a feature needs, configuration only
carries the deltas, and a deployment file that says nothing is a deployment
file that gets your defaults.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 04_configuration_options ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — which environment am I?

Edit `src/Api/L04_ConfigurationOptions/Ex3.cs`. Implement `GetEnvironment` so
that `GET /l04/environment` answers **200** with:

- `name` — the current environment's name
- `isDevelopment` — whether that environment is Development, asked via
  `IHostEnvironment`'s own method rather than by comparing strings yourself
- `catalogTitle` — `Dojo:Catalog:Title`, read straight from `IConfiguration`
  with its colon-separated key

The gate boots the app twice: once normally, where the environment is
`Development`, and once with the environment forced to `Staging`. Anything
hard-coded will pass the first and fail the second.

`IHostEnvironment` is how a well-behaved app decides to show a detailed error
page, seed test data, or refuse to start with a development connection string.
The environment name is not magic: it is just the `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`
variable, and `Development`, `Staging` and `Production` are conventions with
helper methods, not a closed set.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 04_configuration_options ex3
```

## Challenge — named options

Honest difficulty note: the loop in `Register` is three lines; knowing that
`IOptionsMonitor.Get(name)` never fails is the part that catches people.

Edit `src/Api/L04_ConfigurationOptions/Challenge.cs`. `Dojo:Feeds` holds two
child sections, `primary` and `fallback`, each with the shape of `FeedOptions`.
Register one **named** options instance per child — without hard-coding the
names — and implement `GET /l04/feeds/{name}` to answer **200** with that
feed's settings, or **404** when no such feed is configured.

`services.Configure<FeedOptions>(name, section)` registers a named instance;
`monitor.Get(name)` retrieves one. The trap is that `Get` on an unknown name
does not throw and does not return null — it hands back a `FeedOptions` full of
your defaults, which would make `/l04/feeds/nope` a cheerful 200 describing a
feed that does not exist. So ask configuration whether the section is there
before you answer.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 04_configuration_options challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this lesson; the scheduler brings it back
later. Edit `src/Api/L04_ConfigurationOptions/Review1.cs`: give `MailerOptions`
the defaults `DisplayName = "Dojo"` and `RetryCount = 3`, bind it to
`Dojo:Mailer` (which sets only `FromAddress`), and implement `GetMailer`. Note
the parameter type — `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` rather than `IOptions<T>` — and be
able to say what that changes.
