# Reading - dotnet/04_configuration_options

Configuration looks like the least interesting subject in ASP.NET Core and is
one of the highest-leverage. Almost every "it works on my machine" incident,
every leaked secret and every deploy that needed a code change to flip a flag
traces back to a decision made here.

## Notes

**One `IConfiguration`, many providers.** `ConfigurationBuilder` holds an
ordered list of `IConfigurationProvider`s, each of which contributes a flat
`IDictionary<string, string>`. Reading a key walks the providers *backwards*
and returns the first hit, which is what "later wins" means mechanically. The
defaults `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` installs are, in order: `appsettings.json`,
`appsettings.{Environment}.json`, user secrets (Development only), environment
variables, command-line arguments. Adding your own — an INI file, a key vault,
a database — is one `builder.Configuration.Add…` call, and nothing downstream
notices.

**Everything is a string, and the hierarchy is fake.** `configuration["a:b:c"]`
is a dictionary lookup on the literal key `"a:b:c"`. `GetSection("a:b")` does
not return a subtree object; it returns a view that prefixes keys. This is why
JSON, INI, environment variables and command-line arguments can all feed the
same system despite having wildly different notions of structure, and why an
array in JSON becomes the keys `Items:0`, `Items:1`, `Items:2`.

**Environment variables use `__`.** `Dojo__Catalog__PageSize=50` sets
`Dojo:Catalog:PageSize`, because colons are illegal in environment-variable
names on some platforms. Every container orchestrator's documentation assumes
you know this.

**Secrets do not go in `appsettings.json`.** That file is committed. Locally,
use `dotnet user-secrets`, which stores JSON in your user profile outside the
repository and is loaded automatically in Development. In production, use
environment variables injected by the platform, or a real secret store (Azure
Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) added as a configuration provider — the code
that reads them does not change, which is the whole point of the provider
abstraction.

**Validation belongs at startup, not at first use.** `AddOptions<T>().Bind(…)
.ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()` makes a misconfigured application
fail to start rather than fail on the request that first touches the setting.
"Fail fast, at deploy time, with a message naming the key" is worth a great
deal at three in the morning. (This lesson does not gate it, because a
deliberately broken configuration would stop the whole course app from booting —
but it is the first thing to add in real code.)

**`IOptions` versus `IOptionsSnapshot` versus `IOptionsMonitor`.**
`IOptions<T>` is a singleton computed once; a configuration file edited while
the app runs will not reach it. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is scoped and recomputed
per request, so file changes appear on the next request — at the cost of
rebinding on every request, and it cannot be injected into a singleton.
`IOptionsMonitor<T>` is a singleton that tracks changes and exposes
`OnChange`, plus `Get(name)` for named options. Knowing which one to use, and
why `IOptionsSnapshot` in a singleton is a compile-time-legal runtime mistake,
is a standard interview exchange.

## ex1 - binding is name matching, and nothing else

`services.Configure<CatalogOptions>(configuration.GetSection("Dojo:Catalog"))`
registers three things at once: an `IOptions<CatalogOptions>` you can inject, a
`IConfigureOptions<CatalogOptions>` that does the binding lazily on first
access, and a change token so `IOptionsMonitor` can react. Nothing binds at
registration time — which is why a wrong section path is not an error, just an
object full of defaults.

The binder matches **public settable properties** to keys, case-insensitively.
That is the entire algorithm, and its failure modes follow from it: a `readonly`
field is skipped, a property whose name does not match the key is skipped, a
constructor-only record property cannot be written (records *can* be bound if
they have settable properties or a matching constructor, but a positional
record with `init` accessors is a common source of surprise). When a value is
present but unconvertible — `"twenty-five"` for an `int` — the binder throws,
with the key in the message.

The reason to bind at all, rather than read `configuration["Dojo:Catalog:PageSize"]`
where you need it: the class is a *contract*. It can be validated, it can be
injected into a constructor so the dependency is visible, it can be
substituted in a test with `Options.Create(new CatalogOptions { … })`, and it
does not spread magic strings across twenty files.

## ex2 - defaults in code, deltas in configuration

The behaviour you measured — configured `MaxRows` wins, unconfigured `Format`
keeps `"csv"` — falls out of "the binder only writes properties it finds keys
for". It has a big consequence for how you should write options classes: **put
the sensible value in the class**, not in `appsettings.json`. Then a deployment
that says nothing gets a working system, and every line in a real environment's
configuration file is a deliberate deviation you can review.

The opposite habit — defaults in `appsettings.json`, empty class — looks
equivalent and is not. The defaults are now invisible to anyone reading the
class; every environment file has to repeat every key; and forgetting one gives
you `0`, `false` or `null` in production rather than the value everyone
assumed.

`IncludeHeaders` is the pointed case. Its type default is `false`, which is a
perfectly plausible-looking answer, so a missing default here would produce a
report with no header row and no error anywhere. Booleans are where "I forgot
to set a default" hides best.

## ex3 - environments, and what they are actually for

`IHostEnvironment.EnvironmentName` is a string read from `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`,
defaulting to `Production` when unset — which is a deliberately safe default,
because the dangerous behaviours are the development ones. `IsDevelopment()`,
`IsStaging()` and `IsProduction()` are convenience methods over an ordinal
comparison, and `IsEnvironment("QA")` handles your own names.

Two things the environment actually decides in a real app. It selects
`appsettings.{Environment}.json`, which is how one binary gets three
configurations. And it gates behaviour that must never reach users: the
developer exception page (which is why an unhandled exception in this course
returns the exception text rather than a bare 500), scope validation in the DI
container, detailed database errors, and Swagger UI.

The habit to avoid is scattering `if (env.IsDevelopment())` through your
business logic. Environment checks belong in `Program.cs`, where they choose
*which components to wire up*; below that, code should depend on configuration
and on services, not on which environment it happens to be in. A handler that
behaves differently in Development is a handler that is not tested in
Production.

## challenge - named options, and the trap in `Get`

Named options exist because one options *class* often has several
*configurations*: two feeds, three payment providers, four HTTP clients with
different timeouts. `services.Configure<FeedOptions>("primary", section)` binds
one; `monitor.Get("primary")` retrieves it. `IOptions<T>.Value` and
`monitor.CurrentValue` are shorthand for the unnamed instance, whose name is
`Options.DefaultName` — the empty string.

The trap is that `Get` is total: every string is a valid name, and an unknown
one returns a freshly constructed `FeedOptions` with your defaults rather than
throwing. That is the right design for the options system — a name with no
configuration is legitimately "all defaults" — and completely wrong for an API
endpoint, where a client asking about a feed that does not exist deserves a
404. Hence asking `configuration.GetSection(...).Exists()` first.

Enumerating `GetSection("Dojo:Feeds").GetChildren()` instead of hard-coding the
two names is the other half. It means adding a third feed is a configuration
change and not a deployment, which is precisely the promise configuration is
supposed to make.

## review1 - the same idea, and a different delivery interface

Binding `Dojo:Mailer` is ex1 and ex2 again, deliberately. What is new is the
parameter type: `IOptionsSnapshot<MailerOptions>` rather than
`IOptions<MailerOptions>`.

`IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is registered as **scoped**, so it is recomputed once per
request and every service inside that request sees the same value even if a
configuration file changes mid-request. That consistency is the real feature;
the "picks up changes without a restart" part is the advertised one. The price
is a rebind per request, and the constraint that it cannot be injected into a
singleton — try it and you get the captive-dependency error from lesson 02, at
startup, in Development.

For a value you would never change without a deployment — this one, honestly —
`IOptions<T>` is the better choice. Knowing why you would ever pick differently
is the point of the exercise.

## Further reading

- [Configuration in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/) — the provider stack, precedence and the environment-variable spelling.
- [The options pattern in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options) — binding, named options, `IOptionsSnapshot` and `IOptionsMonitor`.
- [Options pattern validation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/options#options-validation) — `ValidateDataAnnotations`, custom validators and `ValidateOnStart`.
- [Use multiple environments in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/environments) — `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`, per-environment files and what changes in Development.
- [Safe storage of app secrets in development](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/app-secrets) — `dotnet user-secrets`, and why the connection string does not belong in `appsettings.json`.

```csharp
using System.Net;
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting;

namespace DotnetDojo.Gates;

public class L04_ConfigurationOptionsTests(DojoWebFactory factory) : IClassFixture<DojoWebFactory>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex1_CatalogOptionsComeFromAppsettings()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/l04/catalog-options");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, response,
            "GET /l04/catalog-options must answer 200 - reread README ex1.");

        var body = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<CatalogDto>();
        Teach.Equal("Dojo Catalog", body?.Title,
            "Title comes from Dojo:Catalog:Title in appsettings.json. An empty string means "
                + "nothing was bound - check the section path you passed to GetSection.");
        Teach.Equal(25, body?.PageSize,
            "PageSize is 25 in appsettings.json, and it is written there as a number, which "
                + "the binder converts to an int for you.");
        Teach.Equal("EUR", body?.Currency,
            "Currency is EUR. If Title bound and this did not, the property name does not "
                + "match the key.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex2_APartialSectionLeavesTheDefaultsAlone()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/l04/report-options");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, response,
            "GET /l04/report-options must answer 200 - reread README ex2.");

        var body = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<ReportDto>();
        Teach.Equal(500, body?.MaxRows,
            "Dojo:Reports sets MaxRows to 500, so the configured value must win over your "
                + "default of 100.");
        Teach.Equal("csv", body?.Format,
            "Dojo:Reports says nothing about Format, so your default has to survive. The "
                + "binder only writes properties it finds keys for; it does not blank the "
                + "rest.");
        Teach.Equal(true, body?.IncludeHeaders,
            "IncludeHeaders is not in configuration either, and its default is true. A false "
                + "here means you left it as the type's default rather than setting one.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex3_TheAppKnowsWhichEnvironmentItIsRunningIn()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/l04/environment");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, response,
            "GET /l04/environment must answer 200 - reread README ex3.");

        var body = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<EnvironmentDto>();
        Teach.Equal("Development", body?.Name,
            "The gate boots the app in the Development environment, so IHostEnvironment "
                + "reports \"Development\".");
        Teach.Equal(true, body?.IsDevelopment,
            "IHostEnvironment has a method that answers this question - do not compare the "
                + "name to a string literal yourself.");
        Teach.Equal("Dojo Catalog", body?.CatalogTitle,
            "Read Dojo:Catalog:Title straight out of IConfiguration with the colon-separated "
                + "key. Configuration is a flat dictionary of paths, not a tree of objects.");

        using var staging = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder => builder.UseEnvironment("Staging"));
        using var stagingClient = staging.CreateClient();

        var stagingBody = await stagingClient.GetFromJsonAsync<EnvironmentDto>("/l04/environment");
        Teach.Equal("Staging", stagingBody?.Name,
            "The same code, booted with a different environment name, must report that name. "
                + "A hard-coded \"Development\" passes the first check and fails here.");
        Teach.Equal(false, stagingBody?.IsDevelopment,
            "Staging is not Development, so IsDevelopment() is false.");
    }
```

In plain English: ex1 and ex2 read values that live in `appsettings.json`, so
they prove binding actually happened rather than that you typed the right
constants. ex3 boots the application a second time with
`WithWebHostBuilder(… UseEnvironment("Staging") …)` — a whole second host, in
memory, in the same test — which is how you assert that behaviour really does
follow the environment. The challenge checks that two names give two different
answers, and that an unconfigured name is a 404 rather than a bag of defaults.

## The teaching point

The rule to carry out of this lesson: **anything that differs between
environments is configuration, and anything that is configuration gets a
default in code.** Connection strings, external URLs, timeouts, feature flags,
page sizes, retry counts. Not secrets in `appsettings.json`, though — that file
is in source control, and the answer for a real secret is user secrets locally
and environment variables or a key vault in production.

The options pattern's quieter benefit is that it turns "what does this feature
need?" into a class you can read. A new colleague can open `CatalogOptions` and
see the complete list of knobs, with their defaults, in one place — which is a
much better answer than grepping for `configuration[`.

Next: **05_efcore_basics**, where the data stops being a static list and starts
being a database, and everything you know about SQL becomes relevant again.

# Reading - dotnet/04_configuration_options

Configuration looks like the least interesting subject in ASP.NET Core and is
one of the highest-leverage. Almost every "it works on my machine" incident,
every leaked secret and every deploy that needed a code change to flip a flag
traces back to a decision made here.

## Notes

**One `IConfiguration`, many providers.** `ConfigurationBuilder` holds an
ordered list of `IConfigurationProvider`s, each of which contributes a flat
`IDictionary<string, string>`. Reading a key walks the providers *backwards*
and returns the first hit, which is what "later wins" means mechanically. The
defaults `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` installs are, in order: `appsettings.json`,
`appsettings.{Environment}.json`, user secrets (Development only), environment
variables, command-line arguments. Adding your own — an INI file, a key vault,
a database — is one `builder.Configuration.Add…` call, and nothing downstream
notices.

**Everything is a string, and the hierarchy is fake.** `configuration["a:b:c"]`
is a dictionary lookup on the literal key `"a:b:c"`. `GetSection("a:b")` does
not return a subtree object; it returns a view that prefixes keys. This is why
JSON, INI, environment variables and command-line arguments can all feed the
same system despite having wildly different notions of structure, and why an
array in JSON becomes the keys `Items:0`, `Items:1`, `Items:2`.

**Environment variables use `__`.** `Dojo__Catalog__PageSize=50` sets
`Dojo:Catalog:PageSize`, because colons are illegal in environment-variable
names on some platforms. Every container orchestrator's documentation assumes
you know this.

**Secrets do not go in `appsettings.json`.** That file is committed. Locally,
use `dotnet user-secrets`, which stores JSON in your user profile outside the
repository and is loaded automatically in Development. In production, use
environment variables injected by the platform, or a real secret store (Azure
Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) added as a configuration provider — the code
that reads them does not change, which is the whole point of the provider
abstraction.

**Validation belongs at startup, not at first use.** `AddOptions<T>().Bind(…)
.ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()` makes a misconfigured application
fail to start rather than fail on the request that first touches the setting.
"Fail fast, at deploy time, with a message naming the key" is worth a great
deal at three in the morning. (This lesson does not gate it, because a
deliberately broken configuration would stop the whole course app from booting —
but it is the first thing to add in real code.)

**`IOptions` versus `IOptionsSnapshot` versus `IOptionsMonitor`.**
`IOptions<T>` is a singleton computed once; a configuration file edited while
the app runs will not reach it. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is scoped and recomputed
per request, so file changes appear on the next request — at the cost of
rebinding on every request, and it cannot be injected into a singleton.
`IOptionsMonitor<T>` is a singleton that tracks changes and exposes
`OnChange`, plus `Get(name)` for named options. Knowing which one to use, and
why `IOptionsSnapshot` in a singleton is a compile-time-legal runtime mistake,
is a standard interview exchange.

## ex1 - binding is name matching, and nothing else

`services.Configure<CatalogOptions>(configuration.GetSection("Dojo:Catalog"))`
registers three things at once: an `IOptions<CatalogOptions>` you can inject, a
`IConfigureOptions<CatalogOptions>` that does the binding lazily on first
access, and a change token so `IOptionsMonitor` can react. Nothing binds at
registration time — which is why a wrong section path is not an error, just an
object full of defaults.

The binder matches **public settable properties** to keys, case-insensitively.
That is the entire algorithm, and its failure modes follow from it: a `readonly`
field is skipped, a property whose name does not match the key is skipped, a
constructor-only record property cannot be written (records *can* be bound if
they have settable properties or a matching constructor, but a positional
record with `init` accessors is a common source of surprise). When a value is
present but unconvertible — `"twenty-five"` for an `int` — the binder throws,
with the key in the message.

The reason to bind at all, rather than read `configuration["Dojo:Catalog:PageSize"]`
where you need it: the class is a *contract*. It can be validated, it can be
injected into a constructor so the dependency is visible, it can be
substituted in a test with `Options.Create(new CatalogOptions { … })`, and it
does not spread magic strings across twenty files.

## ex2 - defaults in code, deltas in configuration

The behaviour you measured — configured `MaxRows` wins, unconfigured `Format`
keeps `"csv"` — falls out of "the binder only writes properties it finds keys
for". It has a big consequence for how you should write options classes: **put
the sensible value in the class**, not in `appsettings.json`. Then a deployment
that says nothing gets a working system, and every line in a real environment's
configuration file is a deliberate deviation you can review.

The opposite habit — defaults in `appsettings.json`, empty class — looks
equivalent and is not. The defaults are now invisible to anyone reading the
class; every environment file has to repeat every key; and forgetting one gives
you `0`, `false` or `null` in production rather than the value everyone
assumed.

`IncludeHeaders` is the pointed case. Its type default is `false`, which is a
perfectly plausible-looking answer, so a missing default here would produce a
report with no header row and no error anywhere. Booleans are where "I forgot
to set a default" hides best.

## ex3 - environments, and what they are actually for

`IHostEnvironment.EnvironmentName` is a string read from `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`,
defaulting to `Production` when unset — which is a deliberately safe default,
because the dangerous behaviours are the development ones. `IsDevelopment()`,
`IsStaging()` and `IsProduction()` are convenience methods over an ordinal
comparison, and `IsEnvironment("QA")` handles your own names.

Two things the environment actually decides in a real app. It selects
`appsettings.{Environment}.json`, which is how one binary gets three
configurations. And it gates behaviour that must never reach users: the
developer exception page (which is why an unhandled exception in this course
returns the exception text rather than a bare 500), scope validation in the DI
container, detailed database errors, and Swagger UI.

The habit to avoid is scattering `if (env.IsDevelopment())` through your
business logic. Environment checks belong in `Program.cs`, where they choose
*which components to wire up*; below that, code should depend on configuration
and on services, not on which environment it happens to be in. A handler that
behaves differently in Development is a handler that is not tested in
Production.

## challenge - named options, and the trap in `Get`

Named options exist because one options *class* often has several
*configurations*: two feeds, three payment providers, four HTTP clients with
different timeouts. `services.Configure<FeedOptions>("primary", section)` binds
one; `monitor.Get("primary")` retrieves it. `IOptions<T>.Value` and
`monitor.CurrentValue` are shorthand for the unnamed instance, whose name is
`Options.DefaultName` — the empty string.

The trap is that `Get` is total: every string is a valid name, and an unknown
one returns a freshly constructed `FeedOptions` with your defaults rather than
throwing. That is the right design for the options system — a name with no
configuration is legitimately "all defaults" — and completely wrong for an API
endpoint, where a client asking about a feed that does not exist deserves a
404. Hence asking `configuration.GetSection(...).Exists()` first.

Enumerating `GetSection("Dojo:Feeds").GetChildren()` instead of hard-coding the
two names is the other half. It means adding a third feed is a configuration
change and not a deployment, which is precisely the promise configuration is
supposed to make.

## review1 - the same idea, and a different delivery interface

Binding `Dojo:Mailer` is ex1 and ex2 again, deliberately. What is new is the
parameter type: `IOptionsSnapshot<MailerOptions>` rather than
`IOptions<MailerOptions>`.

`IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is registered as **scoped**, so it is recomputed once per
request and every service inside that request sees the same value even if a
configuration file changes mid-request. That consistency is the real feature;
the "picks up changes without a restart" part is the advertised one. The price
is a rebind per request, and the constraint that it cannot be injected into a
singleton — try it and you get the captive-dependency error from lesson 02, at
startup, in Development.

For a value you would never change without a deployment — this one, honestly —
`IOptions<T>` is the better choice. Knowing why you would ever pick differently
is the point of the exercise.

## Further reading

- [Configuration in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/) — the provider stack, precedence and the environment-variable spelling.
- [The options pattern in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options) — binding, named options, `IOptionsSnapshot` and `IOptionsMonitor`.
- [Options pattern validation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/options#options-validation) — `ValidateDataAnnotations`, custom validators and `ValidateOnStart`.
- [Use multiple environments in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/environments) — `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`, per-environment files and what changes in Development.
- [Safe storage of app secrets in development](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/app-secrets) — `dotnet user-secrets`, and why the connection string does not belong in `appsettings.json`.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — named options

Honest difficulty note: the loop in `Register` is three lines; knowing that
`IOptionsMonitor.Get(name)` never fails is the part that catches people.

Edit `src/Api/L04_ConfigurationOptions/Challenge.cs`. `Dojo:Feeds` holds two
child sections, `primary` and `fallback`, each with the shape of `FeedOptions`.
Register one **named** options instance per child — without hard-coding the
names — and implement `GET /l04/feeds/{name}` to answer **200** with that
feed's settings, or **404** when no such feed is configured.

`services.Configure<FeedOptions>(name, section)` registers a named instance;
`monitor.Get(name)` retrieves one. The trap is that `Get` on an unknown name
does not throw and does not return null — it hands back a `FeedOptions` full of
your defaults, which would make `/l04/feeds/nope` a cheerful 200 describing a
feed that does not exist. So ask configuration whether the section is there
before you answer.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 04_configuration_options challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves. In `Register`, you need one options registration per child section
of `Dojo:Feeds` — and you are not allowed to type the names, because the point
is that adding a third feed should be a configuration change.

In the handler, you need to turn a name into options, and to notice when the
name is not one you have.

## Hint 2

`configuration.GetSection(ChallengeServices.Section).GetChildren()` gives you an
`IConfigurationSection` per feed. Each one has a `Key` (`"primary"`) and *is*
itself a configuration section you can bind — so a `foreach` with
`services.Configure<FeedOptions>(child.Key, child)` inside is the whole
registration.

In the handler, `feeds.Get(name)` returns the named instance. It never throws
and never returns null, so it cannot tell you whether the feed exists — ask
configuration that question instead. `IConfigurationSection` has an `Exists()`
extension method.

## Hint 3

```csharp
foreach (var feed in configuration.GetSection(Section).GetChildren())
{
    services.Configure<FeedOptions>(feed.Key, feed);
}
```

and in the handler, build the section path with interpolation
(`$"{ChallengeServices.Section}:{name}"`), return `TypedResults.NotFound()`
when it does not exist, and otherwise read `feeds.Get(name)` into a
`FeedResponse`. Note that `name` goes into the response too — the gate does not
check it, but a client that asked for one feed and got another's URL would
never know.

## Hint 1

Two halves. In `Register`, you need one options registration per child section
of `Dojo:Feeds` — and you are not allowed to type the names, because the point
is that adding a third feed should be a configuration change.

In the handler, you need to turn a name into options, and to notice when the
name is not one you have.

## Hint 2

`configuration.GetSection(ChallengeServices.Section).GetChildren()` gives you an
`IConfigurationSection` per feed. Each one has a `Key` (`"primary"`) and *is*
itself a configuration section you can bind — so a `foreach` with
`services.Configure<FeedOptions>(child.Key, child)` inside is the whole
registration.

In the handler, `feeds.Get(name)` returns the named instance. It never throws
and never returns null, so it cannot tell you whether the feed exists — ask
configuration that question instead. `IConfigurationSection` has an `Exists()`
extension method.

## Hint 3

```csharp
foreach (var feed in configuration.GetSection(Section).GetChildren())
{
    services.Configure<FeedOptions>(feed.Key, feed);
}
```

and in the handler, build the section path with interpolation
(`$"{ChallengeServices.Section}:{name}"`), return `TypedResults.NotFound()`
when it does not exist, and otherwise read `feeds.Get(name)` into a
`FeedResponse`. Note that `name` goes into the response too — the gate does not
check it, but a client that asked for one feed and got another's URL would
never know.

## Exercise 2 — defaults, and what a partial section leaves alone

Edit `src/Api/L04_ConfigurationOptions/Ex2.cs`. The `Dojo:Reports` section
contains exactly one key, `MaxRows`. Give `ReportOptions` these defaults —
`MaxRows = 100`, `Format = "csv"`, `IncludeHeaders = true` — bind the class to
the section, and implement `GetReportOptions`.

The result should be `maxRows` **500** (configuration wins), `format` **"csv"**
and `includeHeaders` **true** (your defaults survive, because configuration says
nothing about them).

This is the property that makes the options pattern pleasant to live with: your
class is the complete specification of what a feature needs, configuration only
carries the deltas, and a deployment file that says nothing is a deployment
file that gets your defaults.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 04_configuration_options ex2
```

binding and the handler are exactly ex1 with different names.

## Hint 2

A default is just a property initialiser: `public string Format { get; set; } = "csv";`.
The binder overwrites a property only when it finds a matching key, so anything
configuration does not mention keeps whatever the initialiser set.

`MaxRows` needs one too, even though configuration overrides it — that default
is what the application would use if someone deleted the section.


looks like a deliberate choice and is not. Then bind with

and return `options.Value`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three jobs: give two properties defaults, bind the class, return it. The
binding and the handler are exactly ex1 with different names.

The defaults are the interesting part. Look at `Dojo:Reports` in
`appsettings.json` and notice how few keys are in it, then look at the values
the gate expects.

## Hint 2

A default is just a property initialiser: `public string Format { get; set; } = "csv";`.
The binder overwrites a property only when it finds a matching key, so anything
configuration does not mention keeps whatever the initialiser set.

`MaxRows` needs one too, even though configuration overrides it — that default
is what the application would use if someone deleted the section.

## Hint 3

```csharp
public int MaxRows { get; set; } = 100;
public string Format { get; set; } = "csv";
public bool IncludeHeaders { get; set; } = true;
```

The `IncludeHeaders` one is the trap: leave it alone and it is `false`, which
looks like a deliberate choice and is not. Then bind with
`services.Configure<ReportOptions>(configuration.GetSection("Dojo:Reports"))`
and return `options.Value`.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — which environment am I?

Edit `src/Api/L04_ConfigurationOptions/Ex3.cs`. Implement `GetEnvironment` so
that `GET /l04/environment` answers **200** with:

- `name` — the current environment's name
- `isDevelopment` — whether that environment is Development, asked via
  `IHostEnvironment`'s own method rather than by comparing strings yourself
- `catalogTitle` — `Dojo:Catalog:Title`, read straight from `IConfiguration`
  with its colon-separated key

The gate boots the app twice: once normally, where the environment is
`Development`, and once with the environment forced to `Staging`. Anything
hard-coded will pass the first and fail the second.

`IHostEnvironment` is how a well-behaved app decides to show a detailed error
page, seed test data, or refuse to start with a development connection string.
The environment name is not magic: it is just the `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT`
variable, and `Development`, `Staging` and `Production` are conventions with
helper methods, not a closed set.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 04_configuration_options ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Nothing to register here — both `IHostEnvironment` and `IConfiguration` are
already in the container, put there by the host itself. The whole exercise is
one `TypedResults.Ok(...)` with three values in it.

Two of them come from the environment object and one from configuration.

## Hint 2

`IHostEnvironment` has an `EnvironmentName` property and a set of extension
methods — `IsDevelopment()`, `IsStaging()`, `IsProduction()` — that do the
comparison for you. Use the method; the gate boots a second host in Staging,
and a string comparison you wrote by hand is where a typo hides.

For the title, `configuration["Dojo:Catalog:Title"]` is a plain indexer lookup
and returns `string?`, so you need a fallback for the null.

## Hint 3

```csharp
private static IResult GetEnvironment(IHostEnvironment environment, IConfiguration configuration) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(new EnvironmentResponse(
        environment.EnvironmentName,
        environment./* … */(),
        configuration[/* … */] ?? ""));
```

The record `EnvironmentResponse` is already declared with the three properties
in the order the gate reads them.

lessons.briefing:
# 05 — EF Core basics

Your data has been a static list for five lessons. That was on purpose — it let
routing, DI, middleware and configuration be about themselves. It ends here.
From this lesson on the products live in a real relational database, real SQL
gets generated and executed, and the questions change: not "which element of the
list", but "what query did that turn into, how many round trips did it take, and
did anything actually get written".

If you did the SQL track, you already know the hard half of this. Entity
Framework Core is an **object-relational mapper**: you write LINQ against C#
objects, it translates that into SQL, sends it, and turns the rows back into
objects. Everything you learned about `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `JOIN` and indexes is
still true and still your responsibility — the ORM changes who *types* the SQL,
not who is accountable for it.

The database in this lesson is SQLite, held entirely in memory, created fresh
for every single test. That is why an exercise can insert and delete rows
without leaking into the next one.

## Concept — the entity, the context, the query

Three declarations, all in `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Model.cs`, which is given
code you should read now.

**The entity** is a plain class. No base class, no attributes, no interface:

```csharp
public class Product
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public int PriceCents { get; set; }
    public string Category { get; set; } = "";
}
```

EF infers the table name from the `DbSet` property, the column names from the
property names, and — by convention — that a property called `Id` is the
primary key and is generated by the database. Money is an `int` of cents rather
than a `decimal` or a `double` because floating-point money is a bug waiting for
a rounding error.

**The context** is the unit of work:

```csharp
public class CatalogDb(DbContextOptions<CatalogDb> options) : DbContext(options)
{
    public DbSet<Product> Products => Set<Product>();
}
```

A `DbContext` holds an open-ish connection, a change tracker, and one `DbSet`
per table. It is registered with `AddDbContext<CatalogDb>(...)`, which makes it
**scoped** — one instance per HTTP request. That is not a detail: everything a
request loads goes into that one change tracker, and `SaveChangesAsync` writes
all of it in a single transaction. A `DbContext` is emphatically not
thread-safe, and lesson 02's rule about not capturing shorter-lived services
exists largely because of it.

**The query** is LINQ, executed asynchronously:

```csharp
var cheap = await db.Products
    .Where(p => p.PriceCents < 5000)
    .OrderBy(p => p.Name)
    .Select(p => new ProductSummary(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceCents))
    .ToListAsync();
```

Nothing happens until `ToListAsync()`. Up to that point you are building an
expression tree; the `await` is the moment EF turns it into
`SELECT "p"."Id", "p"."Name", "p"."PriceCents" FROM "Products" AS "p" WHERE …
ORDER BY "p"."Name"` and runs it. This is **deferred execution**, and its most
important consequence is the one in the example: because the `Select` is part of
the expression tree, only three columns are ever fetched. Move the `Select`
after a `.ToList()` and you have loaded every column of every row into memory
first, then thrown most of it away.

Every terminal operator has an async twin — `ToListAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync`,
`SingleAsync`, `CountAsync`, `AnyAsync`, `SaveChangesAsync` — and you should use
them, always. A blocking call to a database inside a request handler holds a
thread pool thread hostage for the whole round trip.

### Writing, and the change tracker

```csharp
db.Products.Add(product);          // nothing has happened yet
await db.SaveChangesAsync();       // INSERT, inside a transaction
```

`SaveChangesAsync` returns the **number of rows written**, which ex4 uses as
evidence. Between loading an entity and saving, EF keeps a snapshot of what it
looked like; on save it compares, generates an `UPDATE` for the differences, and
writes nothing at all if there are none. You never call an `Update` method for
an entity you loaded — assigning to the property is the whole edit.

That only works if the entity is being **tracked**. `AsNoTracking()` tells EF
not to keep the snapshot, which makes read-only queries faster and lighter — and
makes any change you then make to the object invisible to `SaveChangesAsync`.
Silently. That is ex4.

### A word about migrations

In a real project you do not create tables by hand. You change your entity
classes, run `dotnet ef migrations add AddCategory`, and EF generates a C# class
describing the schema delta, which `dotnet ef database update` applies. The
migrations are checked in, run in order, and are the reason a new developer's
database and production's database have the same shape.

This course uses `EnsureCreated()` instead — it builds the schema from the model
in one step, with no history — because a course with a migrations folder would
spend its time on tooling rather than on queries. Know the difference, and know
that `EnsureCreated` is for tests and demos only: it cannot evolve a database
that already exists.

## Exercise 1 — a query and a projection

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Ex1.cs`. Implement `ListProducts` so that
`GET /l05/products` answers **200** with every product as a `ProductSummary`,
ordered by name ascending:

```json
[{"id":2,"name":"Bokken","priceCents":5900}, … ]
```

Two things the gate checks. The order — the seeded rows are deliberately not in
name order, and a database makes no promise about the order of an unsorted
`SELECT`. And the shape: `category` must not appear in the response, which means
the `Select` has to be part of the query, not a `.Select(...)` after a
`.ToList()`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — one row, or an honest 404

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Ex2.cs`. Implement `GetProduct` so that
`GET /l05/products/{id}` answers **200** with the whole `Product` row — category
included this time — or **404** when there is no such id.

`FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == id)` gives you `null` when nothing matches.
Its siblings are worth knowing now: `FirstAsync` throws when there is no match,
`SingleOrDefaultAsync` throws when there is *more than one*, and `FindAsync`
looks in the change tracker before going to the database, which makes it the
fastest way to load by primary key and the only one of the four that is not a
LINQ query.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — Add, Remove, SaveChangesAsync

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Ex3.cs`. Two handlers.

`POST /l05/products` takes `{"name":…,"priceCents":…,"category":…}` and answers
**201** with a `Location` header of `/l05/products/{new id}` and the created
product as the body. A blank name or a non-positive `priceCents` is **400**, and
nothing may be written.

`DELETE /l05/products/{id}` answers **204** when the row was there, **404** when
it was not.

The id in that `Location` header is the interesting part: you do not know it
until after `SaveChangesAsync`, because the database generates it. Read
`product.Id` *after* the save and EF will have filled it in for you.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — tracking, proved

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`POST /l05/products/{id}/rename?name=…&tracked=true|false` so that it loads the
product — **with tracking when `tracked` is true, with `AsNoTracking()` when it
is false** — assigns the new name, saves, and answers **200** with:

```json
{"changes": <what SaveChangesAsync returned>, "name": <the name on your object>}
```

…or **404** when there is no such product.

Run it both ways and look at what comes back. Tracked: `changes` is 1 and the
row really changes. Untracked: `name` is the new name — the assignment
obviously worked — `changes` is **0**, and the database is untouched. No
exception, no warning, nothing in the log. This is the single most expensive
beginner mistake with EF Core, and the point of making you produce it on purpose
is that you will recognise it in the wild.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics ex4
```

## Challenge — a page and its total

Honest difficulty note: the query is four operators; the validation and the
1-based arithmetic are where the bugs are.

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Challenge.cs`. Implement
`GET /l05/products/page?page=&size=` returning:

```json
{"items":[…],"total":5,"page":2,"size":2}
```

`items` is one page of `ProductSummary`, name ascending. `total` is the number
of rows in the table, not the number you returned — that is what lets a client
render page numbers. `page` defaults to 1 and `size` to 2, both are echoed back,
and **page < 1, size < 1 or size > 50 is a 400**.

That upper bound is not busywork. An endpoint that will happily accept

# Reading - dotnet/05_efcore_basics

EF Core is two things wearing one name: a **query translator** that turns
expression trees into SQL, and a **change tracker** that turns object mutation
into `UPDATE` statements. Almost everything surprising about it comes from not
knowing which of the two you are currently talking to.

## Notes

**Deferred execution, and where the boundary is.** `db.Products.Where(...)` does
not query anything; it returns an `IQueryable<Product>`, which is an expression
tree plus a provider that knows how to translate it. The translation happens at
the terminal operator — `ToListAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, `CountAsync`,
`AnyAsync` — and everything before that boundary becomes SQL. Everything *after*
it happens in your process, on rows already fetched. Being able to point at that
boundary in someone else's code is most of what "understanding EF" means.

**Client evaluation is now an error, and that is good.** In EF Core 2, a `Where`
the provider could not translate would be silently evaluated in memory, after
loading the whole table. Since EF Core 3 it throws instead, with a message
naming the expression it could not translate. Fixing it usually means calling a
translatable method (`EF.Functions.Like`), restructuring the predicate, or
deciding that this genuinely is client-side work and calling `AsEnumerable()` to
say so out loud.

**Parameterisation is automatic.** `Where(p => p.Name == name)` becomes
`WHERE "Name" = @__name_0` with the value bound, not interpolated — so LINQ
queries are structurally immune to SQL injection. The exception is
`FromSqlRaw("... " + input)`, which is exactly as dangerous as it looks;
`FromSql($"...{input}")` with an interpolated *FormattableString* is the safe
form, because EF turns the holes into parameters.

**The context is scoped, short-lived and not thread-safe.** One per request is
the rule, and it is enforced by `AddDbContext`'s default lifetime. Two concurrent
operations on one context throw `InvalidOperationException: A second operation
was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed` —
which in practice means you forgot an `await`, or you fanned out with
`Task.WhenAll` over the same context. For background work, resolve a fresh
context inside a fresh scope (lesson 02) or use `AddDbContextFactory`.

**Async all the way, for real reasons.** A database round trip is milliseconds
of doing nothing. `ToList()` parks a thread-pool thread for the duration;
`ToListAsync()` returns it to the pool. Under load the difference is the
difference between a service that scales and one that thread-pool-starves. The
rule "if there is an async version, use it, and await it" has almost no
exceptions in web code.

**`EnsureCreated` versus migrations.** `EnsureCreated()` builds the schema from
the current model in one shot and records nothing; it is for tests and throwaway
demos, and it cannot update a database that already exists. Migrations
(`dotnet ef migrations add`, `dotnet ef database update`) generate versioned,
reviewable, ordered deltas and a `__EFMigrationsHistory` table. Real projects use
migrations, apply them in a deployment step rather than at application startup,
and treat a migration as code that gets reviewed like any other.

## ex1 - projection is the whole lesson

`Select` before `ToListAsync` puts the projection *inside* the SQL:

```sql
SELECT "p"."Id", "p"."Name", "p"."PriceCents" FROM "Products" AS "p" ORDER BY "p"."Name"
```

`Select` after `ToListAsync` fetches every column of every row, materialises a
full entity graph, tracks all of it, and then throws most of it away in memory.
On five rows with four columns you cannot measure the difference. On a table
with a `text` blob column, or a hundred thousand rows, it is the difference
between a fast endpoint and an incident. It also stops entities leaking into
your response contract, which lesson 07 turns into a rule.

The ordering half is worth stating plainly because it catches people in every
language: **a `SELECT` without an `ORDER BY` has no defined order.** Not
"insertion order", not "primary key order" — undefined. It will often *look*
like primary key order on a small table, right up until the query planner picks
an index scan and it does not. If the order matters to your API, it is part of
your API and you write it down.

## ex2 - four ways to load one row

`FirstOrDefaultAsync` takes a predicate and returns `null` when nothing matches.
`FirstAsync` throws `InvalidOperationException`. `SingleOrDefaultAsync` returns
null for zero rows and *throws* for two — which makes it the right choice when
"more than one" would mean your data is corrupt, and the wrong one for a query
you expect to filter loosely. `FindAsync(key)` is different in kind: it checks
the change tracker first and only queries if the entity is not already loaded,
so it is the cheapest lookup by primary key and the only one that can return
without touching the database.

The 404 decision is the same one as lesson 01, and the reason to repeat it is
that the ORM makes the wrong answer easier: returning the nullable entity
directly gives a 200 with `null`, compiles fine, and pushes the problem onto
every caller.

## ex3 - what `SaveChangesAsync` actually does

On save, EF walks the change tracker, finds every entity whose state is Added,
Modified or Deleted, generates the corresponding `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`,
opens a transaction, executes them in dependency order, commits, and updates the
tracked entities with anything the database generated. That last step is why
`product.Id` is populated after the save and not before: the column is
`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` and only the database knows the value.

The transaction is free and implicit, and it is the reason the unit-of-work
shape matters. Two `Add` calls and one `SaveChangesAsync` is atomic; two `Add`
calls each followed by its own save is not, and a failure in the middle leaves
half a change behind.

`Remove` requires a loaded entity because EF needs the key and, for concurrency
tokens, the original values. The pattern "load, check for null, remove, save" is
therefore also the pattern that gives you a free 404. (For bulk work, EF 7 and
later add `ExecuteDeleteAsync`/`ExecuteUpdateAsync`, which issue a single SQL
statement and bypass the change tracker entirely — much faster, and they do not
give you the 404.)

The validation-before-`Add` ordering matters more than it looks. `Add` on a
context whose request then returns 400 is usually harmless, because nobody
saves — but "usually" is doing work there, and any later code that calls
`SaveChangesAsync` for its own reasons would flush your rejected entity too.
Validate first, then touch the context.

## ex4 - the AsNoTracking trap

When EF materialises a tracked entity it stores a snapshot of every property in
the change tracker. `SaveChangesAsync` compares current values against that
snapshot; the differences become the `SET` clause of an `UPDATE`. That is why
you never call `Update()` on an entity you loaded, and why an untracked entity is
invisible to save: there is no snapshot, so there is nothing to compare, so EF
believes there is nothing to write.

The failure mode is the worst kind: *silent*. `changes` is 0, no exception is
thrown, no warning is logged, and the response looks fine because the in-memory
object really does have the new name. The bug surfaces later, as "the edit
didn't stick", usually from a user.

So when should you use `AsNoTracking()`? On every read-only query, and that is
most of them. It skips snapshotting, uses less memory, and is measurably faster
on large result sets. Note that a **projection** to a non-entity type
(`Select(p => new ProductSummary(...))`) is not tracked either — there is no
entity to track — which means ex1's query already had the benefit without asking
for it. `AsNoTracking` is for when you want whole entities and know you will not
change them.

The related trick worth knowing: `AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution()` gives you
untracked entities that still share instances for the same key, which matters for
graphs. Lesson 06 measures exactly that difference.

## challenge - paging, and the two queries you are allowed

`Skip((page - 1) * size).Take(size)` translates to `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`. Two things
to know about it. First, `OFFSET` gets slower as it grows, because the database
still walks the skipped rows; deep paging on a big table is a real problem, and
the professional answer is *keyset* (or "cursor") pagination — `WHERE Name >
@lastSeen ORDER BY Name LIMIT 20` — which stays fast at any depth and is what
"infinite scroll" APIs actually do. Offset paging is fine for a UI with page
numbers over a modest table, which is why it is still everywhere.

Second, `total` costs a second query. That is the honest price of "page 3 of 47"
and there is no way around it; APIs that cannot afford it return "has more" by
fetching `size + 1` rows and checking whether the extra one came back. Both
answers are defensible, and being able to name the trade is worth more than
knowing one of them.

The `size > 50` rejection is the security half. Any endpoint with a
caller-controlled result size and no cap has a denial-of-service switch on it,
and "nobody would do that" is not a control. Cap it, document the cap, and
return 400 rather than silently clamping — silently clamping means a client that
asked for 1000 and got 50 has no idea it is missing data.

## review1 - filter, order, limit, project

The one new operator is `ThenBy`, and it is there because ties in an ordering are
where non-deterministic APIs come from. Two products at the same price with no
tie-breaker can come back in either order, on either run, and the test that
depends on it will fail exactly once a month. Any `ORDER BY` that does not end
in something unique — a name, an id — is a flaky ordering waiting to happen.

`Take` before or after `OrderBy` is the other thing to be careful about: `Take`
first means "any three rows, then sort those three", which is almost never what
anyone wants. LINQ composes in the order you write it, and so does the SQL.

## Further reading

- [Entity Framework Core documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/) — the front door; the "Querying" and "Saving Data" sections cover this lesson.
- [Tracking vs. no-tracking queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking) — snapshots, identity resolution, and when to turn tracking off.
- [Saving data — basic save](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/basic) — `Add`/`Update`/`Remove`, `SaveChanges`, and what the return value means.
- [Migrations overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/managing-schemas/migrations/) — what this course skipped, and how real schema changes ship.
- [Efficient querying](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) — projection, paging, tracking and the round-trip habits that keep EF fast.

## Challenge — a page and its total

Honest difficulty note: the query is four operators; the validation and the
1-based arithmetic are where the bugs are.

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Challenge.cs`. Implement
`GET /l05/products/page?page=&size=` returning:

```json
{"items":[…],"total":5,"page":2,"size":2}
```

`items` is one page of `ProductSummary`, name ascending. `total` is the number
of rows in the table, not the number you returned — that is what lets a client
render page numbers. `page` defaults to 1 and `size` to 2, both are echoed back,
and **page < 1, size < 1 or size > 50 is a 400**.

That upper bound is not busywork. An endpoint that will happily accept
`?size=1000000` is a denial-of-service vector that any client can trigger by
accident.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four beats: resolve the defaults, validate, count, fetch the page.

Both parameters are `int?` so that "not sent" is distinguishable from "sent as
0" — one is a default, the other is a 400.

Watch the arithmetic. Pages are 1-based and `Skip` is 0-based, so page 1 skips
nothing.

## Hint 2

```csharp
int wanted = page ?? 1;
int perPage = size ?? 2;
```

then one guard covering three conditions, then `await db.Products.CountAsync()`
for the total — that is a second query, and it is unavoidable if you want to
report a total.

For the page itself: `OrderBy`, then `Skip`, then `Take`, then `Select`, then
`ToListAsync`. The order of those five is not interchangeable.

## Hint 3

```csharp
var items = await db.Products
    .OrderBy(p => p.Name)
    .Skip((wanted - 1) * perPage)
    .Take(perPage)
    .Select(p => new ProductSummary(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceCents))
    .ToListAsync();

return TypedResults.Ok(new ProductPage(items, total, wanted, perPage));
```

`ProductPage` is already declared in `Model.cs` with exactly those four
properties. If page 2 comes back with the first two rows, the `Skip` expression
is missing its `- 1`.

## Exercise 1 — a query and a projection

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Ex1.cs`. Implement `ListProducts` so that
`GET /l05/products` answers **200** with every product as a `ProductSummary`,
ordered by name ascending:

```json
[{"id":2,"name":"Bokken","priceCents":5900}, … ]
```

Two things the gate checks. The order — the seeded rows are deliberately not in
name order, and a database makes no promise about the order of an unsorted
`SELECT`. And the shape: `category` must not appear in the response, which means
the `Select` has to be part of the query, not a `.Select(...)` after a
`.ToList()`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — one row, or an honest 404

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Ex2.cs`. Implement `GetProduct` so that
`GET /l05/products/{id}` answers **200** with the whole `Product` row — category
included this time — or **404** when there is no such id.

`FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == id)` gives you `null` when nothing matches.
Its siblings are worth knowing now: `FirstAsync` throws when there is no match,
`SingleOrDefaultAsync` throws when there is *more than one*, and `FindAsync`
looks in the change tracker before going to the database, which makes it the
fastest way to load by primary key and the only one of the four that is not a
LINQ query.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — Add, Remove, SaveChangesAsync

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Ex3.cs`. Two handlers.

`POST /l05/products` takes `{"name":…,"priceCents":…,"category":…}` and answers
**201** with a `Location` header of `/l05/products/{new id}` and the created
product as the body. A blank name or a non-positive `priceCents` is **400**, and
nothing may be written.

`DELETE /l05/products/{id}` answers **204** when the row was there, **404** when
it was not.

The id in that `Location` header is the interesting part: you do not know it
until after `SaveChangesAsync`, because the database generates it. Read
`product.Id` *after* the save and EF will have filled it in for you.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics ex3
```

## Hint 1

Two handlers, same three-beat rhythm: check, change the context, save.

For the create, validate *before* you touch `db` at all — the gate counts rows
after two rejected requests and expects nothing to have been inserted.

For the delete, you cannot remove a row you have not loaded, which is also
conveniently how you find out it does not exist.

## Hint 2

Create: build a `Product` from the request, `db.Products.Add(product)`, then
`await db.SaveChangesAsync()`. Only *after* that save does `product.Id` have a
real value — the database generated it — so build the `Location` string from it
afterwards.

Delete: `await db.Products.FindAsync(id)`, return `TypedResults.NotFound()` when
it is null, otherwise `db.Products.Remove(product)` and save, then
`TypedResults.NoContent()`.

`request.Category` is `string?`; the entity's `Category` is not nullable.

## Hint 3

```csharp
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(request.Name) || request.PriceCents <= 0)
{
    return TypedResults.BadRequest();
}

var product = new Product { Name = request.Name, /* … */ };
db.Products.Add(product);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();

return TypedResults.Created($"/l05/products/{product.Id}", product);
```

If the gate says the new product 404s on the next request, you called `Add` and
forgot `SaveChangesAsync` — nothing left the change tracker.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — tracking, proved

Edit `src/Api/L05_EfcoreBasics/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`POST /l05/products/{id}/rename?name=…&tracked=true|false` so that it loads the
product — **with tracking when `tracked` is true, with `AsNoTracking()` when it
is false** — assigns the new name, saves, and answers **200** with:

```json
{"changes": <what SaveChangesAsync returned>, "name": <the name on your object>}
```

…or **404** when there is no such product.

Run it both ways and look at what comes back. Tracked: `changes` is 1 and the
row really changes. Untracked: `name` is the new name — the assignment
obviously worked — `changes` is **0**, and the database is untouched. No
exception, no warning, nothing in the log. This is the single most expensive
beginner mistake with EF Core, and the point of making you produce it on purpose
is that you will recognise it in the wild.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 05_efcore_basics ex4
```

lessons.briefing:
# 06 — Relationships, Include and the N+1

One table was never the interesting case. Real data is a graph: a customer has
orders, an order has lines, a line points at a product, a product carries tags.
The moment a second table appears, so do the two questions that dominate every
performance conversation about an ORM — *what did you load*, and *how many times
did you ask*.

This lesson has five entities and every relationship shape you will meet:

```
Customer  1 ──── *  Order  1 ──── *  OrderLine  * ──── 1  Product  * ──── *  Tag
```

Read `src/Api/L06_EfcoreRelationships/Model.cs` before you start; it is given
code and every expected value below comes from the seed data in the gate.

## Concept — navigations, and the four ways to fill them

A **navigation property** is a property whose type is another entity, or a
collection of them. `Order.Customer` is a reference navigation; `Customer.Orders`
and `Order.Lines` are collection navigations. `Order.CustomerId` is the
**foreign key**, and naming it `<Navigation>Id` is the entire reason EF knows how
these two are related — no attributes, no configuration.

`Product.Tags` and `Tag.Products` are a **many-to-many**. EF creates and manages
the join table by itself; there is no `ProductTag` class in the model, and the
navigations that skip over it are called *skip navigations*.

Now, the important part. **EF never loads a navigation unless you ask.** Load an
order and `order.Lines` is an empty list — not null, not lazy, just empty. That
is a deliberate design choice, and it means "how do I fill this in" is a
question you answer explicitly, four ways:

```csharp
// 1. Eager loading - one query with a JOIN
var customer = await db.Customers
    .Include(c => c.Orders)
        .ThenInclude(o => o.Lines)
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync(c => c.Id == id);

// 2. Projection - one query, and only the columns you named
var summary = await db.Orders
    .Select(o => new { o.Id, Customer = o.Customer!.Name, Lines = o.Lines.Count })
    .ToListAsync();

// 3. Explicit loading - a second query, on demand
await db.Entry(order).Collection(o => o.Lines).LoadAsync();

// 4. Lazy loading - a query per navigation, automatically, behind your back
```

Lazy loading is off by default and this course leaves it off. It is the feature
that turns a loop over a hundred orders into a hundred and one queries without a
single line of code saying so, which is why most teams that turn it on turn it
off again.

### The N+1 problem

This is the one to be able to explain in an interview, so here it is precisely.
You need a list of orders with their customer's name. You write:

```csharp
var orders = await db.Orders.ToListAsync();                       // 1 query
foreach (var order in orders)
{
    var customer = await db.Customers.FindAsync(order.CustomerId); // N queries
}
```

One query for the list, plus one per row: **N+1**. Every answer is correct.
Every test on the response body passes. And each of those N queries is a network
round trip, so at four orders it is invisible and at four thousand it is a
ten-second endpoint. Nothing in the code says "slow"; the cost is in the count.

The fix is always the same shape: **ask the database once, for exactly the shape
you want.** Either `Include` (bring the related entities back with the parents)
or a projection (let SQL compute the answer and return three columns). Projection
is usually better, because `Include` on several collections multiplies rows —
the cartesian explosion — while a projection with aggregates returns one row per
result.

`Ex3.cs` ships with a working N+1 implementation, on purpose. Your job is to
make the same numbers come out of one query.

## Exercise 1 — load the "many" side

Edit `src/Api/L06_EfcoreRelationships/Ex1.cs`. Implement
`GET /l06/customers/{id}` to answer **200** with a `CustomerDetail` — the
customer's id and name, plus their orders (id and reference), id ascending:

```json
{"id":1,"name":"Ada","orders":[{"id":1,"reference":"A-1001"},{"id":3,"reference":"A-1003"}]}
```

**404** when the customer does not exist. A customer who exists and has never
ordered is a **200 with an empty list** — the customer is there, the collection
is empty, and those are different facts.

Write it once without `Include` and look at what comes back. An empty `orders`
array, no exception, no warning. That silence is the thing to remember.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 06_efcore_relationships ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — many-to-many, from both ends

Edit `src/Api/L06_EfcoreRelationships/Ex2.cs`. Two endpoints, both answering
**200** with a plain array of strings sorted A–Z, and **404** when the thing in
the route does not exist:

- `GET /l06/products/{id}/tags` — that product's tag names
- `GET /l06/tags/{name}/products` — the names of products carrying that tag

The join table never appears in your code. `SelectMany` is the operator that
walks a collection navigation and flattens it, and it works identically in both
directions — which is the point of the exercise.

Note that "does not exist" needs its own check: a product with no tags and a
product that is not there both produce an empty list, so you have to ask
separately.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 06_efcore_relationships ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — kill the N+1

Edit `src/Api/L06_EfcoreRelationships/Ex3.cs`. The handler already works and
already returns the right numbers: one `OrderTotals` per order, id ascending,
carrying the order id, the customer's name, the number of lines, and
quantity × unit price summed over those lines.

Run the gate first and read the failure. The values are all correct; the gate
fails because it counted the SQL commands, and there were nine.

Rewrite it as a single query. Everything you need is expressible in one
`Select`: `o.Customer!.Name` becomes a join, `o.Lines.Count` becomes a
correlated subquery, and `o.Lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity * l.UnitPriceCents)`
becomes another. All of it is computed by the database, and what comes back over
the wire is four rows of four columns.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 06_efcore_relationships ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the identity map, made visible

Edit `src/Api/L06_EfcoreRelationships/Ex4.cs`. Implement
`GET /l06/identity?tracked=true|false` so that it loads orders 1 and 3 — both
Ada's — with their `Customer` navigation filled in, tracked or not according to
the flag, and answers **200** with:

```json
{"sameInstance": <ReferenceEquals of the two Customer objects>, "customerName":"Ada"}
```

Run it both ways. Tracked gives you `true`; `AsNoTracking` gives you `false`.
Same rows, same data, and two objects instead of one — because tracking
maintains an **identity map** keyed on the primary key, and no-tracking does not.

This matters in practice more than it sounds. Mutate `order1.Customer!.Name` in
a tracked graph and `order3.Customer!.Name` changes too, because it is the same
object; do it in an untracked graph and the second one does not. Memory is the
other half: an untracked query over ten thousand order lines can materialise ten
thousand copies of the same handful of products.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 06_efcore_relationships ex4
```

## Challenge — an aggregate across three tables, in one query

Honest difficulty note: the LINQ is six lines. Getting it to translate is the
work, and the trick you need is in the hints.

Edit `src/Api/L06_EfcoreRelationships/Challenge.cs`. Implement
`GET /l06/customers/top?limit=` returning the top `limit` customers by total
spend — quantity × unit price, over every line of every order they placed —
highest first, name ascending to break ties:

```json
[{"customerId":1,"name":"Ada","totalCents":30500}, … ]
```

`limit` defaults to 3, and `limit < 1` is **400**. A customer who has never
ordered still appears, with a total of **0** — that is the difference between a
left join and an inner one, and dropping people who have not bought anything is
a classic reporting bug.

And it has to be **one** SQL command. The gate counts.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 06_efcore_relationships challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this lesson; the scheduler brings it back
later. Edit `src/Api/L06_EfcoreRelationships/Review1.cs`: implement
`GET /l06/review/orders/{id}/lines` returning one `LineDetail` per line — the
product's name, the quantity, and quantity × unit price — product name
ascending, with **404** for an order that does not exist.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/06_efcore_relationships

Every ORM's hard problem is the same one: objects are a graph and tables are
sets, and something has to decide how much of the graph a given query drags
along. EF Core's answer is "nothing you did not ask for", which is safe,
explicit, and the source of both the empty-collection surprise and the N+1.

## Notes

**Conventions do the wiring.** A property called `CustomerId` alongside a
navigation called `Customer` is enough for EF to infer a required one-to-many
with `Customer` as the principal and `Order` as the dependent. Make the FK
`int?` and the relationship becomes optional, with `ON DELETE SET NULL` instead
of cascade. Everything conventions infer can be overridden in `OnModelCreating`
with the fluent API — `HasOne(...).WithMany(...).HasForeignKey(...)` — and in a
real project you will, for delete behaviour and indexes if nothing else.

**Many-to-many without a join entity.** Since EF Core 5, two collection
navigations pointing at each other produce a join table EF manages itself, and
the navigations are called *skip navigations* because they skip over it. The
moment the relationship needs a payload of its own — a quantity, a date added,
a role — you promote it to a real entity with two one-to-many relationships, and
the skip navigations become optional sugar on top.

**Split queries.** `Include`ing two collections at once produces a cartesian
product: an order with 3 lines and 4 tags returns 12 rows, and EF de-duplicates
in memory. On wide rows that is real waste, and `AsSplitQuery()` tells EF to
issue one `SELECT` per collection instead — more round trips, far less data.
Neither is universally right, which is why it is a per-query decision. Knowing
the phrase "cartesian explosion" and what to do about it is a good interview
answer.

**Filtered includes.** `Include(c => c.Orders.Where(o => o.IsOpen))` works and
is often what you actually wanted; without the filter you have loaded every
order a customer has ever placed in order to show the three open ones.

**`ExecuteUpdate` / `ExecuteDelete`.** EF 7 added bulk operations that compile to
a single `UPDATE … WHERE` or `DELETE … WHERE` with no loading and no change
tracking. They are dramatically faster for "close all orders older than a year"
and they bypass everything the change tracker would have done — including
concurrency tokens and `SaveChanges` interceptors. Use them deliberately.

**Counting queries is a real technique.** The `CommandCounter` in this lesson's
gate is thirty lines of `ILoggerProvider`. The production versions of the same
idea are EF's `LogTo`, the `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command`
category at Information level, and OpenTelemetry spans per command. Putting an
assertion on query count around a hot endpoint is one of the highest-value tests
a team can write, because N+1 regressions are invisible in every other kind of
test.

## ex1 - navigations are empty until you ask

The first time you write this without `Include`, `customer.Orders` comes back as
an empty list and nothing complains. That is worth sitting with, because it is
the shape of a whole family of bugs: EF is not lying to you, it is telling you
about the rows it loaded, and it loaded one row from `Customers`. The empty list
is the truthful answer to a question you did not ask.

Contrast that with lazy loading, which would have silently issued a second query
when you touched `.Orders` — correct output, hidden cost. Off by default is the
right default, and the reason is that "correct but mysteriously slow" is harder
to find than "obviously empty".

The 404-versus-empty-list decision returns from lesson 01, now with a cleaner
test for it: does the *thing named in the URL* exist? `/l06/customers/99` names
a customer that does not exist, so 404. `/l06/customers/3` names one that does,
whose collection happens to be empty, so 200 and `[]`. Linus is in the seed data
precisely to force you to write that distinction.

## ex2 - one join table, two directions

`SelectMany` is the LINQ operator for "walk a collection navigation and flatten
the result", and it is what a `JOIN` looks like from the object side.
`db.Products.Where(p => p.Id == id).SelectMany(p => p.Tags)` becomes a join
through the hidden `ProductTag` table to `Tags`, and the mirror-image query
becomes the same join read the other way. You never named the join table, and if
you look at the generated SQL you will see it there.

The `AnyAsync` existence check before the real query is a second round trip, and
it is worth being clear-eyed about why it is there rather than defending it as
free. An empty list is ambiguous — no tags, or no product — and the API has to
disambiguate. The single-query alternative is to load the product with
`Include(p => p.Tags)` and check for null, which trades a round trip for
loading a row you do not need. Both are defensible; what is not defensible is
returning `[]` for a product that does not exist.

## ex3 - the N+1, named and killed

The shipped implementation is nine queries for four orders: one for the list,
then a customer lookup and a lines lookup per order. Scale that to a page of 50
orders and it is 101 round trips. At a millisecond each on a LAN — optimistic —
that is a tenth of a second of pure latency for a query the database could
answer in one.

The rewrite is one `Select`, and what makes it work is that everything inside it
is an *expression*, translated rather than executed:

```sql
SELECT "o"."Id", "c"."Name",
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "OrderLines" AS "l" WHERE "o"."Id" = "l"."OrderId"),
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM("l"."Quantity" * "l"."UnitPriceCents"), 0) FROM "OrderLines" …)
FROM "Orders" AS "o"
INNER JOIN "Customers" AS "c" ON "o"."CustomerId" = "c"."Id"
ORDER BY "o"."Id"
```

Four rows, four columns, one round trip, and the arithmetic done by the engine
that is holding the data. If you did the SQL course, this is the same lesson
from the other side: the fastest way to move data is not to move it.

Two things to watch for when you write it. `o.Customer!.Name` needs the
null-forgiving `!` because the navigation is declared nullable, but nothing is
dereferenced at runtime — it is an expression tree, and the `!` is purely a
message to the compiler. And the projection must stay inside the `IQueryable`;
one stray `ToListAsync()` before the `Select` and you are back to loading
everything.

## ex4 - the identity map

A tracked query keeps a dictionary from (entity type, primary key) to object.
When a row for `Customer` id 1 comes back a second time — as the parent of a
second order, say — EF finds the existing instance and reuses it rather than
materialising a new one. That is the identity map, and it is what makes
`ReferenceEquals` return true.

Three consequences worth carrying:

- **Consistency.** In a tracked graph there is exactly one object per row, so an
  edit is visible everywhere that row appears. Untracked, you can hold two
  copies of the same customer with different values and save neither.
- **Memory.** A tracked query over 10,000 order lines materialises each distinct
  product once. The same query untracked materialises one product object per
  line. For read-heavy endpoints over wide graphs that difference is measurable.
- **The middle option.** `AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution()` gives you the
  de-duplication without the change tracking, at the cost of maintaining the map.
  It exists exactly for "read-only, but I care about the graph".

So the rule of thumb is not "always use AsNoTracking". It is: no-tracking for
read-only queries that project or return flat lists; tracking when you intend to
save; identity resolution when you want a coherent read-only graph.

## challenge - the aggregate, and why it would not translate

The interesting failure in this exercise is not the SQL, it is the LINQ
provider. This does not translate:

```csharp
.Select(c => new CustomerSpend(c.Id, c.Name, total))
.OrderByDescending(s => s.TotalCents)     // ← s is a CustomerSpend, in memory
```

EF has to turn `OrderByDescending` into `ORDER BY`, and to do that it must map
`s.TotalCents` back to a column or expression. It cannot see inside your
record's constructor, so the whole tree becomes untranslatable and you get an
exception naming the expression. Project to an **anonymous type** instead — EF
does know how to look inside those — sort, take, and build the record in memory
afterwards. That is a genuinely useful piece of EF folklore.

The other half is the left join. `db.Customers.Select(c => … c.Orders …)` starts
from customers, so a customer with no orders still produces a row, with a sum
of 0. Starting from orders and grouping by customer — the more obvious way to
write it — silently drops Linus, and reports that are missing the zero rows are
a bug that survives review remarkably often, because the numbers that *are* there
are all correct.

## review1 - two hops in one projection

`l.Product!.Name` from an `OrderLine` is a single join, and putting it inside the
`Select` means the product's name is a column in the result rather than a
`Product` entity you loaded and then read one field from.

The trap this exercise sets is the ordering, and it is the same one the challenge
sets: `OrderBy` has to come *before* the projection into `LineDetail`, or the
provider cannot translate it. Ordering by `l.Product!.Name` on the entity side
translates to `ORDER BY "p"."Name"`; ordering by `l.ProductName` on the record
side does not translate at all. Order first, project last.

## Further reading

- [Relationships in EF Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/relationships) — conventions, foreign keys, navigations and the fluent overrides.
- [Loading related data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/related-data/) — eager, explicit and lazy loading, filtered includes, and `ThenInclude`.
- [Single vs. split queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/single-split-queries) — the cartesian explosion and `AsSplitQuery`.
- [Efficient querying](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) — projection, N+1, buffering and the round-trip habits.
- [Many-to-many relationships](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/relationships/many-to-many) — skip navigations, the implicit join entity, and when to make it explicit.
