lessons.briefing:
# 09 — Authentication, authorization, and testing them

Everything you have built so far has been open to the world. This lesson closes
it, and it is the capstone: routing, DI, middleware, configuration, EF Core, REST
semantics and ProblemDetails all show up again, now with a caller attached.

Two words that sound alike and mean different things, and this lesson is mostly
about keeping them apart:

- **Authentication** — *who is calling?* A bearer token arrives, the server
  verifies its signature and expiry, and produces a `ClaimsPrincipal`. Failure is
  **401 Unauthorized**, which is badly named: it means "I do not know who you
  are, authenticate and try again".
- **Authorization** — *may this caller do this?* Failure is **403 Forbidden**: "I
  know exactly who you are, and no".

If you send a 401 to someone who is already logged in, you are telling them to do
something that cannot help. If you send a 403 to an anonymous caller, you are
telling them logging in would not help, which is usually false. Interviewers ask
this; the exercises grade it.

Read `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Notes.cs` first — it is given code, and it holds
the note store plus the signing key the gate's tokens are made with.

## Concept — a JWT, and the two middlewares that read it

A **JSON Web Token** is three base64url chunks separated by dots:

```
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9 . eyJzdWIiOiJhZGEiLCJleHAiOjE3...} . 4pLzGm-vTn...
└──────── header ────────┘             └──────────── payload ────────┘   └── signature ──┘
```

The header names the algorithm. The payload is the **claims** — `sub` (who),
`exp` (until when), `iss` (who issued it), `aud` (who it is for), plus anything
else, such as `role`. The signature is an HMAC or an RSA signature over the first
two parts.

Three things follow, and all three are exam questions:

- **A JWT is signed, not encrypted.** Anyone holding one can read every claim in
  it — paste one into jwt.io and see. Never put anything secret in a token.
- **The signature is the whole security model.** It proves the payload has not
  been altered since the issuer made it. Skip `ValidateIssuerSigningKey` and any
  caller can mint a token saying `"role": "admin"`.
- **Validation is stateless.** The server needs no session store and no database
  lookup; it checks a signature and some dates. That is why JWTs scale — and why
  you cannot revoke one before it expires, which is why access tokens are
  short-lived and paired with a refresh token.

Registering the scheme looks like this:

```csharp
services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.MapInboundClaims = false;         // keep the claim names as written
        options.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters
        {
            ValidateIssuer = true,            ValidIssuer = JwtSettings.Issuer,
            ValidateAudience = true,          ValidAudience = JwtSettings.Audience,
            ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true,  IssuerSigningKey = JwtSettings.SigningKey,
            ValidateLifetime = true,
            NameClaimType = "sub",
            RoleClaimType = "role",
        };
    });

services.AddAuthorization();
```

Every `Validate…` there is a real attack it stops. No issuer check and you
accept tokens from any system sharing your key; no audience check and a token
minted for a different service of yours works here; no lifetime check and a
stolen token is valid forever.

`NameClaimType` and `RoleClaimType` tell ASP.NET Core which claims to treat as
the caller's name and roles, which is what makes `user.Identity!.Name` and
`user.IsInRole("admin")` work.

You never touch `Program.cs` for any of this: `WebApplication` adds
`UseAuthentication()` and `UseAuthorization()` to the pipeline automatically when
it sees those services registered, in the right order, before your endpoints.

### Requiring it

`.RequireAuthorization()` on an endpoint (or a whole `MapGroup`) means "any
authenticated caller". `.RequireAuthorization("policy-name")` means a **policy**,
registered up front:

```csharp
services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("admin-only", policy => policy.RequireRole("admin"));
```

Policies are the extension point: `RequireRole`, `RequireClaim`,
`RequireAssertion(ctx => …)`, or a full `IAuthorizationRequirement` with a
handler. Naming the policy rather than repeating a role string across twenty
endpoints is what lets "who may see reports" change in one place.

### Testing it

There is no login page here and no identity provider. The gate **issues its own
tokens** with the same key the application validates against, which is exactly
how you would test a real API: a helper that mints a token for a given user and
role, and every test asking a question in the form "as this person, what
happens?".

## Exercise 1 — who is calling?

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Ex1.cs`. Register JWT bearer authentication and
authorization in `Ex1Services`, then implement `WhoAmI` so that
`GET /l09/whoami` answers **200** with `{"name": "<the sub claim>"}`.

The endpoint is already marked `.RequireAuthorization()`. Until you register a
scheme it answers **500**, not 401 — asking for authorization when nothing in the
application can authorize is a configuration error, not a rejected request. That
first failure is worth reading.

The gate then tries four bad tokens: none at all, one signed with a different
key, one that expired two hours ago, and one from the wrong issuer. All four must
be **401**. Each corresponds to one `Validate…` flag.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — 401 is not 403

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Ex2.cs`. Add an authorization policy named
`Ex2Services.AdminOnly` requiring the `admin` role, and apply it to
`GET /l09/admin/reports`.

- no token → **401**
- a valid token whose role is `user` → **403**
- a valid token whose role is `admin` → **200** with the report

You write neither status code. Both come from the framework: the authentication
handler *challenges* (401) when there is no identity, and the authorization
middleware *forbids* (403) when there is one and it fails the policy. Getting the
pair right is a matter of letting the right mechanism handle each case rather
than writing `if`s in your handler.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the token decides what you can see

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Ex3.cs`. Implement `GET /l09/notes` to answer
**200** with the caller's own notes, id ascending — and nobody else's.

The filter comes from `user.Identity!.Name`, which is the `sub` claim, and *not*
from a query parameter. Three notes are seeded: 1 and 3 are Ada's, 2 is Grace's.
Ada must see `1,3`; Grace must see `2`; a caller with no notes gets `200` and an
empty list.

Returning the whole store here would pass any test that only checks the status
code, and is the most common data-exposure bug there is. Filtering on an
identifier the *client* supplies is the same bug wearing a disguise: the client
can change it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the client does not choose the owner

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Ex4.cs`. Implement `POST /l09/notes`:

- blank text → **400** (authentication does not exempt anyone from validation)
- otherwise → **201** with a `Location` of `/l09/notes/{new id}` and the created
  note as the body

`NewNote` has an `Owner` property, and it is a trap. The gate posts as Ada with
`{"text":"not mine","owner":"grace"}` and checks that the created note belongs to
**ada**. The request body is attacker-controlled; the token is signed. Any field
that says who you are, what you may do, or what you are worth must come from the
token, never from the payload.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing ex4
```

## Challenge — ownership, admin override, and no information leak

Honest difficulty note: five outcomes, and the interesting one is a 404 where
your instinct says 403.

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Challenge.cs`. Implement
`PUT /l09/notes/{id}`:

| situation | answer |
|---|---|
| no token | **401** |
| blank text | **400** |
| no such note | **404** |
| someone else's note, ordinary caller | **404** |
| the caller's own note | **204** |
| someone else's note, `admin` role | **204** |

Rows three and four are the exercise. Answering 403 for a note you do not own
*confirms that the note exists*, so an attacker can walk the id space and map
your data without ever reading a byte of it. When the existence of a resource is
itself privileged information, "you may not" and "there is nothing here" have to
look identical. (When it is not privileged — a public document you cannot edit —
403 is friendlier and correct. Knowing which case you are in is the skill.)

Note also that the 400 comes first: a malformed request is malformed whoever sent
it, and checking it before you look anything up keeps the logic honest.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing challenge
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/09_auth_and_testing

Security is the one area where a bug that never fires is still a bug, and where
"it works" and "it is correct" can be very far apart. This page is about the
mechanisms underneath the five exercises, and about the handful of decisions
that come up in every code review of a protected endpoint.

## Notes

**Schemes, handlers and the two middlewares.**
`AddAuthentication("Bearer").AddJwtBearer(...)` registers a *scheme*: a name plus
a handler that knows how to turn a request into a `ClaimsPrincipal`.
`UseAuthentication()` runs the default scheme's handler and assigns
`HttpContext.User`; it does not reject anything. `UseAuthorization()` looks at
the selected endpoint's metadata and, if it demands authorization, evaluates the
policy against `HttpContext.User` — challenging (401) when there is no identity
and forbidding (403) when there is one that fails. Both are added automatically
by `WebApplication` when the corresponding services are present, in that order,
after routing and before the endpoint. Authorization needs routing to have run
first, because until an endpoint is selected there is nothing to know the
requirements of.

**Claims are just key/value pairs.** A `ClaimsPrincipal` holds one or more
`ClaimsIdentity`, each holding claims. `user.Identity.Name` and
`user.IsInRole(...)` are conveniences over "find the claim whose type is the
configured name/role type" — which is why `NameClaimType` and `RoleClaimType`
matter, and why turning `MapInboundClaims` off (so `sub` stays `sub` instead of
becoming a long XML-schema URI) makes everything more legible.

**Roles versus policies versus resource-based checks.** Roles are coarse and
static (`admin`, `support`). Policies are named, composable rules evaluated
against the principal — claims, assertions, or custom requirements with
handlers — and are what you should reach for by default, because the rule lives
in one place. Neither can express "may this user edit *this note*", because that
depends on data the authorization system has not loaded. That is
**resource-based authorization**, and it either lives in your handler (as in the
challenge) or uses `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policy)`
after you have fetched the resource.

**Access tokens are short-lived on purpose.** Validation is stateless, so there
is no list of revoked tokens to consult — a token is valid until `exp`. The
industry answer is a short-lived access token (minutes) plus a long-lived refresh
token held somewhere revocable, and a token-revocation list only for the cases
that truly need it. "How do you log someone out immediately?" is a favourite
follow-up; the honest answer is that with pure JWT you cannot, and that you
either accept the window or keep server-side state.

**Where the token lives in a browser matters.** `localStorage` is readable by any
script on the page, so one XSS is total account compromise. An `HttpOnly`,
`Secure`, `SameSite` cookie is not readable by script, but reintroduces CSRF,
which is why cookie auth needs antiforgery tokens and bearer auth does not. There
is no free option; there is only knowing which attack you have chosen to defend
against.

**CORS is not authorization.** `AddCors`/`UseCors` tells a *browser* which
origins may read a response. It stops nothing else — curl, a server, a mobile app
and a proxy all ignore it — and a permissive CORS policy is not a vulnerability
by itself, while a missing authorization check is. The classic mistake is
`AllowAnyOrigin()` together with credentials, which the spec forbids and the
runtime will refuse. `UseCors` also has to run before authentication, or a
browser preflight gets a 401 with no CORS headers on it and the browser reports a
CORS failure for what is really an auth ordering bug.

**HTTPS or nothing.** A bearer token in a header over plain HTTP is a password in
cleartext. `UseHttpsRedirection` and HSTS are the minimum, and in production TLS
usually terminates at the load balancer — in which case `UseForwardedHeaders`
matters so the app sees the real scheme and client IP.

## ex1 - each validation flag is an attack it stops

The four rejected tokens map one-to-one onto the four `Validate…` settings, and
it is worth being able to say what each one prevents.

**Signature** (`ValidateIssuerSigningKey`): without it, anyone can base64 a
payload saying `"role": "admin"` and be believed. The historic version of this
bug is the `alg: none` attack, where a library accepted a token that declared it
had no signature; modern libraries refuse, but the lesson is that the *token
says* which algorithm to use and you must not simply obey it.

**Lifetime** (`ValidateLifetime`): without it, a token leaked from a log file two
years ago still works. Note the default five minutes of clock skew, which is why
the gate expires its token by two hours rather than by one minute.

**Issuer** (`ValidateIssuer`): without it, any system sharing your signing key —
another service of yours, a partner, a test environment — can mint credentials
for production.

**Audience** (`ValidateAudience`): without it, a token your identity provider
issued for a *different* one of your APIs is accepted here. This is the one
people skip most often, and it is how privilege escalates sideways between
services.

The 500-before-401 detail is worth understanding too. `RequireAuthorization()`
adds metadata to the endpoint; `EndpointMiddleware` checks that some authorization
middleware actually ran, and throws if not. That is deliberate: silently serving
an endpoint you asked to protect would be far worse than a loud failure.

## ex2 - the framework produces both status codes

You wrote no status codes in this exercise, and that is the point. The
authentication handler's `ChallengeAsync` produces the 401 (with a
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` header saying how to authenticate); the authorization
middleware's `ForbidAsync` produces the 403. Handling these yourself with `if`s
in the handler means re-deriving, per endpoint, a distinction the framework
already models — and getting it wrong somewhere.

The naming really is unfortunate. 401 "Unauthorized" means *unauthenticated*; 403
"Forbidden" means *unauthorized*. Everyone gets this wrong once, and the way to
keep it straight is the sentence in the README: 401 says *try again with
credentials*, 403 says *credentials will not help*.

`AddAuthorizationBuilder().AddPolicy(name, …)` is the modern registration API.
The reason to name a policy rather than write `RequireRole("admin")` at each call
site is that "who may see reports" is a business rule that will change, and when
it does you want one edit and not a grep. It is also what lets a policy grow from
a role check to "role admin, or the support team during business hours" without
touching a single endpoint.

## ex3 - the filter has to come from the credential

`store.All().Where(n => n.Owner == user.Identity!.Name)` looks trivial, and the
class of bug it avoids is the most commonly exploited one in web APIs. OWASP
calls it **Broken Object Level Authorization**, and it is number one on their API
Security Top 10 for a reason: it is invisible in code review unless you are
looking for it, and every test that checks only status codes passes.

Three versions of the mistake, in increasing subtlety:

- Return everything. The endpoint is authenticated, so it *feels* protected.
- Filter by `?owner=ada` from the query string. Now the client picks, and
  `?owner=grace` works.
- Filter by an id taken from the request body or a header the client controls.
  Same bug, better disguised.

The rule: **anything that scopes data to a caller must come from the signed
token**, not from anywhere the caller can write. In a real codebase the more
robust version pushes it lower — an EF Core global query filter driven by the
current user, so that forgetting the `Where` is impossible rather than merely
discouraged.

The empty-list-and-200 case matters too: a caller with no notes has not failed at
anything, and 404 would be a lie about a collection that exists.

## ex4 - trust the token, never the payload

`NewNote.Owner` exists in this exercise purely to be ignored. That is the shape
of the real bug: a DTO acquires a field because some internal caller needed it,
and nobody notices that the field decides who owns the resulting row.

The general rule covers more than ownership. Any field that answers *who are
you*, *what may you do*, *what tier are you on*, *how much is this*, or *which
tenant is this* must be derived server-side, from the token or from your own
database. The request body is a statement of intent from an untrusted party.
"But our frontend always sends the right value" is not a control — the frontend
is not the only client, and anyone can send a request.

This is the same family as lesson 07's mass assignment, and the same defence
works: enumerate what you accept, and construct the entity yourself.

## challenge - when 404 is the right answer to "not allowed"

The instinct is 403, and for most resources 403 is right and friendlier. The
exception is when *the existence of the resource is itself privileged
information*, and then a 403 is an oracle: an attacker walks `/notes/1`,
`/notes/2`, `/notes/3` and learns exactly which ids exist and roughly how much
data you hold, without reading a single note. GitHub does this deliberately —
a private repository you cannot see returns 404, not 403 — and so does every
system where "does account X exist" is worth knowing.

So the test is: *would telling this caller "it exists but you may not have it"
give them something they should not have?* For a document in a shared workspace,
no — 403, and they can go and ask for access. For another tenant's record, yes —
404, always.

The other decision in the challenge is that validation comes first. Checking the
payload before the lookup means a malformed request gets the same answer whoever
sent it, which keeps the endpoint's behaviour explainable and avoids a subtler
oracle: if a blank body returned 400 for notes you own and 404 for notes you do
not, the *validation* would leak existence.

The admin override is deliberately a role check rather than a special case in the
ownership test, because it is exactly the kind of rule that grows. Today it is
`admin`; tomorrow it is `admin` or the note's workspace moderator, and at that
point the check wants to be a policy or an `IAuthorizationService` call against
the loaded resource rather than a boolean in a handler.

## Further reading

# Reading - dotnet/09_auth_and_testing

Security is the one area where a bug that never fires is still a bug, and where
"it works" and "it is correct" can be very far apart. This page is about the
mechanisms underneath the five exercises, and about the handful of decisions
that come up in every code review of a protected endpoint.

## Notes

**Schemes, handlers and the two middlewares.**
`AddAuthentication("Bearer").AddJwtBearer(...)` registers a *scheme*: a name plus
a handler that knows how to turn a request into a `ClaimsPrincipal`.
`UseAuthentication()` runs the default scheme's handler and assigns
`HttpContext.User`; it does not reject anything. `UseAuthorization()` looks at
the selected endpoint's metadata and, if it demands authorization, evaluates the
policy against `HttpContext.User` — challenging (401) when there is no identity
and forbidding (403) when there is one that fails. Both are added automatically
by `WebApplication` when the corresponding services are present, in that order,
after routing and before the endpoint. Authorization needs routing to have run
first, because until an endpoint is selected there is nothing to know the
requirements of.

**Claims are just key/value pairs.** A `ClaimsPrincipal` holds one or more
`ClaimsIdentity`, each holding claims. `user.Identity.Name` and
`user.IsInRole(...)` are conveniences over "find the claim whose type is the
configured name/role type" — which is why `NameClaimType` and `RoleClaimType`
matter, and why turning `MapInboundClaims` off (so `sub` stays `sub` instead of
becoming a long XML-schema URI) makes everything more legible.

**Roles versus policies versus resource-based checks.** Roles are coarse and
static (`admin`, `support`). Policies are named, composable rules evaluated
against the principal — claims, assertions, or custom requirements with
handlers — and are what you should reach for by default, because the rule lives
in one place. Neither can express "may this user edit *this note*", because that
depends on data the authorization system has not loaded. That is
**resource-based authorization**, and it either lives in your handler (as in the
challenge) or uses `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policy)`
after you have fetched the resource.

**Access tokens are short-lived on purpose.** Validation is stateless, so there
is no list of revoked tokens to consult — a token is valid until `exp`. The
industry answer is a short-lived access token (minutes) plus a long-lived refresh
token held somewhere revocable, and a token-revocation list only for the cases
that truly need it. "How do you log someone out immediately?" is a favourite
follow-up; the honest answer is that with pure JWT you cannot, and that you
either accept the window or keep server-side state.

**Where the token lives in a browser matters.** `localStorage` is readable by any
script on the page, so one XSS is total account compromise. An `HttpOnly`,
`Secure`, `SameSite` cookie is not readable by script, but reintroduces CSRF,
which is why cookie auth needs antiforgery tokens and bearer auth does not. There
is no free option; there is only knowing which attack you have chosen to defend
against.

**CORS is not authorization.** `AddCors`/`UseCors` tells a *browser* which
origins may read a response. It stops nothing else — curl, a server, a mobile app
and a proxy all ignore it — and a permissive CORS policy is not a vulnerability
by itself, while a missing authorization check is. The classic mistake is
`AllowAnyOrigin()` together with credentials, which the spec forbids and the
runtime will refuse. `UseCors` also has to run before authentication, or a
browser preflight gets a 401 with no CORS headers on it and the browser reports a
CORS failure for what is really an auth ordering bug.

**HTTPS or nothing.** A bearer token in a header over plain HTTP is a password in
cleartext. `UseHttpsRedirection` and HSTS are the minimum, and in production TLS
usually terminates at the load balancer — in which case `UseForwardedHeaders`
matters so the app sees the real scheme and client IP.

## ex1 - each validation flag is an attack it stops

The four rejected tokens map one-to-one onto the four `Validate…` settings, and
it is worth being able to say what each one prevents.

**Signature** (`ValidateIssuerSigningKey`): without it, anyone can base64 a
payload saying `"role": "admin"` and be believed. The historic version of this
bug is the `alg: none` attack, where a library accepted a token that declared it
had no signature; modern libraries refuse, but the lesson is that the *token
says* which algorithm to use and you must not simply obey it.

**Lifetime** (`ValidateLifetime`): without it, a token leaked from a log file two
years ago still works. Note the default five minutes of clock skew, which is why
the gate expires its token by two hours rather than by one minute.

**Issuer** (`ValidateIssuer`): without it, any system sharing your signing key —
another service of yours, a partner, a test environment — can mint credentials
for production.

**Audience** (`ValidateAudience`): without it, a token your identity provider
issued for a *different* one of your APIs is accepted here. This is the one
people skip most often, and it is how privilege escalates sideways between
services.

The 500-before-401 detail is worth understanding too. `RequireAuthorization()`
adds metadata to the endpoint; `EndpointMiddleware` checks that some authorization
middleware actually ran, and throws if not. That is deliberate: silently serving
an endpoint you asked to protect would be far worse than a loud failure.

## ex2 - the framework produces both status codes

You wrote no status codes in this exercise, and that is the point. The
authentication handler's `ChallengeAsync` produces the 401 (with a
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` header saying how to authenticate); the authorization
middleware's `ForbidAsync` produces the 403. Handling these yourself with `if`s
in the handler means re-deriving, per endpoint, a distinction the framework
already models — and getting it wrong somewhere.

The naming really is unfortunate. 401 "Unauthorized" means *unauthenticated*; 403
"Forbidden" means *unauthorized*. Everyone gets this wrong once, and the way to
keep it straight is the sentence in the README: 401 says *try again with
credentials*, 403 says *credentials will not help*.

`AddAuthorizationBuilder().AddPolicy(name, …)` is the modern registration API.
The reason to name a policy rather than write `RequireRole("admin")` at each call
site is that "who may see reports" is a business rule that will change, and when
it does you want one edit and not a grep. It is also what lets a policy grow from
a role check to "role admin, or the support team during business hours" without
touching a single endpoint.

## ex3 - the filter has to come from the credential

`store.All().Where(n => n.Owner == user.Identity!.Name)` looks trivial, and the
class of bug it avoids is the most commonly exploited one in web APIs. OWASP
calls it **Broken Object Level Authorization**, and it is number one on their API
Security Top 10 for a reason: it is invisible in code review unless you are
looking for it, and every test that checks only status codes passes.

Three versions of the mistake, in increasing subtlety:

- Return everything. The endpoint is authenticated, so it *feels* protected.
- Filter by `?owner=ada` from the query string. Now the client picks, and
  `?owner=grace` works.
- Filter by an id taken from the request body or a header the client controls.
  Same bug, better disguised.

The rule: **anything that scopes data to a caller must come from the signed
token**, not from anywhere the caller can write. In a real codebase the more
robust version pushes it lower — an EF Core global query filter driven by the
current user, so that forgetting the `Where` is impossible rather than merely
discouraged.

The empty-list-and-200 case matters too: a caller with no notes has not failed at
anything, and 404 would be a lie about a collection that exists.

## ex4 - trust the token, never the payload

`NewNote.Owner` exists in this exercise purely to be ignored. That is the shape
of the real bug: a DTO acquires a field because some internal caller needed it,
and nobody notices that the field decides who owns the resulting row.

The general rule covers more than ownership. Any field that answers *who are
you*, *what may you do*, *what tier are you on*, *how much is this*, or *which
tenant is this* must be derived server-side, from the token or from your own
database. The request body is a statement of intent from an untrusted party.
"But our frontend always sends the right value" is not a control — the frontend
is not the only client, and anyone can send a request.

This is the same family as lesson 07's mass assignment, and the same defence
works: enumerate what you accept, and construct the entity yourself.

## challenge - when 404 is the right answer to "not allowed"

The instinct is 403, and for most resources 403 is right and friendlier. The
exception is when *the existence of the resource is itself privileged
information*, and then a 403 is an oracle: an attacker walks `/notes/1`,
`/notes/2`, `/notes/3` and learns exactly which ids exist and roughly how much
data you hold, without reading a single note. GitHub does this deliberately —
a private repository you cannot see returns 404, not 403 — and so does every
system where "does account X exist" is worth knowing.

So the test is: *would telling this caller "it exists but you may not have it"
give them something they should not have?* For a document in a shared workspace,
no — 403, and they can go and ask for access. For another tenant's record, yes —
404, always.

The other decision in the challenge is that validation comes first. Checking the
payload before the lookup means a malformed request gets the same answer whoever
sent it, which keeps the endpoint's behaviour explainable and avoids a subtler
oracle: if a blank body returned 400 for notes you own and 404 for notes you do
not, the *validation* would leak existence.

The admin override is deliberately a role check rather than a special case in the
ownership test, because it is exactly the kind of rule that grows. Today it is
`admin`; tomorrow it is `admin` or the note's workspace moderator, and at that
point the check wants to be a policy or an `IAuthorizationService` call against
the loaded resource rather than a boolean in a handler.

## Further reading

- [Overview of ASP.NET Core authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authentication/) — schemes, handlers, and how `HttpContext.User` gets populated.
- [Introduction to authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/introduction) — simple, role-based, claims-based and policy-based, with the differences spelled out.
- [Policy-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/policies) — requirements, handlers, and `IAuthorizationService` for resource-based checks.

- [Enable CORS in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/cors) — what CORS does and, more importantly, what it does not.

## Challenge — ownership, admin override, and no information leak

Honest difficulty note: five outcomes, and the interesting one is a 404 where
your instinct says 403.

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Challenge.cs`. Implement
`PUT /l09/notes/{id}`:

| situation | answer |
|---|---|
| no token | **401** |
| blank text | **400** |
| no such note | **404** |
| someone else's note, ordinary caller | **404** |
| the caller's own note | **204** |
| someone else's note, `admin` role | **204** |

Rows three and four are the exercise. Answering 403 for a note you do not own
*confirms that the note exists*, so an attacker can walk the id space and map
your data without ever reading a byte of it. When the existence of a resource is
itself privileged information, "you may not" and "there is nothing here" have to
look identical. (When it is not privileged — a public document you cannot edit —
403 is friendlier and correct. Knowing which case you are in is the skill.)

it, and checking it before you look anything up keeps the logic honest.

## Hint 1

Write the checks in the order the README lists them: payload, existence,
permission, then the work. Each one has exactly one early return.

The 401 needs no code at all — `.RequireAuthorization()` on the route already
handles it.

## Hint 2

Validation first, and its 400 is the same `ValidationProblem` you wrote in ex4.

Then `store.Find(id)`; null is a 404.

Then permission: the caller may proceed if they own the note **or** they are in
the `admin` role. `user.IsInRole("admin")` works because ex1 set
`RoleClaimType = "role"`.

And when they may not proceed, the answer is `TypedResults.NotFound()` — the same
result as "no such note", on purpose.

## Hint 3

```csharp
var note = store.Find(id);
if (note is null) { return TypedResults.NotFound(); }

string caller = user.Identity?.Name ?? "";
bool allowed = note.Owner == caller || user.IsInRole("admin");
if (!allowed)
{
    // Not 403: telling this caller the note exists is itself a leak.
    return TypedResults.NotFound();
}

store.Replace(id, request.Text);
return TypedResults.NoContent();
```

Before you move on, be able to say out loud when 403 would have been the better
answer — `reading.md` has the test, and it is a standard interview follow-up.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — who is calling?

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Ex1.cs`. Register JWT bearer authentication and
authorization in `Ex1Services`, then implement `WhoAmI` so that
`GET /l09/whoami` answers **200** with `{"name": "<the sub claim>"}`.

The endpoint is already marked `.RequireAuthorization()`. Until you register a
scheme it answers **500**, not 401 — asking for authorization when nothing in the
application can authorize is a configuration error, not a rejected request. That
first failure is worth reading.

The gate then tries four bad tokens: none at all, one signed with a different
key, one that expired two hours ago, and one from the wrong issuer. All four must
be **401**. Each corresponds to one `Validate…` flag.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two places to edit. `Ex1Services.Register` needs to tell the container about a
bearer scheme and about authorization; `WhoAmI` needs to read one value off the
`ClaimsPrincipal` it was handed.

Start with the registration, run the gate, and watch the 500 become a 401. That
transition is the proof that the pipeline picked up your services.

## Hint 2

The registration is a chain:

```csharp
services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options => { /* … */ });

services.AddAuthorization();
```

Inside the options, set `MapInboundClaims = false` and build a
`TokenValidationParameters` with all four validations turned on and pointed at
`JwtSettings.Issuer`, `JwtSettings.Audience` and `JwtSettings.SigningKey`. Set
`NameClaimType = "sub"` and `RoleClaimType = "role"` so the framework knows which
claims mean "name" and "role".

You will need `using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer;` and
`using Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens;`.

## Hint 3

Each gate failure maps to one flag: a wrong-key token needs
`ValidateIssuerSigningKey`, an old token needs `ValidateLifetime`, a
`somebody-else` token needs `ValidateIssuer`. All of them default to true, but
supplying a `TokenValidationParameters` without setting them turns them off, so
write them out.

The handler is one line:

```csharp
private static IResult WhoAmI(ClaimsPrincipal user) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(new WhoAmIResponse(user.Identity?.Name ?? ""));
```

`Identity.Name` is the `sub` claim *because* you set `NameClaimType`.

## Hint 1

Two places to edit. `Ex1Services.Register` needs to tell the container about a
bearer scheme and about authorization; `WhoAmI` needs to read one value off the
`ClaimsPrincipal` it was handed.

Start with the registration, run the gate, and watch the 500 become a 401. That
transition is the proof that the pipeline picked up your services.

## Hint 2

The registration is a chain:

```csharp
services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options => { /* … */ });

services.AddAuthorization();
```

Inside the options, set `MapInboundClaims = false` and build a
`TokenValidationParameters` with all four validations turned on and pointed at
`JwtSettings.Issuer`, `JwtSettings.Audience` and `JwtSettings.SigningKey`. Set
`NameClaimType = "sub"` and `RoleClaimType = "role"` so the framework knows which
claims mean "name" and "role".

You will need `using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer;` and
`using Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens;`.

## Hint 3

Each gate failure maps to one flag: a wrong-key token needs
`ValidateIssuerSigningKey`, an old token needs `ValidateLifetime`, a
`somebody-else` token needs `ValidateIssuer`. All of them default to true, but
supplying a `TokenValidationParameters` without setting them turns them off, so
write them out.

The handler is one line:

```csharp
private static IResult WhoAmI(ClaimsPrincipal user) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(new WhoAmIResponse(user.Identity?.Name ?? ""));
```

`Identity.Name` is the `sub` claim *because* you set `NameClaimType`.

## Exercise 2 — 401 is not 403

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Ex2.cs`. Add an authorization policy named
`Ex2Services.AdminOnly` requiring the `admin` role, and apply it to
`GET /l09/admin/reports`.

- no token → **401**
- a valid token whose role is `user` → **403**
- a valid token whose role is `admin` → **200** with the report

You write neither status code. Both come from the framework: the authentication
handler *challenges* (401) when there is no identity, and the authorization
middleware *forbids* (403) when there is one and it fails the policy. Getting the
pair right is a matter of letting the right mechanism handle each case rather
than writing `if`s in your handler.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing ex2
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the token decides what you can see

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Ex3.cs`. Implement `GET /l09/notes` to answer
**200** with the caller's own notes, id ascending — and nobody else's.

The filter comes from `user.Identity!.Name`, which is the `sub` claim, and *not*
from a query parameter. Three notes are seeded: 1 and 3 are Ada's, 2 is Grace's.
Ada must see `1,3`; Grace must see `2`; a caller with no notes gets `200` and an
empty list.

Returning the whole store here would pass any test that only checks the status
code, and is the most common data-exposure bug there is. Filtering on an
identifier the *client* supplies is the same bug wearing a disguise: the client
can change it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`store.All()` gives you every note in the system. Your job is the `Where`.

The only question is where the value you filter on comes from — and there is
exactly one source in this method that a caller cannot forge.

## Hint 2

`user.Identity?.Name` is the `sub` claim from the validated token. That is the
owner to compare against.

It is *not* a query parameter, a header, or a field in a body, because all three
are written by the caller. A filter the client controls is not a filter.

Then `OrderBy(n => n.Id)`, `ToList()`, and `TypedResults.Ok(...)`.

## Hint 3

```csharp
string owner = user.Identity?.Name ?? "";

var mine = store.All()
    .Where(n => n.Owner == owner)
    .OrderBy(n => n.Id)
    .ToList();

return TypedResults.Ok(mine);
```

A caller with no notes ends up with an empty list, which is correct: they exist

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`store.All()` gives you every note in the system. Your job is the `Where`.

The only question is where the value you filter on comes from — and there is
exactly one source in this method that a caller cannot forge.

## Hint 2

`user.Identity?.Name` is the `sub` claim from the validated token. That is the
owner to compare against.

It is *not* a query parameter, a header, or a field in a body, because all three
are written by the caller. A filter the client controls is not a filter.

Then `OrderBy(n => n.Id)`, `ToList()`, and `TypedResults.Ok(...)`.

## Hint 3

```csharp
string owner = user.Identity?.Name ?? "";

var mine = store.All()
    .Where(n => n.Owner == owner)
    .OrderBy(n => n.Id)
    .ToList();

return TypedResults.Ok(mine);
```

A caller with no notes ends up with an empty list, which is correct: they exist
and own nothing. Do not turn that into a 404.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the client does not choose the owner

Edit `src/Api/L09_AuthAndTesting/Ex4.cs`. Implement `POST /l09/notes`:

- blank text → **400** (authentication does not exempt anyone from validation)
- otherwise → **201** with a `Location` of `/l09/notes/{new id}` and the created
  note as the body

`NewNote` has an `Owner` property, and it is a trap. The gate posts as Ada with
`{"text":"not mine","owner":"grace"}` and checks that the created note belongs to
**ada**. The request body is attacker-controlled; the token is signed. Any field
that says who you are, what you may do, or what you are worth must come from the
token, never from the payload.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet 09_auth_and_testing ex4
```

## Hint 1

Validate, then create, then report — lesson 07's create endpoint with one extra
rule.

The extra rule is about a property you must *not* use. Read `NewNote` again and
ask which of its two fields a caller is entitled to decide.

## Hint 2

The validation failure is a ProblemDetails, keyed by field:

```csharp
return TypedResults.ValidationProblem(
    new Dictionary<string, string[]> { ["text"] = ["Text is required."] });
```

For the create, `store.Add(owner, text)` returns the new note with its id. The
`owner` argument is `user.Identity?.Name` — the token — and `request.Owner` is
never read at all. Deleting the temptation is the exercise.

Then `TypedResults.Created($"/l09/notes/{note.Id}", note)`.

## Hint 3

```csharp
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(request.Text))
{
    return TypedResults.ValidationProblem(/* … */);
}

string owner = user.Identity?.Name ?? "";
var note = store.Add(owner, request.Text);

return TypedResults.Created($"/l09/notes/{note.Id}", note);
```

Worth a comment in your own code saying that `request.Owner` is deliberately
ignored — otherwise the next person to read the file will "fix" it.

# d01 — Routing drills

Eight problems on route templates: parameters, constraints, verbs, optional
segments, catch-alls, precedence, link generation and binding sources. They
drill lesson **01_routing_endpoints** — redo that one first if this set feels
like guessing rather than recalling.

Every endpoint lives under `/d01/…` and every answer comes from
`src/Api/D01_Routing/Network.cs`: five stops, six departures, three lines. Read
that file once and you never have to read it again.

## Exercise 1 — one stop, by id

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d01/stops/{id:int}` answers **200**
with the stop that has that id, **404** when the network has no such stop. The
`{id:int}` constraint stays where it is.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — two parameters, one constraint

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d01/departures/{line}/{hour}` answers
**200** with a JSON array of the destinations leaving on that line at that
hour, sorted A–Z.

A line the network does not run is a **404**. A line that runs but has nothing
at that hour is a **200 with an empty array** — those are different claims.
`hour` is constrained to `range(0,23)`; leave it constrained and notice what
that does to hour 24.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the verb is half of the route

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex3.cs`. Map exactly two endpoints on
`/d01/stops/{id:int}/watch`: **PUT** and **DELETE**, both **204** when the stop
exists and **404** when it does not.

Map nothing else there. What the framework then does about `POST` and `GET` is
the point of the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — an optional segment

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex4.cs`. `GET /d01/lines/{line}/timetable/{day?}`
answers **200** with `{"line": …, "day": …, "hours": [ … ]}` where `hours` is
that line's departure hours, distinct and ascending.

`day` defaults to `weekday`. `weekend` drops every hour before 09:00. Any other
day is a **400**. A line the network does not run is a **404**.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the catch-all

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d01/tiles/…` answers **200** with
`{"path": …, "segments": …}` for *any* number of trailing segments, including
none: `/d01/tiles/a/b/c.png` is `"a/b/c.png"` and 3, `/d01/tiles` is `""` and 0.

The template as shipped only matches one segment. Two characters fix that.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — literal beats parameter

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex6.cs`. Two endpoints under `/d01/zones`:

- `GET /d01/zones/all` — **200** with every zone, distinct and sorted A–Z
- `GET /d01/zones/{zone}` — **200** with the names of that zone's stops, sorted
  A–Z; **404** when no stop is in it

The parameterised one is registered first on purpose. Leave it that way.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — name a route, then generate its URL

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex7.cs`. Give `GET /d01/routes/{id:int}` the name
`Ex7.RouteName` and have it answer **200** with `{"id": …, "line": …}` (route 1
is `Network.Lines[0]`), **404** otherwise.

Then `GET /d01/routes/{id:int}/link` answers **200** with
`{"self": …, "next": …}`, both produced by the injected `LinkGenerator` from
that *name*, never by concatenating strings. `next` is `null` for the last
route. **404** when there is no such route.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — say where each parameter comes from

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d01/search/{scope}` answers **200**
with `{"scope": …, "term": …, "zone": …, "matches": [ … ]}`.

- `scope` comes from the route and is `stops` or `lines`; anything else is a
  **400**
- `term` comes from the query parameter **`q`** — not from one called `term`
- `zone` comes from the **`X-Zone`** request header, narrows stops to that zone,
  and is ignored for lines
- `term` keeps names containing it, case-insensitively; no term keeps
  everything; `matches` is sorted A–Z

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d01_routing

## Notes

Every problem in this set is the same question asked eight ways: *what does the
route table do before your handler exists?* Routing runs first. It picks one
endpoint out of every candidate template, and by the time your code is called
the decision is already made — which is why so many "my endpoint is not being
hit" bugs are not bugs in the endpoint at all.

The two ideas that unify the set are **matching** and **precedence**.
Constraints, verbs, optional segments and catch-alls all change what a template
*matches*; when two templates match the same URL, precedence decides which one
wins, and it is never "whichever I wrote first". Keep those two words separate
in your head and the whole subsystem stops being mysterious.

The corollary worth memorising: a route constraint can only ever produce a
**404 or a 405**, never a 400. If your API needs to tell a client that a value
was the wrong shape, that is validation, and validation happens in the handler.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that a route parameter is *data* your handler
receives, and that a missing row is a 404 rather than a 200 carrying null. The
classic mistake is returning `Ok(stop)` unconditionally, which serialises
`null` and hands the client a 200 that means "not found" — a distinction no HTTP
client can recover. The model answer looks the stop up, and the `is null` branch
is the whole answer.

The second thing this drills is that `{id:int}` is not validation. `CEN` does
not produce a 400 and never reaches you; it simply fails to match the template,
and routing has nothing else to try, so it is a 404.

## ex2

Two route values, and both of them have to narrow the result — filtering by only
one is the classic mistake, because with this data it still returns something
plausible. The other half of the drill is the 404-versus-empty distinction: a
line the network does not run is a 404, and a line that runs but is quiet at
midday is a 200 with `[]`. Those are different claims about the world, and
clients branch on them.

`range(0,23)` is the model answer's third teaching point. Hour 24 is a 404
because the constraint is part of *matching*; wanting a 400 there means wanting
validation, which means an unconstrained `{hour:int}` and an explicit check.

## ex3

The verb is part of the route key, so `PUT /watch` and `DELETE /watch` are two
endpoints on one path. The payoff is what you get for free: because *something*
maps that path, an unmapped `POST` gets **405 Method Not Allowed** with an
`Allow` header, not a 404. The classic mistake is reaching for `MapMethods` or
`Map` to "handle everything and switch on the method", which throws that away
and makes your API answer 404 for a request that was merely addressed to the
wrong verb.

## ex4

`{day?}` makes the last segment optional, so one template matches two URLs, and
the absent value arrives as `null`. The model answer's first line is
`day ?? "weekday"` — resolve the default *once*, at the top, then work with a
non-null value. The classic mistake is scattering `day == null` checks through
the rest of the method and getting one of them wrong.

Note the deliberate contrast with ex2: `tuesday` is a 400, because your handler
received it and refused it, while hour 24 was a 404, because routing refused to
call you. Same "bad input", different layer, different code.

## ex5

`{**path}` is the catch-all, and it is the only route parameter that can contain
a `/`. The single-star form `{*path}` is the legacy spelling that does not
re-encode slashes on the way out; prefer the double star. The classic mistake is
`{path}`, which matches exactly one segment, so `a/b/c.png` 404s and the fix
looks like a data problem rather than a template problem.

Also worth keeping: a catch-all matches **zero** segments too, so the bare
prefix is a 200 with an empty string — which is why the model answer coalesces
to `""` before splitting rather than assuming a value is there.

## ex6

Precedence, stated once: routing scores each segment, and a **literal beats a
parameter**, which beats a catch-all. Registration order is not a tiebreaker,
which is why the exercise registers `{zone}` first and `all` still wins. The
classic mistake is believing order matters and "fixing" a precedence problem by
shuffling `MapGet` calls — it works by accident in frameworks that match
top-down, and teaches a rule that is false here.

The model answer's second decision is the 404 for zone `Z`: a zone with no stops
is not an empty zone, it is not a zone, and saying so with a 404 keeps the
resource model honest.

## ex7

`WithName` makes an endpoint *addressable*, and `LinkGenerator.GetPathByName`
turns a name plus values into a URL from the route table itself. The point is
not convenience, it is that the template becomes changeable: move
`/d01/routes/{id}` tomorrow and every generated link moves with it, while every
string you concatenated by hand quietly rots.

Two details in the model answer. Names must be unique across the whole
application — that is why this one is `d01-route` and not `route`. And `next` is
`null` on the last route rather than a link to a 404: absence of a link is how a
client learns it has reached the end, which is the whole idea behind hypermedia
controls, `Link` headers and the `next` field in every paged API you have used.

## ex8

Minimal APIs infer binding sources, and the inference is good enough that people
forget it exists — until a name does not line up. `q` in the URL and `term` in
C# are different names, so `[FromQuery(Name = "q")]` is the only thing that
connects them; without it the parameter silently binds to a query parameter
called `term` that nobody sends, and you get `null` and no error. Headers are
worse: they are *never* inferred, so `zone` binds from nothing at all unless you
write `[FromHeader]`.

The model answer's reasoning is "make every source explicit at the boundary".
The classic mistake is trusting the inference on a public API and discovering
the mismatch in production, where a silently-null filter looks like a data bug.

## Further reading

- [Routing in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/routing) — templates, constraints, precedence and URL generation, in one place.
- [Route constraint reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/routing#route-constraint-reference) — every built-in constraint, including `range`, `alpha` and `regex`.
- [Parameter binding in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding) — the inference rules and the `[From*]` attributes that override them.
- [Routing in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/routing) — route groups, named endpoints and `LinkGenerator`.
- [RFC 9110 §15.5.6 — 405 Method Not Allowed](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-405-method-not-allowed) — what the status actually promises, and the `Allow` header it owes the client.

## Exercise 1 — one stop, by id

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d01/stops/{id:int}` answers **200**
with the stop that has that id, **404** when the network has no such stop. The
`{id:int}` constraint stays where it is.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The route already hands you the id — the whole exercise is the two-branch answer
that follows. One of the five stops has that id, or none of them does, and those
two cases get different status codes.

Do not touch the `{id:int}` constraint. The last check in the gate is about what
that constraint already does for you.

`Network.Stops.FirstOrDefault(...)` gives you the stop or `null`. `First` throws,
and a thrown exception is a 500, not a 404.

Then `TypedResults.NotFound()` or `TypedResults.Ok(stop)`. Both branches must be
returned from the same method, so let the null check pick between them rather
than returning `Ok` and hoping.

## Exercise 3 — the verb is half of the route

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex3.cs`. Map exactly two endpoints on
`/d01/stops/{id:int}/watch`: **PUT** and **DELETE**, both **204** when the stop
exists and **404** when it does not.

the point of the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two `Map…` calls, one per verb, on the same template. The two handlers are
already written for you to fill in; the mapping is the part that is missing.

Resist the urge to map the path once and switch on `context.Request.Method` —
the last two checks in the gate exist to catch exactly that.

## Hint 2

`app.MapPut(template, Watch)` and `app.MapDelete(template, Unwatch)`.

Both handlers answer `TypedResults.NoContent()` when a stop with that id exists
and `TypedResults.NotFound()` when it does not. `Network.Stops.Any(...)` is
enough — you do not need the stop itself.

The 405s then happen without you: routing sees candidates for the path, none of
which accept POST, and says so.

## Hint 1

A normal route parameter matches exactly one segment, which is why
`/d01/tiles/a/b/c.png` currently 404s. There is a spelling of a route parameter
that matches the entire remainder of the path, slashes included.

The handler itself is four lines once the template is right.

## Hint 2

`{**path}` is the catch-all. It also matches *zero* segments, so `/d01/tiles`
reaches the handler with `path` bound to `null`.

Coalesce first (`path ?? ""`), then count with
`value.Split('/', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Length` — the option is
what keeps a stray trailing slash from counting as a segment.

## Exercise 8 — say where each parameter comes from

Edit `src/Api/D01_Routing/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d01/search/{scope}` answers **200**
with `{"scope": …, "term": …, "zone": …, "matches": [ … ]}`.

- `scope` comes from the route and is `stops` or `lines`; anything else is a
  **400**
- `term` comes from the query parameter **`q`** — not from one called `term`
- `zone` comes from the **`X-Zone`** request header, narrows stops to that zone,
  and is ignored for lines
- `term` keeps names containing it, case-insensitively; no term keeps
  everything; `matches` is sorted A–Z

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d01_routing ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three parameters, three different places in the request: the path, the query
string, and a header. Two of those the framework can guess; one of them it never
guesses. And one of the guessable ones is guessing *wrong*, because the name in
the URL is not the name in your C#.

Say what you mean on all three, then write the filtering.

## Hint 2

The attributes live in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc` (already imported in the
stub): `[FromRoute]`, `[FromQuery(Name = "q")]`, `[FromHeader(Name = "X-Zone")]`.

The `Name` argument is the whole point of the exercise — without it the
parameter binds by its C# name, so `?q=ar` does nothing and `?term=ar` does
something, which is precisely backwards.

Then: reject an unknown scope with `TypedResults.BadRequest(...)`, build the
candidate names (`Network.Lines`, or stop names narrowed by zone when the header
is present), filter with
`Contains(term, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` when there is a term, and
sort.

## Hint 3

Build the candidates as an `IEnumerable<string>` and layer the filters onto it,
rather than writing four near-identical LINQ queries:

```csharp
IEnumerable<string> candidates = scope == "lines"
    ? Network.Lines
    : Network.Stops.Where(s => zone is null || s.Zone == zone).Select(s => s.Name);
```

`zone is null || …` is what makes an absent header mean "no filter" instead of
"match the empty zone".

Left for you: the exact shape of the response record, and whether `term` and
`zone` are echoed as sent or as resolved. The gate expects them as sent.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three parameters, three different places in the request: the path, the query
string, and a header. Two of those the framework can guess; one of them it never
guesses. And one of the guessable ones is guessing *wrong*, because the name in
the URL is not the name in your C#.

Say what you mean on all three, then write the filtering.

## Hint 2

The attributes live in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc` (already imported in the
stub): `[FromRoute]`, `[FromQuery(Name = "q")]`, `[FromHeader(Name = "X-Zone")]`.

The `Name` argument is the whole point of the exercise — without it the
parameter binds by its C# name, so `?q=ar` does nothing and `?term=ar` does
something, which is precisely backwards.

Then: reject an unknown scope with `TypedResults.BadRequest(...)`, build the
candidate names (`Network.Lines`, or stop names narrowed by zone when the header
is present), filter with
`Contains(term, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` when there is a term, and
sort.

## Hint 3

Build the candidates as an `IEnumerable<string>` and layer the filters onto it,
rather than writing four near-identical LINQ queries:

```csharp
IEnumerable<string> candidates = scope == "lines"
    ? Network.Lines
    : Network.Stops.Where(s => zone is null || s.Zone == zone).Select(s => s.Name);
```

`zone is null || …` is what makes an absent header mean "no filter" instead of
"match the empty zone".

Left for you: the exact shape of the response record, and whether `term` and
`zone` are echoed as sent or as resolved. The gate expects them as sent.

# d02 — Route group drills

Eight problems on `MapGroup`: prefixes, nesting, parameters in a prefix, and the
endpoint filters a group hangs on everything inside it. They drill lesson
**01_routing_endpoints** — go back to it if the group root and the group prefix
still feel like the same thing.

Everything lives under `/d02/…`. The data is five recipes in
`src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Kitchen.cs`, plus the two filter types ex6 asks you to
arrange.

## Exercise 1 — one group, two endpoints

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex1.cs`. A group for `/d02/recipes` with:

- the group **root** — **200** with every recipe title, sorted A–Z
- `/{id:int}` — **200** with the whole recipe, **404** when there is none

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — groups inside groups

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex2.cs`. A `/d02/admin` group holding two more:

- `/recipes` with `/count` on it — **200** with `{"count": …}`
- `/courses` with its own root — **200** with every course, distinct, sorted A–Z

Nothing else may answer. `/d02/recipes/count` and `/d02/admin/recipes` are both
**404**.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a parameter in the prefix

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex3.cs`. A group whose prefix is
`/d02/courses/{course}`:

- the group root — **200** with that course's titles, sorted A–Z
- `/longest` — **200** with the title of that course's slowest recipe

A course no recipe has is a **404** at both.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — one filter for the whole group

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex4.cs`. Add **one** endpoint filter to the
`/d02/kitchen` group:

- no `X-Chef` request header → **401**, and the handler must not run
- otherwise → set the response header `X-Chef-Ack` to that chef's name and let
  the request through unchanged

Both endpoints are already mapped. Do not touch them.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — a filter that reads the handler's arguments

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex5.cs`. Add **one** endpoint filter to the
`/d02/pantry` group that rejects an `id` above **100** with a **400** before
either handler runs. Ids of 100 or less pass through untouched.

Both handlers take the id as their first parameter.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the order they run in

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex6.cs`. Attach the given `ReportFilter` and three
`MarkFilter`s — named `a`, `b` and `c` — so that `GET /d02/trace/run` answers
with exactly:

```
a>,b>,c>,handler,c<,b<,a<
```

Two of the marks belong on the group and one belongs on the endpoint. The
`ReportFilter` has to see the finished trace.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — rewrite the result on the way out

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex7.cs`. Add **one** endpoint filter to the
`/d02/menu` group that wraps a `List<string>` result in an `Envelope`
(`{"items": [ … ], "count": …}`) and hands anything else back untouched.

`/d02/menu/health` does not return a list, and its body must come out exactly as
the handler wrote it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — nested groups, and a filter each

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex8.cs`. Build this, in one method:

- a `/d02/v1` group whose filter answers **400** unless the request carries
  `X-Api-Version: 1`
- inside it, a `/kitchens/{kitchen}` group whose filter sets the response header
  `X-Kitchen-Checked: yes` and then answers **404** unless the kitchen is one of
  `Cookbook.Kitchens`
- `/recipes` — **200** with the titles that kitchen's courses cover, sorted A–Z
- `/recipes/{id:int}` — **200** with `{"title": …}` when that kitchen serves that
  recipe, **404** otherwise

When the version header is missing, the inner filter must never run.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d02_route_groups

## Notes

A route group is two things at once, and keeping them apart is most of this
lesson. It is a **prefix** — `MapGroup("/d02/recipes")` means every endpoint
below it starts there — and it is a **place to hang conventions**: filters,
metadata, authorization, anything that applies to a set of endpoints rather than
to one.

The prefix half is mechanical. The convention half is where the design payoff
is: a rule written on a group applies to endpoints that do not exist yet. That
is the difference between security (or validation, or versioning) that is
opt-out and security that is opt-in, and opt-in is the one that eventually ships
with a hole in it.

Endpoint filters are the mechanism, and they compose like an onion:
group filters wrap endpoint filters, outer groups wrap inner groups, and within
one builder the first filter added is the outermost. Every filter gets to act on
the way in, on the way out, or both — and any of them can decline to call `next`
and become the response.

## ex1

Really testing one thing: the group root is `""`, not the prefix again. Writing
`group.MapGet("/recipes", …)` inside a group that already says `/recipes` gives
you `/d02/recipes/recipes` and a 404 that looks like the group did not work. The
model answer maps `""` and `"/{id:int}"`, and the prefix appears exactly once, in
exactly one place — which is the reason to use a group at all.

## ex2

Nesting concatenates, and nothing else. `MapGroup` on a group returns another
group whose prefix is the parent's plus its own, so three levels give you three
segments. The classic mistake is hanging the inner group off `app` out of habit,
which still compiles, still maps, and quietly produces `/d02/recipes/count`
instead of `/d02/admin/recipes/count`.

The other check is worth noticing: `/d02/admin/recipes` is a 404 because nothing
is mapped there. A group is a prefix, not a resource — it never answers on its
own.

## ex3

A group prefix is a route template like any other, so it can carry parameters,
and those parameters bind into every handler underneath by name. This is the
tidy way to express a nested resource: say `{course}` once, and every endpoint
below is scoped to it.

The model answer's reasoning: the same route value has to *narrow* both
endpoints, so both handlers take `string course` and neither has to know it came
from a group. The classic mistake is reading it out of `HttpContext.RouteValues`
by hand, which works and throws away the binding, the nullability and the
compiler's help.

## ex4

The drill is the shape of a guard: read something, decide, and either return
your own result or `await next(context)`. Returning a result *without* awaiting
`next` is what short-circuiting means, and the gate checks the body is empty
precisely because "set the status and carry on anyway" is the classic mistake —
the work you were trying to prevent still happens.

The reason this belongs on the group is the sentence in the failure message: the
next endpoint someone adds is guarded by default. Per-endpoint guards are one
forgotten line away from a hole.

## ex5

`EndpointFilterInvocationContext.GetArgument<T>(index)` gives a filter the
arguments the handler is about to receive, already bound and converted. That is
what makes filters a validation layer rather than a header-inspection layer: you
can reject `id = 101` without re-parsing the URL.

The status code is the teaching point. A route constraint could have kept 101
out, but it would have produced a 404 — "no such endpoint" — when what you mean
is "that id is out of range", which is a 400. Choose the layer by the answer you
want to give.

Positional arguments are the sharp edge: `GetArgument<T>(0)` is a promise about
the handler's signature that the compiler cannot check, so a reordered parameter
list breaks the filter silently. In a larger codebase, prefer reading the route
value or using a filter factory that inspects the method's parameters.

## ex6

The ordering rules, stated once and worth memorising: **group filters run
outside endpoint filters**, an **outer group runs outside an inner group**, and
within one builder **the first filter added is the outermost**. So marks appear
in the order you added them and unwind in reverse — `a>,b>,c>,handler,c<,b<,a<`.

The classic mistake is assuming the last one added wins, by analogy with
`services.Add…` replacements. Filters do not replace each other; they nest.

The practical consequence: put the things that must always happen — correlation
ids, exception handling, timing — outermost, because a filter that returns early
takes every filter inside it with it.

## ex7

A filter sees the handler's return value as `object?` and may return something
else, which makes response shaping a cross-cutting concern rather than eight
copies of the same wrapper. This is how envelopes, HATEOAS links and
compatibility shims get added to an existing API without touching a handler.

The model answer's important line is the `is List<string>` test. A filter that
wraps *everything* it sees also wraps the 400s, the 404s and the health check,
and every one of those is a client-visible break. Narrow what you transform, and
pass the rest through by returning the object you were given.

## ex8

Everything at once: two nested groups, a filter on each, a parameterised inner
prefix, and a route value that has to narrow the data rather than decorate the
URL.

The check that matters is the last one. When the outer filter returns without
awaiting `next`, the inner filter never runs — proved here by the absent
`X-Kitchen-Checked` header. That is the property you rely on when you put
authentication outermost: everything inside it is unreachable to an
unauthenticated caller, including code written next year by someone who never
read this file.

The other judgement call is the 404 for recipe 1 in the south kitchen. It exists,
but not *here*, and answering 404 rather than 403 avoids telling a caller that a
resource they may not see exists — the same reasoning that makes per-user
filtering a 404 rather than a leak.

## Further reading

- [Route groups in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/route-handlers#route-groups) — `MapGroup`, nesting, and what a group does to metadata.
- [Filters in minimal API apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/min-api-filters) — `IEndpointFilter`, `EndpointFilterInvocationContext`, short-circuiting and ordering.
- [Routing in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/routing) — how prefixes and templates combine into the route table.
- [Parameter binding in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding) — why a group's route parameter binds into a handler by name.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — one group, two endpoints

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex1.cs`. A group for `/d02/recipes` with:

- the group **root** — **200** with every recipe title, sorted A–Z
- `/{id:int}` — **200** with the whole recipe, **404** when there is none

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`app.MapGroup(prefix)` hands you back something you map on instead of `app`.
Everything you map on it starts with the prefix — which means the prefix belongs
in exactly one place, and the endpoints must not repeat it.

Two endpoints: the list, and one recipe.

## Hint 2

The group root is the **empty string**, not `"/"` and not the prefix again:

```csharp
var group = app.MapGroup("/d02/recipes");
group.MapGet("", List);
group.MapGet("/{id:int}", GetRecipe);
```

The handlers are ordinary: sort the titles with `StringComparer.Ordinal`, and
let `FirstOrDefault` plus a null check pick between `Ok` and `NotFound`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A group prefix is a route template, so it may contain a parameter. Put
`{course}` in the prefix and both endpoints below inherit it — including the one
mapped on the group root.

The handlers already declare a `string course` parameter. Nothing else is needed
to receive it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var group = app.MapGroup("/d02/courses/{course}");
group.MapGet("", Titles);
group.MapGet("/longest", Longest);
```

Both handlers filter `Cookbook.Recipes` on the course first. An empty result is
not an empty course — it means no such course — so both return
`TypedResults.NotFound()` in that case.

"Longest" is by `Minutes`: `OrderByDescending(r => r.Minutes).FirstOrDefault()`.

## Hint 1

A group prefix is a route template, so it may contain a parameter. Put
`{course}` in the prefix and both endpoints below inherit it — including the one
mapped on the group root.

The handlers already declare a `string course` parameter. Nothing else is needed
to receive it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var group = app.MapGroup("/d02/courses/{course}");
group.MapGet("", Titles);
group.MapGet("/longest", Longest);
```

Both handlers filter `Cookbook.Recipes` on the course first. An empty result is
not an empty course — it means no such course — so both return
`TypedResults.NotFound()` in that case.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`group.AddEndpointFilter(async (context, next) => { … })` wraps every endpoint in
the group. Inside, `context.HttpContext` is the request you are guarding and
`next(context)` is the rest of the pipeline, including the handler.

Two outcomes: return your own result *without* calling `next`, or set a header
and return what `next` gives you.

## Hint 2

Read the header with `context.HttpContext.Request.Headers["X-Chef"].ToString()`
— an absent header is an empty string, so `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` covers
both cases at once.

Refuse with `TypedResults.StatusCode(StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized)`, and
note that returning it is the whole short-circuit: there is no `next` call on
that path.

On the accepted path, write `Response.Headers["X-Chef-Ack"]` *before* awaiting
`next`, then `return await next(context);` so the handler's own result survives.

## Hint 1

The filter does not have to re-read the URL. By the time it runs, the framework
has already bound the handler's parameters, and the filter can see them — in
order, by position.

Both handlers take the id first.

## Hint 2

`context.GetArgument<int>(0)` is the id.

Then it is the same two-branch shape as ex4: `TypedResults.BadRequest(…)` for
anything over 100, `await next(context)` otherwise.

Note what you are *not* doing: a `{id:int:max(100)}` constraint would keep 101
out too, but it would answer 404 — "no such endpoint" — when the honest answer
is "that id is out of range".

## Exercise 6 — the order they run in

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex6.cs`. Attach the given `ReportFilter` and three
`MarkFilter`s — named `a`, `b` and `c` — so that `GET /d02/trace/run` answers
with exactly:

```
a>,b>,c>,handler,c<,b<,a<
```

Two of the marks belong on the group and one belongs on the endpoint. The
`ReportFilter` has to see the finished trace.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Filters nest rather than queue. Work out which one has to be *outermost* — the
one that must still be running when everything else has finished — and which one
has to be *innermost*, closest to the handler.

Then remember there are two places to attach a filter: the group, and the
endpoint.

## Hint 2

Three rules decide everything here:

- a group's filters run outside the endpoint's filters
- within one builder, the first filter added is the outermost
- the mark in the trace goes on the way in, and again on the way out

So `c` — the only one between the innermost group filter and the handler — has
to be attached with `.AddEndpointFilter(...)` on the `MapGet` itself, and `a`
has to be added to the group before `b`.

## Hint 3

`ReportFilter` answers with `D02Trace.Read(...)` after awaiting `next`, so it has
to be outside every mark or it will report a half-finished trace — which means
adding it to the group **first**, before `a`.

```csharp
group.AddEndpointFilter(new ReportFilter());
group.AddEndpointFilter(new MarkFilter("a"));
…
```

Left for you: the remaining two lines, and convincing yourself why swapping any
two of them changes the answer.

## Hint 1

Filters nest rather than queue. Work out which one has to be *outermost* — the
one that must still be running when everything else has finished — and which one
has to be *innermost*, closest to the handler.

Then remember there are two places to attach a filter: the group, and the
endpoint.

## Hint 2

Three rules decide everything here:

- a group's filters run outside the endpoint's filters
- within one builder, the first filter added is the outermost
- the mark in the trace goes on the way in, and again on the way out

So `c` — the only one between the innermost group filter and the handler — has
to be attached with `.AddEndpointFilter(...)` on the `MapGet` itself, and `a`
has to be added to the group before `b`.

## Hint 3

`ReportFilter` answers with `D02Trace.Read(...)` after awaiting `next`, so it has
to be outside every mark or it will report a half-finished trace — which means
adding it to the group **first**, before `a`.

```csharp
group.AddEndpointFilter(new ReportFilter());
group.AddEndpointFilter(new MarkFilter("a"));
…
```

Left for you: the remaining two lines, and convincing yourself why swapping any
two of them changes the answer.

## Exercise 8 — nested groups, and a filter each

Edit `src/Api/D02_RouteGroups/Ex8.cs`. Build this, in one method:

- a `/d02/v1` group whose filter answers **400** unless the request carries
  `X-Api-Version: 1`
- inside it, a `/kitchens/{kitchen}` group whose filter sets the response header
  `X-Kitchen-Checked: yes` and then answers **404** unless the kitchen is one of
  `Cookbook.Kitchens`
- `/recipes` — **200** with the titles that kitchen's courses cover, sorted A–Z
- `/recipes/{id:int}` — **200** with `{"title": …}` when that kitchen serves that
  recipe, **404** otherwise

When the version header is missing, the inner filter must never run.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d02_route_groups ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Nothing here is new — it is ex2's nesting, ex3's parameterised prefix and ex4's
guard in one method. Build it outside in: the version group, its filter, the
kitchen group inside it, its filter, then the two endpoints.

The last check in the gate is about what does *not* happen when the outer filter
refuses.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var api = app.MapGroup("/d02/v1");
api.AddEndpointFilter(async (context, next) => { … });

var kitchens = api.MapGroup("/kitchens/{kitchen}");
kitchens.AddEndpointFilter(async (context, next) => { … });
```

The version filter compares
`context.HttpContext.Request.Headers["X-Api-Version"]` to `"1"` and returns
`TypedResults.BadRequest(…)` when it does not match.

The kitchen filter cannot use `GetArgument`, because it needs a value the
*group* supplied: read
`context.HttpContext.Request.RouteValues["kitchen"]?.ToString()`. Set the
`X-Kitchen-Checked` header before you decide, so the gate can see it ran.

## Hint 3

Both handlers start from the same lookup:

```csharp
string[] courses = Cookbook.Kitchens[kitchen];
```

The indexer is safe because the filter has already rejected every kitchen that
is not a key — that is what a guard buys you, and it is why the handlers can be
this short.

For the single recipe, put both conditions in one predicate
(`r.Id == id && courses.Contains(r.Course)`), so a recipe this kitchen does not
serve is indistinguishable from one that does not exist.

Left for you: the response shape for the single recipe, and which of the two
filters owns which failure.
