exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Nothing here is new — it is ex2's nesting, ex3's parameterised prefix and ex4's
guard in one method. Build it outside in: the version group, its filter, the
kitchen group inside it, its filter, then the two endpoints.

The last check in the gate is about what does *not* happen when the outer filter
refuses.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var api = app.MapGroup("/d02/v1");
api.AddEndpointFilter(async (context, next) => { … });

var kitchens = api.MapGroup("/kitchens/{kitchen}");
kitchens.AddEndpointFilter(async (context, next) => { … });
```

The version filter compares
`context.HttpContext.Request.Headers["X-Api-Version"]` to `"1"` and returns
`TypedResults.BadRequest(…)` when it does not match.

The kitchen filter cannot use `GetArgument`, because it needs a value the
*group* supplied: read
`context.HttpContext.Request.RouteValues["kitchen"]?.ToString()`. Set the
`X-Kitchen-Checked` header before you decide, so the gate can see it ran.

## Hint 3

Both handlers start from the same lookup:

```csharp
string[] courses = Cookbook.Kitchens[kitchen];
```

The indexer is safe because the filter has already rejected every kitchen that
is not a key — that is what a guard buys you, and it is why the handlers can be
this short.

For the single recipe, put both conditions in one predicate
(`r.Id == id && courses.Contains(r.Course)`), so a recipe this kitchen does not
serve is indistinguishable from one that does not exist.

Left for you: the response shape for the single recipe, and which of the two
filters owns which failure.

lessons.briefing:
# d03 — Results and status code drills

Eight problems on picking the right status code and the right `TypedResults`
helper: 200 versus 404 for an empty collection, 201 and its `Location`, 204,
409, 400 versus 422, content types, the union return type, and `CreatedAtRoute`.
They drill lesson **01_routing_endpoints** — go back to it if the choice between
these codes still feels like taste rather than a rule.

Everything is under `/d03/…` against `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Desk.cs`:
three bookings, three rooms, and a store that really mutates. Each gate gets its
own application, so an exercise that deletes something cannot affect the others.

## Exercise 1 — empty is not missing

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex1.cs`.

- `GET /d03/bookings` — **200** with the bookings, id ascending. An optional
  `state` filters them, and a filter that matches nothing is **still a 200**.
- `GET /d03/bookings/{id:int}` — **200**, or **404** when there is none.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — 201, and the header that makes it useful

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex2.cs`. `POST /d03/bookings` with
`{"room": …, "guest": …}`:

- **201** with `Location: /d03/bookings/{id}` and the created booking as the body
- a blank room or a blank guest is a **400**, and nothing is written

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — 204 has nothing to say

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex3.cs`. `DELETE /d03/bookings/{id:int}` is
**204 with an empty body** when the booking was there and **404** when it was
not — including the second time you delete the same one.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — four outcomes, one endpoint

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex4.cs`.
`PUT /d03/bookings/{id:int}/state` with `{"state": …}`:

- **400** when the state is not one of `Desk.States` — *even if the id is also
  wrong*
- **404** when there is no such booking
- **409** when the booking is already `cancelled`
- **204** otherwise, and the change sticks

The order those checks go in is the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — 400 for malformed, 422 for impossible

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex5.cs`. `POST /d03/bookings/quote` with
`{"room": …, "nights": …}`:

- a blank room or `nights` below 1 → **400 validation problem**
  (`application/problem+json`) keyed `room` / `nights`
- a well-formed request naming a room the desk does not have → **422**
- otherwise **200** with `{"room": …, "nights": …, "totalCents": …}`, where the
  total is `capacity * Desk.NightlyRatePerHead * nights`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the same data, two content types

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex6.cs`.
`GET /d03/bookings/{id:int}/receipt?format=…`:

- `json` (the default) → **200 `application/json`** with
  `{"bookingId": …, "guest": …, "room": …}`
- `text` → **200 `text/plain`** with exactly `Booking 1: Ada in Sakura`
- anything else → **400**
- a booking that does not exist → **404**, whichever format was asked for

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — the return type lists every outcome

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex7.cs`. Keep the signature's union return
type — `Results<Ok<DeskRoom>, NotFound, BadRequest<string>>` — and fill in
`GET /d03/rooms/{id:int}`:

- an id above **100** → **400** whose body names the id
- an id the desk has no room for → **404**
- otherwise → **200** with the room

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — CreatedAtRoute, and a conflict that explains itself

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex8.cs`. Give
`GET /d03/desk/rooms/{id:int}` the name `Ex8.RoomRouteName` (**200** with the
room, **404** otherwise), then `POST /d03/desk/rooms` with
`{"name": …, "capacity": …}`:

- **201** whose `Location` is generated **from that route name**, body = the room
- a blank name or a capacity below 1 → **400**
- a name the desk already has → **409 ProblemDetails** whose `detail` names it

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d03_results_statuscodes

## Notes

A status code is the only part of your response every client understands without
reading your documentation. Proxies, caches, retry libraries, browsers and
monitoring dashboards all branch on it, which is why "200 with an error inside"
is not a style choice — it is a lie the whole ecosystem believes.

Two questions decide almost every code in this set. **Whose fault is it?** 4xx
means the caller has to change something, 5xx means you do. **What changed?**
201 says something new exists at a URL, 204 says it worked and there is nothing
to send, 409 says the request was fine and the current state refuses it.

The pattern that unites the eight problems is the same three lines every time:
validate the request, find the resource, then act — and each stage has its own
status code. Doing them in a different order gives a caller the wrong thing to
fix, which is exactly what ex4 is built to catch.

## ex1

A collection and an item fail differently, and this is the single most commonly
confused pair in REST. `/bookings?state=pending` matching nothing is a **200
with `[]`**: the collection exists, and its current contents are none. A missing
`/bookings/99` is a **404**: no such resource.

The classic mistake is a 404 for the empty list, usually written to be
"helpful". It forces every client to treat "no results" as an error path, breaks
the natural `for` loop over the response, and makes an empty filter
indistinguishable from a typo in the URL. The model answer simply never checks
whether the list is empty.

## ex2

Two things make a 201 useful, and only one of them is the status. The
`Location` header tells the client where the thing it just created now lives;
without it the client has to guess, re-fetch the collection, or parse the id out
of the body and rebuild the URL itself. Returning the created resource in the
body as well saves that round trip.

The other half of the drill is ordering: validate, then write. The gate lists
the bookings afterwards precisely because "return a 400 *after* calling
`store.Add`" passes every status-code check and corrupts the data.

## ex3

204 means *no content*, and it is a promise: there is no body, and the client
should not try to read one. Writing `{"deleted":true}` alongside a 204 is
malformed — some HTTP stacks will discard it, some will error, and none of them
will use it.

The second delete being a 404 is a deliberate choice worth being able to defend.
DELETE is meant to be idempotent, and many APIs answer 204 every time so that a
retried delete looks successful; that is defensible too, because the *end state*
is what the client asked for. Whichever you pick, pick it once and write it down,
because a client's retry logic depends on it.

## ex4

Four outcomes, and the exercise is really about the order you check them in. The
gate's `nonsenseOnMissing` case is the trap: a bad state *and* a bad id must be a
400, because you should reject a request you cannot understand before you go
looking for a resource. Answering 404 there tells the caller to fix the id when
the actual problem is the body.

409 is the code most APIs forget. The request is well formed and the resource
exists — so it is not a 400 and not a 404 — and the *current state* refuses the
transition. Anything modelled as a state machine has 409s in it: cancelled
bookings, closed accounts, already-shipped orders, stale ETags.

## ex5

400 and 422 split "I could not understand your request" from "I understood it and
it cannot be done". A blank room is a shape problem: 400. A perfectly-shaped
request naming a room that does not exist is a semantic problem: 422
Unprocessable Content.

The line is genuinely blurry — plenty of good APIs use 400 for both, and the
distinction only earns its keep when clients act on it differently (retry after
fixing the field, versus retry never). What is not optional is the *body*:
`ValidationProblem` produces an RFC 9457 document with an `errors` dictionary
keyed by field, which is a machine-readable contract, unlike a sentence.

Note that the model answer collects **all** the errors before returning. An
endpoint that fails on the first problem makes the client play twenty questions.

## ex6

`TypedResults.Json`, `Text`, `Content`, `File`, `Stream` and `Bytes` are the
shape-choosing helpers, and the thing they really control is the `Content-Type`
header. `TypedResults.Text(s, "text/plain")` sends the string as-is;
`TypedResults.Ok(s)` sends it as a *JSON* string, quotes included, which is a
different document.

The 400 for `format=xml` is the judgement call. Falling back to JSON is
friendlier and worse: a client that asked for XML and silently got JSON has no
way to detect the mismatch until something downstream breaks. Real content
negotiation lives in the `Accept` header and answers **406 Not Acceptable**; a
`format` query parameter is the pragmatic version, and it should be just as
strict.

## ex7

`Results<Ok<T>, NotFound, BadRequest<string>>` puts the endpoint's possible
outcomes into its *signature*. Two things fall out. The compiler stops you
returning anything else — a fourth outcome is a build error, not a surprise in
production — and the OpenAPI document gets all three response types with their
schemas, without an attribute per code.

The classic mistake is reaching for `IResult` everywhere because it is shorter.
It is, and it buys nothing: `IResult` documents nothing and checks nothing.
Reach for the union when an endpoint has a small, fixed set of outcomes, and for
`IResult` when it genuinely does not.

## ex8

`CreatedAtRoute` is `Created` plus link generation: name the GET endpoint, and
the `Location` is produced from the route table rather than from a format string,
so the URL keeps working when the template changes. Note it emits an **absolute**
URL — both forms are legal per RFC 9110, and knowing which one you emit matters
to clients that join it against a base.

The 409 is the other half. A conflict a caller has to act on deserves a
`ProblemDetails` body: `TypedResults.Problem(detail:, statusCode:, title:)`
gives you the RFC 9457 document with a `detail` naming the collision, so the
client can show a message instead of "409". Note the detail says *what*
collided; it does not echo anything the caller could not already see, which is
the line to hold when the conflicting record belongs to someone else.

## Further reading

- [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses) — `TypedResults`, the union return type, and every built-in result.
- [Handle errors in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling) — `AddProblemDetails`, `ValidationProblem` and the RFC 9457 body.
- [RFC 9110 §15 — HTTP status codes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-status-codes) — what 201, 204, 409 and 422 actually promise, in the words that settle arguments.
- [RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html) — the error format ASP.NET Core emits by default.

`format` query parameter is the pragmatic version, and it should be just as
strict.

## ex7

`Results<Ok<T>, NotFound, BadRequest<string>>` puts the endpoint's possible
outcomes into its *signature*. Two things fall out. The compiler stops you
returning anything else — a fourth outcome is a build error, not a surprise in
production — and the OpenAPI document gets all three response types with their
schemas, without an attribute per code.

The classic mistake is reaching for `IResult` everywhere because it is shorter.
It is, and it buys nothing: `IResult` documents nothing and checks nothing.
Reach for the union when an endpoint has a small, fixed set of outcomes, and for
`IResult` when it genuinely does not.

## ex8

`CreatedAtRoute` is `Created` plus link generation: name the GET endpoint, and
the `Location` is produced from the route table rather than from a format string,
so the URL keeps working when the template changes. Note it emits an **absolute**
URL — both forms are legal per RFC 9110, and knowing which one you emit matters
to clients that join it against a base.

The 409 is the other half. A conflict a caller has to act on deserves a
`ProblemDetails` body: `TypedResults.Problem(detail:, statusCode:, title:)`
gives you the RFC 9457 document with a `detail` naming the collision, so the
client can show a message instead of "409". Note the detail says *what*
collided; it does not echo anything the caller could not already see, which is
the line to hold when the conflicting record belongs to someone else.

- [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses) — `TypedResults`, the union return type, and every built-in result.
- [Handle errors in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling) — `AddProblemDetails`, `ValidationProblem` and the RFC 9457 body.
- [RFC 9110 §15 — HTTP status codes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-status-codes) — what 201, 204, 409 and 422 actually promise, in the words that settle arguments.
- [RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html) — the error format ASP.NET Core emits by default.

## Exercise 1 — empty is not missing

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex1.cs`.

- `GET /d03/bookings` — **200** with the bookings, id ascending. An optional
  `state` filters them, and a filter that matches nothing is **still a 200**.
- `GET /d03/bookings/{id:int}` — **200**, or **404** when there is none.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two endpoints, and the interesting one is the list. There is no branch in it at
all: an optional filter narrows the set, and whatever is left is the answer —
including nothing.

The single-item endpoint is where the 404 lives.

## Hint 2

Start from `store.Bookings().AsEnumerable()` and add the filter only when
`state` has a value:

```csharp
if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(state)) { bookings = bookings.Where(...); }
```

Then `OrderBy(b => b.Id)` and `TypedResults.Ok(...)`. No `Count == 0` check
anywhere: an empty list is a perfectly good 200.

For the item, `store.Find(id)` gives null when there is none — and *that* is the
404.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One line of logic: did the store actually remove something? That question has a
boolean answer, and the two status codes follow from it directly.

Resist adding a body to the success case.

## Hint 2

`store.Remove(id)` returns `true` when a booking was there and `false` when it
was not, so:

```csharp
return store.Remove(id) ? TypedResults.NoContent() : TypedResults.NotFound();
```

`TypedResults.NoContent()` writes a 204 and no body. `TypedResults.Ok()` would
be a 200 with an empty body, which is a different — and less precise — claim.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — four outcomes, one endpoint

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex4.cs`.
`PUT /d03/bookings/{id:int}/state` with `{"state": …}`:

- **400** when the state is not one of `Desk.States` — *even if the id is also
  wrong*
- **404** when there is no such booking
- **409** when the booking is already `cancelled`
- **204** otherwise, and the change sticks

The order those checks go in is the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d03_results_statuscodes ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four outcomes, and the exercise is the *order*. Read the gate's
`nonsenseOnMissing` check before you write anything: a bad state and a bad id
together must produce the code for the bad state.

That tells you which check has to come first.

## Hint 2

The order is: validate the body, find the resource, check whether its state
allows the change, then act.

- `Desk.States.Contains(state)` decides the 400
- `store.Find(id)` being null decides the 404
- `booking.State == "cancelled"` decides the 409
- otherwise `store.SetState(id, state)` and `TypedResults.NoContent()`

`TypedResults.Conflict(...)` is the 409. Note that a null `State` in the body
should behave like an unknown one — `request.State ?? ""` handles it.

## Hint 2

The order is: validate the body, find the resource, check whether its state
allows the change, then act.

- `Desk.States.Contains(state)` decides the 400
- `store.Find(id)` being null decides the 404
- `booking.State == "cancelled"` decides the 409
- otherwise `store.SetState(id, state)` and `TypedResults.NoContent()`

should behave like an unknown one — `request.State ?? ""` handles it.

## Hint 1

Resolve the default format first, then reject an unsupported one, then look up
the booking — the same "validate the request before you hunt for the resource"
order as ex4.

Two different result helpers produce the two content types. `TypedResults.Ok`
produces neither of them correctly for the text case.

## Hint 2

`format ?? "json"`, then reject anything that is not `json` or `text` with a 400.

For the text branch, `TypedResults.Text(body, "text/plain")` writes the string
as-is. `TypedResults.Ok(body)` would send `"Booking 1: Ada in Sakura"` — a JSON
string, quotes and all, under `application/json`.

For the JSON branch, `TypedResults.Json(new Receipt(...))` is explicit about what
it is doing; `TypedResults.Ok(receipt)` produces the same bytes.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The signature is already written and it is the interesting part: three outcomes,
named in the return type. Your job is to return one of exactly those three — and
the compiler will not let you do anything else.

Order the checks so the cheapest, most obviously-wrong case goes first.

## Hint 2

`TypedResults.BadRequest("…")`, `TypedResults.NotFound()` and
`TypedResults.Ok(room)` each convert implicitly to the union type, so you can
return them directly with no cast.

That implicit conversion is why `TypedResults` matters here: `Results.Ok(room)`
returns a plain `IResult`, which does **not** convert, and the method will not
compile.

## Hint 3

```csharp
if (id > 100) { return TypedResults.BadRequest($"id {id} is out of range."); }

var room = store.FindRoom(id);
if (room is null) { return TypedResults.NotFound(); }

return TypedResults.Ok(room);
```

Worth trying once you have it passing: add a fourth outcome — say a
`TypedResults.Conflict()` — and watch the compiler reject it. That error is the
feature you are buying by writing the union out.

Still yours to decide: whether the 400 body should name the id, and what it
should say.

The signature is already written and it is the interesting part: three outcomes,
named in the return type. Your job is to return one of exactly those three — and
the compiler will not let you do anything else.

Order the checks so the cheapest, most obviously-wrong case goes first.

## Hint 2

`TypedResults.BadRequest("…")`, `TypedResults.NotFound()` and
`TypedResults.Ok(room)` each convert implicitly to the union type, so you can
return them directly with no cast.

That implicit conversion is why `TypedResults` matters here: `Results.Ok(room)`
returns a plain `IResult`, which does **not** convert, and the method will not
compile.

## Hint 3

```csharp
if (id > 100) { return TypedResults.BadRequest($"id {id} is out of range."); }

var room = store.FindRoom(id);
if (room is null) { return TypedResults.NotFound(); }

return TypedResults.Ok(room);
```

Worth trying once you have it passing: add a fourth outcome — say a
`TypedResults.Conflict()` — and watch the compiler reject it. That error is the
feature you are buying by writing the union out.

Still yours to decide: whether the 400 body should name the id, and what it
should say.

Edit `src/Api/D03_ResultsStatuscodes/Ex8.cs`. Give
`GET /d03/desk/rooms/{id:int}` the name `Ex8.RoomRouteName` (**200** with the
room, **404** otherwise), then `POST /d03/desk/rooms` with
`{"name": …, "capacity": …}`:

- **201** whose `Location` is generated **from that route name**, body = the room
- a blank name or a capacity below 1 → **400**
- a name the desk already has → **409 ProblemDetails** whose `detail` names it

`Location` from that name rather than from a string, and give the duplicate case
a body a client can act on.

The order of checks in the POST is ex4's again — shape first, then state.

`app.MapGet(...).WithName(RoomRouteName)` is the naming.

which the gate's content-type check rejects.

The duplicate check is `store.FindRoom(request.Name)` — the string overload,
which matches case-insensitively, because "kiri" and "Kiri" are the same room to
anyone but a computer.

or `FindRoom("")` gets asked a question that means nothing.

Left for you: what the `detail` sentence says. It should name the room that
collided and nothing else — a conflict message is a place people accidentally
leak the contents of a record the caller was not allowed to see.

# d04 — DI lifetime drills

Eight problems on singleton, scoped and transient: choosing them from a
requirement, spotting a captive dependency, opening a scope by hand, disposal,
registration order, and the two ways a singleton can still see the current
request. They drill lesson **02_dependency_injection** — go back to it if
"scoped" still means "per request" and nothing more.

Everything is under `/d04/…`. Each exercise owns one file in
`src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/`, registrations included, so nothing you do here can
break another exercise.

## Exercise 1 — three requirements, three lifetimes

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex1.cs`, `Ex1Services` only. Read the doc comment
on each interface and pick the lifetime it describes:

- `IWarmCache` — expensive to build, and the whole application shares one
- `ICorrelation` — one object for the whole of *this* request, wherever it is
  asked for
- `IReading` — fresh at every single resolution

Two of the three registrations as shipped are wrong.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the captive dependency

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex2.cs`. `IStamp` is transient and
`IReportBuilder` is a singleton, and both of those are correct — yet
`GET /d04/report` reports the same stamp for both builds, forever.

Fix `ReportBuilder` so every `Build()` uses a fresh stamp. Do not change either
lifetime, and do not make the builder resolve the stamp in its constructor.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a singleton that needs a scoped service

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex3.cs`. `IJobRunner` is a singleton and
`IJobUnit` is scoped, and both are correct. `RunOnce()` must give each run its
own unit of work:

- two runs in one request → two different units
- neither of them is the **request's** unit

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — who disposes what

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex4.cs`, `Ex4Services` only. Pick the lifetime for
`ILease` that gives every caller its own lease **and** lets the container return
it when the request ends:

- two leases in one request are different objects
- by the next request, both of the previous request's leases have been disposed

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — Add, the last one wins, and TryAdd

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex5.cs`, `Ex5Services` only. Write **three**
registration calls so that:

- `IGreeter` resolves to the **casual** greeter
- `IEnumerable<IGreeter>` holds exactly `formal` then `casual`, in that order
- the third call is a `TryAdd` of `LoudGreeter` that changes nothing

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — why a unit of work is scoped

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex6.cs`, the `IWorkUnit` registration only. Both
repositories and the handler must share **one** unit of work per request, and no
two requests may ever share one.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — a singleton that can see the current request

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex7.cs`. `IRequestReporter` stays a **singleton**
and `Describe()` must return the `X-Trace` header of the request being handled
right now, or `"none"` when there is not one.

One more line is needed in `Ex7Services`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — four registrations, four different answers

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex8.cs`, `Ex8Services` only. All four TODO
registrations are wrong. `GET /d04/audit` must report, over three requests:

- `parserBuilds` — **1**, and still 1 on the third request
- `basketA` and `basketB` — equal within a request, different across requests
- `ticketA` and `ticketB` — always different
- `handled` — 1, then 2, then 3

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d04_di_lifetimes

## Notes

A lifetime is not a performance setting. It is a statement about **what an
object is allowed to remember**, and every bug in this set is the same bug seen
from a different angle: something remembered longer than it should have, or
shorter.

Three rules cover almost everything. A **singleton** may remember nothing about
any particular request. A **scoped** object may remember everything about one
request and must forget it when the request ends. A **transient** may remember
nothing at all, because it will be thrown away.

The corollary is the rule that catches people: a service may only depend on
things that live **at least as long as it does**. A singleton holding a scoped
service is a captive dependency, and ASP.NET Core refuses to start in
Development rather than let you ship it. A singleton holding a *transient* is
the quiet version of the same mistake — it compiles, it starts, and the
"transient" is a singleton in practice, which is ex2.

## ex1

Three sentences, three lifetimes, and the drill is translating requirements into
registrations without thinking about mechanics. "The whole application shares
one" is singleton. "One object for the whole of this request" is scoped. "Fresh
at every use" is transient.

The classic mistake is registering everything as scoped because it is the safe
middle. It is safe, and it silently makes the expensive cache expensive again on
every request. The model answer chooses each one from the *sentence*, not from
habit.

## ex2

The captive dependency, in its most common form. `ReportBuilder` takes an
`IStamp` in its constructor; the builder is a singleton, so the container
resolves one stamp at startup and the builder holds it forever. The transient
registration is not wrong and the singleton registration is not wrong — the
*capture* is.

The fix is to resolve per call rather than per construction:
`IServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IStamp>()` inside `Build()`. The classic
mistake is making the builder scoped instead, which "fixes" the symptom by
rebuilding an expensive object per request and still returns one stamp for the
whole request.

Two footnotes worth having. `Func<IStamp>` does **not** work — the built-in
container has no factory support, unlike Autofac. And injecting
`IServiceProvider` is the service locator pattern, which is a smell everywhere
except exactly here: a long-lived object that needs short-lived collaborators.

## ex3

Same shape as ex2, one level harder, because the dependency is *scoped* rather
than transient. A singleton cannot take it in its constructor at all — the
container throws at startup in Development — and it cannot resolve it from the
root provider either, because the root provider has no scope. That second
failure is the error the shipped stub produces, and it is worth reading once:
"Cannot resolve scoped service … from root provider".

The answer is `IServiceScopeFactory`: create a scope per unit of work, resolve
inside it, dispose it. This is precisely how a `BackgroundService` uses a
`DbContext`, and it is the single most useful DI pattern in a hosted-service
codebase.

The `using` matters. A scope you open is a scope you own; forgetting to dispose
it leaks everything created inside it until the process ends.

## ex4

Transient does not mean untracked. When the container creates an `IDisposable`,
the **scope that created it** takes ownership and disposes it when it ends — so
two transient leases resolved during a request are both disposed when the
request finishes. That is the behaviour the gate counts.

Scoped fails the first check (both callers get the same lease). Singleton fails
the second (nothing is ever disposed, because the root scope only ends at
shutdown). Transient is the only lifetime that satisfies both.

The production consequence: a transient `IDisposable` resolved from the **root**
provider — the mistake ex2 and ex3 skirt around — is never disposed until the
application stops, which is a slow memory leak that looks like nothing until it
looks like an outage.

## ex5

Three mechanics, in one exercise. `Add…` **appends** a registration rather than
replacing one. Resolving a single service gives you the **last** registration.
Resolving `IEnumerable<T>` gives you **all** of them, in registration order. And
`TryAdd…` does nothing at all if any registration for that service type already
exists.

# Reading - dotnet/d04_di_lifetimes

## Notes

A lifetime is not a performance setting. It is a statement about **what an
object is allowed to remember**, and every bug in this set is the same bug seen
from a different angle: something remembered longer than it should have, or
shorter.

Three rules cover almost everything. A **singleton** may remember nothing about
any particular request. A **scoped** object may remember everything about one
request and must forget it when the request ends. A **transient** may remember
nothing at all, because it will be thrown away.

The corollary is the rule that catches people: a service may only depend on
things that live **at least as long as it does**. A singleton holding a scoped
service is a captive dependency, and ASP.NET Core refuses to start in
Development rather than let you ship it. A singleton holding a *transient* is
the quiet version of the same mistake — it compiles, it starts, and the
"transient" is a singleton in practice, which is ex2.

every request. The model answer chooses each one from the *sentence*, not from
habit.

mistake is making the builder scoped instead, which "fixes" the symptom by

whole request.

container has no factory support, unlike Autofac. And injecting

## Hint 1

Do not think about mechanics; translate the three sentences. "The whole
application shares one", "one object for the whole of this request" and "fresh
at every use" each name exactly one lifetime, and the doc comments say which
sentence belongs to which interface.

The handler is given and correct. Only the three registration lines change.

## Hint 2

`AddSingleton`, `AddScoped` and `AddTransient` — one of each, and the shipped
file already has the transient one in the right place.

Check yourself against the gate rather than against intuition: a singleton is
the same across two requests, a scoped is the same *within* one request and
different across two, and a transient differs even when resolved twice in the
same request.

## Exercise 2 — the captive dependency

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex2.cs`. `IStamp` is transient and
`IReportBuilder` is a singleton, and both of those are correct — yet
`GET /d04/report` reports the same stamp for both builds, forever.

Fix `ReportBuilder` so every `Build()` uses a fresh stamp. Do not change either
lifetime, and do not make the builder resolve the stamp in its constructor.

uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex2

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both lifetimes are right, so the bug is not in `Ex2Services`. Ask when
`ReportBuilder`'s constructor runs, and how many times: once, at startup,
because it is a singleton — and whatever it was handed then is what it still
holds now.

"Transient" describes how often the container *creates* one, not how often your
object *asks* for one.

## Hint 2

Move the resolution from construction time to call time. Take an
`IServiceProvider` in the constructor and call
`services.GetRequiredService<IStamp>()` inside `Build()`.

Two things this is not: `Func<IStamp>` is not supported by the built-in
container, and making the builder scoped would fix the symptom by rebuilding the
singleton every request — and still hand out one stamp per request rather than
one per build.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two requirements, and they pull in different directions. Every caller needs its
*own* lease, which rules one lifetime out. And every lease must be handed back
when the request ends, which rules out the one whose scope never ends.

Only one line changes.

## Hint 2

Transient. Each resolution creates a new lease — and, crucially, the **scope
that resolved it** takes ownership and disposes it when the request finishes.

That last part surprises people: transient does not mean the container forgets
about you. It means you get a new instance; if that instance is `IDisposable`,
the resolving scope still owns it.

The consequence worth remembering: a transient `IDisposable` resolved from the
*root* provider is owned by the root scope, which only ends when the process
does.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two requirements, and they pull in different directions. Every caller needs its
*own* lease, which rules one lifetime out. And every lease must be handed back
when the request ends, which rules out the one whose scope never ends.

Only one line changes.

## Hint 2

Transient. Each resolution creates a new lease — and, crucially, the **scope
that resolved it** takes ownership and disposes it when the request finishes.

That last part surprises people: transient does not mean the container forgets
about you. It means you get a new instance; if that instance is `IDisposable`,
the resolving scope still owns it.

The consequence worth remembering: a transient `IDisposable` resolved from the
*root* provider is owned by the root scope, which only ends when the process
does.

## Exercise 5 — Add, the last one wins, and TryAdd

Edit `src/Api/D04_DiLifetimes/Ex5.cs`, `Ex5Services` only. Write **three**
registration calls so that:

- `IGreeter` resolves to the **casual** greeter
- `IEnumerable<IGreeter>` holds exactly `formal` then `casual`, in that order
- the third call is a `TryAdd` of `LoudGreeter` that changes nothing

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d04_di_lifetimes ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three calls, and the exercise is what each one does to the *list* of
registrations behind `IGreeter`. One of them appends. One of them appends again.
One of them looks first and does nothing.

Order matters for two of the three checks.

## Hint 2

```csharp
services.AddSingleton<IGreeter, FormalGreeter>();
services.AddSingleton<IGreeter, CasualGreeter>();
services.TryAddSingleton<IGreeter, LoudGreeter>();
```

`TryAdd…` lives in `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions`, so the
file needs that `using`.

The three facts being drilled: `Add` appends rather than replaces; a single
resolve gets the **last** registration; `IEnumerable<IGreeter>` gets **all** of
them in the order they were added. `TryAdd` does nothing because `IGreeter`
already has registrations — which is exactly how framework defaults get out of
your way.

```csharp

```

file needs that `using`.

resolve gets the **last** registration; `IEnumerable<IGreeter>` gets **all** of

## Hint 1

The reporter is built once, at startup, long before any of these requests
existed — so nothing it receives in its constructor can be "the current
request". It needs something that is itself a singleton but *answers
differently* depending on which request is in flight.

ASP.NET Core ships exactly one such thing, and it needs registering.

## Hint 2

`services.AddHttpContextAccessor();` in `Ex7Services`, and
`IHttpContextAccessor` in the reporter's constructor.

`accessor.HttpContext` is `null` outside a request — a background thread, a
health probe, a startup task — so handle that rather than assuming. Then read
`http.Request.Headers["X-Trace"].ToString()`; an absent header is an empty
string, which is the `"none"` case.

The accessor works because it wraps an `AsyncLocal<HttpContext>`: the value
follows the async flow of one request, not the instance.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reporter is built once, at startup, long before any of these requests
existed — so nothing it receives in its constructor can be "the current
request". It needs something that is itself a singleton but *answers
differently* depending on which request is in flight.

ASP.NET Core ships exactly one such thing, and it needs registering.

## Hint 2

`services.AddHttpContextAccessor();` in `Ex7Services`, and
`IHttpContextAccessor` in the reporter's constructor.

`accessor.HttpContext` is `null` outside a request — a background thread, a
health probe, a startup task — so handle that rather than assuming. Then read
`http.Request.Headers["X-Trace"].ToString()`; an absent header is an empty
string, which is the `"none"` case.

The accessor works because it wraps an `AsyncLocal<HttpContext>`: the value
follows the async flow of one request, not the instance.

lessons.briefing:
# d05 — DI pattern drills

Eight problems on the shapes you register rather than the lifetimes you give
them: a set of strategies, a factory, a decorator, an open generic, keyed
services, `TryAddEnumerable`, `ActivatorUtilities`, and decorating a
registration you did not write. They drill lesson
**02_dependency_injection** — go back to it if `IEnumerable<T>` injection is
still a surprise.

Everything is under `/d05/…`, and each exercise owns one file in
`src/Api/D05_DiPatterns/` with its own registrations.

## Exercise 1 — a set of strategies, one chosen at runtime

Edit `src/Api/D05_DiPatterns/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d05/notify/{channel}?message=…`
answers **200** with `{"sent": …, "channels": [ … ]}`:

- `sent` is what the notifier whose `Channel` matches the route produced
- `channels` is every channel the application knows, sorted A–Z
- a channel nobody implements is a **404**

All three notifiers have to be reachable through `IEnumerable<INotifier>`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d05_di_patterns ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a factory registration

Edit `src/Api/D05_DiPatterns/Ex2.cs`, `Ex2Services` only. `Pricer` takes an
`int`, so the container cannot build it by convention. Register `IPricer` so it
is constructed with the rate that `IRateSource` reports — 250 — rather than a
number typed into the registration.

`GET /d05/price?units=4` then answers **200** with a quote of **1000**.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d05_di_patterns ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the decorator

# Reading - dotnet/d05_di_patterns

## Notes

Lifetimes decide *how long* an object lives. This set is about the other half of
a registration: **what the container builds, and out of what**. Every problem
here is a different answer to "the default `AddScoped<IFoo, Foo>()` cannot
express this".

The pattern that unites them is composition at the composition root. A strategy
set, a decorator chain, an open generic and a keyed lookup are all ways of
saying "the shape of this dependency is decided in one place, at startup, and
the code that uses it stays ignorant". That ignorance is the payoff: the handler
in ex8 has no idea it is talking to two decorators, and it never needs to.

The one thing worth internalising about the built-in container: it is
deliberately small. No `Func<T>`, no automatic decoration, no assembly scanning,
no property injection. Everything in this lesson is done with the four
primitives it does have — a type, a factory lambda, an open generic, and a key —
and knowing exactly where that ceiling is tells you when a third-party container
or Scrutor actually earns its dependency.

## ex1

Registering the same service type more than once is not a mistake — it builds a
**set**. `IEnumerable<INotifier>` gets every registration in order, which is how
strategies, validation rules, health checks and pipeline stages get plugged in
without a central list anyone has to remember to edit.

The classic mistake is expecting the second `Add` to replace the first. It never
does; the *single* resolve takes the last one, and the enumerable takes all of
them. Here that shows up as a 404 for `sms`, because only one notifier was
registered.

The model answer's other decision: `FirstOrDefault` and a 404, rather than
`First` and a 500. An unknown channel is a client mistake, not a server one.

## ex2

Sometimes the constructor needs a **value**, not a service — a rate, a
connection string, a size limit — and the container has no way to guess it. The
factory overload, `AddSingleton<IPricer>(sp => …)`, is the escape hatch: you get
the provider, you resolve what you need, you build the object yourself.

The classic mistake is hard-coding the value in the registration to make it
compile, which is exactly what the shipped stub does. It works, it passes a
smoke test, and it silently ignores the configured rate forever.

Worth knowing: the factory runs **once per instance created**, respecting the
lifetime you registered — so a singleton factory runs once, a scoped factory
once per request. And whatever the factory returns is owned by the container: if
it is `IDisposable`, the scope will dispose it.

## ex3

A decorator implements the same interface it wraps, so callers cannot tell the
difference. Caching, retries, logging, metrics, authorization checks and audit
trails are all decorators, and none of them belong inside the class doing the
real work.

Composing them by hand in a factory lambda is the honest way to do it in the
built-in container: `new AuditSink(new UppercaseSink(new CoreSink()), trail)`.
It reads inside-out, which is the usual source of the classic mistake — getting
the nesting backwards, so the audit trail records the shouted message instead of
the original one.

Two things to notice in the gate. The order shows up in the *result string*, and
also in *what the audit layer saw* — a decorator's position decides which
version of the data it observes. That is exactly why an authorization decorator
goes outside a caching one, and a retry decorator goes inside a timeout one.

## ex4

`services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(InMemoryRepository<>))` is the
open-generic registration: one line that the container closes on demand for
`IRepository<Widget>`, `IRepository<Gadget>` and anything else asked for later.
This is how `ILogger<T>`, `IOptions<T>` and `IValidator<T>` are registered.

The classic mistake is registering closed forms one at a time, which compiles,
works for the types you remembered, and produces a runtime "unable to resolve"
for the one you did not — usually in the feature added six months later.

Note the non-generic overload: open generics cannot be expressed with the
generic `AddScoped<TService, TImplementation>()` form, and they cannot use a
factory lambda either. Type arguments only.

One aside worth having, because it bites hard the first time. The handler's
parameters carry `[FromServices]` explicitly. Without it, minimal APIs infer the
binding source by asking the container whether the type is a service — and a
type it has never heard of is inferred as the request **body**. A `GET` endpoint
with an inferred body is a *startup* failure, not a request failure, so one
missing registration takes the whole application down with a message about
bodies rather than about DI. Being explicit turns that into an ordinary
"unable to resolve service" 500 on the one endpoint that is broken.

## ex5

Keyed services (.NET 8+) let one interface have several registrations
distinguished by a key, without an enumerable and without a marker interface per
implementation. `[FromKeyedServices("email")]` picks one at *composition* time;
`GetKeyedService<T>(key)` picks one at *request* time.

The distinction the gate draws is worth keeping: the pinned parameter never
changes, the runtime lookup does. Reach for the attribute when the choice is
structural ("this handler always uses the primary database") and the runtime
lookup when the key comes from data.

The classic mistake is `GetRequiredKeyedService` for a key that came from user
input — that throws, and a thrown exception is a 500 for what is really a 404.
`KeyedService.AnyKey` is the wildcard for "give me all of them regardless of
key", which is how you enumerate a keyed set.

## ex6

`Add` appends unconditionally, `TryAdd` does nothing if *any* registration
exists for the service type, and `TryAddEnumerable` adds only if that exact
**implementation type** is not already registered. The third is the one for
plugin sets, and it exists because the first two both get it wrong: `Add`
duplicates, and `TryAdd` would stop the second, different check from registering
at all.

The practical failure this prevents is not academic. Two modules that both
depend on "the disk check" and both register it means the check runs twice —
twice the log lines, twice the load, and a health endpoint that reports the same
component twice.

`ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<TService, TImplementation>()` is how you build the
descriptor `TryAddEnumerable` wants; it needs the descriptor, not the type
arguments, because it has to compare implementation types.

## ex7

`ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<T>(provider, args)` builds a type that is
**not registered**, filling constructor parameters from the container and
matching the extra arguments you pass by type. That is the standard answer to
"half of this object's constructor is DI and half is runtime data" — a job with
a label, a strategy with a tenant id, a command with its payload.

The classic mistake is `new ExportJob(new FixedClock(), label)`, which works
until the clock has dependencies, or the singleton matters, or a test wants to
replace it. The gate checks the clock is the container's instance for exactly
that reason.

Worth knowing: `ActivatorUtilities.CreateFactory` pre-compiles the same thing
when you are going to build many instances, and that the type must have a public
constructor — this is not a way around encapsulation.

## ex8

The hardest one, and the most useful. You are handed a registration you did not
write and must wrap it without knowing what it names. The move is: find the
`ServiceDescriptor` in the collection, remove it, and register a factory that
builds the original from that descriptor and wraps the result.

Building the original is the fiddly part, because a descriptor can carry an
*instance*, a *factory*, or an *implementation type* — the model answer handles
all three, and `ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance` covers the last one because
the type is no longer registered for the container to resolve.

Applying `Decorate` twice gives you `counting>shouting>core`: each call wraps
whatever the previous one left, so the **last** decorator applied is the
outermost. That is the same nesting rule as d02's endpoint filters, and getting
it backwards is the classic mistake.

This is precisely what Scrutor's `services.Decorate<IFoo, FooDecorator>()` does,
and having written it once is the reason to be comfortable reaching for it.

## Further reading

- [Dependency injection in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection) — factory registrations, open generics, `IEnumerable<T>` and multiple registrations.
- [Keyed dependency injection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection#keyed-services) — `AddKeyed*`, `[FromKeyedServices]` and `KeyedService.AnyKey`.
- [Dependency injection guidelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection-guidelines) — what the built-in container deliberately does not do, and when to replace it.
- [ActivatorUtilities](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.dependencyinjection.activatorutilities) — constructing unregistered types with a mix of DI and explicit arguments.
- [Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/dependency-injection) — `TryAdd`, `TryAddEnumerable` and the service descriptor model.

## Exercise 1 — a set of strategies, one chosen at runtime

Edit `src/Api/D05_DiPatterns/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d05/notify/{channel}?message=…`
answers **200** with `{"sent": …, "channels": [ … ]}`:

- `sent` is what the notifier whose `Channel` matches the route produced
- `channels` is every channel the application knows, sorted A–Z
- a channel nobody implements is a **404**

All three notifiers have to be reachable through `IEnumerable<INotifier>`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d05_di_patterns ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Registering the same interface more than once does not replace anything — it
builds a set, and `IEnumerable<INotifier>` is how you get the whole set. The
stub only registers one of the three.

Then the handler is a lookup: which member of the set has this channel?

## Hint 2

Three `AddSingleton<INotifier, …>()` calls, one per implementation.

In the handler, materialise the enumerable once (`notifiers.ToList()`) because
you need it twice: `FirstOrDefault(n => n.Channel == channel)` to pick, and
`Select(n => n.Channel)` to list.

`FirstOrDefault` plus a null check gives you the 404; `First` would throw and
turn a client mistake into a 500.

## Exercise 2 — a factory registration

Edit `src/Api/D05_DiPatterns/Ex2.cs`, `Ex2Services` only. `Pricer` takes an
`int`, so the container cannot build it by convention. Register `IPricer` so it
is constructed with the rate that `IRateSource` reports — 250 — rather than a
number typed into the registration.

`GET /d05/price?units=4` then answers **200** with a quote of **1000**.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d05_di_patterns ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Pricer`'s constructor takes an `int`. The container has no idea which int, so
the type-based registration cannot work — you have to build the object yourself,
in a lambda the container calls when it needs one.

That lambda is handed the thing you need to look the value up in.

## Hint 2

The factory overload gives you an `IServiceProvider`:

```csharp
services.AddSingleton<IPricer>(sp => new Pricer(sp.GetRequiredService<IRateSource>().Cents));
```

The lambda runs once, because the registration is a singleton — the rate is read
at first use and captured, which is the right behaviour for a value that does
not change.

Anything you construct in there is owned by the container, so an `IDisposable`
result is still disposed with the scope that created it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Pricer`'s constructor takes an `int`. The container has no idea which int, so
the type-based registration cannot work — you have to build the object yourself,
in a lambda the container calls when it needs one.

That lambda is handed the thing you need to look the value up in.

## Hint 2

The factory overload gives you an `IServiceProvider`:

```csharp
services.AddSingleton<IPricer>(sp => new Pricer(sp.GetRequiredService<IRateSource>().Cents));
```

The lambda runs once, because the registration is a singleton — the rate is read
at first use and captured, which is the right behaviour for a value that does
not change.

Anything you construct in there is owned by the container, so an `IDisposable`
result is still disposed with the scope that created it.

## Exercise 3 — the decorator

Edit `src/Api/D05_DiPatterns/Ex3.cs`, `Ex3Services` only. Make `IMessageSink`
resolve to `AuditSink` wrapping `UppercaseSink` wrapping `CoreSink`, with the
audit trail coming from the container.

uv run dojo test dotnet d05_di_patterns ex3

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each decorator takes the next one in its constructor, so composing them is one
nested expression — and it reads inside-out, which is where the mistakes come
from.

Write down the required chain first: audit on the outside, uppercase in the
middle, core at the centre. Then build it from the centre out.

## Hint 2

A factory registration, because you are constructing the whole chain yourself:

```csharp
services.AddSingleton<IMessageSink>(sp => new AuditSink(
    new UppercaseSink(new CoreSink()),
    sp.GetRequiredService<IAuditTrail>()));
```

The trail comes from the provider — it is a registered singleton and the gate
reads the same instance the endpoint does.

Check yourself on the second assertion: the audit layer records what *it* was
handed. Because it is outside the uppercase layer, that is the original `hi`. If
your trail holds `HI`, the two layers are the wrong way round.

`services.AddKeyedSingleton<IChannel, EmailChannel>("email");` and the same for
`"sms"`.

- `services.GetKeyedServices<IChannel>(KeyedService.AnyKey)` for all of them

service type, whatever its key".

## Exercise 6 — a set that must not gain duplicates

Edit `src/Api/D05_DiPatterns/Ex6.cs`, `Ex6Services` only. Three calls: disk,
clock, then disk again. The third must change nothing, because two modules

uv run dojo test dotnet d05_di_patterns ex6

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three calls, and you need one that appends *unless this exact implementation is
already in the set*. `Add` always appends. `TryAdd` would refuse the second
check too, because by then something is registered for `IStartupCheck`.

There is a third method, and it compares implementation types.

## Hint 2

```csharp
services.TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IStartupCheck, DiskCheck>());
```

…three times, with `DiskCheck`, `ClockCheck`, `DiskCheck`. The third is a no-op.

It takes a `ServiceDescriptor` rather than type arguments precisely because it
has to look at the implementation type to decide. `TryAddEnumerable` lives in
`Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions`, so the file needs that
`using`.

This is the registration method for any set two independent modules might both
want to contribute to.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`IServiceCollection` is a `List<ServiceDescriptor>` — you can read it, search it,
and remove from it, right up until the provider is built. That is the whole
trick: find the descriptor that is already there, take it out, and put back a
factory that builds the original and wraps it.

Write one small helper and call it twice.

## Hint 2

The shape of the helper:

```csharp
var existing = services.Last(d => d.ServiceType == typeof(IGreetingService));
services.Remove(existing);
services.AddSingleton<IGreetingService>(sp => wrap(sp, Build(sp, existing)));
```

`wrap` is a `Func<IServiceProvider, IGreetingService, IGreetingService>` so the
counting decorator can pull `IGreetCounter` out of the provider and the shouting
one can ignore it.

Call it with the shouting wrapper first and the counting wrapper second: each
call wraps whatever the previous one left, so the **last** one applied ends up
outermost.

## Hint 3

`Build` is the fiddly part, because a descriptor can carry any of three things:

```csharp
if (descriptor.ImplementationInstance is IGreetingService instance) return instance;
if (descriptor.ImplementationFactory is not null)
    return (IGreetingService)descriptor.ImplementationFactory(sp);
return (IGreetingService)ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance(sp, descriptor.ImplementationType!);
```

The third line is why ex7 came first: the original implementation type is no
longer registered — you removed it — so the container cannot resolve it and you
have to construct it yourself.

Left for you: assembling the helper, and predicting the chain before you run it.
This is exactly what Scrutor's `Decorate` does, and writing it once is the point.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`IServiceCollection` is a `List<ServiceDescriptor>` — you can read it, search it,
and remove from it, right up until the provider is built. That is the whole
trick: find the descriptor that is already there, take it out, and put back a
factory that builds the original and wraps it.

Write one small helper and call it twice.

## Hint 2

The shape of the helper:

```csharp
var existing = services.Last(d => d.ServiceType == typeof(IGreetingService));
services.Remove(existing);
services.AddSingleton<IGreetingService>(sp => wrap(sp, Build(sp, existing)));
```

`wrap` is a `Func<IServiceProvider, IGreetingService, IGreetingService>` so the
counting decorator can pull `IGreetCounter` out of the provider and the shouting
one can ignore it.

Call it with the shouting wrapper first and the counting wrapper second: each
call wraps whatever the previous one left, so the **last** one applied ends up
outermost.

## Hint 3

`Build` is the fiddly part, because a descriptor can carry any of three things:

```csharp
if (descriptor.ImplementationInstance is IGreetingService instance) return instance;
if (descriptor.ImplementationFactory is not null)
    return (IGreetingService)descriptor.ImplementationFactory(sp);
return (IGreetingService)ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance(sp, descriptor.ImplementationType!);
```

The third line is why ex7 came first: the original implementation type is no
longer registered — you removed it — so the container cannot resolve it and you
have to construct it yourself.

Left for you: assembling the helper, and predicting the chain before you run it.
This is exactly what Scrutor's `Decorate` does, and writing it once is the point.

lessons.briefing:
# d06 — Middleware order drills

Eight problems on the shape of the pipeline: registration order, where a
short-circuit belongs, why `Run` is last, branches that rejoin and branches that
do not, headers written too late, and what an exception does to the way out.
They drill lesson **03_middleware** — go back to it if "in, then out again" is
not yet a picture in your head.

Every exercise builds its own pipeline with `app.CreateApplicationBuilder()` and
hangs it off one path under `/d06/…`. `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Pipeline.cs`
holds the trace helper and the middleware types you are arranging; most
exercises only ask you to reorder three lines.

Unless an exercise says otherwise, the response body **is** the finished trace.

## Exercise 1 — the order is the design

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex1.cs`, `Configure` only. Two requirements
decide the order of `timing`, `auth` and `cache`:

- timing has to measure everything, including auth
- auth has to run before the cache is consulted

`GET /d06/order` then answers `timing>,auth>,cache>,handler,cache<,auth<,timing<`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — where a short-circuit belongs

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex2.cs`, `Configure` only. Both middlewares
belong in the pipeline; only the order is wrong.

- `GET /d06/guard` with `X-Key: d06-key` → **200**,
  `guard>,expensive>,handler,expensive<,guard<`
- without the header → **401**, and the trace is exactly `guard>` — the
  expensive middleware must not have run at all

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — nothing runs after the terminal delegate

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex3.cs`, `Configure` only. All three lines are
needed; exactly one of them can be last.

`GET /d06/terminal` must answer `outer>,inner>,handler,inner<,outer<`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a branch that rejoins

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex4.cs`, `Configure` only. Add an `admin`
marker that runs **only** for paths under `/d06/when/admin`, before the existing
`common` marker — and both kinds of request must still reach the terminal
handler.

- `/d06/when/admin/reports` → `admin>,common>,handler,common<,admin<`
- `/d06/when/reports` → `common>,handler,common<`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — a branch that does not come back

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex5.cs`, `Configure` only. A request carrying
a `beta` query parameter takes a branch that marks `beta`, ends in its own
terminal handler marking `beta-handler`, and **never** reaches `common` or the
shared handler.

- `/d06/beta/thing?beta=1` → `beta>,beta-handler,beta<`
- `/d06/beta/thing` → `common>,handler,common<`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a header that depends on what happens later

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex6.cs`, `MarksHeaderMiddleware` only.
`GET /d06/headers` must answer **200** with the body `payload` and a header
`X-Marks` holding `work>,handler`.

Writing the header before `next` gives you an empty string; writing it after
`next` throws, because by then the response has started. There is a hook for
exactly this.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — what an exception does to the way out

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex7.cs`, `Configure` only. Three middlewares,
and only the order is wrong. The `audit` marker has to finish **even when the
request blows up**, and the risky one has to sit somewhere its exception can be
caught.

- `/d06/errors/fine` → **200**, `audit>,catch>,risky,handler,catch<,audit<`
- `/d06/errors/boom` → **503**, `audit>,catch>,risky,caught,catch<,audit<`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the whole pipeline, in one order

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex8.cs`, `Configure` only. Four things go in,
and there is one order that satisfies all of this. Here the trace arrives in the
`X-Marks` header, not the body.

- every response carries `X-Marks`, **including the 401 and the 503**
- an exception from the handler becomes a **503** with the body `failed`
- a request without `X-Key: d06-key` is **401** with the body `no key`, and the
  handler never runs
- paths under `/d06/full/admin` pick up an `admin` marker, and that branch is
  inside the guard

Expected: `/d06/full/reports` → `catch>,guard>,handler`;
`/d06/full/admin/reports` → `catch>,guard>,admin>,handler`; no key →
`catch>,guard>`; `/d06/full/boom` → `catch>,guard>,handler,caught`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/d06_middleware_order

## Notes

The pipeline is a stack of nested function calls, not a queue. Each middleware
gets a chance to act **on the way in**, hands control to `next`, and then gets a
chance to act **on the way out** — so registration order is inside-out order,
and the first thing registered is the last thing to finish.

Every problem in this set is that one picture, tested from a different side. A
guard must be outside the work it guards. A terminal delegate has nothing after
it. A branch either rejoins or it does not. A header must be written before the
response starts. And code after `await next(...)` is not a `finally` — it is
ordinary code that a downstream exception skips entirely.

The habit worth building: when you place a middleware, ask two questions. What
must it wrap? And what must still run if the thing inside it fails? The answers
put it in exactly one place.

## ex1

The two requirements are real ones. Timing that does not wrap authentication
does not measure authentication, and the slow request you are trying to explain
looks fast. Authentication that runs *after* the cache means a cache hit is
served to someone who was never allowed to ask — an authorization bypass that no
test of the handler will ever catch, because the handler never runs.

The classic mistake is treating order as an implementation detail and putting
new middleware at the end because that is where the cursor was. The model
answer picks each position from a sentence about what must wrap what.

## ex2

Short-circuiting only saves you something if it happens before the cost.
`ExpensiveMiddleware` after the guard is a rate limiter that rate-limits nothing,
an auth check that authenticates after the database query, a request-size check
that runs once the body is already buffered.

The gate asserts the *absence* of a mark, which is the honest way to test a
short-circuit: it is easy to write a guard that sets a 401 and calls `next`
anyway, and the status code alone will not tell you.

Note the trace stops at `guard>` and never reaches `guard<`. That is not a bug —
the guard returns before its own post-`next` line, which is the same mechanism
ex7 explores from the other end.

## ex3

`Use` passes control on; `Run` does not. `Run` takes a `RequestDelegate` with no
`next` parameter at all, which is the API telling you it is terminal. Anything
registered after it is unreachable, and nothing warns you — no compiler error,
no startup failure, just a trace with one entry in it.

The classic mistake is subtler than the shipped stub: writing
`app.Run(...)` early "temporarily" while debugging and leaving it in, or calling
`app.UseRouting()` after something that already terminated. The rule is one
line: terminal delegates last, always.

## ex4

`UseWhen` runs a branch when a predicate matches, and the branch **rejoins** the
main pipeline afterwards. That is the one to reach for when a subset of requests
needs extra treatment but the same handling in the end — a stricter rate limit
for one path prefix, an extra header for one tenant, request logging only for
API routes.

The classic mistake is using it as if it were terminal and being surprised that
the rest of the pipeline still ran. The other one is a predicate that is too
loose: `Path.StartsWithSegments` respects segment boundaries, so it matches
`/admin/reports` but not `/administrators` — `Path.Value.StartsWith("/admin")`
would match both, which is a security bug the day someone adds that route.

## ex5

`MapWhen` is the terminal cousin: the branch is a pipeline of its own, and
control never comes back. Everything after it in the main pipeline is skipped
for matching requests, which is right when the branch is an *alternative* rather
than an addition — a legacy compatibility shim, a maintenance-mode responder, a
feature-flagged v2 implementation.

Because it does not rejoin, a `MapWhen` branch must terminate itself. A branch
with no `Run` at the end produces a 404, which is a confusing way to discover
the rule.

Worth having straight for interviews: `Use` (wrap), `Run` (terminate),
`Map` (branch on a path prefix, and rebase `Request.Path`/`PathBase`),
`MapWhen` (branch on a predicate, terminal), `UseWhen` (branch on a predicate,
rejoins).

## ex6

Headers are part of the response *start line block*: once a single byte of body
has been written, they have been sent, and the framework throws if you try to
change them. So the natural-looking `await next(...); Response.Headers[…] = …`
is wrong, and the equally natural "write it up front" produces an empty value
because nothing has happened yet.

`HttpResponse.OnStarting` is the hook: register a callback before `next`, and it
runs at the last possible instant — after the handler has decided everything and
before the first byte leaves. This is how timing headers, correlation ids and
`Server-Timing` are added in real services.

Look closely at the expected value: `work>,handler` and not `work<`. The
callback fires when the handler writes, which is *before* the pipeline unwinds.
A header can only ever describe what has already happened.

## ex7

The mark to stare at is `audit<`. Code placed after `await next(context)` is not
a `finally` block — if `next` throws, that line is skipped and the exception
keeps propagating. So a logging or metrics middleware written the obvious way
silently stops recording exactly the requests that failed.

Two fixes, and knowing both is the point. Put a `try/finally` in the middleware
itself, which is what `CatchMiddleware` does for its own closing mark. Or put
something that swallows the exception *between* you and the danger, which is what
this exercise's ordering does.

The other half is the catcher's own position: a `try/catch` can only see what is
downstream of it, so exception handling belongs near the outside of the pipeline
— which is exactly where `UseExceptionHandler` tells you to put it.

## ex8

Everything at once, and each of the four positions is forced by a sentence.

The header middleware is **outermost** because every response must carry the
trace — and the responses you most want to trace are the 401s and 503s, which
are produced by middleware further in. Put it inside the guard and the failing
requests are the ones missing the header.

The catcher is **outside the guard and the handler** because it can only catch
what is downstream. The guard is **outside the branch** because a branch that
runs before authentication is work done for callers who never proved anything.
The branch is innermost because it is an addition to the handled path, not a
replacement for it.

That ordering — observability, then error handling, then authentication, then
routing-shaped concerns, then the handler — is close to the order ASP.NET
Core's own documentation recommends for a real application, and it is worth
being able to justify each step out loud.

## Further reading

- [ASP.NET Core Middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware) — `Use`, `Run`, `Map`, and the recommended order for a real pipeline.
- [Write custom middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/write) — the convention-based class, `next`, and short-circuiting.
- [HttpResponse.OnStarting](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.http.httpresponse.onstarting) — the hook for anything that must be decided before the first byte.
- [Handle errors in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling) — `UseExceptionHandler` and why it belongs near the outside.
- [Request and response operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-response) — what "the response has started" actually means, and what stops being possible after it.

# Reading - dotnet/d06_middleware_order

## Notes

The pipeline is a stack of nested function calls, not a queue. Each middleware
gets a chance to act **on the way in**, hands control to `next`, and then gets a
chance to act **on the way out** — so registration order is inside-out order,
and the first thing registered is the last thing to finish.

Every problem in this set is that one picture, tested from a different side. A
guard must be outside the work it guards. A terminal delegate has nothing after
it. A branch either rejoins or it does not. A header must be written before the
response starts. And code after `await next(...)` is not a `finally` — it is
ordinary code that a downstream exception skips entirely.

The habit worth building: when you place a middleware, ask two questions. What
must it wrap? And what must still run if the thing inside it fails? The answers
put it in exactly one place.

## ex1

The two requirements are real ones. Timing that does not wrap authentication
does not measure authentication, and the slow request you are trying to explain
looks fast. Authentication that runs *after* the cache means a cache hit is
served to someone who was never allowed to ask — an authorization bypass that no
test of the handler will ever catch, because the handler never runs.

The classic mistake is treating order as an implementation detail and putting
new middleware at the end because that is where the cursor was. The model
answer picks each position from a sentence about what must wrap what.

## ex2

Short-circuiting only saves you something if it happens before the cost.
`ExpensiveMiddleware` after the guard is a rate limiter that rate-limits nothing,
an auth check that authenticates after the database query, a request-size check
that runs once the body is already buffered.

The gate asserts the *absence* of a mark, which is the honest way to test a
short-circuit: it is easy to write a guard that sets a 401 and calls `next`
anyway, and the status code alone will not tell you.

Note the trace stops at `guard>` and never reaches `guard<`. That is not a bug —
the guard returns before its own post-`next` line, which is the same mechanism
ex7 explores from the other end.

## ex3

`Use` passes control on; `Run` does not. `Run` takes a `RequestDelegate` with no
`next` parameter at all, which is the API telling you it is terminal. Anything
registered after it is unreachable, and nothing warns you — no compiler error,
no startup failure, just a trace with one entry in it.

The classic mistake is subtler than the shipped stub: writing
`app.Run(...)` early "temporarily" while debugging and leaving it in, or calling
`app.UseRouting()` after something that already terminated. The rule is one
line: terminal delegates last, always.

## ex4

`UseWhen` runs a branch when a predicate matches, and the branch **rejoins** the
main pipeline afterwards. That is the one to reach for when a subset of requests
needs extra treatment but the same handling in the end — a stricter rate limit
for one path prefix, an extra header for one tenant, request logging only for
API routes.

The classic mistake is using it as if it were terminal and being surprised that
the rest of the pipeline still ran. The other one is a predicate that is too
loose: `Path.StartsWithSegments` respects segment boundaries, so it matches
`/admin/reports` but not `/administrators` — `Path.Value.StartsWith("/admin")`
would match both, which is a security bug the day someone adds that route.

## ex5

`MapWhen` is the terminal cousin: the branch is a pipeline of its own, and
control never comes back. Everything after it in the main pipeline is skipped
for matching requests, which is right when the branch is an *alternative* rather
than an addition — a legacy compatibility shim, a maintenance-mode responder, a
feature-flagged v2 implementation.

Because it does not rejoin, a `MapWhen` branch must terminate itself. A branch
with no `Run` at the end produces a 404, which is a confusing way to discover
the rule.

Worth having straight for interviews: `Use` (wrap), `Run` (terminate),
`Map` (branch on a path prefix, and rebase `Request.Path`/`PathBase`),
`MapWhen` (branch on a predicate, terminal), `UseWhen` (branch on a predicate,
rejoins).

## ex6

Headers are part of the response *start line block*: once a single byte of body
has been written, they have been sent, and the framework throws if you try to
change them. So the natural-looking `await next(...); Response.Headers[…] = …`
is wrong, and the equally natural "write it up front" produces an empty value
because nothing has happened yet.

`HttpResponse.OnStarting` is the hook: register a callback before `next`, and it
runs at the last possible instant — after the handler has decided everything and
before the first byte leaves. This is how timing headers, correlation ids and
`Server-Timing` are added in real services.

Look closely at the expected value: `work>,handler` and not `work<`. The
callback fires when the handler writes, which is *before* the pipeline unwinds.
A header can only ever describe what has already happened.

## ex7

The mark to stare at is `audit<`. Code placed after `await next(context)` is not
a `finally` block — if `next` throws, that line is skipped and the exception
keeps propagating. So a logging or metrics middleware written the obvious way
silently stops recording exactly the requests that failed.

Two fixes, and knowing both is the point. Put a `try/finally` in the middleware
itself, which is what `CatchMiddleware` does for its own closing mark. Or put
something that swallows the exception *between* you and the danger, which is what
this exercise's ordering does.

The other half is the catcher's own position: a `try/catch` can only see what is
downstream of it, so exception handling belongs near the outside of the pipeline
— which is exactly where `UseExceptionHandler` tells you to put it.

## ex8

Everything at once, and each of the four positions is forced by a sentence.

The header middleware is **outermost** because every response must carry the
trace — and the responses you most want to trace are the 401s and 503s, which
are produced by middleware further in. Put it inside the guard and the failing
requests are the ones missing the header.

The catcher is **outside the guard and the handler** because it can only catch
what is downstream. The guard is **outside the branch** because a branch that
runs before authentication is work done for callers who never proved anything.
The branch is innermost because it is an addition to the handled path, not a
replacement for it.

That ordering — observability, then error handling, then authentication, then
routing-shaped concerns, then the handler — is close to the order ASP.NET
Core's own documentation recommends for a real application, and it is worth
being able to justify each step out loud.

- [ASP.NET Core Middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware) — `Use`, `Run`, `Map`, and the recommended order for a real pipeline.
- [Write custom middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/write) — the convention-based class, `next`, and short-circuiting.
- [HttpResponse.OnStarting](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.http.httpresponse.onstarting) — the hook for anything that must be decided before the first byte.
- [Handle errors in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling) — `UseExceptionHandler` and why it belongs near the outside.
- [Request and response operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-response) — what "the response has started" actually means, and what stops being possible after it.
