## Exercise 1 — the order is the design

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex1.cs`, `Configure` only. Two requirements
decide the order of `timing`, `auth` and `cache`:

- timing has to measure everything, including auth
- auth has to run before the cache is consulted

`GET /d06/order` then answers `timing>,auth>,cache>,handler,cache<,auth<,timing<`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the two requirements as sentences about wrapping. "Timing must measure
everything" means timing wraps the other two. "Auth must run before the cache is
consulted" means auth wraps the cache.

That fixes all three positions without you having to think about the trace at
all.

## Hint 2

The first middleware registered is the outermost, so the registration order is
the same as the wrapping order: timing, auth, cache.

The trace then falls out: each one marks `>` on the way in, in that order, and
`<` on the way out, in reverse. A pipeline is a stack of nested calls, not a
queue.

## Hint 1

Read the two requirements as sentences about wrapping. "Timing must measure
everything" means timing wraps the other two. "Auth must run before the cache is
consulted" means auth wraps the cache.

That fixes all three positions without you having to think about the trace at
all.

## Hint 2

The first middleware registered is the outermost, so the registration order is
the same as the wrapping order: timing, auth, cache.

The trace then falls out: each one marks `>` on the way in, in that order, and
`<` on the way out, in reverse. A pipeline is a stack of nested calls, not a
queue.

## Hint 1

Run it as shipped and read the trace: one entry. Two middlewares were registered
and neither of them ran, and nothing warned you.

```csharp
pipeline.UseMiddleware<MarkMiddleware>("outer");

pipeline.Run(D06Pipeline.Handler);
```

same mistake looks like an `app.Run(...)` left in from debugging, or routing
registered after something that already terminated.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run it as shipped and read the trace: one entry. Two middlewares were registered
and neither of them ran, and nothing warned you.

Look at what `Run` takes as an argument compared with `Use`. One of them has a
`next` and one does not.

## Hint 2

`Run` is terminal — it never calls `next`, so everything registered after it is
unreachable. Move it to the bottom:

```csharp
pipeline.UseMiddleware<MarkMiddleware>("outer");
pipeline.UseMiddleware<MarkMiddleware>("inner");
pipeline.Run(D06Pipeline.Handler);
```

The rule is one line: terminal delegates last, always. In a real application the
same mistake looks like an `app.Run(...)` left in from debugging, or routing
registered after something that already terminated.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You need a branch that runs for some requests and then puts them back on the
main road, so the terminal handler is still reached either way. One of the
`IApplicationBuilder` branching methods does exactly that; the other one does
not come back.

The predicate is about the request path.

## Hint 2

```csharp
pipeline.UseWhen(
    context => context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/d06/when/admin"),
    branch => branch.UseMiddleware<MarkMiddleware>("admin"));
```

…registered *before* the `common` marker, because the expected trace has `admin`
outside it.

Use `StartsWithSegments`, not `Path.Value.StartsWith("/d06/when/admin")`: the
first respects segment boundaries, so it will not match a future
`/d06/when/administrators`. That difference has been a real security bug in real
applications.

## Hint 1

You need a branch that runs for some requests and then puts them back on the
main road, so the terminal handler is still reached either way. One of the
`IApplicationBuilder` branching methods does exactly that; the other one does
not come back.

## Hint 2

```csharp
pipeline.UseWhen(
    context => context.Request.Path.StartsWithSegments("/d06/when/admin"),
    branch => branch.UseMiddleware<MarkMiddleware>("admin"));
```

…registered *before* the `common` marker, because the expected trace has `admin`
outside it.

Use `StartsWithSegments`, not `Path.Value.StartsWith("/d06/when/admin")`: the
first respects segment boundaries, so it will not match a future
`/d06/when/administrators`. That difference has been a real security bug in real
applications.

## Exercise 6 — a header that depends on what happens later

Edit `src/Api/D06_MiddlewareOrder/Ex6.cs`, `MarksHeaderMiddleware` only.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d06_middleware_order ex6
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two obvious placements and both are wrong. Before `next`, nothing has happened
yet, so the value is empty. After `next`, the handler has already written the
body — the headers went out with it and are read-only.

You need to *register* the work early and *run* it late.

## Hint 2

`context.Response.OnStarting(callback)` registers a callback that fires at the
instant the response starts — the last moment the headers are still writable:

```csharp
context.Response.OnStarting(() =>
{
    context.Response.Headers[HeaderName] = D06Trace.Read(context);
    return Task.CompletedTask;
});

return next(context);
```

Check the expected value against your mental model: it is `work>,handler`, with
no `work<`. The callback runs when the handler writes, which is before the
pipeline unwinds — a header can only ever describe what has already happened.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two placement questions, and answering them in order fixes all three lines.

First: a `try/catch` can only catch what happens *inside* the call it wraps, so
where must the catcher be relative to the thing that throws?

Second: `MarkMiddleware` writes its closing mark on the line after
`await next(...)` — which is skipped entirely if `next` throws. So where must
audit be for that line to still run?

## Hint 2

Audit outermost, then the catcher, then the risky one:

```csharp
pipeline.UseMiddleware<MarkMiddleware>("audit");
pipeline.UseMiddleware<CatchMiddleware>();
pipeline.UseMiddleware<RiskyMiddleware>();
```

The catcher swallows the exception and returns normally, so by the time control
reaches audit's post-`next` line there is nothing propagating and the mark runs.

The general lesson is worth writing down: code after `await next(...)` is **not**
a `finally`. If you need it to run on failures too, either wrap it in your own
`try/finally` or make sure something between you and the danger handles the
exception.

- every response carries `X-Marks`, **including the 401 and the 503**
- an exception from the handler becomes a **503** with the body `failed`
- a request without `X-Key: d06-key` is **401** with the body `no key`, and the
  handler never runs
- paths under `/d06/full/admin` pick up an `admin` marker, and that branch is
  inside the guard

Expected: `/d06/full/reports` → `catch>,guard>,handler`;
`/d06/full/admin/reports` → `catch>,guard>,admin>,handler`; no key →
`catch>,guard>`; `/d06/full/boom` → `catch>,guard>,handler,caught`.

lessons.briefing:
# d07 — Writing middleware drills

Eight problems on writing the middleware itself rather than arranging it: the
convention-based class, constructor arguments, `IMiddleware`, refusing properly,
reading a request body without stealing it, capturing a response, answering from
a cache, and one component that does all of it. They drill lesson
**03_middleware** — go back to it if `next` is still mysterious.

Every exercise builds its own pipeline with `app.CreateApplicationBuilder()` and
hangs it off one path under `/d07/…`.

## Exercise 1 — the convention-based class

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex1.cs`, `HandledMiddleware` only.

- always add the response header `X-D07-Handled: yes`
- when the query string contains `trace`, put `true` in `HttpContext.Items`
  under `HandledMiddleware.ItemKey`
- then let the rest of the pipeline run

`GET /d07/handled` answers `plain`; `GET /d07/handled?trace=1` answers `traced`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — one type, two configurations

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex2.cs`. Implement `BannerMiddleware` (set
the named header to the given value, then call `next`) and add it to the branch
in `Branch`, passing the arguments through.

`GET /d07/banner/a` gets `X-Banner: alpha`; `/d07/banner/b` gets
`X-Banner: beta`. Same class, two configurations.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — factory-based middleware

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex3.cs`. `TagMiddleware` implements
`IMiddleware` and takes a **scoped** `IRequestTag`. Put this request's tag in
`X-Tag`, call `next`, and register the middleware so the container can build it.

The gate checks the header equals the body — the middleware and the handler must
share one tag — and that two requests get different ones.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — refusing properly

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex4.cs`, `BearerGateMiddleware` only.

- no `Authorization` header → **401** carrying `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`
- an `Authorization` that is not `BearerGateMiddleware.ValidToken` → **403**
- the valid token → call `next`

Neither refusal writes a body or calls `next`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — read the body without stealing it

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex5.cs`, `BodyLengthMiddleware` only. Put the
request body's length in `X-Body-Length` **and** leave the body readable for the
handler, which echoes it back.

As shipped the header is right and the echo is empty.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — rewrite what the handler wrote

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex6.cs`, `ShoutMiddleware` only. Capture
everything the rest of the pipeline writes, report its length in
`X-Original-Length`, and send the **upper-cased** version to the client.

`GET /d07/shout` → body `HELLO FROM THE HANDLER`, header `22`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — answer from a cache

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex7.cs`, `CacheMiddleware` only. Key on
`Request.Path`:

- a hit → `X-Cache: HIT`, write the stored body, **do not call `next`**
- a miss → capture what the pipeline writes, store it, `X-Cache: MISS`, and send
  it on

The handler's answer changes every time it runs, so a cached response is easy to
tell from a fresh one: `made 1` for the first path, `made 2` for the second, and
never a `made 3`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — one component that does all of it

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex8.cs`. `RecordMiddleware` is factory-based
and holds a **scoped** `IRecorder`. It must:

- put `recorder.Id` in `X-Record-Id` on every response
- buffer the request body so the handler can still read it
- refuse a request body longer than `MaxRequestChars` (20) with **413**, the
  body `too large`, and no call to `next`
- capture the response and set `X-Record` to `"{request length}:{response
  length}"` — `25:9` on the refusal, since `too large` is nine characters

`POST /d07/record/one` with `hello` → `echo:hello` and `X-Record: 5:10`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/d07_middleware_custom

## Notes

A middleware is a function from `HttpContext` to `Task` that happens to be
allowed to call another one. Everything in this set follows from that: you hold
the request before anyone else sees it, you hold the response after everyone
else has written it, and you decide whether "everyone else" runs at all.

The skill being drilled is the *mechanics* — the exact shape of the class, where
its dependencies come from, how to read a stream twice, how to hold the pen
while something downstream writes. Order was d06's job; this set assumes the
position is already right and asks whether you can write the component.

The one distinction to carry away: a **convention-based** middleware is built
once, at startup, and lives for the life of the application. A **factory-based**
one (`IMiddleware`) is resolved from the container on every request. That single
fact decides what each of them is allowed to depend on.

## ex1

The convention: a public class, a constructor whose first parameter is
`RequestDelegate next`, and a public `InvokeAsync(HttpContext)` returning
`Task`. No interface, no base class, no registration — `UseMiddleware<T>` finds
the method by name and shape at startup, and gets it wrong at *runtime* rather
than at compile time if you misspell it.

The other half is `HttpContext.Items`: a per-request dictionary that is the
normal way one middleware hands a fact to something downstream. It is thrown
away when the request ends, which is exactly the lifetime you want for
"this request is being traced".

The classic mistake is a `static` field instead — which works perfectly until
two requests arrive at once.

## ex2

`UseMiddleware<T>(args…)` passes extra arguments to the constructor after
`next`, and anything it does not supply is resolved from the container. That is
how one middleware class serves two configurations, and it is why the same type
can appear twice in a pipeline with different behaviour.

The idiomatic version wraps this in an extension method
(`app.UseBanner("X-Banner", "alpha")`) and often takes an options object rather
than loose strings, so the call site reads as a sentence and new settings do not
change the signature. That is the shape almost every published middleware
package uses.

The classic mistake is a static or captured configuration field, which quietly
makes the second registration overwrite the first.

## ex3

`IMiddleware` exists for one reason: a convention-based middleware is a
**singleton**, so a scoped dependency in its constructor is a captive dependency
— and in Development the container refuses to start rather than let it happen.
An `IMiddleware` implementation is resolved per request from
`context.RequestServices`, so it can hold whatever the request holds.

The price is that it must be **registered** — the shipped stub's 500 is the
container saying exactly that — and that resolving it costs a little on every
request.

Which to use, in one sentence: convention-based by default, `IMiddleware` when
the middleware needs a scoped service or you want it constructed by the
container so it can be replaced in a test. The third option is neither: take
`IServiceProvider` in a convention-based middleware and resolve per call, which
is d04 ex2's trick and works when you only need it occasionally.

## ex4

Two status codes people confuse. **401 Unauthorized** means "I do not know who
you are", and RFC 9110 requires it to carry `WWW-Authenticate` naming the
scheme, so a client knows *how* to try again. **403 Forbidden** means "I know who
you are and the answer is still no", and it carries nothing, because there is no
retry that would help.

The other rule the gate enforces is the short-circuit: no body, no `next`. A
refusal that still runs the handler is not a refusal, and the status code alone
will not tell you — which is why the gate reads the body rather than trusting
the code.

In a real application this whole middleware is `UseAuthentication` and
`UseAuthorization`, and you would write a scheme handler rather than this.
Writing it once is how you know what those are doing.

## ex5

A request body is a forward-only stream. Read it to the end in middleware and
the handler finds nothing left — with no error, no warning, and a `null` model
that looks like a client bug.

`HttpRequest.EnableBuffering()` wraps the stream in one that can seek, spilling
to disk past a threshold. After that, read what you like and set
`Body.Position = 0` so the next reader starts at the beginning. The `leaveOpen:

than streamed — so this belongs in middleware that needs it (request logging,
signature verification, idempotency hashing) and nowhere else.

pen. Swap `Response.Body` for a `MemoryStream` **before** calling `next`, let
everything write into it, then read it, restore the real stream, and write what
you actually want.

rewriting is a last resort; prefer an endpoint filter (d02 ex7) that transforms

# Reading - dotnet/d07_middleware_custom

## Notes

A middleware is a function from `HttpContext` to `Task` that happens to be
allowed to call another one. Everything in this set follows from that: you hold
the request before anyone else sees it, you hold the response after everyone
else has written it, and you decide whether "everyone else" runs at all.

The skill being drilled is the *mechanics* — the exact shape of the class, where
its dependencies come from, how to read a stream twice, how to hold the pen
while something downstream writes. Order was d06's job; this set assumes the
position is already right and asks whether you can write the component.

The one distinction to carry away: a **convention-based** middleware is built
once, at startup, and lives for the life of the application. A **factory-based**
one (`IMiddleware`) is resolved from the container on every request. That single
fact decides what each of them is allowed to depend on.

## ex1

The convention: a public class, a constructor whose first parameter is
`RequestDelegate next`, and a public `InvokeAsync(HttpContext)` returning
`Task`. No interface, no base class, no registration — `UseMiddleware<T>` finds
the method by name and shape at startup, and gets it wrong at *runtime* rather
than at compile time if you misspell it.

The other half is `HttpContext.Items`: a per-request dictionary that is the
normal way one middleware hands a fact to something downstream. It is thrown
away when the request ends, which is exactly the lifetime you want for
"this request is being traced".

The classic mistake is a `static` field instead — which works perfectly until
two requests arrive at once.

## ex2

`UseMiddleware<T>(args…)` passes extra arguments to the constructor after
`next`, and anything it does not supply is resolved from the container. That is
how one middleware class serves two configurations, and it is why the same type
can appear twice in a pipeline with different behaviour.

container so it can be replaced in a test. The third option is neither: take
`IServiceProvider` in a convention-based middleware and resolve per call, which
is d04 ex2's trick and works when you only need it occasionally.

Two status codes people confuse. **401 Unauthorized** means "I do not know who

retry that would help.

Writing it once is how you know what those are doing.

## Hint 1

Three things in one method, and the last one is the easiest to forget: call
`next`. A middleware that does its work and returns has short-circuited the
request, which is not what this one is for.

The header goes on `context.Response.Headers`; the fact for the handler goes
somewhere that lives exactly as long as this request.

## Hint 2

```csharp
context.Response.Headers[HeaderName] = "yes";

if (context.Request.Query.ContainsKey("trace"))
{
    context.Items[ItemKey] = true;
}

return next(context);
```

`HttpContext.Items` is a per-request dictionary — the normal way one middleware
tells a handler something. A static field would work for one request and break
the moment two arrive at once.

Setting the header before `next` is deliberate: after the handler has written a
body, the headers have already gone out.

## Hint 1

The middleware's constructor already declares the two settings it needs. The
question is how they get there — `UseMiddleware` takes more than a type
argument.

Everything you do not pass is resolved from the container; everything you do
pass fills the constructor after `next`.

## Hint 2

`pipeline.UseMiddleware<BannerMiddleware>(headerName, value);`

The arguments line up with the constructor parameters *after* `RequestDelegate
next`, which the framework always supplies itself.

`InvokeAsync` is then two lines: set the named header, `return next(context);`.

In a published middleware package this would be wrapped in an extension method —
`app.UseBanner("X-Banner", "alpha")` — and usually take an options object rather
than loose strings, so adding a setting does not change the signature.

## Hint 1

The middleware's constructor already declares the two settings it needs. The
question is how they get there — `UseMiddleware` takes more than a type
argument.

Everything you do not pass is resolved from the container; everything you do
pass fills the constructor after `next`.

## Hint 2

`pipeline.UseMiddleware<BannerMiddleware>(headerName, value);`

The arguments line up with the constructor parameters *after* `RequestDelegate
next`, which the framework always supplies itself.

`InvokeAsync` is then two lines: set the named header, `return next(context);`.

In a published middleware package this would be wrapped in an extension method —
`app.UseBanner("X-Banner", "alpha")` — and usually take an options object rather
than loose strings, so adding a setting does not change the signature.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three branches, and two of them return without calling `next`. Get the status
codes right first: one of them means "I do not know who you are" and the other
means "I know, and no".

Only one of the two owes the client an extra header.

## Hint 2

Read `context.Request.Headers.Authorization.ToString()` — an absent header is an
empty string, so `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` covers it.

- absent → `StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized` **and**
  `context.Response.Headers.WWWAuthenticate = "Bearer";`
- present but wrong → `StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden`
- correct → `return next(context);`

Both refusals `return Task.CompletedTask;` — setting a status and then calling
`next` anyway runs the handler you were trying to protect, and the status code
alone will not reveal it. The gate reads the body for exactly that reason.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three branches, and two of them return without calling `next`. Get the status
codes right first: one of them means "I do not know who you are" and the other
means "I know, and no".

Only one of the two owes the client an extra header.

## Hint 2

Read `context.Request.Headers.Authorization.ToString()` — an absent header is an
empty string, so `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` covers it.

- absent → `StatusCodes.Status401Unauthorized` **and**
  `context.Response.Headers.WWWAuthenticate = "Bearer";`
- present but wrong → `StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden`
- correct → `return next(context);`

Both refusals `return Task.CompletedTask;` — setting a status and then calling
`next` anyway runs the handler you were trying to protect, and the status code
alone will not reveal it. The gate reads the body for exactly that reason.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The header is already right, so the reading works. The problem is what is left
afterwards: a request body is a forward-only stream, and you just read it to the
end.

Two things are missing — one that makes the stream rewindable, and one that
rewinds it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
context.Request.EnableBuffering();

using var reader = new StreamReader(context.Request.Body, leaveOpen: true);
string body = await reader.ReadToEndAsync();

context.Response.Headers[HeaderName] = body.Length.ToString();

context.Request.Body.Position = 0;

await next(context);
```

`EnableBuffering()` wraps the body in a seekable stream (spilling to disk past a
threshold), and `Position = 0` puts the next reader back at the start.

`leaveOpen: true` matters too: disposing the reader would close the request
stream out from under everyone downstream.

The cost is real — the body is now held rather than streamed — so do this only
in middleware that genuinely needs the body.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The header is already right, so the reading works. The problem is what is left
afterwards: a request body is a forward-only stream, and you just read it to the
end.

Two things are missing — one that makes the stream rewindable, and one that
rewinds it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
context.Request.EnableBuffering();

using var reader = new StreamReader(context.Request.Body, leaveOpen: true);
string body = await reader.ReadToEndAsync();

context.Response.Headers[HeaderName] = body.Length.ToString();

context.Request.Body.Position = 0;

await next(context);
```

`EnableBuffering()` wraps the body in a seekable stream (spilling to disk past a
threshold), and `Position = 0` puts the next reader back at the start.

`leaveOpen: true` matters too: disposing the reader would close the request
stream out from under everyone downstream.

The cost is real — the body is now held rather than streamed — so do this only
in middleware that genuinely needs the body.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You cannot change bytes that have already gone to the client. So do not let them
go: give the rest of the pipeline a stream of *yours* to write into, and decide
what the real client sees afterwards.

`context.Response.Body` is a settable property.

## Hint 2

Swap it before `next`, read it after, restore it, then write:

```csharp
var real = context.Response.Body;
using var buffer = new MemoryStream();
context.Response.Body = buffer;

await next(context);

buffer.Position = 0;
string written = await new StreamReader(buffer).ReadToEndAsync();

context.Response.Body = real;
context.Response.Headers[HeaderName] = written.Length.ToString();
await context.Response.WriteAsync(written.ToUpperInvariant());
```

The rewind before reading is ex5's rule again.

## Hint 3

Wrap it in `try`/`finally` and restore `context.Response.Body = real;` in the
`finally`. If the handler throws, leaving a dead `MemoryStream` on the context
breaks every middleware above you — including the one whose job is to turn that
exception into a response.

Notice why the header assignment is legal here at all: nothing has been written
to the *real* response yet, so its headers are still open. Capturing the response
is what buys you the right to change your mind.

Left for you: assembling it, and noticing what this costs. The whole response is
now in memory and streaming is gone — which is why an endpoint filter that
transforms the result object (d02 ex7) is the better tool whenever it applies.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — answer from a cache

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex7.cs`, `CacheMiddleware` only. Key on
`Request.Path`:

- a hit → `X-Cache: HIT`, write the stored body, **do not call `next`**
- a miss → capture what the pipeline writes, store it, `X-Cache: MISS`, and send
  it on

The handler's answer changes every time it runs, so a cached response is easy to
tell from a fresh one: `made 1` for the first path, `made 2` for the second, and
never a `made 3`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two paths, and you have written both before. The hit is ex4's short-circuit:
write something and return, without calling `next`. The miss is ex6's capture:
hold the pen, let the pipeline write, then keep a copy.

The key is `context.Request.Path`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (cache.TryGet(key, out string cached))
{
    context.Response.Headers[HeaderName] = "HIT";
    await context.Response.WriteAsync(cached);
    return;                       // no next - that is the whole point
}
```

The miss path is ex6's swap, plus a `cache.Set(key, written)` before you write
the captured body on to the real response.

Set `X-Cache` before writing in both branches: once a byte of body has gone, the
headers have gone with it.

## Hint 3

Restore `context.Response.Body` in a `finally`, exactly as in ex6.

Then read the gate: the handler's answer changes every time it runs, so `made 2`
coming back from a supposed hit means the handler ran again and nothing was
saved. A cache that still does the work is not a cache.

Worth thinking about before you move on — none of this is required to pass, and
all of it is required in production. Keying on the path alone ignores the query
string, the `Accept` headers and *who is asking*, and that last one turns a
cache into a data leak. Nothing here ever expires. Nothing coordinates two
instances behind a load balancer. `builder.Services.AddOutputCache()` handles
all three, and knowing that is half of the interview answer.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two paths, and you have written both before. The hit is ex4's short-circuit:
write something and return, without calling `next`. The miss is ex6's capture:
hold the pen, let the pipeline write, then keep a copy.

The key is `context.Request.Path`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (cache.TryGet(key, out string cached))
{
    context.Response.Headers[HeaderName] = "HIT";
    await context.Response.WriteAsync(cached);
    return;                       // no next - that is the whole point
}
```

The miss path is ex6's swap, plus a `cache.Set(key, written)` before you write
the captured body on to the real response.

Set `X-Cache` before writing in both branches: once a byte of body has gone, the
headers have gone with it.

## Hint 3

Restore `context.Response.Body` in a `finally`, exactly as in ex6.

Then read the gate: the handler's answer changes every time it runs, so `made 2`
coming back from a supposed hit means the handler ran again and nothing was
saved. A cache that still does the work is not a cache.

Worth thinking about before you move on — none of this is required to pass, and
all of it is required in production. Keying on the path alone ignores the query
string, the `Accept` headers and *who is asking*, and that last one turns a
cache into a data leak. Nothing here ever expires. Nothing coordinates two
instances behind a load balancer. `builder.Services.AddOutputCache()` handles
all three, and knowing that is half of the interview answer.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — one component that does all of it

Edit `src/Api/D07_MiddlewareCustom/Ex8.cs`. `RecordMiddleware` is factory-based
and holds a **scoped** `IRecorder`. It must:

- put `recorder.Id` in `X-Record-Id` on every response
- buffer the request body so the handler can still read it
- refuse a request body longer than `MaxRequestChars` (20) with **413**, the
  body `too large`, and no call to `next`
- capture the response and set `X-Record` to `"{request length}:{response
  length}"` — `25:9` on the refusal, since `too large` is nine characters

`POST /d07/record/one` with `hello` → `echo:hello` and `X-Record: 5:10`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d07_middleware_custom ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Nothing here is new. It is ex3's `IMiddleware` with a scoped dependency, ex5's
request buffering, ex4's short-circuit and ex6's response capture, in one
method — plus the registration ex3 taught you.

The exercise is the *order of the steps inside the method*.

## Hint 2

Work through what each requirement forces:

1. `X-Record-Id` must be on **every** response, including the 413 — so write it
   first, before any branch.
2. The decision depends on the request's length — so buffer and read before
   deciding.
3. The refusal must set its own `X-Record` and write its body, then `return`.
4. Only then swap `Response.Body`, call `next`, read the capture, restore, set
   `X-Record`, and write the captured body on.

And in `Ex8Services`: `services.AddScoped<RecordMiddleware>();`

## Hint 3

The two lengths:

```csharp
context.Response.Headers[RecordHeader] = $"{request.Length}:{response.Length}";
```

…and on the refusal path the response is the literal `too large`, which is nine
characters — so `25:9`.

Remember `context.Request.Body.Position = 0;` after reading, or the handler's
echo comes back empty; and the `finally` that restores `context.Response.Body`,
or a throwing handler leaves a dead stream behind.

Left for you: assembling it, and checking the `X-Record-Id` behaviour. Two
requests with the same id means the middleware was registered as a singleton and
the "scoped" recorder inside it has been captive since startup — which is the
bug `IMiddleware` exists to prevent.

## Hint 1

Nothing here is new. It is ex3's `IMiddleware` with a scoped dependency, ex5's
request buffering, ex4's short-circuit and ex6's response capture, in one
method — plus the registration ex3 taught you.

## Hint 2

Work through what each requirement forces:

1. `X-Record-Id` must be on **every** response, including the 413 — so write it
   first, before any branch.
2. The decision depends on the request's length — so buffer and read before
   deciding.
3. The refusal must set its own `X-Record` and write its body, then `return`.
4. Only then swap `Response.Body`, call `next`, read the capture, restore, set
   `X-Record`, and write the captured body on.

The two lengths:

```csharp

```

characters — so `25:9`.

echo comes back empty; and the `finally` that restores `context.Response.Body`,
or a throwing handler leaves a dead stream behind.

requests with the same id means the middleware was registered as a singleton and
the "scoped" recorder inside it has been captive since startup — which is the
bug `IMiddleware` exists to prevent.

# d08 — Configuration drills

Eight problems on `IConfiguration`: reading keys, binding sections, arrays,
connection strings, missing sections, walking keys you did not write, the
binder's conversions, and an environment-aware override chain. They drill lesson
**04_configuration_options** — go back to it if "configuration is a flat
dictionary" is not yet how you picture it.

Every endpoint is under `/d08/…` and takes `IConfiguration` (and, in ex8,
`IHostEnvironment`) as a handler parameter. The gate boots the application with
its own in-memory settings for each exercise, which is also the answer to "how
do I test configuration-dependent code".

## Exercise 1 — read three keys

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d08/site` → **200** with
`{"title": …, "pageSize": …, "beta": …}` from `Dojo:D08:Site:Title`,
`:PageSize` and `:Beta`.

Missing values fall back to `(untitled)`, `10` and `false`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — bind a section onto an object

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d08/mailer` → **200** with
`{"from": …, "retries": …}` bound from `Dojo:D08:Mailer` onto `MailerSettings`.

Keys the section does not mention must keep the class defaults.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — arrays

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex3.cs`. `GET /d08/mirrors` → **200** with
`{"mirrors": [ … ], "count": …}` from `Dojo:D08:Mirrors`, in configuration
order. No section at all is an empty list and a count of 0 — never null, never a
404.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — connection strings

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex4.cs`. `GET /d08/connections/{name}` →
**200** with `{"name": …, "value": …}` for a connection string this application
has, **404** for one it does not.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — a section that is not there

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d08/limits` → **200** with
`{"section": …, "maxItems": …, "timeoutSeconds": …}`:

- `section` — whether `Dojo:D08:Limits` exists at all
- `maxItems` — `Dojo:D08:Limits:MaxItems`, or **50**
- `timeoutSeconds` — `Dojo:D08:Limits:TimeoutSeconds`, or **30**

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — walk keys you did not write

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex6.cs`. `Dojo:D08:Features` maps feature names
to booleans, and nothing in your code knows the names. `GET /d08/features` →
**200** with `{"enabled": [ … ], "known": …}` — the true ones, sorted A–Z, and a
count of every key in the section.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — one bind, a whole tree

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex7.cs`. Bind `Dojo:D08:Feed` onto
`FeedSettings` in **one** call — an enum, two `TimeSpan`s, a list of objects and
a nested object — and report it as
`{"mode": …, "intervalSeconds": …, "endpoints": ["url|weight", …], "retryCount": …, "backoffSeconds": …}`.

Anything configuration does not mention keeps its default, at every depth.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the environment picks the override

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d08/effective/{key}` → **200**
with `{"key": …, "value": …, "source": …, "environment": …}`, where the value is
the first of these configuration actually has:

1. `Dojo:D08:Overrides:{environment}:{key}` → source `environment`
2. `Dojo:D08:Overrides:Default:{key}` → source `default`
3. neither → value `none`, source `none`

The environment name comes from `IHostEnvironment`, never from a literal — the
gate boots the same configuration twice, as Staging and as Development.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d08_configuration

## Notes

`IConfiguration` is a **flat dictionary of string keys to string values**, and
almost every confusion about it dissolves once that sentence is believed. The
colons in `Dojo:D08:Site:Title` are part of the key, not navigation. The
"objects" and "arrays" in `appsettings.json` are a convenience for writing keys —
an array is keys named `0`, `1`, `2`, and a nested object is a key with a longer
prefix.

The second idea is **layering**. Several providers — JSON files,
environment-specific JSON, user secrets, environment variables, command line —
are stacked, and a later one wins key by key. That is why a `docker run -e
Dojo__D08__Site__Title=…` overrides a file without the file changing, and why
you cannot *remove* an array element from a later layer, only overwrite it.

The third is that **absence is normal**. `GetSection` never returns null,
`GetValue<T>` has an overload that takes a default, and a missing key is not an
exception. Configuration is the one place in an application where "not there" is
an ordinary answer rather than a bug, which is exactly why d09 exists — some
values really are required, and that has to be said explicitly.

## ex1

Three reads and three conversions. `configuration["path"]` is the raw string or
`null`; `GetValue<int>("path", 10)` parses and falls back in one call.

The classic mistake is `int.Parse(configuration["…"]!)`, which is a
`NullReferenceException` or a `FormatException` waiting for the first deployment
that forgets the key — and it happens at the moment the value is *used*, which
is usually not startup.

Worth remembering the environment-variable spelling: a colon is not legal in an
environment variable name on Linux, so `Dojo__D08__Site__Title` (double
underscore) maps to the same key. That is how the same configuration is written
in a Dockerfile, a Kubernetes manifest and an App Service setting.

## ex2

`GetSection(path).Get<T>()` constructs the object — running its property
initialisers — and then writes **only** the properties it found keys for. That
is why defaults survive a partial section, and it is the single most useful
thing to know about the binder.

The classic mistake is expecting the opposite and "defending" against it by
checking every property for null afterwards. The model answer instead puts the
defaults where they belong, in the class, and lets configuration override what
it wants to.

The one null to handle: `Get<T>()` returns `null` when the section does not
exist at all, so `?? new MailerSettings()` is not paranoia.

## ex3

Arrays are numbered keys, which explains two things people find surprising.
Order is the key order, so `Mirrors:0` comes before `Mirrors:1` whatever the
file looked like. And a later configuration layer overwrites **by index** — it
cannot shorten a list, so a three-element default and a one-element override
leave you with one new value and two stale ones.

The classic mistake here is treating a missing list as an error. An application
with no mirrors configured is a valid application; the model answer coalesces to
an empty list and returns 200.

## ex4

`GetConnectionString(name)` is exactly `GetSection("ConnectionStrings")[name]`,
and it exists because that path is a convention every hosting platform writes
into — Azure App Service, Docker Compose, Aspire, and every CI system's secret
store. Using the convention means an operator can set your connection string
without reading your code.

The 404 is the design decision worth defending: a connection string that is not
configured is not an empty connection string. Returning `""` and letting the
database driver fail three layers down turns a configuration problem into a
mystery.

## ex5

`GetSection` **never returns null** — it hands back an empty section — which is
why there is an `Exists()` method at all. `Exists()` is true when the section has
a value or at least one child.

That design means missing configuration cannot crash you by accident, and it
also means it cannot warn you. Reading a required value with `GetValue<int>` and
no default silently gives you `0`, and `0` is a plausible-looking timeout. The
model answer supplies a default for each value *and* reports whether the section
was there, which is the shape of a real "is this thing configured" health check.

## ex6

`GetChildren()` enumerates a section whose keys your code does not know: feature
flags, per-tenant settings, named clients, rate-limit policies. Each child is
itself an `IConfigurationSection` with a `Key` and a value, so
`child.Get<bool>()` converts properly.

The classic mistake is reading `child.Value` and testing it for
truthiness — `"false"` is a non-empty string, so the feature you switched off
stays on. Conversion is not optional just because the value looks like a
sentence.

The design note: `known` counts every key, not just the enabled ones, because a
feature switched off is still a feature the application knows about. That
distinction is what lets an admin page list flags rather than guess them.

## ex7

One `Get<T>()` call handles an enum, two `TimeSpan`s, a list of objects and a
nested object, and knowing the conversion rules saves writing a parser.

Enums bind **by name, case-insensitively** — and also by number, which is the
sharp edge: `"Mode": "3"` on a two-value enum binds silently to `(FeedMode)3`
and fails much later. `TimeSpan` binds from `"hh:mm:ss"` (and `"d.hh:mm:ss"`),
`DateTime` from ISO-8601, and anything with a `TypeConverter` from its string
form.

Lists of objects bind index-first: `Endpoints:0:Url`, `Endpoints:0:Weight`. And
the defaults rule from ex2 applies **at every depth** — `Retry:Count` was
configured, `Retry:Backoff` was not, and the nested object's own default
survives.

## ex8

The chain — environment-specific, then default, then nothing — is the shape of
almost every real feature-flag or per-tenant override system, and building it
from `IHostEnvironment.EnvironmentName` rather than a literal is what makes it
work in all four environments.

Note the framework does this for you at the *file* level:
`appsettings.json` then `appsettings.{Environment}.json`, layered so the second
wins. Reach for that first. Build an in-configuration chain like this one when
the branching is per-key rather than per-file — a tenant, a region, a rollout
ring — because layering files cannot express "this key, for this tenant".

The `source` field in the response is the part worth stealing. When something is
configured wrongly in production, "what is the value" is half the question;
"where did it come from" is the half that takes an afternoon. Exposing the
provenance — as this endpoint does, or as `IConfigurationRoot.GetDebugView()`
does — turns that afternoon into a request.

## Further reading

- [Configuration in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration) — providers, layering, environment variables and the key spelling rules.
- [Configuration in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/configuration) — the flat-dictionary model, `GetSection`, `Exists`, `GetChildren`.
- [Configuration binder](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/configuration-binder) — `Get<T>`, `Bind`, arrays, nested objects and the type conversions.
- [Use multiple environments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/environments) — `IHostEnvironment`, `appsettings.{Environment}.json` and how the name is chosen.
- [Integration tests in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests) — `WithWebHostBuilder` and `ConfigureAppConfiguration`, the gate's own trick.

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d08/site` → **200** with
`{"title": …, "pageSize": …, "beta": …}` from `Dojo:D08:Site:Title`,

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The whole colon-separated path is the key — configuration is a flat dictionary,
so there is nothing to navigate into. Three reads, three fallbacks.

Two of the three values are not strings, and every configuration value is stored
as one.

## Hint 2

```csharp
string title = configuration["Dojo:D08:Site:Title"] ?? "(untitled)";
int pageSize = configuration.GetValue("Dojo:D08:Site:PageSize", 10);
bool beta = configuration.GetValue("Dojo:D08:Site:Beta", false);
```

The indexer gives you `string?`; `GetValue<T>(key, default)` converts and falls
back in one call.

Avoid `int.Parse(configuration["…"]!)`: it throws on a missing key, and it
throws at the moment the value is *used* rather than at startup, which is the
worst possible time to find out.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One call turns a section into an instance of your class. You do not have to read
the keys individually, and you do not have to defend the defaults — the binder
only writes what it found.

There is a null to handle: a section that does not exist at all.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var settings = configuration.GetSection("Dojo:D08:Mailer").Get<MailerSettings>()
               ?? new MailerSettings();
```

`Get<T>` constructs the object — running the property initialisers that hold
your defaults — and then overwrites only the properties configuration mentions.
That is why `Retries` stays 3.

`Bind(existingInstance)` is the other spelling, and it is the one to use when
you already have an object to fill.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One call turns a section into an instance of your class. You do not have to read
the keys individually, and you do not have to defend the defaults — the binder
only writes what it found.

There is a null to handle: a section that does not exist at all.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var settings = configuration.GetSection("Dojo:D08:Mailer").Get<MailerSettings>()
               ?? new MailerSettings();
```

`Get<T>` constructs the object — running the property initialisers that hold
your defaults — and then overwrites only the properties configuration mentions.
That is why `Retries` stays 3.

`Bind(existingInstance)` is the other spelling, and it is the one to use when
you already have an object to fill.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An array in `appsettings.json` is stored as keys named `0`, `1`, `2`. The binder
knows that, so a section binds straight to a `List<string>` — you do not have to
loop over indices yourself.

An absent section is not an error. Decide what it becomes before you write the
response.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var mirrors = configuration.GetSection("Dojo:D08:Mirrors").Get<List<string>>() ?? [];
```

`Get<List<string>>()` returns `null` for a section that is not there, and the
gate wants an empty list and a 200 — an application with no mirrors configured is
not a broken application.

Worth knowing while you are here: because the keys are indices, a later
configuration layer overwrites an array *element by element*. It cannot make the
list shorter, which is a real source of stale values in layered configuration.

## Hint 1

An array in `appsettings.json` is stored as keys named `0`, `1`, `2`. The binder
knows that, so a section binds straight to a `List<string>` — you do not have to
loop over indices yourself.

An absent section is not an error. Decide what it becomes before you write the
response.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var mirrors = configuration.GetSection("Dojo:D08:Mirrors").Get<List<string>>() ?? [];
```

`Get<List<string>>()` returns `null` for a section that is not there, and the
gate wants an empty list and a 200 — an application with no mirrors configured is
not a broken application.

Worth knowing while you are here: because the keys are indices, a later
configuration layer overwrites an array *element by element*. It cannot make the
list shorter, which is a real source of stale values in layered configuration.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`GetSection` never returns null, so `section == null` is not the question. There
is a method that answers "is there anything here at all".

The two numbers are ex1 again: read with a default rather than reading and
hoping.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var section = configuration.GetSection("Dojo:D08:Limits");
section.Exists();                                            // has a value or children
configuration.GetValue("Dojo:D08:Limits:MaxItems", 50);
configuration.GetValue("Dojo:D08:Limits:TimeoutSeconds", 30);
```

`Exists()` is true when the section has a value or at least one child.

The reason to supply a default on every read is in the failure message:
`GetValue<int>` with no default silently gives you `0`, and `0` is a
plausible-looking timeout that nothing will warn you about.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is ex2 with a bigger class. One `Get<T>()` call handles all of it — the
enum, both `TimeSpan`s, the list of objects and the nested object — and you write
no parsing at all.

The rest of the exercise is projecting the bound object into the response shape.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var feed = configuration.GetSection("Dojo:D08:Feed").Get<FeedSettings>() ?? new FeedSettings();
```

Then read `feed.Mode.ToString()`, `(int)feed.Interval.TotalSeconds`, the
endpoints as `$"{e.Url}|{e.Weight}"`, and the two retry values.

The conversion rules doing the work: enums bind **by name**, case-insensitively;
`TimeSpan` binds from `"hh:mm:ss"`; a list of objects binds from
`Endpoints:0:Url`, `Endpoints:0:Weight`, index first.

## Hint 3

The check worth predicting before you run it is `backoffSeconds`. Configuration
sets `Retry:Count` and says nothing about `Retry:Backoff` — and the nested
object's own default of two seconds survives, because the binder never blanks a
property it found no key for, **at any depth**.

One sharp edge to file away: enums also bind by *number*, so `"Mode": "3"` on a
two-value enum silently produces `(FeedMode)3` and fails somewhere far from the
configuration file. If that matters, validate — which is exactly what d09 is
about.

Left for you: the projection, and deciding whether `?? new FeedSettings()` is
paranoia or necessary. (Run the gate's no-configuration case and find out.)

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is ex2 with a bigger class. One `Get<T>()` call handles all of it — the
enum, both `TimeSpan`s, the list of objects and the nested object — and you write
no parsing at all.

The rest of the exercise is projecting the bound object into the response shape.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var feed = configuration.GetSection("Dojo:D08:Feed").Get<FeedSettings>() ?? new FeedSettings();
```

Then read `feed.Mode.ToString()`, `(int)feed.Interval.TotalSeconds`, the
endpoints as `$"{e.Url}|{e.Weight}"`, and the two retry values.

The conversion rules doing the work: enums bind **by name**, case-insensitively;
`TimeSpan` binds from `"hh:mm:ss"`; a list of objects binds from
`Endpoints:0:Url`, `Endpoints:0:Weight`, index first.

## Hint 3

The check worth predicting before you run it is `backoffSeconds`. Configuration
sets `Retry:Count` and says nothing about `Retry:Backoff` — and the nested
object's own default of two seconds survives, because the binder never blanks a
property it found no key for, **at any depth**.

One sharp edge to file away: enums also bind by *number*, so `"Mode": "3"` on a
two-value enum silently produces `(FeedMode)3` and fails somewhere far from the
configuration file. If that matters, validate — which is exactly what d09 is
about.

Left for you: the projection, and deciding whether `?? new FeedSettings()` is
paranoia or necessary. (Run the gate's no-configuration case and find out.)

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the environment picks the override

Edit `src/Api/D08_Configuration/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d08/effective/{key}` → **200**
with `{"key": …, "value": …, "source": …, "environment": …}`, where the value is
the first of these configuration actually has:

1. `Dojo:D08:Overrides:{environment}:{key}` → source `environment`
2. `Dojo:D08:Overrides:Default:{key}` → source `default`
3. neither → value `none`, source `none`

The environment name comes from `IHostEnvironment`, never from a literal — the
gate boots the same configuration twice, as Staging and as Development.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d08_configuration ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three lookups in order, and the first one that has a value wins. Build the two
keys with string interpolation — the environment name is part of the path.

The name has to come from `IHostEnvironment`, because the gate boots the same
configuration twice under two different names.

## Hint 2

```csharp
string name = environment.EnvironmentName;

string? specific = configuration[$"Dojo:D08:Overrides:{name}:{key}"];
string? fallback = configuration[$"Dojo:D08:Overrides:Default:{key}"];
```

Check `specific` first, then `fallback`, then give up with `"none"` — and report
which branch answered in `source`.

`string.IsNullOrEmpty` rather than `is not null`: a key present with an empty
value should behave like an absent one here.

## Hint 3

Write the three returns as three early exits rather than a nested conditional —
the chain reads as the rule it implements, and adding a fourth layer later is
one more block instead of a rewrite.

Two things worth taking away once it passes. The framework already does this at
the *file* level (`appsettings.json` then
`appsettings.{Environment}.json`), so reach for that before building a chain in
configuration; this shape earns its keep when the branching is per-key — a
tenant, a region, a rollout ring — which file layering cannot express.

And the `source` field is the part to steal. When a value is wrong in
production, "what is it" is half the question and "where did it come from" is
the half that costs you an afternoon.

The name has to come from `IHostEnvironment`, because the gate boots the same
configuration twice under two different names.

## Hint 2

```csharp

string? specific = configuration[$"Dojo:D08:Overrides:{name}:{key}"];
string? fallback = configuration[$"Dojo:D08:Overrides:Default:{key}"];
```

Check `specific` first, then `fallback`, then give up with `"none"` — and report
which branch answered in `source`.

`string.IsNullOrEmpty` rather than `is not null`: a key present with an empty
value should behave like an absent one here.

## Hint 3

Write the three returns as three early exits rather than a nested conditional —
the chain reads as the rule it implements, and adding a fourth layer later is
one more block instead of a rewrite.

Two things worth taking away once it passes. The framework already does this at
the *file* level (`appsettings.json` then
`appsettings.{Environment}.json`), so reach for that before building a chain in
configuration; this shape earns its keep when the branching is per-key — a
tenant, a region, a rollout ring — which file layering cannot express.

And the `source` field is the part to steal. When a value is wrong in
production, "what is it" is half the question and "where did it come from" is
the half that costs you an afternoon.

# d09 — Options and validation drills

Eight problems on the options pattern: binding a section, data annotations, a
predicate, a validator class, named instances, `PostConfigure`,
`ValidateOnStart`, and all of it at once. They drill lesson
**04_configuration_options** — go back to it if `IOptions<T>` still feels like
a wrapper for no reason.

Everything is under `/d09/…`. Every endpoint is already written: it resolves the
options and answers with them, or answers **500** with `{"messages": [ … ]}` when
validation refused — see `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Support.cs`. Your work is
in the `IServiceRegistrar` of each file.

The gate boots the application with its own in-memory settings per case, which
is also the answer to "how do I test a configuration-dependent service".

## Exercise 1 — a section, a class, an `IOptions<T>`

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex1.cs`, `Ex1Services` only. Bind
`ArchiveOptions` to `Dojo:D09:Archive`.

`GET /d09/archive` then reports the configured bucket and retention — and the
class defaults when nothing is configured.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — data annotations

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex2.cs`. Make `Host` required and `Port`
between 1 and 65535, bind `Dojo:D09:Smtp`, and make those attributes actually
run.

Valid settings → **200**. A missing host or an out-of-range port → **500** whose
`messages` name the property.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a rule no attribute can express

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex3.cs`, `Ex3Services` only. Bind
`Dojo:D09:Window` and add the rule that `End` must be greater than `Start`, with
exactly this message:

```
End must be after Start.
```

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a validator class

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex4.cs`. Fill in `QuotaOptionsValidator` so
it returns **every** reason at once, and register it:

- `Daily must be at least 1.` — when `Daily` is below 1
- `Burst must not exceed Daily.` — when it does
- `Tier '…' is not a tier.` — when `Tier` is not one of `QuotaOptionsValidator.Tiers`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — named instances

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex5.cs`. One named registration per name in
`Ex5Services.Names`, each bound to `Dojo:D09:Feeds:{name}` and each carrying the
rule that `Url` must not be blank, with the message `Url is required.`

Then `GET /d09/feeds/{name}` → **200** with `{"name": …, "url": …,
"timeoutSeconds": …}`, **404** for a name this application does not configure,
and **500** when that named instance fails validation.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the pass that runs last

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex6.cs`, `Ex6Services` only. After binding,
fill in the blanks: a blank `FileName` becomes `report.csv`, and `FullPath`
becomes `{Folder}/{FileName}`.

A configured file name must survive.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — fail at startup, not at 3am

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex7.cs`, `Ex7Services` only. Bind
`Dojo:D09:License`, require that `Seats` is positive with the message
`Seats must be positive.`, and make that check run when the application
**starts**.

The class defaults are deliberately valid, so an unconfigured application still
boots. A configured `Seats` of 0 must stop it dead.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — bind, derive, validate twice

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex8.cs`. Bind `Dojo:D09:Pipeline`, then:

- `Name` is required and `Workers` must be between 1 and 64 (annotations)
- `Label` is derived as `{Name}:{Mode}:{Workers}` after binding
- `Mode` must be one of `Ex8Services.Modes`, with the message
  `Mode must be batch or stream.`

Both kinds of validation have to be registered: adding one does not imply the
other.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d09_options_validation

## Notes

The options pattern is three ideas wearing one name. **Binding** turns a
configuration section into a typed object. **Validation** decides whether that
object is usable. **Lifetime** decides when either of those happens, and it is
the part people skip.

`IOptions<T>` is a singleton, built once, on first use. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is
scoped and re-binds per request. `IOptionsMonitor<T>` is a singleton that tracks
changes and can be injected into other singletons. Which one you take is a
statement about how often the values may change underneath you.

The thread that runs through all eight problems: **configuration is input, and
input is validated at the boundary**. A missing bucket name, a port of 70000, an
end time before a start time — these are not exotic; they are the ordinary
result of a deploy script with a typo, and the only question is whether you find
out at startup, at first request, or in a bug report.

## ex1

`AddOptions<T>().BindConfiguration(path)` binds a section by path, resolving
`IConfiguration` from the container when it does. `services.Configure<T>(
configuration.GetSection(path))` is the older spelling of the same thing and is
just as good.

The failure worth noticing is the silent one: `IOptions<T>` **always resolves**,
even when nothing was bound, and hands back a default-constructed object. A
blank bucket name is the only symptom, and it will not look like a
configuration bug when you meet it in production.

Class defaults survive a partial section, exactly as in d08 ex2 — the binder
writes what it found and leaves the rest.

## ex2

Attributes on their own do nothing. `ValidateDataAnnotations()` is what makes
`[Required]` and `[Range]` run, and forgetting it is the classic mistake — the
code *looks* validated, and a 200 with an empty host is the only clue.

When it does run, the failure arrives as an `OptionsValidationException` on the
first `.Value`, carrying a `Failures` collection. That timing matters: it is not
at startup unless you ask (ex7), so a rarely-used option can sit broken for
weeks.

Note `[Required]` on a `string` rejects `""` by default, which is what you want
for configuration — a key present and empty is the same as absent.

## ex3

Some rules are about the *object*, not a property: an end after a start, a
maximum above a minimum, a retry count that makes sense against a timeout. No
attribute can see two properties at once, and `.Validate(predicate, message)` is
the escape hatch.

The message is the whole user interface of this failure. It is what an operator
reads at 3am, so "End must be after Start." beats "Validation failed" by more
than it looks.

The limit worth knowing: `Validate` gives you exactly one message per call. Add
several `Validate` calls for several rules, or move to a validator class.

## ex4

`IValidateOptions<T>` is the full version: a class, resolvable from the
container so it can take dependencies, and able to return **every** failure at
once via `ValidateOptionsResult.Fail(collection)`.

That last part is the real lesson. An operator who fixes one setting, redeploys,
waits for the pipeline and then discovers the next problem has had a bad
afternoon — and it was avoidable, because you knew about all three the first
time.

The classic mistake is writing the validator and never registering it. It is a
plain class; nothing runs it unless it is in the container.

## ex5

Named options let one class serve several configured instances — `primary` and
`backup` feeds, per-tenant settings, several named HTTP clients. Each name binds
separately **and validates separately**, which is why the gate can have one feed
healthy and the other refusing.

The sharp edge is `Get(name)`: it does **not** throw for a name nobody
registered. It builds an unbound instance with default values and hands it over
happily, so an endpoint that takes the name from a client has to know which
names exist. That check is the difference between a 404 and a confidently wrong
answer.

`IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is the scoped one, which is what makes it safe to
re-evaluate per request; `IOptionsMonitor<T>.Get(name)` is the singleton-safe
equivalent.

## ex6

The order is: every `Configure`, then every binding, then every `PostConfigure`,
then validation. `PostConfigure` is therefore the only place that can see the
final state — which makes it the right home for defaults that depend on other
values, and for derived fields like a full path.

The model answer *fills in* rather than overwrites: a configured file name
survives. A `PostConfigure` that assigns unconditionally silently takes the
operator's setting away, which is a genuinely confusing bug to be on the
receiving end of.

`PostConfigureAll<T>` does the same for every named instance at once.

## ex7

Without `ValidateOnStart()`, validation happens on first `.Value` — which for a
rarely-used option means the first *user* to hit that code path finds the
problem, in production, possibly weeks after the deploy.

`ValidateOnStart()` moves it to host startup, so a bad setting is a failed
deploy instead: the container never becomes healthy, the rollout halts, and the
message is in the startup log where someone is already looking.

The condition for using it is the one this exercise builds in: **the defaults
must be valid**, or an application with no configuration at all cannot start. If
a value genuinely has no safe default, that is the point — you *want* it to
refuse.

## ex8

Everything in one chain, and the thing to take away is that each link is opt-in.
`BindConfiguration` does not imply `ValidateDataAnnotations`;
`ValidateDataAnnotations` does not imply your `Validate` predicate; neither
implies `ValidateOnStart`. Four separate decisions, four separate calls.

The ordering inside the pipeline is what makes `Label` work: `PostConfigure`
runs before validation, so the derived value exists by the time the rules look at
the object — and a rule could validate the derived value too.

In a real service this whole block lives next to the class it configures, often
as an extension method (`services.AddPipelineOptions(configuration)`), so the
composition root reads as a list of features rather than a list of framework
calls.

## Further reading

- [Options pattern in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options) — `IOptions`, `IOptionsSnapshot`, `IOptionsMonitor` and named options.
- [Options pattern in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/options) — binding, `PostConfigure`, and the order the pipeline runs in.
- [Options validation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/options-library-authors#options-validation) — data annotations, `Validate`, `IValidateOptions<T>` and `ValidateOnStart`.
- [Configuration in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration) — where the sections these options bind to come from.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves. Put the constraints on the class as attributes — and then add the
one call that makes anything actually run them.

Attributes on an options class are inert by default. That is the whole trap.

## Hint 2

```csharp
[Required]
public string Host { get; set; } = "";

[Range(1, 65535)]
public int Port { get; set; } = 25;
```

…from `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations`, which the file already imports.

Then:

```csharp
services.AddOptions<SmtpOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Dojo:D09:Smtp")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations();
```

The failure arrives as an `OptionsValidationException` the first time something
reads `.Value` — which the given endpoint already catches and turns into the
500 the gate is looking for.

`[Required]` on a string rejects `""` too, which is what you want: a key present
and empty is the same as absent.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two halves. Put the constraints on the class as attributes — and then add the
one call that makes anything actually run them.

Attributes on an options class are inert by default. That is the whole trap.

## Hint 2

```csharp
[Required]
public string Host { get; set; } = "";

[Range(1, 65535)]
public int Port { get; set; } = 25;
```

…from `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations`, which the file already imports.

Then:

```csharp
services.AddOptions<SmtpOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Dojo:D09:Smtp")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations();
```

The failure arrives as an `OptionsValidationException` the first time something
reads `.Value` — which the given endpoint already catches and turns into the
500 the gate is looking for.

`[Required]` on a string rejects `""` too, which is what you want: a key present
and empty is the same as absent.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

No attribute can see two properties at once. This rule is about the *object*, so
it needs something that receives the whole object.

The message the gate checks is exact — copy it from the README.

## Hint 2

```csharp
services.AddOptions<WindowOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Dojo:D09:Window")
    .Validate(options => options.End > options.Start, "End must be after Start.");
```

`Validate` takes a predicate over the bound instance and one message, and chains
after the binding.

That message is the entire user interface of this failure — it is what an
operator reads when a deploy goes wrong at 3am. "Validation failed" would be
technically true and useless.

For several such rules, chain several `Validate` calls, or move to a validator
class (ex4).

## Exercise 5 — named instances

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex5.cs`. One named registration per name in
`Ex5Services.Names`, each bound to `Dojo:D09:Feeds:{name}` and each carrying the
rule that `Url` must not be blank, with the message `Url is required.`

Then `GET /d09/feeds/{name}` → **200** with `{"name": …, "url": …,

and **500** when that named instance fails validation.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`AddOptions<T>()` has an overload that takes a **name**, and each named
registration binds and validates independently. Loop over `Ex5Services.Names`
and register one per name.

Then the endpoint. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>.Get(name)` looks the instance up — and it
is far more forgiving than you want it to be.

## Hint 2

```csharp
foreach (string name in Names)
{
    services.AddOptions<FeedOptions>(name)
        .BindConfiguration($"Dojo:D09:Feeds:{name}")
        .Validate(options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.Url), "Url is required.");
}
```

In the handler, check `Ex5Services.Names.Contains(name)` **first** and return
`TypedResults.NotFound()` if not: `Get("nope")` does not throw, it invents an
unbound instance with defaults and hands it over.

Then `D09Options.Read(() => feeds.Get(name), value => …)` — the given helper
turns the validation failure into the 500 for you.

## Hint 3

The check the gate is really making is that validation is **per named
instance**: primary answers 200 while backup answers 500, from one options
class. That is what makes named options the right tool for "the same settings,
several times" — two feeds, several tenants, a set of named HTTP clients.

`IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is scoped, which is why it is safe to re-evaluate per
request. A singleton would need `IOptionsMonitor<T>.Get(name)` instead.

Left for you: the loop, the existence check, and deciding what should happen if
`Names` ever came from configuration rather than a constant.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`AddOptions<T>()` has an overload that takes a **name**, and each named
registration binds and validates independently. Loop over `Ex5Services.Names`
and register one per name.

Then the endpoint. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>.Get(name)` looks the instance up — and it
is far more forgiving than you want it to be.

## Hint 2

```csharp
foreach (string name in Names)
{
    services.AddOptions<FeedOptions>(name)
        .BindConfiguration($"Dojo:D09:Feeds:{name}")
        .Validate(options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.Url), "Url is required.");
}
```

In the handler, check `Ex5Services.Names.Contains(name)` **first** and return
`TypedResults.NotFound()` if not: `Get("nope")` does not throw, it invents an
unbound instance with defaults and hands it over.

Then `D09Options.Read(() => feeds.Get(name), value => …)` — the given helper
turns the validation failure into the 500 for you.

## Hint 3

The check the gate is really making is that validation is **per named
instance**: primary answers 200 while backup answers 500, from one options
class. That is what makes named options the right tool for "the same settings,
several times" — two feeds, several tenants, a set of named HTTP clients.

`IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is scoped, which is why it is safe to re-evaluate per
request. A singleton would need `IOptionsMonitor<T>.Get(name)` instead.

Left for you: the loop, the existence check, and deciding what should happen if
`Names` ever came from configuration rather than a constant.

## Exercise 6 — the pass that runs last

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex6.cs`, `Ex6Services` only. After binding,
fill in the blanks: a blank `FileName` becomes `report.csv`, and `FullPath`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`FullPath` is derived from two other values, so it can only be computed once
those values are final — after binding, after any `Configure`.

There is a registration whose whole purpose is "run last".

## Hint 2

```csharp
services.PostConfigure<ReportOptions>(options =>
{
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.FileName))
    {
        options.FileName = "report.csv";
    }

    options.FullPath = $"{options.Folder}/{options.FileName}";
});
```

The order in the options pipeline is: `Configure` → binding → `PostConfigure` →
validation. So this sees the final values, and anything validating afterwards
sees the derived ones.

Note the `if`. Assigning `FileName` unconditionally would take the operator's
configured value away — and that is a confusing bug to be on the receiving end
of, because the setting is right there in the file doing nothing.

## Exercise 7 — fail at startup, not at 3am

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex7.cs`, `Ex7Services` only. Bind
`Dojo:D09:License`, require that `Seats` is positive with the message
`Seats must be positive.`, and make that check run when the application
**starts**.

The class defaults are deliberately valid, so an unconfigured application still
boots. A configured `Seats` of 0 must stop it dead.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The rule itself is ex3's. The new part is *when* it runs: by default, on first
use — which for a rarely-read option means the first user to reach that code
path finds the problem, in production.

One more call in the chain moves it to host startup.

## Hint 2

```csharp
services.AddOptions<LicenseOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Dojo:D09:License")
    .Validate(options => options.Seats > 0, "Seats must be positive.")
    .ValidateOnStart();
```

With `ValidateOnStart`, a bad setting is a failed deploy: the host never becomes
healthy, the rollout halts, and the message is in the startup log where somebody
is already watching.

The precondition is the one this class is built around: **the defaults must be
valid**, or an application with no configuration at all cannot boot. `Seats`
defaults to 5 for exactly that reason.

And when a value genuinely has no safe default, refusing to start is the correct
behaviour rather than a problem to work around.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The rule itself is ex3's. The new part is *when* it runs: by default, on first
use — which for a rarely-read option means the first user to reach that code
path finds the problem, in production.

One more call in the chain moves it to host startup.

## Hint 2

```csharp
services.AddOptions<LicenseOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Dojo:D09:License")
    .Validate(options => options.Seats > 0, "Seats must be positive.")
    .ValidateOnStart();
```

With `ValidateOnStart`, a bad setting is a failed deploy: the host never becomes
healthy, the rollout halts, and the message is in the startup log where somebody
is already watching.

The precondition is the one this class is built around: **the defaults must be
valid**, or an application with no configuration at all cannot boot. `Seats`
defaults to 5 for exactly that reason.

And when a value genuinely has no safe default, refusing to start is the correct
behaviour rather than a problem to work around.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — bind, derive, validate twice

Edit `src/Api/D09_OptionsValidation/Ex8.cs`. Bind `Dojo:D09:Pipeline`, then:

- `Name` is required and `Workers` must be between 1 and 64 (annotations)
- `Label` is derived as `{Name}:{Mode}:{Workers}` after binding
- `Mode` must be one of `Ex8Services.Modes`, with the message
  `Mode must be batch or stream.`

Both kinds of validation have to be registered: adding one does not imply the
other.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d09_options_validation ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four things, and each one is a separate call you have already made in an earlier
exercise: bind (ex1), derive (ex6), annotations (ex2), predicate (ex3).

Nothing here implies anything else. That is the lesson.

## Hint 2

The attributes go on the class:

```csharp
[Required] public string Name { get; set; } = "";
[Range(1, 64)] public int Workers { get; set; } = 1;
```

…and the chain does the rest:

```csharp
services.AddOptions<PipelineOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Dojo:D09:Pipeline")
    .PostConfigure(options => options.Label = $"{options.Name}:{options.Mode}:{options.Workers}")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .Validate(options => Modes.Contains(options.Mode), "Mode must be batch or stream.");
```

`PostConfigure` is available on the `OptionsBuilder` too, so it can sit in the
chain rather than as a separate `services.PostConfigure<T>(...)` call.

## Hint 3

Check the ordering claim yourself: `PostConfigure` runs **before** validation, so
`Label` exists by the time the rules look at the object — which means a rule
could validate the derived value if you wanted it to.

Worth doing once the gate is green: pull the whole block into an extension
method, `services.AddPipelineOptions()`, and see how much better the composition
root reads as a list of features than as a list of framework calls. That is what
you would actually ship.

Left for you: assembling the chain, and predicting which of the three bad
configurations produces which message before you run it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Four things, and each one is a separate call you have already made in an earlier
exercise: bind (ex1), derive (ex6), annotations (ex2), predicate (ex3).

Nothing here implies anything else. That is the lesson.

## Hint 2

The attributes go on the class:

```csharp
[Required] public string Name { get; set; } = "";
[Range(1, 64)] public int Workers { get; set; } = 1;
```

…and the chain does the rest:

```csharp
services.AddOptions<PipelineOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Dojo:D09:Pipeline")
    .PostConfigure(options => options.Label = $"{options.Name}:{options.Mode}:{options.Workers}")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .Validate(options => Modes.Contains(options.Mode), "Mode must be batch or stream.");
```

`PostConfigure` is available on the `OptionsBuilder` too, so it can sit in the
chain rather than as a separate `services.PostConfigure<T>(...)` call.

## Hint 3

Check the ordering claim yourself: `PostConfigure` runs **before** validation, so
`Label` exists by the time the rules look at the object — which means a rule
could validate the derived value if you wanted it to.

Worth doing once the gate is green: pull the whole block into an extension
method, `services.AddPipelineOptions()`, and see how much better the composition
root reads as a list of features than as a list of framework calls. That is what
you would actually ship.

Left for you: assembling the chain, and predicting which of the three bad
configurations produces which message before you run it.
