lessons.briefing:
# d10 — EF Core CRUD drills

Eight problems on reading and writing rows: projection, lookups by key and by
another column, create, update, delete, a set-based update that loads nothing,
the unit of work, PUT-as-upsert, and an all-or-nothing batch. They drill lesson
**05_efcore_basics** — go back to it if `SaveChangesAsync` still feels like
magic.

Everything is under `/d10/…` against `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Model.cs`: one
`Member` entity, one `D10Db`. The gates give each test a private in-memory
SQLite database seeded with five members — Ada 120 (black), Grace 80 (brown),
Linus 200 (black), Mia 80 (white), Noor 45 (brown).

## Exercise 1 — project, then order

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d10/members` → **200** with every
member as a `MemberSummary` — id, name and credits only — most credits first,
ties broken by name A–Z.

The gate reads the raw body: `email` or `grade` appearing anywhere means whole
entities went over the wire.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — by key, and by another column

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex2.cs`.

- `GET /d10/members/{id:int}` — **200** with the whole row, **404** otherwise
- `GET /d10/members/by-email/{email}` — the same, matching on a column that is
  not the primary key

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — create

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex3.cs`. `POST /d10/members` with
`{"name": …, "email": …, "credits": …}` → **201** with
`Location: /d10/members/{id}` and the created member, at grade `white`.

A blank name, a blank email or negative credits is a **400** that writes
nothing.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — update and delete

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex4.cs`.

- `PUT /d10/members/{id:int}/credits` with `{"credits": …}` — **204** when it
  stuck, **404** when there is no such member, **400** for negative credits
  (writing nothing)
- `DELETE /d10/members/{id:int}` — **204** when the row is now gone, **404**
  when it was not there

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — change many rows without loading any

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex5.cs`.
`POST /d10/members/regrade?from=…&to=…` → **200** with `{"changed": …}`, the
number of rows that moved from one grade to the other.

Both parameters are required (**400** otherwise), and it must cost the database
**exactly one command** however many rows match.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — two rows, one save

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex6.cs`. `POST /d10/transfer` with
`{"from": …, "to": …, "credits": …}` moves credits between two members and
answers **200** with `{"changed": …}` taken from `SaveChangesAsync` itself.

**404** when either member is missing; **400** when the amount is not positive
or the sender cannot afford it — and a refused transfer leaves both rows exactly
as they were.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — PUT as upsert

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex7.cs`. `PUT /d10/roster/{email}` with
`{"name": …, "credits": …}`:

- nobody has that email → **201**, `Location: /d10/members/{id}`, the member, at
  grade `white`
- somebody does → **204**, and their name and credits are replaced
- blank name or negative credits → **400**, writing nothing

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the whole batch or none of it

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex8.cs`. `POST /d10/members/batch` with an array of
new members → **201** with `{"created": [ids]}` in request order and a
`Location` naming the first.

If **any** item is invalid — blank name, blank email, negative credits, or an
email that is already taken, *including by an earlier item in the same batch* —
the whole request is a **400** with `{"index": …, "message": …}` for the first
bad one, and not a single row is written.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d10_efcore_crud

## Notes

Two ideas hold this whole set together. The first is the **unit of work**: a
`DbContext` is not a connection, it is a change tracker. You load entities,
assign to their properties, and one `SaveChangesAsync` writes everything at once
inside a transaction. That is why ex6's transfer is safe and why ex8's batch can
be all-or-nothing without you writing a single `BEGIN`.

The second is that **the query and the write are different tools**. Reading is
LINQ that becomes SQL and should fetch only what you need (ex1). Writing is
either "load, change, save" (ex4, ex6, ex7) or, when there is nothing to load,
a set-based `ExecuteUpdateAsync` (ex5). Reaching for the wrong one is the most
common EF Core performance mistake there is.

The habit worth building: after every endpoint, ask *how many round trips did
that cost, and could the database have done it in one?*

## ex1

`Select` before `ToListAsync` and the projection becomes part of the SQL — the
database stops fetching the columns you did not ask for, and nothing is tracked,
because there is no entity to track.

The classic mistake is `ToListAsync()` first and `Select` after, which is a
`SELECT *` and an in-memory transform. It works, and it ships every column of
every row over the wire; the gate reads the raw body for exactly that reason.

And ordering is not optional. A database makes no promise about the order rows
come back in unless you say `OrderBy`, and "it looked sorted in testing" is a bug
waiting for the first index change.

## ex2

`FindAsync` is the primary-key lookup and it has one property nothing else has:
if that entity is already in the change tracker, it answers **without a round
trip**. `FirstOrDefaultAsync` always goes to the database, and it can filter on
anything.

So: `FindAsync` for a key, `FirstOrDefaultAsync` for everything else. The classic
mistake is `First` instead of `FirstOrDefault`, which throws on no match — and a
thrown exception is a 500 for what is really a 404.

## ex3

Three lines: `Add`, `SaveChangesAsync`, read the id. The id does not exist until
the save, because the database generates it — which is why the `Location` header
can only be built afterwards.

The order that matters is validate-then-`Add`. The gate counts rows after three
rejected requests because "return a 400 after calling `Add`" leaves an entity in
the change tracker; nothing has been written *yet*, but the next
`SaveChangesAsync` in that request would write it.

## ex4

There is no `Update` call in the model answer, and that surprises people. The
context tracks the entity you loaded, notices the assignment, and works out the
`UPDATE` itself. `db.Update(entity)` exists for *detached* entities — one that
arrived over the wire rather than out of a query — and using it on a tracked
entity marks every property modified, which writes columns you did not change.

Delete is the same shape: you have to `Remove` an entity, so you have to have
loaded one, which is why deleting something that is not there is a 404 rather
than a silent success.

## ex5

`ExecuteUpdateAsync` (and `ExecuteDeleteAsync`) send one `UPDATE … WHERE`
straight to the database. Nothing is loaded, nothing is tracked, `SaveChanges` is
not involved — and the command count proves it.

The trade is real and worth saying out loud: because nothing is tracked, the
change tracker does not know about it. Entities you already loaded keep their old
values, so a bulk update followed by work on stale entities in the same context
is a genuine footgun. There are no interceptors, no `SaveChanges` overrides and
no automatic audit columns either.

Use it for what it is for: "change this set of rows", where the set may be large
and you never needed the rows themselves.

## ex6

The unit of work, demonstrated. Two entities change, one `SaveChangesAsync`
writes both inside a transaction, and its return value is the number of rows it
touched — which is why the gate can tell a half-done transfer from a whole one.

The subtle part is the validation order. Once you have assigned `sender.Credits
-= amount`, the change tracker is holding that edit; returning a 400 afterwards
without saving is *usually* harmless, because the context dies with the request
— but it is only harmless by accident, and it stops being true the moment
anything else in the request saves. Check first, mutate second.

In a real system this is also where you would think about concurrency: two
transfers from the same account at once both read 120 and both write, and the
answer to that is a rowversion token and `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`.

## ex7

PUT-as-upsert, over a database. The rule is the same as anywhere else: PUT means
"make the resource at this URL be this", and when the **client** names the
resource — an email, a slug, a device id — creating it is legitimate. The 201
versus 204 branch is a statement about what happened, not about what was asked.

The EF-specific part is that "does it exist" is a query, so an upsert is
inherently two round trips. If that matters, databases have a native answer
(`MERGE`, `INSERT … ON CONFLICT`) that EF does not expose, and you reach for raw
SQL. And under real concurrency two simultaneous upserts can both see "not
there" — which is what unique indexes are for.

## ex8

All-or-nothing, and there are two halves to it. `SaveChangesAsync` gives you the
transaction for free: either every `Add` in this batch commits or none does.
What it does *not* give you is the validation discipline — the model answer
checks every item **before** adding any, so a rejection cannot leave half a batch
staged in the change tracker.

The check the gate insists on is the one people miss: a duplicate *within the
batch*. Comparing each item against the database misses two items in the same
request claiming the same email, because neither of them is in the database yet.
The fix is to accumulate as you validate.

And the error names the **index**. "One of your 500 rows is wrong" is not an
error message anybody can act on.

## Further reading

- [Saving data in EF Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/) — the change tracker, `SaveChanges`, and what it does in one transaction.
- [ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/execute-insert-update-delete) — set-based writes, and everything they deliberately skip.
- [Efficient querying](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) — projection, tracking, and counting round trips.
- [Disconnected entities](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/disconnected-entities) — when `Update` is the right call and when it writes too much.
- [Handling concurrency conflicts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/concurrency) — the ex6 follow-up an interviewer will ask.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — project, then order

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d10/members` → **200** with every
member as a `MemberSummary` — id, name and credits only — most credits first,
ties broken by name A–Z.

The gate reads the raw body: `email` or `grade` appearing anywhere means whole
entities went over the wire.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two things, and the order they appear in the query is what matters. Sort while
it is still a database query, and cut the columns down before the rows come
back.

The gate reads the raw JSON, so "project after materialising" is visible.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await db.Members
    .OrderByDescending(m => m.Credits)
    .ThenBy(m => m.Name)
    .Select(m => new MemberSummary(m.Id, m.Name, m.Credits))
    .ToListAsync();
```

Everything before `ToListAsync` becomes SQL, so the `SELECT` really does name
three columns and the `ORDER BY` really is the database's.

Putting `ToListAsync()` first and `Select` after is a `SELECT *` plus an
in-memory transform: the same answer, every column fetched.

## Hint 1

Two things, and the order they appear in the query is what matters. Sort while
it is still a database query, and cut the columns down before the rows come
back.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await db.Members
    .OrderByDescending(m => m.Credits)
    .ThenBy(m => m.Name)
    .Select(m => new MemberSummary(m.Id, m.Name, m.Credits))
    .ToListAsync();
```

Everything before `ToListAsync` becomes SQL, so the `SELECT` really does name
three columns and the `ORDER BY` really is the database's.

Putting `ToListAsync()` first and `Select` after is a `SELECT *` plus an
in-memory transform: the same answer, every column fetched.

client's.

## Hint 1

The update is shorter than you expect — there is no `Update` call in it at all.
Load the entity, assign to the property, save.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var member = await db.Members.FindAsync(id);
if (member is null) { return TypedResults.NotFound(); }

member.Credits = request.Credits;
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
```

The change tracker noticed the assignment and works out the `UPDATE` itself.
`db.Update(member)` on a tracked entity marks *every* property modified, so it
writes columns you never touched.

Validate the negative credits before the lookup, so a bad body is a 400 whatever
the id is.

## Exercise 6 — two rows, one save

Edit `src/Api/D10_EfcoreCrud/Ex6.cs`. `POST /d10/transfer` with
`{"from": …, "to": …, "credits": …}` moves credits between two members and
answers **200** with `{"changed": …}` taken from `SaveChangesAsync` itself.

**404** when either member is missing; **400** when the amount is not positive

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d10_efcore_crud ex6
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both sides of the transfer change, and both changes belong to one
`SaveChangesAsync` — that is the unit of work, and it is what makes the transfer
atomic without you writing a transaction.

The order of the checks is the part the gate is really testing.

## Hint 2

Check the amount, load both members, check they exist, check the balance — and
only then touch either entity:

```csharp
sender.Credits -= request.Credits;
receiver.Credits += request.Credits;

int changed = await db.SaveChangesAsync();
```

`SaveChangesAsync` returns the number of rows it wrote, so `changed` is 2.

Assigning before the balance check and returning a 400 afterwards leaves the
change tracker holding an edit you did not mean. It happens not to be written
here, because the context dies with the request — but that is luck, not design.

## Hint 3

The four outcomes, in order: non-positive amount → 400; either member missing →
404; sender cannot afford it → 400; otherwise move and save.

Worth thinking about once it passes: two transfers from Ada at the same instant
both read 120, both subtract, and one of them is lost. The answer is optimistic
concurrency — a `[Timestamp]` rowversion column and a
`DbUpdateConcurrencyException` you handle — and "how would you make this safe
under load" is the standard follow-up to this exact question.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both sides of the transfer change, and both changes belong to one
`SaveChangesAsync` — that is the unit of work, and it is what makes the transfer
atomic without you writing a transaction.

The order of the checks is the part the gate is really testing.

## Hint 2

Check the amount, load both members, check they exist, check the balance — and
only then touch either entity:

```csharp
sender.Credits -= request.Credits;
receiver.Credits += request.Credits;

int changed = await db.SaveChangesAsync();
```

`SaveChangesAsync` returns the number of rows it wrote, so `changed` is 2.

Assigning before the balance check and returning a 400 afterwards leaves the
change tracker holding an edit you did not mean. It happens not to be written
here, because the context dies with the request — but that is luck, not design.

## Hint 3

The four outcomes, in order: non-positive amount → 400; either member missing →
404; sender cannot afford it → 400; otherwise move and save.

Worth thinking about once it passes: two transfers from Ada at the same instant
both read 120, both subtract, and one of them is lost. The answer is optimistic
concurrency — a `[Timestamp]` rowversion column and a
`DbUpdateConcurrencyException` you handle — and "how would you make this safe
under load" is the standard follow-up to this exact question.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two passes, and keeping them separate is the whole exercise. Validate every item
first, collecting nothing but a verdict; only when the whole batch is good do you
add anything.

One of the gate's cases cannot be caught by comparing items against the
database. Find it before you write the loop.

## Hint 2

Load the taken emails once, up front:

```csharp
var taken = await db.Members.Select(m => m.Email).ToListAsync();
```

…then in the loop, `taken.Add(item.Email)` after each item passes. That is what
catches two items in the same request claiming the same email — neither of them
is in the database yet, so a database-only check sees nothing wrong.

Return `TypedResults.BadRequest(new BatchError(index, "…"))` on the first
failure, from inside the loop, before anything has been added.

## Hint 3

Build the `Member` objects into a local list as you validate, then after the
loop:

```csharp
db.Members.AddRange(members);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
```

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two passes, and keeping them separate is the whole exercise. Validate every item
first, collecting nothing but a verdict; only when the whole batch is good do you
add anything.

One of the gate's cases cannot be caught by comparing items against the
database. Find it before you write the loop.

## Hint 2

Load the taken emails once, up front:

```csharp
var taken = await db.Members.Select(m => m.Email).ToListAsync();
```

…then in the loop, `taken.Add(item.Email)` after each item passes. That is what
catches two items in the same request claiming the same email — neither of them
is in the database yet, so a database-only check sees nothing wrong.

Return `TypedResults.BadRequest(new BatchError(index, "…"))` on the first
failure, from inside the loop, before anything has been added.

## Hint 3

Build the `Member` objects into a local list as you validate, then after the
loop:

```csharp
db.Members.AddRange(members);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
var ids = members.Select(m => m.Id).ToList();
```

One `SaveChangesAsync` inserts all of them in one transaction, and the ids are
populated afterwards, in the order you added them.

Left for you: the four checks and their messages. The index is the part that
matters most — "one of your 500 rows is wrong" is not something anybody can act
on.

lessons.briefing:
# d11 — EF Core query drills

Eight problems on getting the right answer for the right number of round trips:
composing filters, projecting, grouping, aggregating, paging, killing an N+1,
split queries, and a search endpoint that does all of it on the database. They
drill lessons **05_efcore_basics** and **06_efcore_relationships**.

Everything is under `/d11/…` against `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Model.cs`:
students, courses, and the enrolments between them. Half the gates count SQL
commands, so "correct" is not enough on its own.

The seed: **students** Ada (GB), Grace (US), Linus (FI), Mia (US); **courses**
Algebra (math, 5), Calculus (math, 8), Poetry (arts, 3), Sculpture (arts, 4),
Rhetoric (arts, 2); **enrolments** 1–8, with scores 90, 75, 60, 88, 95, 66, 55,
100.

## Exercise 1 — filter, then sort

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d11/students` → **200** with the
names, sorted A–Z. An optional `country` narrows them; a country nobody is from
is an **empty array**, not a 404.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — ask for the columns you need

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d11/courses` → **200** with every
course as a `CourseSummary` — id, title, credits — sorted by title.

`subject` must not appear anywhere in the response.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — let the database do the arithmetic

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex3.cs`. `GET /d11/subjects` → **200** with one
row per subject — `{"subject": …, "courses": …, "totalCredits": …}` — sorted by
subject, in **one** SQL command.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — count and average without loading

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex4.cs`.
`GET /d11/courses/{id:int}/stats` → **200** with
`{"title": …, "enrolled": …, "averageScore": …}`, **404** when there is no such
course.

The average is a whole number, and a course nobody is enrolled on averages
**0** — not an exception.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — a page and its total

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d11/enrolments` → **200** with
`{"items": [{"id": …, "score": …}], "total": …, "page": …, "size": …}`, id
ascending.

`page` is 1-based, default 1; `size` defaults to 3 and may not exceed 50;
anything else is a **400**. It costs **exactly two** SQL commands, however big
the table is.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the N+1

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex6.cs`.
`GET /d11/enrolments/overview` already returns the right rows —
`{"enrolmentId": …, "student": …, "course": …, "score": …}`, id ascending — and
takes seventeen SQL commands to do it.

Make it **one**, without changing the output.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — one query, or one per collection

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex7.cs`.
`GET /d11/students/{id:int}/detail` → **200** with
`{"name": …, "courses": [titles sorted A–Z]}`, **404** when there is no such
student.

The same load, two ways: `split=false` (the default) must cost **one** SQL
command and `split=true` must cost **two**. Use `Include`/`ThenInclude` rather
than a projection, so the difference is visible.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — compose the query, then run it once

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d11/search` → **200** with
`{"items": [{"student": …, "course": …, "score": …}], "total": …}`, where
`total` is how many **matched**:

- `subject` — optional, matches the course's subject
- `minScore` — optional, keeps scores at or above it
- `sort` — `score` (highest first, the default), `student` or `course` (A–Z);
  anything else is a **400**
- `page` — 1-based, default 1; `size` — default 3, maximum 20

Ties break by enrolment id so paging is stable, and the whole thing costs **two**
SQL commands whatever the parameters.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/d11_efcore_queries

## Notes

An EF Core query is a **description** until you make it run. `db.Enrolments` is
an `IQueryable`, and every `Where`, `OrderBy`, `Select`, `Skip` and `Take` you
chain onto it adds to an expression tree that has not touched the database. The
moment you call `ToListAsync`, `CountAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync` — or write a
`foreach` — the tree is translated into SQL and executed.

Every problem in this set turns on where that line falls. Filter before the line
and the database filters; filter after it and you fetched everything and threw
most of it away. The answers look identical, which is exactly why half these
gates count SQL commands instead of just checking values.

Three habits come out of it. **Compose, then execute once.** **Project to what
the caller needs**, so the SELECT lists three columns rather than every one.
And **count the round trips** — an endpoint that is correct at seed size and
issues one query per row is an outage waiting for real data.

## ex1

Conditional filters are the everyday case, and the shape that works is a local
`IQueryable` you add to:

```csharp
var query = db.Students.AsQueryable();
if (…) { query = query.Where(…); }
```

Nothing runs until `ToListAsync`, so the `WHERE` is in the SQL whether the
parameter arrived or not. The classic mistake is `ToListAsync()` first and
`.Where(…)` after, which is correct and reads the whole table.

The empty-versus-missing rule from d03 applies here too: a country nobody is
from is a 200 with `[]`.

## ex2

`Select` before the execution boundary changes the SQL. The database really does
send three columns, nothing is tracked (there is no entity to track), and the
response cannot leak a field you forgot to strip.

The classic mistake is projecting after materialising — same JSON, every column
fetched — which is invisible until the table has fifty columns or one of them is
a blob. The gate reads the raw body because that is the only symptom you can see
from outside.

## ex3

`GroupBy` over an `IQueryable` becomes a real `GROUP BY`: the counting and
summing happen in the database and two rows come back. `GroupBy` after
`ToListAsync` fetches every row and does the arithmetic in your process — same
answer, whole table.

Two restrictions worth knowing, because both produce the same wall of text.

EF only translates a `GroupBy` whose result is *projected to an aggregate*.
`GroupBy(…).ToListAsync()` — grouping without aggregating — cannot be expressed
in SQL at all, and EF will tell you so rather than doing it silently, which is a
deliberate and welcome change from the days of silent client evaluation.

And the projection out of a group has to be an **anonymous type or an object
initialiser**, not a constructor call: `.Select(g => new SubjectTotals(g.Key,
g.Count(), …))` throws, while the same aggregates projected into `new { … }`
translate fine. Build the record from the materialised rows afterwards — two
rows have already arrived by then, so it costs nothing.

## ex4

`CountAsync` and `AverageAsync` push the aggregate into SQL, so nothing is
materialised. The trap is the empty set: `AverageAsync` on no rows throws
`InvalidOperationException`, because there is no average of nothing.

The fix is a cast — `Select(e => (int?)e.Score).AverageAsync()` — which lets the
database's `NULL` come back as `null` and turns the crash into a `?? 0`. That is
the same trick you need for `MaxAsync` and `MinAsync`, and it is a good thing to
have in your fingers before an interviewer asks why a report endpoint 500s at
the start of every month.

## ex5

A page and its total are two queries: one `COUNT`, one `SELECT … LIMIT`. There is
no way to get both in one round trip through EF, and the gate insists on exactly
two so that "materialise everything and count the list" is caught.

The other rules are the ones from d03's search: order **before** `Skip`/`Take`
(paging an unordered query is undefined), cap the page size rather than trusting
the client, and report the total so the client can draw page numbers.

The honest alternative worth naming: fetching `size + 1` rows and reporting only
"there is more" costs one query instead of two, and keyset pagination
(`WHERE id > lastSeen`) beats `Skip` outright once the offsets get large.

## ex6

The N+1, in the shape you will actually meet: a loop that fetches a parent for
each child. Seventeen commands for eight rows here; eight thousand for four
thousand rows in production, at which point the endpoint's latency is a function
of the network rather than the data.

The fix is one projection. `e.Student!.Name` is a **join expressed as a property
access**: the `!` is a message to the compiler, not a dereference, because
nothing in that lambda runs in your process — the whole thing is an expression
tree EF translates.

The follow-up to have ready is "how would you catch this before production", and
the answer is the gate you just ran: count the commands. Turn on the
`Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` category at Information, or
assert a query count in a test around the hot endpoint.

## ex7

`Include` + `ThenInclude` is one query with JOINs, which duplicates the root
row's columns once per related row. With one collection that is fine. With two
collections on the same root it is a **cartesian explosion** — ten orders and ten
addresses become a hundred rows — and that is what `AsSplitQuery()` exists for:
one query per collection, so nothing multiplies.

The trade is round trips against row volume, and there is a correctness footnote
that matters: split queries are **not** executed in one transaction by default,
so another writer can change the data between them. Single query is the default
for that reason.

Also worth having: `AsSplitQuery()` per query, or
`UseSqlite(…, o => o.UseQuerySplittingBehavior(…))` for the whole context.

## ex8

Everything at once, and the shape is worth memorising because almost every list
endpoint you ever write is this: compose the filters onto an `IQueryable`, count

# Reading - dotnet/d11_efcore_queries

## Notes

An EF Core query is a **description** until you make it run. `db.Enrolments` is
an `IQueryable`, and every `Where`, `OrderBy`, `Select`, `Skip` and `Take` you
chain onto it adds to an expression tree that has not touched the database. The
moment you call `ToListAsync`, `CountAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync` — or write a
`foreach` — the tree is translated into SQL and executed.

Every problem in this set turns on where that line falls. Filter before the line
and the database filters; filter after it and you fetched everything and threw
most of it away. The answers look identical, which is exactly why half these
gates count SQL commands instead of just checking values.

Three habits come out of it. **Compose, then execute once.** **Project to what
the caller needs**, so the SELECT lists three columns rather than every one.
And **count the round trips** — an endpoint that is correct at seed size and
issues one query per row is an outage waiting for real data.

## ex1

Conditional filters are the everyday case, and the shape that works is a local
`IQueryable` you add to:

```csharp
var query = db.Students.AsQueryable();
if (…) { query = query.Where(…); }
```

Nothing runs until `ToListAsync`, so the `WHERE` is in the SQL whether the
parameter arrived or not. The classic mistake is `ToListAsync()` first and
`.Where(…)` after, which is correct and reads the whole table.

The empty-versus-missing rule from d03 applies here too: a country nobody is
from is a 200 with `[]`.

## ex2

`Select` before the execution boundary changes the SQL. The database really does
send three columns, nothing is tracked (there is no entity to track), and the
response cannot leak a field you forgot to strip.

The classic mistake is projecting after materialising — same JSON, every column
fetched — which is invisible until the table has fifty columns or one of them is
a blob. The gate reads the raw body because that is the only symptom you can see
from outside.

## ex3

`GroupBy` over an `IQueryable` becomes a real `GROUP BY`: the counting and
summing happen in the database and two rows come back. `GroupBy` after
`ToListAsync` fetches every row and does the arithmetic in your process — same
answer, whole table.

Two restrictions worth knowing, because both produce the same wall of text.

EF only translates a `GroupBy` whose result is *projected to an aggregate*.
`GroupBy(…).ToListAsync()` — grouping without aggregating — cannot be expressed
in SQL at all, and EF will tell you so rather than doing it silently, which is a
deliberate and welcome change from the days of silent client evaluation.

And the projection out of a group has to be an **anonymous type or an object
initialiser**, not a constructor call: `.Select(g => new SubjectTotals(g.Key,
g.Count(), …))` throws, while the same aggregates projected into `new { … }`
translate fine. Build the record from the materialised rows afterwards — two
rows have already arrived by then, so it costs nothing.

## ex4

`CountAsync` and `AverageAsync` push the aggregate into SQL, so nothing is
materialised. The trap is the empty set: `AverageAsync` on no rows throws
`InvalidOperationException`, because there is no average of nothing.

The fix is a cast — `Select(e => (int?)e.Score).AverageAsync()` — which lets the
database's `NULL` come back as `null` and turns the crash into a `?? 0`. That is
the same trick you need for `MaxAsync` and `MinAsync`, and it is a good thing to
have in your fingers before an interviewer asks why a report endpoint 500s at
the start of every month.

## ex5

A page and its total are two queries: one `COUNT`, one `SELECT … LIMIT`. There is
no way to get both in one round trip through EF, and the gate insists on exactly
two so that "materialise everything and count the list" is caught.

The other rules are the ones from d03's search: order **before** `Skip`/`Take`
(paging an unordered query is undefined), cap the page size rather than trusting
the client, and report the total so the client can draw page numbers.

The honest alternative worth naming: fetching `size + 1` rows and reporting only
"there is more" costs one query instead of two, and keyset pagination
(`WHERE id > lastSeen`) beats `Skip` outright once the offsets get large.

## ex6

The N+1, in the shape you will actually meet: a loop that fetches a parent for
each child. Seventeen commands for eight rows here; eight thousand for four
thousand rows in production, at which point the endpoint's latency is a function
of the network rather than the data.

The fix is one projection. `e.Student!.Name` is a **join expressed as a property
access**: the `!` is a message to the compiler, not a dereference, because
nothing in that lambda runs in your process — the whole thing is an expression
tree EF translates.

The follow-up to have ready is "how would you catch this before production", and
the answer is the gate you just ran: count the commands. Turn on the
`Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` category at Information, or
assert a query count in a test around the hot endpoint.

## ex7

`Include` + `ThenInclude` is one query with JOINs, which duplicates the root
row's columns once per related row. With one collection that is fine. With two
collections on the same root it is a **cartesian explosion** — ten orders and ten
addresses become a hundred rows — and that is what `AsSplitQuery()` exists for:
one query per collection, so nothing multiplies.

The trade is round trips against row volume, and there is a correctness footnote
that matters: split queries are **not** executed in one transaction by default,
so another writer can change the data between them. Single query is the default
for that reason.

Also worth having: `AsSplitQuery()` per query, or
`UseSqlite(…, o => o.UseQuerySplittingBehavior(…))` for the whole context.

## ex8

and a SQL injection. And the **tie-break on a unique column** makes paging

another.

The command count is the proof that composition worked. Two: one for the total,
one for the page.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — ask for the columns you need

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d11/courses` → **200** with every
course as a `CourseSummary` — id, title, credits — sorted by title.

`subject` must not appear anywhere in the response.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One query, and the only interesting decision is *where* the projection goes. The
gate reads the raw response body, so the difference between projecting before
and after materialising is visible from outside.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await db.Courses
    .OrderBy(c => c.Title)
    .Select(c => new CourseSummary(c.Id, c.Title, c.Credits))
    .ToListAsync();
```

Because the `Select` is before `ToListAsync`, the SQL names three columns and
`Subject` is never fetched. Nothing is tracked either — there is no entity to
track — which is a small extra saving on every read-only query.

`ToListAsync()` followed by `.Select(...)` gives the same JSON and a `SELECT *`.

## Hint 1

The gate wants one SQL command, so the grouping and the arithmetic both have to
happen in the database. That rules out fetching the courses and grouping the

LINQ's grouping operator translates — as long as what you project out of each

## Hint 2

```csharp
var grouped = await db.Courses
    .GroupBy(c => c.Subject)
    .Select(g => new
    {
        Subject = g.Key,
        Courses = g.Count(),
        TotalCredits = g.Sum(c => c.Credits),
    })
    .OrderBy(t => t.Subject)
    .ToListAsync();
```

`g.Key` is the subject, and `Count`/`Sum` inside the projection become `COUNT`
and `SUM` in the `GROUP BY`.

step is in memory and costs nothing — you are converting two rows, not a table.

The reason for the anonymous type is worth knowing, because the error message is
long and the cause is not obvious: EF **cannot translate a group projection

build the record after `ToListAsync`.

## Hint 1

Two aggregates over the same filtered set, and neither of them should
materialise an enrolment. Build the filtered query once and ask it two questions.

One of the two questions has no answer when the set is empty. Run the gate's
Rhetoric case and see what happens.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var enrolments = db.Enrolments.Where(e => e.CourseId == id);

int enrolled = await enrolments.CountAsync();
double average = await enrolments.Select(e => (int?)e.Score).AverageAsync() ?? 0;
```

The cast to `int?` is the whole trick: averaging a nullable lets the database's
`NULL` come back as `null`, where averaging an `int` over no rows throws
`InvalidOperationException`.

The same applies to `MaxAsync` and `MinAsync`, and it is a very common way for a
reports endpoint to 500 on the first day of a month.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two aggregates over the same filtered set, and neither of them should
materialise an enrolment. Build the filtered query once and ask it two questions.

One of the two questions has no answer when the set is empty. Run the gate's
Rhetoric case and see what happens.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var enrolments = db.Enrolments.Where(e => e.CourseId == id);

int enrolled = await enrolments.CountAsync();
double average = await enrolments.Select(e => (int?)e.Score).AverageAsync() ?? 0;
```

The cast to `int?` is the whole trick: averaging a nullable lets the database's
`NULL` come back as `null`, where averaging an `int` over no rows throws
`InvalidOperationException`.

The same applies to `MaxAsync` and `MinAsync`, and it is a very common way for a
reports endpoint to 500 on the first day of a month.

## Exercise 5 — a page and its total

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d11/enrolments` → **200** with
`{"items": [{"id": …, "score": …}], "total": …, "page": …, "size": …}`, id
ascending.

`page` is 1-based, default 1; `size` defaults to 3 and may not exceed 50;
anything else is a **400**. It costs **exactly two** SQL commands, however big
the table is.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex5
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two questions, two queries: how many are there, and what is on this page. Build
the ordered query once and use it for both.

Resolve and validate the paging values before you touch the database.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var query = db.Enrolments.OrderBy(e => e.Id);

int total = await query.CountAsync();

var items = await query
    .Skip((wanted - 1) * perPage)
    .Take(perPage)
    .Select(e => new EnrolmentItem(e.Id, e.Score))
    .ToListAsync();
```

Order before `Skip`/`Take` — paging an unordered query is undefined, and the
database is free to hand you the same row on two different pages.

`ToListAsync().Count` instead of `CountAsync()` would be one command instead of
two, and would fetch the whole table to get it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var query = db.Enrolments.OrderBy(e => e.Id);

int total = await query.CountAsync();

var items = await query
    .Skip((wanted - 1) * perPage)
    .Take(perPage)
    .Select(e => new EnrolmentItem(e.Id, e.Score))
    .ToListAsync();
```

Order before `Skip`/`Take` — paging an unordered query is undefined, and the
database is free to hand you the same row on two different pages.

`ToListAsync().Count` instead of `CountAsync()` would be one command instead of
two, and would fetch the whole table to get it.

## Hint 1

Load the student with their enrolments and each enrolment's course — two levels,
so two calls. Then one line switches between the two execution strategies.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var query = db.Students
    .Include(s => s.Enrolments)
    .ThenInclude(e => e.Course)
    .Where(s => s.Id == id);

query = split == true ? query.AsSplitQuery() : query.AsSingleQuery();
```

`AsSingleQuery()` is the default, so naming it explicitly is for the reader
rather than the compiler.

Then materialise, null-check for the 404, and sort the titles in memory — they
are already loaded, so there is nothing to gain from doing it in SQL.

## Hint 3

The reason `AsSplitQuery` exists is not this query — it is the one with **two**
collections on the same root. `Include(o => o.Lines).Include(o => o.Addresses)`
in a single query JOINs both, so ten lines and ten addresses come back as a
hundred rows, each repeating the order's columns. That is the cartesian
explosion, and splitting is the cure.

The caveat to know: split queries are not run in one transaction by default, so
another writer can change the data between them. That is why single query is
still the default.

Left for you: the sort, and deciding which you would ship for this shape. (One
collection, small: single.)

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Load the student with their enrolments and each enrolment's course — two levels,
so two calls. Then one line switches between the two execution strategies.

Use `Include`/`ThenInclude`, not a projection: a projection would not show the
difference the gate is measuring.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var query = db.Students
    .Include(s => s.Enrolments)
    .ThenInclude(e => e.Course)
    .Where(s => s.Id == id);

query = split == true ? query.AsSplitQuery() : query.AsSingleQuery();
```

`AsSingleQuery()` is the default, so naming it explicitly is for the reader
rather than the compiler.

Then materialise, null-check for the 404, and sort the titles in memory — they
are already loaded, so there is nothing to gain from doing it in SQL.

## Hint 3

The reason `AsSplitQuery` exists is not this query — it is the one with **two**
collections on the same root. `Include(o => o.Lines).Include(o => o.Addresses)`
in a single query JOINs both, so ten lines and ten addresses come back as a
hundred rows, each repeating the order's columns. That is the cartesian
explosion, and splitting is the cure.

The caveat to know: split queries are not run in one transaction by default, so
another writer can change the data between them. That is why single query is
still the default.

Left for you: the sort, and deciding which you would ship for this shape. (One
collection, small: single.)

## Exercise 8 — compose the query, then run it once

Edit `src/Api/D11_EfcoreQueries/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d11/search` → **200** with
`{"items": [{"student": …, "course": …, "score": …}], "total": …}`, where
`total` is how many **matched**:

- `subject` — optional, matches the course's subject
- `minScore` — optional, keeps scores at or above it
- `sort` — `score` (highest first, the default), `student` or `course` (A–Z);
  anything else is a **400**
- `page` — 1-based, default 1; `size` — default 3, maximum 20

Ties break by enrolment id so paging is stable, and the whole thing costs **two**
SQL commands whatever the parameters.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d11_efcore_queries ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The shape of almost every list endpoint you will ever write: resolve and
validate the parameters, compose the filters onto an `IQueryable`, count it,
order it, page it, project it, execute.

Do the validation first — a bad sort should not cost a database round trip.

## Hint 2

Filters compose the same way as ex1:

```csharp
var query = db.Enrolments.AsQueryable();
if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(subject)) { query = query.Where(e => e.Course!.Subject == subject); }
if (minScore is not null) { query = query.Where(e => e.Score >= minScore); }

int total = await query.CountAsync();
```

The sort is a `switch` over the whitelist, and every branch ends with
`.ThenBy(e => e.Id)`.

Then `Skip`/`Take`/`Select`/`ToListAsync`, exactly as in ex5.

## Hint 3

The two decisions worth being able to defend:

**The whitelist.** Only `score`, `student` and `course` are sortable, so your
column names never become API surface and every supported sort can be indexed.
In a codebase where sorts are built by string concatenation, this is also the
line between an API and a SQL injection.

**The tie-break.** `ThenBy(e => e.Id)` on a unique column makes the ordering
total. An `ORDER BY` with ties can come back in a different order on the next
request, and a client paging through an unstable sort sees one row twice and
never sees another.

Left for you: the switch, and predicting the command count before you run it.
(Two.)

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The shape of almost every list endpoint you will ever write: resolve and
validate the parameters, compose the filters onto an `IQueryable`, count it,
order it, page it, project it, execute.

Do the validation first — a bad sort should not cost a database round trip.

## Hint 2

Filters compose the same way as ex1:

```csharp
var query = db.Enrolments.AsQueryable();
if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(subject)) { query = query.Where(e => e.Course!.Subject == subject); }
if (minScore is not null) { query = query.Where(e => e.Score >= minScore); }

int total = await query.CountAsync();
```

The sort is a `switch` over the whitelist, and every branch ends with
`.ThenBy(e => e.Id)`.

Then `Skip`/`Take`/`Select`/`ToListAsync`, exactly as in ex5.

## Hint 3

The two decisions worth being able to defend:

**The whitelist.** Only `score`, `student` and `course` are sortable, so your
column names never become API surface and every supported sort can be indexed.
In a codebase where sorts are built by string concatenation, this is also the
line between an API and a SQL injection.

**The tie-break.** `ThenBy(e => e.Id)` on a unique column makes the ordering
total. An `ORDER BY` with ties can come back in a different order on the next
request, and a client paging through an unstable sort sees one row twice and
never sees another.

Left for you: the switch, and predicting the command count before you run it.
(Two.)

# d12 — EF Core relationship drills

Eight problems on navigations: loading the "many" side, walking a many-to-many
both ways, creating a child, cascade delete, filtered includes, aggregating
across two hops, nested collection projections, and replacing a many-to-many
set. They drill lesson **06_efcore_relationships**.

Everything is under `/d12/…` against
`src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Model.cs`: `Author 1--* Book 1--* Review`, and
`Book *--* Genre` with no join entity in the model.

The seed: **authors** Ada, Grace, Linus (who has written nothing); **books**
Aurora (Ada, scifi), Bramble (Ada, essay + poetry), Cinder (Grace, scifi +
essay), Dust (Grace, poetry); **reviews** zoe 5 and yan 3 on Aurora, zoe 4 on
Bramble, xu 2 and yan 4 on Cinder, xu 5 on Dust.

## Exercise 1 — an author and their books

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex1.cs`.
`GET /d12/authors/{id:int}` → **200** with
`{"id": …, "name": …, "books": [{"id": …, "title": …}]}`, books by title.

An author who has written nothing is a **200 with an empty list**; an author who
does not exist is a **404**.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — many-to-many, both ways

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex2.cs`.

- `GET /d12/books/{id:int}/genres` — **200** with the genre names, sorted;
  **404** when there is no such book
- `GET /d12/genres/{name}/books` — **200** with the titles, sorted; **404** when
  there is no such genre

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — create a child

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex3.cs`.
`POST /d12/authors/{id:int}/books` with `{"title": …, "year": …}` → **201** with
`Location: /d12/books/{id}` and `{"id": …, "title": …, "year": …}`, attached to
that author.

**404** when the author does not exist; **400** for a blank title or a year
below 1, writing nothing.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — what happens to the children

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex4.cs`.
`DELETE /d12/books/{id:int}` → **204** when the book is now gone, **404** when it
was not there.

Its reviews go with it, and so do its rows in the book–genre join table —
without you writing a line about either.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — load some of the children

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex5.cs`.
`GET /d12/books/{id:int}/reviews?minStars=…` → **200** with
`{"title": …, "reviews": [{"reviewer": …, "stars": …}]}` — only the reviews of at
least `minStars` (default 0), sorted by reviewer. **404** when there is no such
book.

The filtering happens in the database: **one** SQL command, and the reviews that
did not qualify are never fetched.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — aggregate across two hops

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex6.cs`.
`GET /d12/authors/ratings` → **200** with one row per author —
`{"author": …, "books": …, "averageStars": …}` — sorted by name, in **one** SQL
command.

The average is over every review of every one of that author's books, truncated
to a whole number. An author with no reviews averages **0**, and an author with
no books still appears.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — collections inside collections

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex7.cs`. `GET /d12/library` → **200**
with `[{"author": …, "books": [{"title": …, "genres": [ … ]}]}]` — authors by
name, books by title, genres by name, and an author with no books still there.

**One** SQL command for the whole shape.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — replace the set

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex8.cs`.
`PUT /d12/books/{id:int}/genres` takes a JSON array of genre names — the
complete list the book should have afterwards:

- **204** — the book now carries exactly those, no more and no fewer
- **404** — there is no such book
- **400** — a name that is not a genre, quoting it, and nothing changes

An empty array is a valid request: it means "no genres".

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d12_efcore_relationships

## Notes

A navigation property is a **relationship**, not a field that is always there.
EF gives you three ways to fill one — `Include`, a projection, or explicit
loading — and exactly none of them happen by default. A collection you did not
ask for is empty, not null and not lazily fetched, which is why "the author has
no books" is the single most common first bug in this area.

The second idea is that **a foreign key and a navigation are two views of the
same thing**. Setting `book.AuthorId = 1` and setting `book.Author = ada` do the
same work; the FK is enough when you already have the id, and it saves a query.

The third is that relationships have **behaviour**, not just shape. A required
relationship cascades on delete by convention. A many-to-many keeps a join table
you never named and never query directly. Knowing what EF does for you here is
most of what separates a working data layer from a surprising one.

## ex1

Three ways to load the "many" side, and this exercise uses the one that fetches
least: **project the collection**. `a.Books.Select(...)` inside a `Select`
becomes part of the SQL, so you get exactly the columns you named and nothing is
tracked.

`Include(a => a.Books)` is the other route and is right when you need the
entities themselves — to change them, or because you are going to save.

The classic mistake is neither: a plain `FirstOrDefaultAsync` and then reading
`author.Books`, which is an empty list and no error at all. Lazy loading would
have papered over it, which is exactly why it is off by default.

## ex2

The join table exists in the database and not in your model, and `SelectMany`
over the skip navigation walks it in whichever direction you start from.
`db.Books.Where(…).SelectMany(b => b.Genres)` and
`db.Genres.Where(…).SelectMany(g => g.Books)` are the same table, read two ways.

The design decision worth noticing is the 404s. A book with no genres is a 200
with `[]`; a book that does not exist is a 404 — the same empty-versus-missing
rule as everywhere else, and the reason the model answer checks existence
separately before projecting.

## ex3

Setting `AuthorId` is enough. The navigation property is optional sugar: EF fixes
it up when both ends are tracked, and skipping it saves loading the author at
all.

The model answer still checks the author exists, and the reason is the error
message. Inserting with an author id nobody has produces a foreign-key violation
— a `DbUpdateException` wrapping a provider-specific message, which is a 500
that tells the caller nothing. One `AnyAsync` turns it into a 404 that does.

The other route is `author.Books.Add(book)` on a loaded author, which is
natural when you already have the parent in hand.

## ex4

`Review.BookId` is a non-nullable `int`, so EF makes the relationship required,
and a required relationship is **cascade delete** by convention: deleting the
book deletes its reviews, and the join rows go with it.

Two things to know before relying on it. The database enforces this only if the
FK was created with `ON DELETE CASCADE` — EF's migrations do that, and on SQLite
the provider turns foreign keys on for you. And EF *also* cascades in the change
tracker for children it has loaded, which is why a delete can behave differently
depending on what happened to be in memory.

Make the FK nullable and the convention changes to `ClientSetNull`: the children
survive with a null parent. Neither default is wrong; the point is to have
chosen. `OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict)` is the third option, and it is the
right one whenever "delete this and everything under it" should require a human
to say so twice.

## ex5

Filtered include — `Include(b => b.Reviews.Where(...))` — has been available
since EF Core 5, and the projection form used here does the same job with less
ceremony. Either way the filter is in the SQL, so the rows that did not qualify
never cross the wire.

The classic mistake is loading the collection and filtering the materialised
list. Identical JSON, and every review of every book fetched — which is fine at
six rows and ruinous on a book with ten thousand.

The restriction worth knowing about filtered includes: they can only use
`Where`, `OrderBy`, `Skip` and `Take`, and the *same* navigation must be
filtered identically everywhere in one query, or EF throws.

## ex6

Two hops and an aggregate, in one query. `a.Books.SelectMany(b => b.Reviews)`
inside a projection translates into a correlated subquery, so the database does
the averaging and three rows come back.

Two details do the work. The **left join**: starting from `Authors` means Linus
appears with zero books, where starting from `Reviews` and grouping would have
dropped him — and "the customer who has never ordered" is the classic instance of
that bug. And the **nullable average**: `Average(r => (double?)r.Stars) ?? 0`,
because averaging an empty set throws, exactly as in d11 ex4.

## ex7

A projection with a collection inside a collection is still one query. EF sends
the JOINed rows and reassembles the object graph on the way back — you do not
have to choose between "one query" and "the shape I actually want".

The classic mistake is the readable-looking loop: fetch the authors, then for
each one fetch the books, then for each book fetch the genres. That is the N+1
squared, and it looks fine in a test with three authors.

The caveat that connects this to d11 ex7: JOINing two collections at the same
level multiplies rows, so a wide projection can move a surprising amount of data
even in one round trip. One query is usually right; `AsSplitQuery` is the escape
hatch when the multiplication gets out of hand.

## ex8

Replacing a many-to-many set is `Clear()` then `AddRange()`, and EF works out
which join rows to insert and which to delete. That only works if the current
set was **loaded** — `Include(b => b.Genres)` — because there is nothing to clear
otherwise, and a `Clear()` on an unloaded collection silently removes nothing.

The order matters as much as the mechanics: validate every name *before*
clearing. Clearing and then discovering an unknown genre leaves the book with no
genres and the caller with a 400, which is the worst of both.

The design decision is refusing to invent a genre. A `PUT` that creates
vocabulary on the fly means one typo becomes a permanent tag that nothing else
uses — the classic failure of free-text tagging systems. A 400 quoting the name
is friendlier than it looks.

## Further reading

- [Relationships in EF Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/relationships) — conventions for one-to-many, many-to-many, and what a required FK implies.
- [Loading related data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/related-data/) — eager, explicit and lazy loading, and filtered includes.
- [Cascade delete](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/cascade-delete) — the conventions, the database side, and `DeleteBehavior`.
- [Many-to-many relationships](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/relationships/many-to-many) — skip navigations and the join entity you did not write.
- [Efficient querying](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) — projections over includes, and the cost of JOINing two collections.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — an author and their books

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex1.cs`.
`GET /d12/authors/{id:int}` → **200** with
`{"id": …, "name": …, "books": [{"id": …, "title": …}]}`, books by title.

An author who has written nothing is a **200 with an empty list**; an author who
does not exist is a **404**.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A navigation property is not loaded unless you ask. A plain `FirstOrDefaultAsync`
gives you the author with an *empty* Books list — no error, no warning, and a
response that looks like the author wrote nothing.

Two ways to ask; the one that fetches least is a projection.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await db.Authors
    .Where(a => a.Id == id)
    .Select(a => new AuthorDetail(
        a.Id,
        a.Name,
        a.Books.OrderBy(b => b.Title).Select(b => new BookSummary(b.Id, b.Title)).ToList()))
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync();
```

The inner `Select` becomes part of the SQL, so you get two columns per book and
nothing is tracked.

`Include(a => a.Books)` is the other route, and the one to use when you need the
book entities themselves — to change them, or because you are about to save.

Null from `FirstOrDefaultAsync` is your 404; an empty Books list is not.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You do not need to load the author. A `Book` carries its parent's id as an
ordinary property, and setting it is all that attaches the new row.

You do still need to know the author *exists* — think about what happens if you
insert with an id nobody has.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (!await db.Authors.AnyAsync(a => a.Id == id)) { return TypedResults.NotFound(); }

var book = new Book { Title = request.Title, Year = request.Year, AuthorId = id };
db.Books.Add(book);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
```

Without the check, the insert fails on a foreign-key violation: a
`DbUpdateException` wrapping a provider message, which reaches the client as a
500 that explains nothing. One `AnyAsync` turns it into a 404 that does.

Validate the body before the existence check, and read `book.Id` after the save
for the Location.

The other route is `author.Books.Add(book)` on a loaded author — natural when
you already have the parent in hand, and one query more when you do not.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

You do not need to load the author. A `Book` carries its parent's id as an
ordinary property, and setting it is all that attaches the new row.

You do still need to know the author *exists* — think about what happens if you
insert with an id nobody has.

## Hint 2

```csharp
if (!await db.Authors.AnyAsync(a => a.Id == id)) { return TypedResults.NotFound(); }

var book = new Book { Title = request.Title, Year = request.Year, AuthorId = id };
db.Books.Add(book);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
```

Without the check, the insert fails on a foreign-key violation: a
`DbUpdateException` wrapping a provider message, which reaches the client as a
500 that explains nothing. One `AnyAsync` turns it into a 404 that does.

Validate the body before the existence check, and read `book.Id` after the save
for the Location.

The other route is `author.Books.Add(book)` on a loaded author — natural when
you already have the parent in hand, and one query more when you do not.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This one is shorter than it looks. Load the book, remove it, save — and say
nothing about the reviews at all.

If you find yourself deleting reviews by hand, stop and ask what EF already
knows about the relationship.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var book = await db.Books.FindAsync(id);
if (book is null) { return TypedResults.NotFound(); }

db.Books.Remove(book);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
```

`Review.BookId` is a non-nullable `int`, so the relationship is **required**, and
a required relationship cascades on delete by convention. The reviews go, and so
do the book's rows in the join table.

Worth knowing before you rely on it: make that FK nullable and the convention
changes to `ClientSetNull` — the children survive with a null parent. And
`OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict)` is the third option, which is the right one
when "delete this and everything under it" should need saying twice.

## Exercise 5 — load some of the children

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex5.cs`.
`GET /d12/books/{id:int}/reviews?minStars=…` → **200** with
`{"title": …, "reviews": [{"reviewer": …, "stars": …}]}` — only the reviews of at
least `minStars` (default 0), sorted by reviewer. **404** when there is no such
book.

The filtering happens in the database: **one** SQL command, and the reviews that
did not qualify are never fetched.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The gate counts one SQL command and checks that the reviews below the threshold
never appear. Both mean the filter has to be *inside* the query, not applied to a
loaded list.

You can filter a collection while projecting it — the same shape as ex1, with a
`Where` in the middle.

## Hint 2

```csharp
int floor = minStars ?? 0;

await db.Books
    .Where(b => b.Id == id)
    .Select(b => new BookReviews(
        b.Title,
        b.Reviews
            .Where(r => r.Stars >= floor)
            .OrderBy(r => r.Reviewer)
            .Select(r => new ReviewLine(r.Reviewer, r.Stars))
            .ToList()))
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync();
```

`Include(b => b.Reviews.Where(...))` — a filtered include — does the same job
when you want the entities rather than a DTO.

A book whose reviews all fall below the floor is still a 200 with an empty list;
only a missing book is a 404.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — aggregate across two hops

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex6.cs`.
`GET /d12/authors/ratings` → **200** with one row per author —
`{"author": …, "books": …, "averageStars": …}` — sorted by name, in **one** SQL
command.

The average is over every review of every one of that author's books, truncated
to a whole number. An author with no reviews averages **0**, and an author with
no books still appears.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start from the authors, not the reviews — that is what keeps the author who has
written nothing in the result. Then reach two hops down inside the projection.

One of the three authors has no reviews at all, and averaging nothing throws.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await db.Authors
    .OrderBy(a => a.Name)
    .Select(a => new AuthorRating(
        a.Name,
        a.Books.Count,
        (int)(a.Books.SelectMany(b => b.Reviews).Average(r => (double?)r.Stars) ?? 0)))
    .ToListAsync();
```

`SelectMany` flattens the second hop, and the `(double?)` cast is the same trick
as d11 ex4: it lets the database's `NULL` come back as `null` instead of raising
`InvalidOperationException`.

The cast to `int` truncates, which is why Grace's 3.67 is a 3.

## Hint 3

The design point worth taking away is the direction. Starting from `Reviews` and
grouping by author would give the same numbers for Ada and Grace and would
silently **drop Linus** — an inner join, with no error and no obvious symptom.

"The customer who has never ordered" is the same bug, and it is the one that
makes a monthly report quietly under-count.

Left for you: assembling the projection, and predicting the command count before
you run it. (One.)

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the authors, not the reviews — that is what keeps the author who has
written nothing in the result. Then reach two hops down inside the projection.

One of the three authors has no reviews at all, and averaging nothing throws.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await db.Authors
    .OrderBy(a => a.Name)
    .Select(a => new AuthorRating(
        a.Name,
        a.Books.Count,
        (int)(a.Books.SelectMany(b => b.Reviews).Average(r => (double?)r.Stars) ?? 0)))
    .ToListAsync();
```

`SelectMany` flattens the second hop, and the `(double?)` cast is the same trick
as d11 ex4: it lets the database's `NULL` come back as `null` instead of raising
`InvalidOperationException`.

The cast to `int` truncates, which is why Grace's 3.67 is a 3.

## Hint 3

The design point worth taking away is the direction. Starting from `Reviews` and
grouping by author would give the same numbers for Ada and Grace and would
silently **drop Linus** — an inner join, with no error and no obvious symptom.

"The customer who has never ordered" is the same bug, and it is the one that
makes a monthly report quietly under-count.

Left for you: assembling the projection, and predicting the command count before
you run it. (One.)

## Hint 1

This is ex1 with one more level. A projection may contain a collection, and that
collection's projection may contain another one — EF handles the whole shape in
a single query.

Sort at every level, and start from the authors so the empty shelf survives.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await db.Authors
    .OrderBy(a => a.Name)
    .Select(a => new ShelfAuthor(
        a.Name,
        a.Books
            .OrderBy(b => b.Title)
            .Select(b => new ShelfBook(
                b.Title,
                b.Genres.OrderBy(g => g.Name).Select(g => g.Name).ToList()))
            .ToList()))
    .ToListAsync();
```

Three `OrderBy`s, three levels, one `ToListAsync`.

The alternative — fetch authors, loop, fetch books, loop, fetch genres — is the
N+1 squared, and it reads perfectly well right up until the data is real.

## Hint 3

Worth understanding rather than just copying: EF sends the JOINed rows and
reassembles the object graph on the way back, which is why one query can produce
a nested shape at all.

The cost is the flip side of d11 ex7. JOINing collections repeats the parent's
columns once per child row, so a wide projection can move a surprising amount of
data even in a single round trip. One query is usually right; `AsSplitQuery` is
the escape hatch when the multiplication gets out of hand.

Left for you: the three sorts, and checking that Linus still appears.

Edit `src/Api/D12_EfcoreRelationships/Ex8.cs`.
`PUT /d12/books/{id:int}/genres` takes a JSON array of genre names — the
complete list the book should have afterwards:

- **204** — the book now carries exactly those, no more and no fewer
- **404** — there is no such book
- **400** — a name that is not a genre, quoting it, and nothing changes

An empty array is a valid request: it means "no genres".

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d12_efcore_relationships ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

PUT replaces, so the end state is exactly the names in the body — which means
clearing what is there and adding what was asked for.

You cannot clear a collection you did not load. And you must not clear anything
until you know every name is real.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var book = await db.Books
    .Include(b => b.Genres)
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync(b => b.Id == id);
```

The `Include` is not optional: `Clear()` on an unloaded collection removes
nothing at all, silently.

Then look the names up in one query, `db.Genres.Where(g => wanted.Contains(g.Name))`,
and compare counts (or find the first name that came back with no match) to
produce the 400.

Only after that:

```csharp
book.Genres.Clear();
book.Genres.AddRange(genres);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
```

EF works out which join rows to insert and which to delete.

## Hint 3

Two decisions worth being able to defend.

**Validate before clearing.** The gate re-reads the genres after a rejected
request precisely to catch "clear, then discover steampunk is not a genre" —
which leaves the book with nothing and the caller with a 400.

**Refuse to invent a genre.** Creating one on the fly makes every typo a
permanent tag that nothing else uses, which is how free-text tagging systems rot.
A 400 quoting the name is friendlier than it looks.

Left for you: how you detect the unknown name, and whether duplicates in the
request body should be an error or ignored. (The gate does not test it; decide
anyway.)

lessons.briefing:
# d13 - EF Core tracking drills

Eight problems on the change tracker: what gets remembered, what gets written,
what a query really costs, and the two ways the identity map can hand you stale
data. They drill lessons **05_efcore_basics** and **06_efcore_relationships** -
redo those if "tracked" still just means "loaded". Several gates here grade the
number of SQL commands as strictly as the response body.

Everything is under `/d13/...`. The entities, DTOs and the calibration helper
live in `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Model.cs` - given code, read it first. Each
exercise owns one file, so nothing you do here can break another exercise.

## Exercise 1 - reads must not stick

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d13/board` lists every van as a
`BoardRow` - id, plate, status UPPERCASED for the wall display - ordered by
plate A-Z, and records one `BoardView` audit row per view (that part is already
written and must stay).

As shipped, viewing the board twice quietly rewrites every van's status in the
database. Make the uppercase live in the response only.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - load, assign, save

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex2.cs`. `PUT /d13/vans/{id}/mileage` takes a
`MileageChange`: 404 for an unknown van, 400 when the new reading is lower than
the current one, otherwise 204 - having changed the mileage and *nothing else*,
in exactly two round trips.

The shipped version fabricates a `Van` and calls `Update()` on it. Run the gate
once and look at what that did to the plate.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - nothing changed, nothing written

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex3.cs`. `PUT /d13/vans/{id}/depot` answers
200 with a `ChangeReport`: `changed` is whether anything was really written.
Moving a van to the depot it is already in must cost ONE round trip and no
UPDATE at all; a real move costs two and reports `changed: true`. 404 unknown
van, 400 blank depot.

`SaveChangesAsync` returns something useful here.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - the identity map

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex4.cs`. `GET /d13/vans/{id}/recheck` fetches
the van twice - and must answer 200 with a `RecheckReport` where `sameInstance`
is `true`, at a total cost of ONE database query. 404 (for one query) when the
van does not exist.

One of the two fetch APIs checks the tracker before it builds SQL.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - update without loading

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex5.cs`. `PUT /d13/vans/{id}` replaces every
client-visible column from a `VanReplacement`. 400 when plate, depot or status
is blank or mileage is negative; 204 on success in exactly ONE round trip - no
SELECT; 404 when the row does not exist, which without a SELECT you learn from
the UPDATE itself.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - bulk update blindsides the tracker

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex6.cs`. `POST /d13/depots/{depot}/service-bump`
adds `amount` to every van in the depot with one `ExecuteUpdate`, then answers
200 with each van as a `DepotVan` (id ascending) showing the mileage as it is
NOW. 400 when the amount is not positive, 404 when the depot has no vans, at
most three round trips.

The shipped version reports numbers that are 500 out of date. Understand why
before you fix it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - the cache that lied

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex7.cs`. `GET /d13/vans/{id}/tuneup`: 404 for
an unknown van; otherwise call `D13Calibration.Apply` (given code) exactly
once, then answer 200 with a `TuneupReport` carrying the mileage AFTER the
correction.

The shipped version re-queries after the correction and still reports the old
number. The re-query is real; the result is not what you think.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - sync the fleet, all or nothing

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex8.cs`. `POST /d13/sync` takes a list of
`SyncItem`s. 400 for an empty batch; 404 + a `SyncError` naming the first
offending index for an unknown id; 409 + a `SyncError` for a reading lower than
the database's - and in every failure case NOTHING is written. Success applies
the whole batch with one SELECT and one SaveChanges and answers 200 with a
`SyncResult`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d13_efcore_tracking

## Notes

Every problem in this set is the same question asked eight ways: **which
objects does this DbContext remember, and what will it do about them?** A
tracked entity is compared against a snapshot at SaveChanges time; anything
different gets written, whether you meant it or not (ex1). The tracker is also
an identity map: within one context, one primary key maps to at most one
instance, which makes a second fetch free (ex4) and makes a "fresh" re-query
lie to you (ex7). And everything the tracker does costs or saves round trips,
which is why half these gates count SQL commands: the response body can be
right while the query plan is a disaster.

The working rules: reads that only render should not track; writes that start
from a loaded entity should let change detection do the work; writes that start
from a payload do not need the load at all; and anything that bypasses the
tracker - `ExecuteUpdate`, another process, raw SQL - leaves tracked instances
stale until you deliberately read past them.

## ex1

This problem was really testing whether you know that *mutating a tracked
entity is a write waiting to happen*. The handler only wanted to uppercase a
string for a display board, but the vans were tracked, and the audit-row
`SaveChanges` faithfully flushed the "formatting".

The classic mistake is thinking SaveChanges only writes "what you saved". It
writes every detected change on every tracked entity. The model answer reads
the vans with `AsNoTracking()` (projecting into `BoardRow` before formatting is
even better), so the display mutation is invisible to the context and the audit
insert is the only change in the room.

## ex2

The drill is the bread-and-butter update: load, assign, save - and the trap is
`Update()` on a fabricated entity. `db.Update(new Van { Id = id, Mileage = m })`
marks *every* property modified, so the columns you never set are written too,
as `""` and `0`. That is how a mileage correction erases a plate.

The model answer loads the row (which also makes 404 and the
no-going-backwards rule answerable), assigns one property, and saves. The
tracker diffs against the snapshot and the UPDATE touches one column, in
exactly two round trips.

## ex3

What this tests: change detection is a *comparison*, not a recording of your
assignments. Assigning the value a property already has produces no change, no
UPDATE, no transaction - and `SaveChangesAsync` returns `0`, which is precisely
the `ChangeReport`.

The classic mistake is calling `Update(van)` on an already-tracked entity "to
be safe". That stamps every property modified, turns the no-op into a full
UPDATE, and reports a change that never happened. The model answer assigns
unconditionally and reports `written > 0` - the framework already knows whether
anything changed; ask it.

## ex4

The identity map drill. `FirstOrDefaultAsync` tracks the van under its key;
`FindAsync` *checks the tracker first* and only queries when the key is
unknown - so the second fetch costs nothing and returns the very same
instance.

The classic mistake is the reverse order of operations, or `AsNoTracking` on
either fetch: untracked results are never registered, so every fetch pays a
round trip and every result is a distinct object. The rule to keep: `Find` is
the only query API that can answer from memory, and it only helps if the first
read was tracked.

## ex5

The disconnected update. When the payload carries the entire resource, loading
the row first is a round trip that buys you nothing - you are about to
overwrite every column anyway. The model answer builds the entity from the
payload, attaches it as modified (`db.Vans.Update(van)` on an untracked
instance with a set key), and saves: one UPDATE.

The 404 is the interesting half: with no SELECT, "does it exist?" is answered
by the UPDATE's row count, which EF surfaces as `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`
when zero rows matched. Catch it, answer 404. The classic mistake is assuming
you must read before you write; the second mistake is forgetting the catch and
letting the 404 case become a 500.

## ex6

`ExecuteUpdate` goes straight to SQL: nothing is loaded, nothing is tracked,

## Notes

Every problem in this set is the same question asked eight ways: **which
objects does this DbContext remember, and what will it do about them?** A
tracked entity is compared against a snapshot at SaveChanges time; anything
different gets written, whether you meant it or not (ex1). The tracker is also
an identity map: within one context, one primary key maps to at most one
instance, which makes a second fetch free (ex4) and makes a "fresh" re-query
lie to you (ex7). And everything the tracker does costs or saves round trips,
which is why half these gates count SQL commands: the response body can be
right while the query plan is a disaster.

The working rules: reads that only render should not track; writes that start
from a loaded entity should let change detection do the work; writes that start
from a payload do not need the load at all; and anything that bypasses the
tracker - `ExecuteUpdate`, another process, raw SQL - leaves tracked instances
stale until you deliberately read past them.

string for a display board, but the vans were tracked, and the audit-row

writes every detected change on every tracked entity. The model answer reads
the vans with `AsNoTracking()` (projecting into `BoardRow` before formatting is
even better), so the display mutation is invisible to the context and the audit
insert is the only change in the room.
