tracker diffs against the snapshot and the UPDATE touches one column, in
exactly two round trips.

## ex3

assignments. Assigning the value a property already has produces no change, no
UPDATE, no transaction - and `SaveChangesAsync` returns `0`, which is precisely
the `ChangeReport`.

anything changed; ask it.

unknown - so the second fetch costs nothing and returns the very same

read was tracked.

## Hint 1

The uppercase assignment is not the bug on its own - the bug is that the vans
are *tracked* when it happens. The audit `SaveChanges` then writes every
detected change in the context, including your display formatting.

## Hint 2

Make the read invisible to the tracker: `db.Vans.AsNoTracking()` before
materialising, or skip entities entirely and `Select` into `BoardRow` first,
formatting in the projection. The audit add-and-save stays exactly as given.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - load, assign, save

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex2.cs`. `PUT /d13/vans/{id}/mileage` takes a
`MileageChange`: 404 for an unknown van, 400 when the new reading is lower than
the current one, otherwise 204 - having changed the mileage and *nothing else*,
in exactly two round trips.

The shipped version fabricates a `Van` and calls `Update()` on it. Run the gate
once and look at what that did to the plate.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You cannot answer 404, and you cannot compare against the current reading,
without the current row in hand. This endpoint is the two-trip pattern on
purpose: load, then decide, then save.

## Hint 2

`FirstOrDefaultAsync` the van (null means 404), reject a lower reading with
400, then assign `van.Mileage` and `await db.SaveChangesAsync()`. No
`Update()` call anywhere - the change tracker saw the assignment, and the
UPDATE it emits touches only the mileage column, which is why the plate
survives.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The payload carries every column, so the SELECT buys you nothing - you are
about to overwrite whatever it returns. Build the `Van` from the request with
its `Id` set, and tell the context it is a modified entity that exists
elsewhere. The 404 comes from the UPDATE itself, not from a lookup.

## Hint 2

`db.Vans.Update(van)` on an *untracked* instance with a non-zero key attaches
it in the Modified state: SaveChanges sends one UPDATE. When that UPDATE
matches zero rows, EF throws - the exception name starts with
`DbUpdateConcurrency` - and catching it is your 404.

## Hint 3

Validate first (blank strings, negative mileage) and return 400 before
touching the context. Then: construct the entity, `Update`, and wrap only the
`SaveChangesAsync` call in `try/catch (DbUpdateConcurrencyException)`
returning `TypedResults.NotFound()`. Success falls through to `NoContent()`.

## Exercise 6 - bulk update blindsides the tracker

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex6.cs`. `POST /d13/depots/{depot}/service-bump`
adds `amount` to every van in the depot with one `ExecuteUpdate`, then answers
200 with each van as a `DepotVan` (id ascending) showing the mileage as it is
NOW. 400 when the amount is not positive, 404 when the depot has no vans, at
most three round trips.

The shipped version reports numbers that are 500 out of date. Understand why
before you fix it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`ExecuteUpdate` changes rows, not objects. The list the stub loaded before the
bump is a snapshot from before the bump, and nothing will ever update it. Get
the order of operations right and the staleness problem disappears.

## Hint 2

Bump first: `ExecuteUpdateAsync` returns how many rows it hit, and `0` is your
404 - no separate existence query needed. Then build the response with a
`Select(v => new DepotVan(...))` projection: projections are never tracked, so
they always read what the database holds now. That is two round trips of the
three you are allowed.

## Hint 1

`ExecuteUpdate` changes rows, not objects. The list the stub loaded before the
bump is a snapshot from before the bump, and nothing will ever update it. Get
the order of operations right and the staleness problem disappears.

## Hint 2

Bump first: `ExecuteUpdateAsync` returns how many rows it hit, and `0` is your
404 - no separate existence query needed. Then build the response with a
`Select(v => new DepotVan(...))` projection: projections are never tracked, so
they always read what the database holds now. That is two round trips of the
three you are allowed.

## Exercise 7 - the cache that lied

Edit `src/Api/D13_EfcoreTracking/Ex7.cs`. `GET /d13/vans/{id}/tuneup`: 404 for
an unknown van; otherwise call `D13Calibration.Apply` (given code) exactly
once, then answer 200 with a `TuneupReport` carrying the mileage AFTER the
correction.

number. The re-query is real; the result is not what you think.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d13_efcore_tracking ex7
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The stub's re-query genuinely executes SQL and genuinely gets the new mileage
back - and then EF discards those values, because the van is already tracked
and one key maps to one instance. A tracked entity does not refresh by being
queried again.

## Hint 2

The cleanest fix: never track the van. Check existence with
`AsNoTracking().AnyAsync(...)`, call `D13Calibration.Apply` once, then read
the report through a projection (`Select(v => new TuneupReport(...))`) - a
projection has no entity to go stale.

## Hint 3

If you do keep a tracked instance, you must explicitly refresh it:
`await db.Entry(van).ReloadAsync()` before reporting. Either approach passes;
what cannot work is `FirstAsync` again on the same context and hoping.

## Hint 1

The stub's re-query genuinely executes SQL and genuinely gets the new mileage
back - and then EF discards those values, because the van is already tracked
and one key maps to one instance. A tracked entity does not refresh by being
queried again.

## Hint 2

The cleanest fix: never track the van. Check existence with
`AsNoTracking().AnyAsync(...)`, call `D13Calibration.Apply` once, then read
the report through a projection (`Select(v => new TuneupReport(...))`) - a
projection has no entity to go stale.

## Hint 3

If you do keep a tracked instance, you must explicitly refresh it:
`await db.Entry(van).ReloadAsync()` before reporting. Either approach passes;
what cannot work is `FirstAsync` again on the same context and hoping.

lessons.briefing:
# d14 - projection and DTO drills

Eight problems on turning entity graphs into wire shapes: `Select` into a
record, nested collections, conditionals and aggregates computed in the
database, and doing all of it inside a query budget. They drill lessons
**06_efcore_relationships** and **07_rest_crud** - go back to those if
"projection" still sounds like a synonym for `Include`.

The domain is a small cinema: directors, their films, and the screenings of
each film. Two columns exist for the back office only - `Director.Email` and
`Film.BudgetCents` - and several gates read the raw response body looking for
them. The gates also count the SQL commands EF Core sends, so a correct body
assembled by hauling tables into memory still fails. Read
`src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Model.cs` first; everything is under `/d14/...`
and each exercise owns one file.

## Exercise 1 - the list is a contract, not a table dump

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d14/films` must answer 200
with every film as a `FilmCard` - `id`, `title`, `year` and the *director's
name* - newest year first, ties broken by title A-Z.

One SQL query, and neither `email` nor `budget` may appear anywhere in the
body. Run the shipped version once and read what the serializer says about the
`Film` -> `Director` -> `Films` cycle.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - a director and their titles in one query

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d14/directors/{id}` answers
200 with a `DirectorFilms` - the director's `name` and their film *titles*,
oldest year first - or 404 when there is no such director.

The whole answer, name and nested list together, costs exactly one query.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - the status comes out of the database

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex3.cs`. `GET /d14/screenings/board` answers
200 with every screening as a `ScreeningBoardRow`, id ascending, where
`status` is:

- `"sold out"` when `sold >= seats`
- `"filling"` when the house is 80% full or more - integer math,
  `sold * 10 >= seats * 8`, no doubles
- `"open"` otherwise

The shipped version reports everything as open. One query, and the raw seat
counts never reach the client.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - the films nobody is showing

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex4.cs`. `GET /d14/films/quiet` answers 200
with every film that has *no* screenings at all, as a `QuietFilm`, title A-Z.
One query - the absence test runs in the database, not over a list you loaded.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - the earliest screening, inside the projection

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d14/films/next-showing`
answers 200 with EVERY film as a `NextShowing`, title A-Z. `nextDay` and
`nextRoom` come from that film's earliest screening - lowest day, ties broken
by screening id - and a film with no screenings reports `null` for both while
still appearing in the list.

One query for all of it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - two levels of shaping, with a filter inside

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex6.cs`. `GET /d14/directors/slate` answers
200 with every director as a `DirectorSlate`, name A-Z. Inside each: ALL of
their films (title A-Z) as `SlateFilm`s, and inside each film the rooms of its
screenings that still have seats (`sold < seats`), room A-Z.

A film with nothing open still appears, with an empty room list. At most two
SQL queries.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - one search box, two shapes, one contract

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex7.cs`. `GET /d14/search?q=` searches film
titles and director names, case-insensitively, and answers 200 with a list of
`SearchHit`:

- matching FILMS first - `kind` `"film"`, `label` the title, `year` filled,
  title A-Z
- then matching DIRECTORS - `kind` `"director"`, `label` the name, `year`
  null, name A-Z

A missing or blank `q` is 400 as a validation problem whose `errors`
dictionary is keyed `"q"`. At most two queries, and no internal columns in the
body.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - the whole dashboard on a query budget

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d14/dashboard` answers 200
with a `Dashboard`:

- `films` - how many films exist
- `screenings` - how many screenings exist
- `seatsSold` - total tickets sold across all screenings
- `soldOut` - how many screenings have `sold >= seats`
- `top` - the top THREE films by percent sold, as `TopFilm`s:
  `sum(sold) * 100 / sum(seats)` over that film's screenings, integer
  division, films with no screenings excluded, highest percent first, ties
  broken by title A-Z

At most three SQL queries for all of it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d14_projections_dtos

## Notes

Every problem in this set is the same move: put the shape you want to send on
the wire *inside* the query, so the database builds it. That single habit buys
three things at once, and the gates check all three.

It buys a **contract**. A `FilmCard` cannot leak an email or a budget, because
those columns are not in it. Returning entities is not a shortcut, it is
publishing your schema - and every column you add later is published too.

It buys **traffic**. `Select` is the only thing that narrows the SELECT list;
`Include` widens it. A projection reads four columns where an entity graph
reads twenty, and the difference is invisible in the response body, which is
why the gates count commands and read the raw body rather than trusting
equality.

And it buys **no tracking**. A projection into a non-entity type has nothing to
track, so EF takes no snapshot and does no fix-up - it is `AsNoTracking` you
get for free.

The one rule that makes it work: everything inside the projection is still an
expression tree. Ordering, filtering, conditionals, `Sum`, `Any`,
`FirstOrDefault` and even nested `ToList()` are translated. The moment you call
something the provider cannot translate, you get either a runtime error or a
silent client evaluation - which is the same correct answer at ten times the
cost.

## ex1

What this was really testing: whether you reach for `Include` or for `Select`
when the client needs one field from a related row. `Include` says "load the
whole director"; the projection says "give me the name". Both produce the name;
only one of them is a contract.

The classic mistake is the shipped code - hand entities to the serializer.
`Film.Director.Films` points back at the film, so `System.Text.Json` walks a
cycle and throws; and in the versions where it does not throw, the email and
budget columns ride along silently. The model answer's reasoning: name the four
fields you promised, and the JOIN, the narrow SELECT list and the safe body all
follow from that one `Select`.

Worth noticing: with the projection in place the `Include` becomes dead code.
`f.Director!.Name` is enough - EF sees the navigation in the expression tree and
joins for it.

## ex2

What this was really testing: that a nested collection inside a projection is
one query, not two. `d.Films.Select(f => f.Title).ToList()` sits inside the
outer `Select` and EF plans the whole thing together.

The classic mistake is the two-step: load the director, then load the films, and
report a correct body in two round trips - or worse, load the director with
`Include(d => d.Films)` and map in memory, which drags every film column back
for a list of strings. The model answer's reasoning: the shape is one object, so
it is one expression, so it is one query; and `FirstOrDefaultAsync` on the
projected sequence gives the 404 test for free, because a missing director
projects to `null` rather than throwing.

## ex3

What this was really testing: that a ternary in a projection is a SQL `CASE`,
not C#. The database can decide "sold out / filling / open" perfectly well, and
deciding it there means the seat counts never leave the server.

The classic mistake is `ToListAsync()` first and the conditional after - correct
output, whole table on the wire, and the raw seat numbers now inside your
process where somebody will eventually serialize them. The second mistake is
`(double)s.Sold / s.Seats >= 0.8`, which drags floating point into a comparison
that integers answer exactly; `sold * 10 >= seats * 8` is the same predicate
with no rounding to argue about. The model answer's reasoning: nest the two
conditions in the order of severity, sold-out first, and let the provider emit
one `CASE WHEN`.

## ex4

What this was really testing: absence. `!f.Screenings.Any()` translates to `NOT
EXISTS`, which is the cheapest way a relational database can answer "nothing
matches" - it stops at the first row it finds.

The classic mistake is loading films with their screenings and filtering the
result with `Count == 0`, which reads every screening in the database to
discover that two films have none. A subtler one is a `GroupJoin` or a manual
`Except` over ids, both correct and both more query than the question needs. The
model answer's reasoning: the question is a predicate over a navigation, so it
belongs in `Where`, and the projection then only has to carry the two fields the
contract names.

## ex5

What this was really testing: a correlated subquery in a projection. `f.Screenings
.OrderBy(...).Select(...).FirstOrDefault()` runs once per film, inside the single
statement, and the provider is very good at that; the equivalent `foreach` over
films is the N+1 you were hired to remove.

The classic mistake, besides the loop, is the cast. `FirstOrDefault()` over an
empty sequence gives you the CLR default - `0` for `int`, and `""` is what you
will try to explain to the front end. Projecting `(int?)s.Day` and
`(string?)s.Room` makes the empty case genuinely `null`, which is what the
contract promised for a film nobody has scheduled. The model answer's reasoning:
order by day then id so the tie is deterministic, cast to nullable so absence has
a value, and never filter the outer query - every film appears.

## ex6

What this was really testing: where the filter goes. The rooms are filtered, the
films are not, and the directors are not - so the `Where` belongs on the
innermost collection and nowhere else. Move it up one level and Long Meridian
and Vinyl Country vanish from a slate that is supposed to show them as empty.

The classic mistake is exactly that migration of the predicate outward, usually
via `Include(...).ThenInclude(...)` plus filtered includes, which changes what
rows *exist* in the result rather than what rows are *listed inside* one. The
model answer's reasoning: build the tree from the inside out - rooms, then a
`SlateFilm`, then a `DirectorSlate` - and each ordering clause sits next to the
collection it orders. Three levels, one expression, and the query budget is
never in danger.

## ex7

What this was really testing: that "one endpoint contract" and "one query" are
different requirements. Films and directors are different tables with different
shapes, so two queries is the honest answer; what must be unified is the
`SearchHit` they both become and the order they arrive in.

The classic mistakes come in pairs. On the matching side, `Contains` after a
`ToLower()` on both sides works and makes the predicate unsargable - it cannot
use an index on any real database; `EF.Functions.Like` keeps the comparison in
SQL, and SQLite's `LIKE` is already case-insensitive for ASCII. On the validation
side, returning `BadRequest("...")` passes the status check and fails the body
check: the contract asks for a validation problem, which is
`TypedResults.ValidationProblem` with the dictionary keyed by the offending
parameter name. The model answer's reasoning: validate first and return early,
then two narrow projections, then `Concat` - films before directors, because the
order is part of the contract too.

## ex8

What this was really testing: aggregation discipline under a budget you cannot
meet by accident. Five numbers and a ranking, three queries, and the only way
there is to make the database do the arithmetic.

Three techniques carry it. `GroupBy(s => 1)` is the idiom for "aggregate the
whole table" and collapses count, sum and conditional-count into one row -
`Sum(s => cond ? 1 : 0)` is the portable spelling of a counted condition. The
ranking is a projection with `Sum` over a navigation, ordered and `Take(3)`-ed
*before* materialisation, so the database returns three rows rather than six.
And the integer division is not an accident to be tolerated but the specified
rounding: `250 * 100 / 280` is 89 in SQL exactly as the contract says.

The classic mistake is `ToListAsync()` at the top and LINQ-to-Objects
underneath. It is easy to write, it always agrees with the expected numbers, and
it reads the entire schema to produce five integers - which is why the gate
grades the command count rather than the body alone.

## Further reading

- [Complex query operators - EF Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/complex-query-operators) - projections, correlated subqueries and nested collections.
- [Single vs. split queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/single-split-queries) - why a projected collection stays one query and what cartesian explosion costs.
- [Efficient querying](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) - projecting only what you need, `AsNoTracking`, and the N+1 patterns to look for.
- [Client vs. server evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/client-eval) - what happens when the provider cannot translate part of your expression.
- [Database functions and EF.Functions.Like](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/providers/sqlite/functions) - keeping the match in SQL.
- [Handle errors in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/handle-errors) - `TypedResults.ValidationProblem` and the shape of an errors dictionary.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A nested collection is allowed *inside* a projection, and EF plans it together
with the outer shape. That is what makes "the name and the titles" one query
rather than two.

## Hint 2

`db.Directors.Where(d => d.Id == id).Select(d => new DirectorFilms(d.Name,
d.Films.OrderBy(f => f.Year).Select(f => f.Title).ToList()))` and then
`FirstOrDefaultAsync()`. A missing director projects to `null`, so the 404 is
just a null check - no separate existence query.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - the status comes out of the database

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex3.cs`. `GET /d14/screenings/board` answers
200 with every screening as a `ScreeningBoardRow`, id ascending, where
`status` is:

- `"sold out"` when `sold >= seats`
- `"filling"` when the house is 80% full or more - integer math,
  `sold * 10 >= seats * 8`, no doubles
- `"open"` otherwise

The shipped version reports everything as open. One query, and the raw seat
counts never reach the client.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `?:` inside a projection is not C# running over loaded rows - the provider
turns it into a SQL `CASE WHEN`. So the status can be decided in the same
statement that reads the row, and the seat counts never have to travel.

## Hint 2

Nest the two conditions, severest first, in the fourth constructor argument:
sold-out (`s.Sold >= s.Seats`), else filling (`s.Sold * 10 >= s.Seats * 8`),
else open. Keep it in integers - a cast to `double` invites a rounding
argument the gate will win.

## Hint 1

A `?:` inside a projection is not C# running over loaded rows - the provider
turns it into a SQL `CASE WHEN`. So the status can be decided in the same
statement that reads the row, and the seat counts never have to travel.

sold-out (`s.Sold >= s.Seats`), else filling (`s.Sold * 10 >= s.Seats * 8`),
else open. Keep it in integers - a cast to `double` invites a rounding
argument the gate will win.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every film appears, so nothing is filtered - the work happens inside the
projection. A correlated `OrderBy(...).FirstOrDefault()` over the film's
screenings is translated and runs once per film inside the one statement.

Two subqueries, one for the day and one for the room, both ordered
`.OrderBy(s => s.Day).ThenBy(s => s.Id)` so the tie is deterministic.

`FirstOrDefault()` over an empty sequence gives you the CLR default: `0` and
`""`, not `null`. Project the element as nullable first -
`.Select(s => (int?)s.Day).FirstOrDefault()` and
`.Select(s => (string?)s.Room).FirstOrDefault()` - so a film with no
screenings really reports null.

## Hint 1

Every film appears, so nothing is filtered - the work happens inside the
projection. A correlated `OrderBy(...).FirstOrDefault()` over the film's
screenings is translated and runs once per film inside the one statement.

## Hint 2

Two subqueries, one for the day and one for the room, both ordered
`.OrderBy(s => s.Day).ThenBy(s => s.Id)` so the tie is deterministic.

## Hint 3

`FirstOrDefault()` over an empty sequence gives you the CLR default: `0` and
`""`, not `null`. Project the element as nullable first -
`.Select(s => (int?)s.Day).FirstOrDefault()` and
`.Select(s => (string?)s.Room).FirstOrDefault()` - so a film with no
screenings really reports null.

for the guard, so a `q` of one space is rejected too.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two tables, two queries, one wire shape. Validate first and return early;
then project films into `SearchHit`s and directors into `SearchHit`s
separately, and join the two lists in memory - the ordering the contract asks
for is "all films, then all directors", which `Concat` gives you directly.

## Hint 2

`TypedResults.ValidationProblem(new Dictionary<string, string[]> { ["q"] =
["..."] })` is the 400. `BadRequest("...")` has the right status and the wrong
body - the gate reads the `errors` dictionary.

## Hint 3

For the match, `EF.Functions.Like(f.Title, $"%{term}%")` keeps the comparison
in SQL, and SQLite's `LIKE` is already case-insensitive for ASCII, so `VALE`
finds `Mira Vale` without any `ToLower()`. Use `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(q)`
for the guard, so a `q` of one space is rejected too.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - the whole dashboard on a query budget

Edit `src/Api/D14_ProjectionsDtos/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d14/dashboard` answers 200
with a `Dashboard`:

- `films` - how many films exist
- `screenings` - how many screenings exist
- `seatsSold` - total tickets sold across all screenings
- `soldOut` - how many screenings have `sold >= seats`
- `top` - the top THREE films by percent sold, as `TopFilm`s:
  `sum(sold) * 100 / sum(seats)` over that film's screenings, integer
  division, films with no screenings excluded, highest percent first, ties
  broken by title A-Z

At most three SQL queries for all of it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d14_projections_dtos ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Five numbers and a ranking in three queries means nothing may be counted in
memory. Split it the way the database would: one count of films, one grouped
aggregate over all screenings, one ranking query.

## Hint 2

`db.Screenings.GroupBy(s => 1).Select(g => new { Count = g.Count(), Sold =
g.Sum(s => s.Sold), SoldOut = g.Sum(s => s.Sold >= s.Seats ? 1 : 0) })` is the
idiom for aggregating a whole table in one row. `Sum(... ? 1 : 0)` is the
portable way to count a condition inside a group. Handle the empty-table case
(`FirstOrDefaultAsync` can return null).

## Hint 3

The ranking is a projection with `Sum` over the navigation:
`f.Screenings.Sum(s => s.Sold) * 100 / f.Screenings.Sum(s => s.Seats)`,
filtered by `f.Screenings.Any()`, then `OrderByDescending(...).ThenBy(t =>
t.Title).Take(3)` - all before `ToListAsync`, so three rows come back rather
than six. Integer division is not a bug here; it is the specified rounding.

## Hint 1

Five numbers and a ranking in three queries means nothing may be counted in
memory. Split it the way the database would: one count of films, one grouped
aggregate over all screenings, one ranking query.

## Hint 2

`db.Screenings.GroupBy(s => 1).Select(g => new { Count = g.Count(), Sold =
g.Sum(s => s.Sold), SoldOut = g.Sum(s => s.Sold >= s.Seats ? 1 : 0) })` is the
idiom for aggregating a whole table in one row. `Sum(... ? 1 : 0)` is the
portable way to count a condition inside a group. Handle the empty-table case
(`FirstOrDefaultAsync` can return null).

## Hint 3

The ranking is a projection with `Sum` over the navigation:
`f.Screenings.Sum(s => s.Sold) * 100 / f.Screenings.Sum(s => s.Seats)`,
filtered by `f.Screenings.Any()`, then `OrderByDescending(...).ThenBy(t =>
t.Title).Take(3)` - all before `ToListAsync`, so three rows come back rather
than six. Integer division is not a bug here; it is the specified rounding.

lessons.briefing:
# d15 - REST read drills

Eight problems on the read half of an HTTP API: collections and items, 404
against an empty 200, filters that are validated rather than guessed, routing
that decides instead of parsing, conditional GETs, and letting the client
choose its representation. They drill lesson **07_rest_crud** - go back to it
if "404" still means "anything I could not find".

The data is a bike-share network: five docking stations and twelve bikes, all
static and read-only, in `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Model.cs`. Read it first. A
bike out on a ride has no station code; a bike in service is still docked.
Everything is under `/d15/...` and each exercise owns one file.

## Exercise 1 - a collection and an item are two different resources

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex1.cs`.

- `GET /d15/stations` - 200 with every station as a `StationCard`, code A-Z.
  `available` counts the bikes at that station whose status is `available`.
- `GET /d15/stations/{code}` - 200 with that one card, or **404** when no
  station has that code.

The shipped version serializes the seed order and throws on an unknown code.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - empty is not the same as missing

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d15/stations/{code}/bikes` answers
200 with the bikes docked at that station as `BikeCard`s, id ascending -
including the ones in service.

- a station with nothing docked: **200** and `[]`
- a code that names no station at all: **404**

The shipped version cannot tell those two apart.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - an optional filter is still a validated one

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex3.cs`. `GET /d15/bikes` answers 200 with
`BikeCard`s, id ascending. `?status=` narrows to one value from
`D15Network.Statuses`:

- no `status` at all - every bike
- a legal status matching nothing (`retired`) - 200 and `[]`
- a status outside the list - **400** as a validation problem whose `errors`
  dictionary is keyed `"status"`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - let routing decide what a URL means

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex4.cs`. One catch-all route is currently doing
two jobs and parsing its way through them. Split it:

- `GET /d15/bikes/available` - 200 with the available bikes, id ascending
- `GET /d15/bikes/{id}` - 200 with that bike, 404 when there is no such id
- `GET /d15/bikes/abc` - **404**, decided by routing, before any handler runs

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - a conditional GET

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d15/network` answers 200 with a
`NetworkSummary` and an `ETag` header identifying that body - use the given
`Tag(...)` helper, do not invent your own.

When the request carries an `If-None-Match` that matches, answer **304** with
no body, still sending the `ETag`. When it carries one that does not match,
answer the full 200.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - one query key, many values

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex6.cs`. `GET /d15/stations/search` answers 200
with `StationCard`s, code A-Z. `?zone=` may be repeated, and a station matches
if its zone is **any** of the values given, compared case-insensitively. No
`zone` at all means every station.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - the client chooses the representation

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex7.cs`. `GET /d15/export` serves the station list
in whichever representation the client asked for, honouring `Accept`:

- `application/json`, `*/*`, or no `Accept` header - 200, JSON, the cards from
  the given `Cards()` helper
- `text/csv` - 200 with `Content-Type: text/csv` and this exact body: the
  header row `code,name,zone,capacity,available`, then one row per station in
  code order, fields comma separated, rows joined with a single newline
- anything else - **406**, no body

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - one endpoint with the whole read contract

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d15/stations/{code}/report`:

- 404 when `{code}` names no station
- 400 as a validation problem keyed `"model"` when `?model=` is outside
  `D15Network.Models` (the station is checked first)
- otherwise 200 with a `StationReport` over the bikes docked there, narrowed
  by `model` when one was given: `docked`, `available`, `free` =
  `capacity - docked`, and `models` = the distinct models docked, A-Z
- the response carries an `ETag` for the representation it just produced, and
  answers 304 to a matching `If-None-Match` - so two different query strings
  must not share a tag

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d15_rest_reads

## Notes

A read endpoint answers three questions before it answers the client's: does
this resource exist, is this request well formed, and does the caller already
have the answer? The set drills each of those, and the pattern that unites them
is that **the status line is part of the payload**. A client does not parse your
prose; it switches on a number.

The three that people conflate:

- **404** means the resource does not exist. It is not "nothing matched my
  filter" and it is not "your parameter is wrong".
- **400** means the *request* is wrong - a value outside the vocabulary, a
  malformed body. The server understood you and refuses.
- **200 with an empty array** means the collection exists and is empty. Any
  client that renders a list has to handle it, and none of them has to handle a
  404 for the same case.

And the two the drills add: **406** for "I cannot produce anything you said you
would accept", and **304** for "you already have this". The last one is the only
status in HTTP whose entire value is the bytes it does *not* send.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that a collection resource and an item resource
are separate endpoints with separate failure modes, and that neither of them
serializes storage. The seed order in `Model.cs` is deliberately not code order,
because the order rows happen to sit in is never a contract.

The classic mistake is the second half: `First(s => s.Code == code)` throws
`InvalidOperationException` when nothing matches, and an unhandled exception is
a 500 - a claim that *your server* is broken, when in fact the client asked a
perfectly well-formed question with a negative answer. The model answer's
reasoning: `FirstOrDefault` plus a null check, so "not there" is a decision the
handler makes rather than an accident the pipeline reports.

## ex2

What this was really testing: the distinction between an empty child collection
and a missing parent. `GET /d15/stations/zz99/bikes` and
`GET /d15/stations/hs11/bikes` differ in exactly one way, and the shipped code
cannot see it, because filtering a list by a code nobody has gives you the same
empty list as filtering by a code with nothing docked.

The classic mistake is skipping the parent check because the query "works". The
consequence shows up as a bug report in six months: a station is deleted, every
dashboard for it keeps rendering an empty dock instead of an error, and nobody
notices for a quarter. The model answer's reasoning: look up the parent first,
return 404 there, and only then answer the question that was asked.

## ex3

What this was really testing: that an optional parameter still has a
vocabulary. `?status=availble` is not a filter that matches nothing; it is a
request the server cannot honour, and saying 200 to it destroys the client's
only chance of finding the typo.

The classic mistake is exactly the shipped code - `Where(b => status is null ||
b.Status == status)` reads as obviously correct and turns every misspelling into
a silent empty result. The `retired` case in the gate is the counterweight: a
*legal* value with no matches genuinely is 200 and `[]`, so the rule is not "an
empty result is suspicious", it is "an unknown value is". The model answer's
reasoning: check membership against the published list, and when it fails answer
with a validation problem keyed by the parameter name, so the client is told
which knob it turned wrongly.

## ex4

What this was really testing: that routing is a dispatcher, not a suggestion.
The shipped handler binds `{id}` as a string, parses it, and branches - which
works today and is a trap tomorrow, because it has quietly claimed every URL
under `/d15/bikes/`.

Two things follow from splitting it. A literal segment always outranks a
parameter segment, so `available` and `{id:int}` can coexist and the
registration order does not matter. And the `:int` constraint means
`/d15/bikes/abc` matches *no* endpoint, so the 404 comes from routing before any
of your code runs - which is both faster and the correct answer, since there is
no such resource rather than a bad request about one.

The classic mistake is answering 400 to `/d15/bikes/abc`. It is defensible in
isolation and it is wrong here: it asserts that this URL identifies a bike and
you got its id wrong, when the truth is that this URL identifies nothing.

## ex5

What this was really testing: conditional requests. The server hands out an
`ETag` - an opaque token for *this representation* - and a client that keeps it
can ask "still the same?" with `If-None-Match`. If it is, the answer is 304 and
the body is never written.

Three details the gate pins down. The tag must be **quoted**, because that is
the grammar and `HttpClient` will not parse it otherwise. It must go out on the
**304 as well**, or the client has nothing to send on its next request and the
cache degrades to nothing after one hit. And a *non*-matching tag must produce
the full 200 - answering 304 to any `If-None-Match` at all is a cache that can
never update, which is the most expensive bug in this file.

The reasoning behind computing the tag from the serialized body: it is
automatically correct. A version number you maintain by hand is one forgotten
increment away from serving last week's data forever.

## ex6

What this was really testing: query-string binding when a key repeats.
`?zone=north&zone=south` is one key with two values, and binding it to a `string`
takes the first and throws the second away - silently, with a 200, which is the
worst possible way to lose half a filter.

Binding `string[] zone` takes all of them, and binds to an empty array when the
key is absent, which is exactly the "no filter" case with no null check needed.
The case-insensitive half is a `HashSet<string>` with
`StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`: doing it with `ToLower()` on both sides works
too and is the habit that makes database-backed versions of this endpoint
unable to use an index.

## ex7

What this was really testing: content negotiation, which is the part of HTTP
most people have used for years without implementing once. The client sends
`Accept` listing what it can read; the server picks something from that list, or
admits it cannot.

The four cases are all deliberate. No `Accept` header means no preference, so
the server chooses - JSON. `*/*` means the same thing said out loud. `text/csv`
is a representation of the *same resource* - not a different endpoint, not
`?format=csv`, the same URL serving different bytes - and the `Content-Type` on
the way back has to say which one it chose, or the client cannot parse what it
got. And `application/xml` is the case that matters: the client has told you in
advance it will not understand JSON, so sending JSON is sending garbage with a
200 on it. 406 is the honest answer.

The classic mistake is reading `Accept` as a single string and comparing it for
equality. Real clients send lists with quality values -
`text/csv;q=0.9, application/json;q=0.8` - which is why the model answer uses
`GetTypedHeaders().Accept` and walks it in preference order.

## ex8

What this was really testing: everything above, on one endpoint, in the right
order. Existence before validity (a report for a station that does not exist
cannot have a bad `model` parameter), validity before work, work before caching.

The subtle one is the last gate check: the filtered and unfiltered reports must
not share an `ETag`. An entity tag identifies a **representation**, not a URL
path - two different query strings that produce two different bodies are two
different representations. Reusing one tag across them means a client that
fetched `?model=roadster` and then asks for the unfiltered report gets a 304 and
keeps rendering the filtered numbers, forever, with no error anywhere. Computing
the tag from the body that was actually produced makes that impossible by
construction, which is the whole reason to do it that way.

The arithmetic is deliberately stated in the README rather than left to
intuition: `free = capacity - docked` over the *filtered* set. Drills compare
literally, and "obvious" is where two reasonable people disagree.

## Further reading

- [Routing in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/routing) - route templates, constraints, and how precedence between literal and parameter segments is decided.
- [Parameter binding in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding) - query strings, arrays, optional parameters.
- [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses) - `TypedResults`, `Text`, `StatusCode`, `ValidationProblem`.
- [HTTP conditional requests (MDN)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Conditional_requests) - `ETag`, `If-None-Match` and what 304 is for.
- [HTTP content negotiation (MDN)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Content_negotiation) - `Accept`, quality values and 406.
- [RFC 9110 section 15.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-client-error-4xx) - what the 4xx codes actually claim.

construction, which is the whole reason to do it that way.

intuition: `free = capacity - docked` over the *filtered* set. Drills compare
literally, and "obvious" is where two reasonable people disagree.

## Exercise 1 - a collection and an item are two different resources

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex1.cs`.

- `GET /d15/stations` - 200 with every station as a `StationCard`, code A-Z.
  `available` counts the bikes at that station whose status is `available`.
- `GET /d15/stations/{code}` - 200 with that one card, or **404** when no
  station has that code.

The shipped version serializes the seed order and throws on an unknown code.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two independent problems in one file. The collection has to sort and to project
into `StationCard` - `Station` has no `available` field, so serializing it can
never satisfy the gate. The item has to answer "there is no such station"
without throwing.

## Hint 2

`OrderBy(s => s.Code, StringComparer.Ordinal)` then `Select` into a
`StationCard`, using `D15Network.AvailableAt(s.Code)` for the last field.

For the item, swap `First` for `FirstOrDefault` (or the given
`D15Network.Find`) and return `TypedResults.NotFound()` when it comes back
null. An exception is a 500, which claims the fault is yours.

returns 200 with an empty array. That contrast is the whole exercise.

## Exercise 4 - let routing decide what a URL means

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex4.cs`. One catch-all route is currently doing
two jobs and parsing its way through them. Split it:

- `GET /d15/bikes/available` - 200 with the available bikes, id ascending
- `GET /d15/bikes/{id}` - 200 with that bike, 404 when there is no such id
- `GET /d15/bikes/abc` - **404**, decided by routing, before any handler runs

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex4
```

`app.MapGet("/d15/bikes/available", ...)` and

that URL reaches your code and you are back to parsing.

## Exercise 5 - a conditional GET

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d15/network` answers 200 with a
`NetworkSummary` and an `ETag` header identifying that body - use the given
`Tag(...)` helper, do not invent your own.

answer the full 200.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex5
```

Two lines and a branch. Compute `Tag(summary)`, put it on the response, and
compare it against what the client sent in `If-None-Match` before deciding
which status to return.

## Hint 2

`http.Response.Headers.ETag = tag;` sets it - and it has to be set on *both*
paths, so set it before the branch. Read the request side with
`http.Request.Headers.IfNoneMatch`, which is a collection: a client may send
several tags.

## Hint 3

The 304 is `TypedResults.StatusCode(StatusCodes.Status304NotModified)` - a
status and nothing else, which is the point. And a tag that does not match must
still fall through to the full 200; a handler that returns 304 whenever an
`If-None-Match` is present is a cache that never updates.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - one query key, many values

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex6.cs`. `GET /d15/stations/search` answers 200
with `StationCard`s, code A-Z. `?zone=` may be repeated, and a station matches
if its zone is **any** of the values given, compared case-insensitively. No
`zone` at all means every station.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d15_rest_reads ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The handler's signature is the bug. `?zone=north&zone=south` is one key with two
values, and a `string` parameter can only hold one of them.

## Hint 2

Bind `string[] zone` instead. Minimal APIs fill it with every value of that key,
and with an empty array when the key is absent - which is exactly your "no
filter" case, so `zone.Length == 0` replaces the null check.

For the case-insensitive match, build a
`new HashSet<string>(zone, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` once and ask it
whether it contains the station's zone.

## Exercise 8 - one endpoint with the whole read contract

Edit `src/Api/D15_RestReads/Ex8.cs`. `GET /d15/stations/{code}/report`:

## Hint 1

Four checks in one handler, and their order is the exercise: existence (404),
then the query string's validity (400), then the work, then the cache (304).
Getting them out of order gives a 400 for a station that does not exist, which
tells the client to fix the wrong thing.

Reuse what you already wrote. The 404 is ex1's `D15Network.Find`; the 400 is
ex3's membership guard with `D15Network.Models` and the key `"model"`; the ETag
is ex5's `Ex5.Tag(...)` plus the `If-None-Match` comparison.

## Hint 3

Compute the tag from the `StationReport` you just built, not from the code or
the URL. That is what makes `?model=roadster` and the unfiltered call carry
different tags automatically - an entity tag identifies a representation, and
those two are different representations of the same resource.

`models` is `docked.Select(b => b.Model).Distinct().OrderBy(...)` - the distinct
matters, cw01 has two roadsters.

## Hint 1

Four checks in one handler, and their order is the exercise: existence (404),
then the query string's validity (400), then the work, then the cache (304).
Getting them out of order gives a 400 for a station that does not exist, which
tells the client to fix the wrong thing.

## Hint 2

Reuse what you already wrote. The 404 is ex1's `D15Network.Find`; the 400 is
ex3's membership guard with `D15Network.Models` and the key `"model"`; the ETag
is ex5's `Ex5.Tag(...)` plus the `If-None-Match` comparison.

## Hint 3

Compute the tag from the `StationReport` you just built, not from the code or
the URL. That is what makes `?model=roadster` and the unfiltered call carry
different tags automatically - an entity tag identifies a representation, and
those two are different representations of the same resource.

`models` is `docked.Select(b => b.Model).Distinct().OrderBy(...)` - the distinct
matters, cw01 has two roadsters.

# d16 - REST write drills

Eight problems on the write half of an HTTP API: 201 and where it put it, 204
and nothing else, replace against patch, a retry that must not do the work
twice, a state machine that says no, optimistic concurrency, and a batch that
is one write or none. They drill lesson **07_rest_crud** - go back to it if
"POST creates, PUT updates" is still the whole model.

The domain is a print shop's job queue (`src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Model.cs`) -
five jobs, seeded fresh for every gate. Because every exercise changes state,
the gates read the database back afterwards: a right-looking response over a
wrong row fails, and so does a rejected request that wrote something anyway.
Everything is under `/d16/...` and each exercise owns one file.

## Exercise 1 - a create says 201 and says where it put it

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex1.cs`. `POST /d16/jobs` takes a `NewJob` and
answers **201** with the created `JobDto`, a `Location` header of
`/d16/jobs/{newId}`, and the row saved. A new job starts `"queued"`.

The shipped version saves correctly and then undersells it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - a delete is either gone or never there

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex2.cs`. `DELETE /d16/jobs/{id}`:

- the job existed - **204**, with no body, and the row removed
- there was nothing to delete - **404**, including on a second delete of the
  same id

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - PUT replaces the whole thing

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex3.cs`. `PUT /d16/jobs/{id}` takes a
`JobReplacement`:

- unknown id - 404
- blank title, `copies` below 1, or a `status` outside `D16Queue.Statuses` -
  **400** as a validation problem keyed `"title"` / `"copies"` / `"status"`,
  and nothing written
- otherwise **204**, having replaced the job - and a body with no `status`
  leaves it `"queued"`, because that is what replacing means

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - the retry that must not print twice

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex4.cs`. `POST /d16/rush` creates a job with
status `"printing"`, keyed by the `Idempotency-Key` header:

- no header - **400** as a validation problem keyed `"Idempotency-Key"`, and
  nothing created
- a key never seen - **201** + `Location` + the new `JobDto`
- a key already used - **200** with the *same* `JobDto` and the same
  `Location`, no second row, **whatever this request body says**

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - PATCH touches only what was sent

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex5.cs`. `PATCH /d16/jobs/{id}` takes a `JobPatch`
and changes only the fields actually present in the body. Unknown id: 404. A
blank title, `copies` below 1 or an unknown status: 400, keyed as in ex3.
Otherwise **200** with the full updated `JobDto`.

The shipped version treats a missing field as "set it to the default".

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - an action the state can refuse

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex6.cs`. `POST /d16/jobs/{id}/cancel`:

- unknown id - 404
- the job's status is one of `D16Queue.Finished` - **409**, with its status
  left exactly as it was
- otherwise **204**, with the status now `"cancelled"`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - the write that has to prove it read the current one

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex7.cs`. Two endpoints:

- `GET /d16/jobs/{id}` - 200 with the `JobDto` and an `ETag` of
  `Tag(job.Version)`, or 404
- `PUT /d16/jobs/{id}/copies` - 404 for an unknown id; **428** when the request
  carries no `If-Match` at all; **412** when it carries one that is not the
  job's current tag, with nothing written; otherwise **204** with `copies`
  updated and `Version` bumped by one

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - a batch is one write or none of it

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex8.cs`. `POST /d16/batches` takes a `NewBatch`:

- **400** as a validation problem when the reference is blank
  (`"reference"`), the items list is missing or empty (`"items"`), or any item
  has a blank title (`"items[i].title"`) or `copies` below 1
  (`"items[i].copies"`) - every offending key present at once, and **nothing**
  written
- otherwise **201** with `Location: /d16/batches/{id}` and a `BatchDto`: the
  batch id, its reference, and the ids of the jobs it created, ascending. Each
  job is `"queued"` and carries the batch id.

`GET /d16/batches/{id}` answers 200 with the same `BatchDto`, or 404.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d16_rest_writes

## Notes

A write endpoint has to answer two questions the read endpoints never faced:
what changed, and what happens when the same request arrives twice. The set
drills both, and the pattern that unites every exercise is that **the database
is the assertion**. The gates do not trust a 204; they read the rows back
afterwards, including on the failure paths, where the interesting bug lives.

The verbs, in the shape this API uses them:

- **POST** creates something the server names. It answers **201** with a
  `Location` header, because the client cannot know the id it just caused.
- **PUT** replaces a resource the client names. A field left out of the body
  goes back to its default - that is what *replace* means, and it is the one
  thing people reliably get wrong.
- **PATCH** changes only the fields that were actually sent. `null` in the
  parsed body means "not mentioned", never "set it to empty".
- **DELETE** answers **204** and nothing else.

And the failure vocabulary. **400** is "your request is malformed" - a blank
title, zero copies, a status this queue does not have. **404** is "no such
resource". **409** is the one people reach for last and should reach for more:
the request is fine and the resource exists, but its *state* refuses. **412**
and **428** are the concurrency pair from ex7.

Running through all of it: validate before you assign. EF Core tracks the
entity you loaded, so a handler that sets three properties and *then* decides
to return 400 has already staged a change; the next `SaveChanges` anywhere in
that request commits it. Decide first, mutate second.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that a create tells the client where the new
thing is. The shipped code saves correctly and answers 200 with the body, which
leaves the client parsing an id out of JSON - or, more often, refetching the
whole collection to find what it just made.

The classic mistake beyond the status is trying to build the `Location` before
`SaveChangesAsync`. The id does not exist until the insert runs; that is the
whole reason the server, not the client, is the one that names it. The model
answer's reasoning: save, then use the id EF filled in, then
`TypedResults.Created(location, dto)` - which sets the header and the body in
one call.

## ex2

What this was really testing: 204 and the difference between "gone" and "never
there". A successful delete has nothing to say, and 204 is how HTTP says
nothing - a body alongside it contradicts the status line, and some proxies
will simply drop it.

The design decision worth arguing about is the second delete. Answering 204
again is defensible: the end state the client asked for holds, and that makes
DELETE idempotent, which is what the specification wants. This API answers 404
instead, to tell the client its id is stale. Both are shipped in the wild; what
is not defensible is choosing without deciding. The README states it, so the
gate can.

## ex3

What this was really testing: replacement semantics. `PUT /d16/jobs/5` with no
`status` in the body sets the status back to `queued`, because PUT declares the
new state of the whole resource and anything absent from that declaration is
absent from the resource.

The classic mistake is keeping the old value for missing fields - PATCH
behaviour under a PUT. It feels forgiving and it makes a field impossible to
clear: the client sends a body without `status` meaning "remove it", the server
keeps the old one, and the two sides disagree forever.

The other half is the ordering. The gate ends by checking that job 1 is
untouched after three rejected requests, because the natural way to write this
handler - load, assign, validate, return 400 - has already changed the tracked
entity by the time it decides to refuse. The model answer's reasoning: compute
`title`, `copies` and `status` into locals, collect every error, and only
assign once there are none.

## ex4

What this was really testing: idempotency keys, which is how every payment API
you have used survives a mobile network. The client generates a key, sends it
with the request, and retries with the *same* key when it does not see an
answer. The server promises that the second call does not do the work again.

Three details the gate pins down. A missing key is refused outright, because an
endpoint that cannot be retried safely should not accept a request that might
be retried. The replay answers **200**, not 201 - nothing was created this time.
And the replay returns the **stored** result even though its body differs: an
idempotency key says "this is the same request I already sent", so the first
one is the one that happened. A server that applies the new payload has
implemented an upsert and called it idempotency.

The classic mistake in production is storing the key only *after* the work
succeeds, which leaves a window where two concurrent retries both find nothing
and both do the job. The real fix is a unique index on the key column, so the
second insert fails rather than duplicating - worth knowing even though this
drill is single-threaded.

## ex5

What this was really testing: that `null` in a parsed patch body carries
information - "the client did not mention this" - and that flattening it with
`??` destroys that information. The shipped handler does exactly that, and one
PATCH of `copies` wipes the title.

Every rule in the model answer is guarded twice: once by "was this field
present", and once by the same validation PUT applies. That second half is the
part people skip. `copies: 0` is invalid whether it arrives by PUT or PATCH;
the verb changes which fields are *considered*, never which values are *legal*.

The honest limitation: nullable-field patching cannot distinguish "not sent"
from "explicitly sent as null" for a genuinely nullable column. When that
distinction matters, the answer is JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch, or a
wrapper type that records presence separately from value. For a drill of three
non-nullable fields, nullable properties are the right amount of machinery.

## ex6

What this was really testing: 409, the status that says "you are not wrong, but
no". Cancelling a job that is already `done` is not a malformed request (400
would blame the client's payload) and not a missing resource (404 would blame
the id). The job is there, the request is fine, and the state machine refuses.

The reasoning behind the specific transitions: `queued` and `printing` are
in-flight and can still be pulled; `done` and `cancelled` are terminal. Making
a re-cancel a no-op 204 would be defensible too - but this API has decided that
the client asking to cancel a finished job has a stale view worth telling it
about, which is exactly what a conflict is.

`TypedResults.Problem(statusCode: 409, ...)` is the shape: a
`ProblemDetails` body, so the client gets a machine-readable reason rather than
a bare status code and a guess.

## ex7

What this was really testing: optimistic concurrency over HTTP, which is the
same idea as ex5 of the reads drill turned around. There, the client asked "is
my copy still current?" and saved a download. Here it says "only write if my
copy is still current" and saves an overwrite.

The three statuses have distinct jobs. **428 Precondition Required** is the
server refusing to accept a blind write at all: a client that sent no `If-Match`
never read the resource, so there is no version it could have been editing, and
letting it through is last-write-wins by default. **412 Precondition Failed**
is the race actually being lost - somebody wrote between this client's read and
its write, and the correct response is to re-read and decide, not to guess which
edit mattered. **204** is the write going through, and the version moving, which
is what makes the *next* replay of the old tag fail.

The classic mistake is a version that never changes. An ETag derived from
something static is permanently valid, every `If-Match` matches, and the whole
protocol is theatre. The second classic mistake is checking the precondition
after the assignment, which fails the "nothing was written" half of the gate for
the same reason ex3 does.

Worth knowing: EF Core has this built in as `[Timestamp]` / `IsConcurrencyToken`,
which turns the check into a `WHERE Version = @old` on the UPDATE and throws
`DbUpdateConcurrencyException` when it matches no rows. That version is safe
against a race between the check and the write; the hand-rolled one in this
drill is not, and knowing why is the point.

## ex8

What this was really testing: batch semantics, which is ex3's "validate before
you assign" scaled up until it is impossible to fake. Two jobs, one of them
unusable, and the gate checks that the *valid* one was not created either.

Three disciplines stack here. All-or-nothing validation: one pass over every
item collecting every error, so a client with four bad rows learns about four
bad rows rather than bisecting its own payload over four round trips. Keyed
errors: `items[1].copies` names the item and the field, which is the difference
between a usable API and a 400 with the word "invalid" in it. And a single
write: hanging the jobs off `batch.Jobs` means one `SaveChanges` inserts the
batch and its jobs together and EF fills in each `BatchId` - two saves would
leave an orphan batch behind if the second one failed.

The last check is the quiet one: the `Location` the create handed out has to
actually resolve. A 201 pointing at a URL that 404s is a create that lied, and
it is astonishingly common in APIs where the create and the read were written by
different people in different weeks.

## Further reading

- [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses) - `TypedResults.Created`, `NoContent`, `Problem`, `ValidationProblem`, `StatusCode`.
- [Handle errors in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/handle-errors) - the `ProblemDetails` and validation-problem shapes.
- [Saving data with EF Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/) - change tracking, `SaveChanges` as a unit of work, and related-entity inserts.
- [Handling concurrency conflicts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/concurrency) - the database-level version of ex7, and `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`.
- [RFC 9110 section 13](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-conditional-requests) - `If-Match`, `If-None-Match`, 412 and what a precondition means.
- [RFC 6585 section 3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585#section-3) - 428 Precondition Required, and why it exists.

The verbs, in the shape this API uses them:

- **POST** creates something the server names. It answers **201** with a
  `Location` header, because the client cannot know the id it just caused.
- **PUT** replaces a resource the client names. A field left out of the body
  goes back to its default - that is what *replace* means, and it is the one
  thing people reliably get wrong.
- **PATCH** changes only the fields that were actually sent. `null` in the
  parsed body means "not mentioned", never "set it to empty".
- **DELETE** answers **204** and nothing else.

And the failure vocabulary. **400** is "your request is malformed" - a blank
title, zero copies, a status this queue does not have. **404** is "no such
resource". **409** is the one people reach for last and should reach for more:
the request is fine and the resource exists, but its *state* refuses. **412**
and **428** are the concurrency pair from ex7.

Running through all of it: validate before you assign. EF Core tracks the
entity you loaded, so a handler that sets three properties and *then* decides
to return 400 has already staged a change; the next `SaveChanges` anywhere in
that request commits it. Decide first, mutate second.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that a create tells the client where the new
thing is. The shipped code saves correctly and answers 200 with the body, which
leaves the client parsing an id out of JSON - or, more often, refetching the
whole collection to find what it just made.

The classic mistake beyond the status is trying to build the `Location` before
`SaveChangesAsync`. The id does not exist until the insert runs; that is the
whole reason the server, not the client, is the one that names it. The model
answer's reasoning: save, then use the id EF filled in, then
`TypedResults.Created(location, dto)` - which sets the header and the body in
one call.

## ex2

What this was really testing: 204 and the difference between "gone" and "never
there". A successful delete has nothing to say, and 204 is how HTTP says
nothing - a body alongside it contradicts the status line, and some proxies
will simply drop it.

The design decision worth arguing about is the second delete. Answering 204
again is defensible: the end state the client asked for holds, and that makes
DELETE idempotent, which is what the specification wants. This API answers 404
instead, to tell the client its id is stale. Both are shipped in the wild; what
is not defensible is choosing without deciding. The README states it, so the
gate can.

## ex3

What this was really testing: replacement semantics. `PUT /d16/jobs/5` with no
`status` in the body sets the status back to `queued`, because PUT declares the
new state of the whole resource and anything absent from that declaration is
absent from the resource.

The classic mistake is keeping the old value for missing fields - PATCH
behaviour under a PUT. It feels forgiving and it makes a field impossible to
clear: the client sends a body without `status` meaning "remove it", the server
keeps the old one, and the two sides disagree forever.

The other half is the ordering. The gate ends by checking that job 1 is
untouched after three rejected requests, because the natural way to write this
handler - load, assign, validate, return 400 - has already changed the tracked
entity by the time it decides to refuse. The model answer's reasoning: compute
`title`, `copies` and `status` into locals, collect every error, and only
assign once there are none.

## ex4

What this was really testing: idempotency keys, which is how every payment API
you have used survives a mobile network. The client generates a key, sends it
with the request, and retries with the *same* key when it does not see an
answer. The server promises that the second call does not do the work again.

Three details the gate pins down. A missing key is refused outright, because an
endpoint that cannot be retried safely should not accept a request that might
be retried. The replay answers **200**, not 201 - nothing was created this time.
And the replay returns the **stored** result even though its body differs: an
idempotency key says "this is the same request I already sent", so the first
one is the one that happened. A server that applies the new payload has
implemented an upsert and called it idempotency.

The classic mistake in production is storing the key only *after* the work
succeeds, which leaves a window where two concurrent retries both find nothing
and both do the job. The real fix is a unique index on the key column, so the
second insert fails rather than duplicating - worth knowing even though this
drill is single-threaded.

## ex5

What this was really testing: that `null` in a parsed patch body carries
information - "the client did not mention this" - and that flattening it with
`??` destroys that information. The shipped handler does exactly that, and one
PATCH of `copies` wipes the title.

Every rule in the model answer is guarded twice: once by "was this field
present", and once by the same validation PUT applies. That second half is the
part people skip. `copies: 0` is invalid whether it arrives by PUT or PATCH;
the verb changes which fields are *considered*, never which values are *legal*.

The honest limitation: nullable-field patching cannot distinguish "not sent"
from "explicitly sent as null" for a genuinely nullable column. When that
distinction matters, the answer is JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch, or a
wrapper type that records presence separately from value. For a drill of three
non-nullable fields, nullable properties are the right amount of machinery.

## ex6

What this was really testing: 409, the status that says "you are not wrong, but
no". Cancelling a job that is already `done` is not a malformed request (400
would blame the client's payload) and not a missing resource (404 would blame
the id). The job is there, the request is fine, and the state machine refuses.

The reasoning behind the specific transitions: `queued` and `printing` are
in-flight and can still be pulled; `done` and `cancelled` are terminal. Making
a re-cancel a no-op 204 would be defensible too - but this API has decided that
the client asking to cancel a finished job has a stale view worth telling it
about, which is exactly what a conflict is.

`TypedResults.Problem(statusCode: 409, ...)` is the shape: a
`ProblemDetails` body, so the client gets a machine-readable reason rather than
a bare status code and a guess.

## ex7

What this was really testing: optimistic concurrency over HTTP, which is the
same idea as ex5 of the reads drill turned around. There, the client asked "is
my copy still current?" and saved a download. Here it says "only write if my
copy is still current" and saves an overwrite.

The three statuses have distinct jobs. **428 Precondition Required** is the
server refusing to accept a blind write at all: a client that sent no `If-Match`
never read the resource, so there is no version it could have been editing, and
letting it through is last-write-wins by default. **412 Precondition Failed**
is the race actually being lost - somebody wrote between this client's read and
its write, and the correct response is to re-read and decide, not to guess which
edit mattered. **204** is the write going through, and the version moving, which
is what makes the *next* replay of the old tag fail.

The classic mistake is a version that never changes. An ETag derived from
something static is permanently valid, every `If-Match` matches, and the whole
protocol is theatre. The second classic mistake is checking the precondition
after the assignment, which fails the "nothing was written" half of the gate for
the same reason ex3 does.

Worth knowing: EF Core has this built in as `[Timestamp]` / `IsConcurrencyToken`,
which turns the check into a `WHERE Version = @old` on the UPDATE and throws
`DbUpdateConcurrencyException` when it matches no rows. That version is safe
against a race between the check and the write; the hand-rolled one in this
drill is not, and knowing why is the point.

## ex8

What this was really testing: batch semantics, which is ex3's "validate before
you assign" scaled up until it is impossible to fake. Two jobs, one of them
unusable, and the gate checks that the *valid* one was not created either.

Three disciplines stack here. All-or-nothing validation: one pass over every
item collecting every error, so a client with four bad rows learns about four
bad rows rather than bisecting its own payload over four round trips. Keyed
errors: `items[1].copies` names the item and the field, which is the difference
between a usable API and a 400 with the word "invalid" in it. And a single
write: hanging the jobs off `batch.Jobs` means one `SaveChanges` inserts the
batch and its jobs together and EF fills in each `BatchId` - two saves would
leave an orphan batch behind if the second one failed.

The last check is the quiet one: the `Location` the create handed out has to
actually resolve. A 201 pointing at a URL that 404s is a create that lied, and
it is astonishingly common in APIs where the create and the read were written by
different people in different weeks.

## Further reading

- [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses) - `TypedResults.Created`, `NoContent`, `Problem`, `ValidationProblem`, `StatusCode`.
- [Handle errors in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/handle-errors) - the `ProblemDetails` and validation-problem shapes.
- [Saving data with EF Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/) - change tracking, `SaveChanges` as a unit of work, and related-entity inserts.
- [Handling concurrency conflicts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/concurrency) - the database-level version of ex7, and `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`.
- [RFC 9110 section 13](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-conditional-requests) - `If-Match`, `If-None-Match`, 412 and what a precondition means.
- [RFC 6585 section 3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585#section-3) - 428 Precondition Required, and why it exists.

## Exercise 1 - a create says 201 and says where it put it

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex1.cs`. `POST /d16/jobs` takes a `NewJob` and
answers **201** with the created `JobDto`, a `Location` header of
`/d16/jobs/{newId}`, and the row saved. A new job starts `"queued"`.

The shipped version saves correctly and then undersells it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The write itself is already correct - the row is saved. What is wrong is what
the response says about it. Two things are missing: the status that means "a
new thing now exists", and the address of that thing.

## Hint 2

`TypedResults.Created($"/d16/jobs/{job.Id}", D16Queue.ToDto(job))` sets both the
status and the `Location` header in one call.

It has to come *after* `SaveChangesAsync`: `job.Id` is 0 until the insert runs,
so a Location built earlier points at `/d16/jobs/0`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The write itself is already correct - the row is saved. What is wrong is what
the response says about it. Two things are missing: the status that means "a
new thing now exists", and the address of that thing.

## Hint 2

`TypedResults.Created($"/d16/jobs/{job.Id}", D16Queue.ToDto(job))` sets both the
status and the `Location` header in one call.

It has to come *after* `SaveChangesAsync`: `job.Id` is 0 until the insert runs,
so a Location built earlier points at `/d16/jobs/0`.

## Hint 1

Two answers only. Find the row; if it is not there, say so; otherwise remove it,
save, and return the status that carries no body.

`FirstOrDefaultAsync`, then either `TypedResults.NotFound()` or
`db.Jobs.Remove(job)` + `SaveChangesAsync()` + `TypedResults.NoContent()`.

## Exercise 4 - the retry that must not print twice

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex4
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The key is the request's identity, and `Job.IdempotencyKey` is where to keep it.
Read the header with `http.Request.Headers["Idempotency-Key"]`, refuse when it
is missing, and otherwise ask the database whether that key has been used.

## Hint 2

Found: return the job that key already made, with `TypedResults.Ok(...)` - 200,
because nothing was created this time - and set
`http.Response.Headers.Location` yourself, since `Ok` does not.

Not found: create as before, but store the key on the row, and answer 201.

## Hint 3

The retry deliberately sends a *different* body. Return the stored job exactly
as it is; do not apply the new payload. An idempotency key means "this is the
same request I already sent", so the first one is the one that happened -
applying the second makes this an upsert, which is a different contract.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The key is the request's identity, and `Job.IdempotencyKey` is where to keep it.
Read the header with `http.Request.Headers["Idempotency-Key"]`, refuse when it
is missing, and otherwise ask the database whether that key has been used.

## Hint 2

Found: return the job that key already made, with `TypedResults.Ok(...)` - 200,
because nothing was created this time - and set
`http.Response.Headers.Location` yourself, since `Ok` does not.

Not found: create as before, but store the key on the row, and answer 201.

## Hint 3

The retry deliberately sends a *different* body. Return the stored job exactly
as it is; do not apply the new payload. An idempotency key means "this is the
same request I already sent", so the first one is the one that happened -
applying the second makes this an upsert, which is a different contract.

## Exercise 5 - PATCH touches only what was sent

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex5.cs`. `PATCH /d16/jobs/{id}` takes a `JobPatch`
and changes only the fields actually present in the body. Unknown id: 404. A
blank title, `copies` below 1 or an unknown status: 400, keyed as in ex3.
Otherwise **200** with the full updated `JobDto`.

The shipped version treats a missing field as "set it to the default".

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex5
```

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex6.cs`. `POST /d16/jobs/{id}/cancel`:

- unknown id - 404
- the job's status is one of `D16Queue.Finished` - **409**, with its status
  left exactly as it was
- otherwise **204**, with the status now `"cancelled"`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex6
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - the write that has to prove it read the current one

Edit `src/Api/D16_RestWrites/Ex7.cs`. Two endpoints:

- `GET /d16/jobs/{id}` - 200 with the `JobDto` and an `ETag` of
  `Tag(job.Version)`, or 404
- `PUT /d16/jobs/{id}/copies` - 404 for an unknown id; **428** when the request
  carries no `If-Match` at all; **412** when it carries one that is not the
  job's current tag, with nothing written; otherwise **204** with `copies`
  updated and `Version` bumped by one

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d16_rest_writes ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves of one protocol. The read hands out the current version as an ETag;
the write refuses to run unless the client hands that version back and it is
still current.

Set `http.Response.Headers.ETag = Tag(job.Version)` in `Read`, before returning
the DTO.

## Hint 2

In `SetCopies`, the order is: 404 for an unknown id, then look at
`http.Request.Headers.IfMatch`.

- empty - `TypedResults.StatusCode(StatusCodes.Status428PreconditionRequired)`
- present but none of its values equals `Tag(job.Version)` -
  `StatusCodes.Status412PreconditionFailed`
- otherwise write, and `job.Version++`

## Hint 3

Both refusals must leave the row untouched, so both must happen before the
assignment. And the `Version++` is not decoration: if the version never moves,
every ETag stays valid forever, every `If-Match` matches, and the protocol
protects nothing. The gate replays the old tag afterwards to check that it
does not.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two halves of one protocol. The read hands out the current version as an ETag;
the write refuses to run unless the client hands that version back and it is
still current.

Set `http.Response.Headers.ETag = Tag(job.Version)` in `Read`, before returning
the DTO.

## Hint 2

In `SetCopies`, the order is: 404 for an unknown id, then look at
`http.Request.Headers.IfMatch`.

- empty - `TypedResults.StatusCode(StatusCodes.Status428PreconditionRequired)`
- present but none of its values equals `Tag(job.Version)` -
  `StatusCodes.Status412PreconditionFailed`
- otherwise write, and `job.Version++`

## Hint 3

Both refusals must leave the row untouched, so both must happen before the
assignment. And the `Version++` is not decoration: if the version never moves,
every ETag stays valid forever, every `If-Match` matches, and the protocol
protects nothing. The gate replays the old tag afterwards to check that it
does not.
