# d21 - authorization policy drills

Eight problems on the object that decides: policies as an AND of requirements,
requirements as an OR of handlers, a handler that has to see the request, a
handler that has to see the resource, a veto that beats every success, and a
policy applied where it cannot be forgotten. They drill lesson
**09_auth_and_testing** - go back to it if a policy still means
`RequireAuthenticatedUser()`.

The domain is a hospital shift roster (`src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Model.cs`):
four shifts across two wards, one of them locked, a `charge` role, and tokens
carrying `ward` and `grade` claims. The scheme `d21-bearer` is given and
correct - by the time any of these policies run, the token is already valid.
Everything is under `/d21/...` and each exercise owns one file, including its
own policies and handlers.

Note the routing: `/d21/roster/locked` and `/d21/roster/leads` are literal
segments, so they outrank ex2's `/d21/roster/{ward}` and reach ex3 and ex4.

## Exercise 1 - a policy is a list of requirements

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex1.cs`, `Ex1Services` only.
`GET /d21/roster` returns every shift, id ascending - but only for ward staff:

- no token - 401
- a valid token with **no `ward` claim** - **403**
- a token with a `ward` claim - 200

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - a requirement that has to look at the request

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex2.cs`, `Ex2Services` only.
`GET /d21/roster/{ward}` returns that ward's shifts - and the caller may read a
ward when it is **their own**, **or** when they are the charge nurse. That is an
OR, and the ward being asked for is a route value.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - a requirement and the handler that decides it

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex3.cs`. `MinimumGradeRequirement` is
given and the policy is wired; the handler agrees with everybody. Make it
succeed only when the caller's `grade` claim is at least
`requirement.Grade` - the bound comes from the requirement, and `D21Claims.GradeOf`
returns 0 for a caller with no grade. Exactly 5 passes a minimum of 5.

`GET /d21/roster/locked` returns the locked shifts.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - two handlers, one requirement

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex4.cs`. A ward lead is somebody at
grade 8 or above **or** the charge nurse. The grade handler is given. Write
`WardLeadByRoleHandler` and register it - as a second handler, not as an extra
clause in the first.

`GET /d21/roster/leads` returns the wards, alphabetically.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - the decision needs the thing being decided about

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex5.cs`.
`PUT /d21/shifts/{id}/day` takes a `DayChange`, in this order:

1. no such shift - 404
2. `D21Policies.EditShift` refuses this caller for **this shift** - 403
3. `day` outside 1 to 7 - 400 validation problem keyed `"day"`
4. otherwise 204, with the day written

Fill in `ShiftOwnerHandler` (the owner or the charge nurse) and call
`IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, shift, policy)` from the endpoint.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - one policy, a whole group

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex6.cs`. `D21Policies.Ops` is correct
and nothing applies it, so `/d21/ops/summary` and `/d21/ops/wards` are wide
open. Apply it to the **group**, once.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - a handler that says no and means it

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex7.cs`. `DELETE /d21/shifts/{id}` is
given and correct: 404 for an unknown shift, 403 when `D21Policies.DeleteShift`
refuses, otherwise 204.

`ShiftRemovalOwnerHandler` is given: the owner or the charge nurse may remove a
shift. Make `ShiftLockHandler` stop a **locked** shift being removed by anybody
at all - including the charge nurse, whose handler has already succeeded on that
same requirement.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - the policy and the handler agree

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex8.cs`. `POST /d21/shifts` needs a
caller who is on a ward **and** is senior (grade 5 or above) - no handler
required. Then:

- `day` outside 1 to 7 - 400 validation problem keyed `"day"`
- otherwise 201 with `Location: /d21/shifts/{newId}` and the created
  `ShiftDto`, whose `doctor` is the caller's subject and whose `ward` is the
  caller's **ward claim**

`NewShift.Ward` is a trap.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d21_authorization_policies

## Notes

By the time any of this runs, the token is already valid - d20 dealt with that.
This set is about the **policy**: the object that turns a valid identity into a
yes or a no, and where that object lives.

The model has four pieces, and knowing which is which is most of the skill.

- A **policy** is a named bundle of requirements. Every requirement in it must
  be satisfied, so a policy is an **AND**.
- A **requirement** is a marker: a small object saying what has to hold. It
  contains data (`MinimumGradeRequirement.Grade`), never logic.
- A **handler** decides one requirement. Several handlers may look at the same
  requirement, and it is satisfied when **any** of them succeeds - so a
  requirement is an **OR** over its handlers.
- **`context.Fail()`** is a veto. It is not the opposite of `Succeed`; silence
  is. Fail overrides every success, from any handler, in any order.

Two more distinctions the set drills. A requirement that needs the *request* -
a route value, a query string - reaches it through
`AuthorizationHandlerContext.Resource`, which in an endpoint-routing application
is the `HttpContext`. And a requirement that needs the *thing being acted on* -
this shift, this document - cannot run at the endpoint at all, because the
resource has not been loaded yet; that is what `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user,
resource, policy)` inside the handler is for.

Finally: 401 and 403 are produced by the policy, not by you. A refused policy
answers 403 when the caller authenticated and 401 when they did not, and a
handler that returns `Unauthorized()` from inside an endpoint is nearly always
wrong.

## ex1

What this was really testing: the difference between "has a token" and "meets
the requirement". `RequireAuthenticatedUser()` asks only the first, and it is
the line people leave a policy at because it makes the 401 work and the endpoint
stop being open.

The token in the gate is genuine and belongs to somebody real at head office who
has no ward. Nothing about it is suspicious; it simply does not describe
somebody who should be reading a ward roster. `RequireClaim(ward)` is the whole
fix, and it asks for presence rather than a value - which is what you want when
any ward will do.

The model answer's reasoning: write down the requirement the business actually
has, not the one that makes the endpoint compile.

## ex2

What this was really testing: a requirement about the **request**, and the
difference between AND and OR in policy-speak.

Two `RequireX` calls are an AND, and the rule here is an OR - your own ward *or*
being the charge nurse - so it is one `RequireAssertion` rather than two
requirements. That is the shape people get backwards, and the symptom is a
charge nurse who can only see her own ward.

The other half is reaching the route value. Authorization runs inside the
endpoint pipeline, so `context.Resource` is the `HttpContext`, and
`Request.RouteValues["ward"]` is there for the reading. The classic mistake is
to give up and do the check in the handler instead - which works, and moves the
rule out of the place where it can be reused, audited and applied to a group.

## ex3

What this was really testing: writing a handler, and specifically that the
requirement holds the **data** and the handler holds the **logic**. The bound
comes from `requirement.Grade`, so the same handler serves a policy that wants 5
and one that wants 8.

The shipped handler calls `Succeed` unconditionally, which is exactly the state a
half-finished handler is left in - and it is worse than no policy at all,
because the endpoint now looks protected.

Two details the gate pins. A caller with no grade claim must fail:
`D21Claims.GradeOf` returns 0 for that, so it needs no special case, which is
the point of reading a claim through one helper. And exactly 5 must pass -
"minimum" is inclusive, and off-by-one on an authorization bound is a bug you
find in production.

Note what the handler does *not* do: it never calls `Fail`. Not succeeding says
"I am not a reason to allow this"; failing says "nobody may allow this", and
those are very different claims. ex7 is the case where the second one is right.

## ex4

What this was really testing: that a requirement is an OR over its handlers.
Two ways to be a ward lead, two handlers, both registered against
`IAuthorizationHandler`, and the requirement is met as soon as either succeeds.

The classic mistake is to put the second condition inside the first handler with
an `||`. It works, and it means every new way of being a ward lead edits the
code that implements the old ones - so the file grows a chain of unrelated
business rules and nobody dares touch it. Separate handlers can be added,
removed and tested independently, and the one that comes from a different team
does not have to be merged into yours.

Worth knowing: handlers are resolved from DI, so they can take dependencies -
a database, an options object, a clock - which is the other reason not to
collapse them into assertions.

## ex5

What this was really testing: resource-based authorization, which is the case an
endpoint-level policy structurally cannot handle. "May this caller edit **this**
shift" needs the shift, and the shift is not loaded until the handler runs.

The shape is `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement, TResource>` - three parameters
instead of two - plus an explicit
`IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policyName)` call inside
the endpoint. Applying that policy with `RequireAuthorization` would silently
never succeed, because the middleware passes the `HttpContext` as the resource
and the typed handler would not match.

The ordering is the other half. 404 first, because there is nothing to authorize
against; then authorization; then validation - so a caller with no rights is not
told which of their fields were malformed. The gate checks that with a request
that is both unauthorized and invalid.

## ex6

What this was really testing: where a policy is applied. Per-endpoint
`RequireAuthorization` is correct on the day it is written and wrong on the day
somebody adds the ninth endpoint and forgets - and the failure is silent, wide
open, and invisible in review because the surrounding lines all look right.

A policy on the group is a property of the group: every endpoint added under it
is protected the moment it exists. The same argument scales up to
`AddAuthorization(options => options.FallbackPolicy = ...)`, which makes the
whole application authenticated by default and turns forgetting into an
`AllowAnonymous` you have to write on purpose.

## ex7

What this was really testing: `context.Fail()`, and the fact that it is not the
opposite of `Succeed`.

Handlers only ever *add* reasons to allow something. Not succeeding is neutral;
it declines to be such a reason. So a lock handler that quietly says nothing
cannot stop the charge nurse, whose handler has already succeeded on the very
same requirement - and the gate proves it with exactly that request.

`Fail()` is the veto, and it wins unconditionally: order does not matter, and no
later success can undo it. That is what makes it the right tool for a rule that
must hold for everybody - a locked record, a suspended account, a legal hold -
and the wrong tool for "I have nothing to say about this caller".

Worth knowing: `AuthorizationOptions.InvokeHandlersAfterFailure` defaults to
true, so every handler still runs after a failure. That matters when handlers
have side effects like auditing, and it is why `Fail` must be a decision rather
than an early exit.

## ex8

What this was really testing: composition, and the trap this whole part of the
track keeps returning to.

The policy is an AND of two things a token either says or does not -
`RequireClaim` for one, a one-line `RequireAssertion` for the other. No handler
is needed: a rule that depends only on the caller's own claims and on nothing
else does not need the machinery, and reaching for `IAuthorizationRequirement`
when a lambda will do is how policy files become unreadable.

And the trap: `NewShift.Ward` is ignored. The policy has just insisted the
caller has a ward claim, and that claim is the ward the shift goes on. Taking it
from the body would let a senior nurse on cardio place shifts on neuro - which
is not a rule anybody wrote down, and would be the only place in the system
where the ward claim did not mean what it says.

## Further reading

- [Policy-based authorization in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/policies) - requirements, handlers, `Succeed`, `Fail`, and multiple handlers per requirement.
- [Resource-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/resourcebased) - `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement, TResource>` and `IAuthorizationService`.
- [Claims-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/claims) - `RequireClaim` and what a claim requirement actually asks.
- [Simple authorization and RequireAuthorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/simple) - applying policies to endpoints and to route groups.
- [Route groups in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/route-handlers#route-groups) - why metadata on a group is inherited by everything in it.
- [Differentiate 401 from 403](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/introduction) - what the authorization middleware emits, and when.

  contains data (`MinimumGradeRequirement.Grade`), never logic.
- A **handler** decides one requirement. Several handlers may look at the same
  requirement, and it is satisfied when **any** of them succeeds - so a
  requirement is an **OR** over its handlers.
- **`context.Fail()`** is a veto. It is not the opposite of `Succeed`; silence
  is. Fail overrides every success, from any handler, in any order.

Two more distinctions the set drills. A requirement that needs the *request* -
a route value, a query string - reaches it through
`AuthorizationHandlerContext.Resource`, which in an endpoint-routing application
is the `HttpContext`. And a requirement that needs the *thing being acted on* -
this shift, this document - cannot run at the endpoint at all, because the
resource has not been loaded yet; that is what `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user,
resource, policy)` inside the handler is for.

Finally: 401 and 403 are produced by the policy, not by you. A refused policy
answers 403 when the caller authenticated and 401 when they did not, and a
handler that returns `Unauthorized()` from inside an endpoint is nearly always
wrong.

## ex1

What this was really testing: the difference between "has a token" and "meets
the requirement". `RequireAuthenticatedUser()` asks only the first, and it is
the line people leave a policy at because it makes the 401 work and the endpoint
stop being open.

The token in the gate is genuine and belongs to somebody real at head office who
has no ward. Nothing about it is suspicious; it simply does not describe
somebody who should be reading a ward roster. `RequireClaim(ward)` is the whole
fix, and it asks for presence rather than a value - which is what you want when
any ward will do.

The model answer's reasoning: write down the requirement the business actually
has, not the one that makes the endpoint compile.

## ex2

What this was really testing: a requirement about the **request**, and the
difference between AND and OR in policy-speak.

Two `RequireX` calls are an AND, and the rule here is an OR - your own ward *or*
being the charge nurse - so it is one `RequireAssertion` rather than two
requirements. That is the shape people get backwards, and the symptom is a
charge nurse who can only see her own ward.

The other half is reaching the route value. Authorization runs inside the
endpoint pipeline, so `context.Resource` is the `HttpContext`, and
`Request.RouteValues["ward"]` is there for the reading. The classic mistake is
to give up and do the check in the handler instead - which works, and moves the
rule out of the place where it can be reused, audited and applied to a group.

## ex3

What this was really testing: writing a handler, and specifically that the
requirement holds the **data** and the handler holds the **logic**. The bound
comes from `requirement.Grade`, so the same handler serves a policy that wants 5
and one that wants 8.

The shipped handler calls `Succeed` unconditionally, which is exactly the state a
half-finished handler is left in - and it is worse than no policy at all,
because the endpoint now looks protected.

Two details the gate pins. A caller with no grade claim must fail:
`D21Claims.GradeOf` returns 0 for that, so it needs no special case, which is
the point of reading a claim through one helper. And exactly 5 must pass -
"minimum" is inclusive, and off-by-one on an authorization bound is a bug you
find in production.

Note what the handler does *not* do: it never calls `Fail`. Not succeeding says
"I am not a reason to allow this"; failing says "nobody may allow this", and
those are very different claims. ex7 is the case where the second one is right.

## ex4

What this was really testing: that a requirement is an OR over its handlers.
Two ways to be a ward lead, two handlers, both registered against
`IAuthorizationHandler`, and the requirement is met as soon as either succeeds.

The classic mistake is to put the second condition inside the first handler with
an `||`. It works, and it means every new way of being a ward lead edits the
code that implements the old ones - so the file grows a chain of unrelated
business rules and nobody dares touch it. Separate handlers can be added,
removed and tested independently, and the one that comes from a different team
does not have to be merged into yours.

Worth knowing: handlers are resolved from DI, so they can take dependencies -
a database, an options object, a clock - which is the other reason not to
collapse them into assertions.

## ex5

What this was really testing: resource-based authorization, which is the case an
endpoint-level policy structurally cannot handle. "May this caller edit **this**
shift" needs the shift, and the shift is not loaded until the handler runs.

The shape is `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement, TResource>` - three parameters
instead of two - plus an explicit
`IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policyName)` call inside
the endpoint. Applying that policy with `RequireAuthorization` would silently
never succeed, because the middleware passes the `HttpContext` as the resource
and the typed handler would not match.

The ordering is the other half. 404 first, because there is nothing to authorize
against; then authorization; then validation - so a caller with no rights is not
told which of their fields were malformed. The gate checks that with a request
that is both unauthorized and invalid.

## ex6

What this was really testing: where a policy is applied. Per-endpoint
`RequireAuthorization` is correct on the day it is written and wrong on the day
somebody adds the ninth endpoint and forgets - and the failure is silent, wide
open, and invisible in review because the surrounding lines all look right.

A policy on the group is a property of the group: every endpoint added under it
is protected the moment it exists. The same argument scales up to
`AddAuthorization(options => options.FallbackPolicy = ...)`, which makes the
whole application authenticated by default and turns forgetting into an
`AllowAnonymous` you have to write on purpose.

## ex7

What this was really testing: `context.Fail()`, and the fact that it is not the
opposite of `Succeed`.

Handlers only ever *add* reasons to allow something. Not succeeding is neutral;
it declines to be such a reason. So a lock handler that quietly says nothing
cannot stop the charge nurse, whose handler has already succeeded on the very
same requirement - and the gate proves it with exactly that request.

`Fail()` is the veto, and it wins unconditionally: order does not matter, and no
later success can undo it. That is what makes it the right tool for a rule that
must hold for everybody - a locked record, a suspended account, a legal hold -
and the wrong tool for "I have nothing to say about this caller".

Worth knowing: `AuthorizationOptions.InvokeHandlersAfterFailure` defaults to
true, so every handler still runs after a failure. That matters when handlers
have side effects like auditing, and it is why `Fail` must be a decision rather
than an early exit.

## ex8

What this was really testing: composition, and the trap this whole part of the
track keeps returning to.

The policy is an AND of two things a token either says or does not -
`RequireClaim` for one, a one-line `RequireAssertion` for the other. No handler
is needed: a rule that depends only on the caller's own claims and on nothing
else does not need the machinery, and reaching for `IAuthorizationRequirement`
when a lambda will do is how policy files become unreadable.

And the trap: `NewShift.Ward` is ignored. The policy has just insisted the
caller has a ward claim, and that claim is the ward the shift goes on. Taking it
from the body would let a senior nurse on cardio place shifts on neuro - which
is not a rule anybody wrote down, and would be the only place in the system
where the ward claim did not mean what it says.

## Further reading

- [Policy-based authorization in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/policies) - requirements, handlers, `Succeed`, `Fail`, and multiple handlers per requirement.
- [Resource-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/resourcebased) - `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement, TResource>` and `IAuthorizationService`.
- [Claims-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/claims) - `RequireClaim` and what a claim requirement actually asks.
- [Simple authorization and RequireAuthorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/simple) - applying policies to endpoints and to route groups.
- [Route groups in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/route-handlers#route-groups) - why metadata on a group is inherited by everything in it.
- [Differentiate 401 from 403](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/introduction) - what the authorization middleware emits, and when.

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex1.cs`, `Ex1Services` only.
`GET /d21/roster` returns every shift, id ascending - but only for ward staff:

- no token - 401
- a valid token with **no `ward` claim** - **403**
- a token with a `ward` claim - 200

uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex1
```

`RequireAuthenticatedUser()` asks whether there is a valid token. The roster's
actual rule is about the caller: they have to work on a ward.

Add `.RequireClaim(D21Claims.Ward)` to the policy. With one argument it asks

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - a requirement that has to look at the request

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex2.cs`, `Ex2Services` only.
`GET /d21/roster/{ward}` returns that ward's shifts - and the caller may read a
ward when it is **their own**, **or** when they are the charge nurse. That is an
OR, and the ward being asked for is a route value.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two ways in - your own ward, or being the charge nurse - so this is an OR. Two
`RequireX` calls would be an AND and would demand both, which is not the rule.
One `RequireAssertion` expresses an OR directly.

## Hint 2

The assertion is handed an `AuthorizationHandlerContext`. In an
endpoint-routing application its `Resource` is the `HttpContext`, so the ward
being asked for is reachable:

    (context.Resource as HttpContext)?.Request.RouteValues["ward"] as string

Compare it with `D21Claims.WardOf(context.User)`, and short-circuit to true when
`context.User.IsInRole("charge")`.

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex5.cs`.

1. no such shift - 404

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"May this caller edit THIS shift" needs the shift, and the shift does not exist
until the handler has loaded it - which is why an endpoint-level policy
structurally cannot answer it.

## Hint 2

Two halves. Fill in `ShiftOwnerHandler`, whose third parameter is the `Shift`
itself: succeed when `resource.Doctor` is the caller, or the caller is in the
`charge` role.

Then ask, from inside the endpoint:

    var decision = await authorization.AuthorizeAsync(user, shift, D21Policies.EditShift);
    if (!decision.Succeeded) return TypedResults.Forbid(authenticationSchemes: [D21Jwt.Scheme]);

## Hint 3

The order is graded: 404 first (there is nothing to authorize against), then the
authorization check, then the validation. Putting validation first tells a
caller with no rights at all which of their fields were malformed.

Note that `D21Policies.EditShift` is never used with `RequireAuthorization` -
the middleware would pass the `HttpContext` as the resource and the typed
handler would never match.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"May this caller edit THIS shift" needs the shift, and the shift does not exist
until the handler has loaded it - which is why an endpoint-level policy
structurally cannot answer it.

## Hint 2

Two halves. Fill in `ShiftOwnerHandler`, whose third parameter is the `Shift`
itself: succeed when `resource.Doctor` is the caller, or the caller is in the
`charge` role.

Then ask, from inside the endpoint:

    var decision = await authorization.AuthorizeAsync(user, shift, D21Policies.EditShift);
    if (!decision.Succeeded) return TypedResults.Forbid(authenticationSchemes: [D21Jwt.Scheme]);

## Hint 3

The order is graded: 404 first (there is nothing to authorize against), then the
authorization check, then the validation. Putting validation first tells a
caller with no rights at all which of their fields were malformed.

Note that `D21Policies.EditShift` is never used with `RequireAuthorization` -
the middleware would pass the `HttpContext` as the resource and the typed
handler would never match.

locked record, a suspended account - and wrong for "I have nothing to say about
this caller", which is what ex3 and ex4 do by returning without succeeding.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Staying silent will not work here, and the gate proves it: the charge nurse's
handler has already succeeded on this requirement, and a requirement is met as
soon as any handler succeeds. Silence is not a refusal.

## Hint 2

`context.Fail()` is the veto. In `ShiftLockHandler`:

    if (resource.Locked) context.Fail();

That is all. Nothing else in the file changes - the endpoint and the owner
handler are given and correct.

## Hint 3

A failure beats every success, from any handler, whatever order they ran in.
That is what makes `Fail` right for a rule that must hold for everybody - a
locked record, a suspended account - and wrong for "I have nothing to say about
this caller", which is what ex3 and ex4 do by returning without succeeding.

## Exercise 8 - the policy and the handler agree

Edit `src/Api/D21_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex8.cs`. `POST /d21/shifts` needs a
caller who is on a ward **and** is senior (grade 5 or above) - no handler
required. Then:

- `day` outside 1 to 7 - 400 validation problem keyed `"day"`
- otherwise 201 with `Location: /d21/shifts/{newId}` and the created
  `ShiftDto`, whose `doctor` is the caller's subject and whose `ward` is the
  caller's **ward claim**

`NewShift.Ward` is a trap.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d21_authorization_policies ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two things must BOTH hold, so this one is an AND - which is what a policy is by
default. No handler is needed: a rule that depends only on the caller's own
claims is a `RequireClaim` and a one-line assertion.

## Hint 2

    .RequireClaim(D21Claims.Ward)
    .RequireAssertion(context => D21Claims.GradeOf(context.User) >= 5)

Reaching for `IAuthorizationRequirement` when a lambda will do is how a policy
file stops being readable.

## Hint 3

In the handler, `NewShift.Ward` is never read. The policy has just insisted the
caller has a ward claim; that claim is the ward, exactly as the subject is the
doctor. Validate the day first (`ValidationProblem` keyed `"day"`), then
`roster.Add(...)`, then `TypedResults.Created($"/d21/shifts/{shift.Id}", ...)`.

Two things must BOTH hold, so this one is an AND - which is what a policy is by
default. No handler is needed: a rule that depends only on the caller's own
claims is a `RequireClaim` and a one-line assertion.

## Hint 2

    .RequireClaim(D21Claims.Ward)
    .RequireAssertion(context => D21Claims.GradeOf(context.User) >= 5)

Reaching for `IAuthorizationRequirement` when a lambda will do is how a policy
file stops being readable.

## Hint 3

In the handler, `NewShift.Ward` is never read. The policy has just insisted the
caller has a ward claim; that claim is the ward, exactly as the subject is the
doctor. Validate the day first (`ValidationProblem` keyed `"day"`), then
`roster.Add(...)`, then `TypedResults.Created($"/d21/shifts/{shift.Id}", ...)`.

lessons.briefing:
# d22 - integration testing drills

Eight problems on writing application code a test can pin down: state that
belongs to the host instead of the process, a clock that arrives as a
parameter, an identifier that is a function of its inputs, an outbound call
behind an interface, a limit that comes from configuration, and an endpoint
that is safe to call twice. They drill lesson **09_auth_and_testing** - the
testing half of it - and every gate below proves the seam by using it.

You are not writing tests here. You are writing the endpoints, and the gates
substitute things: they build two hosts and demand each one sees only its own
writes, they install a clock stuck at 2026-03-04 and demand the due date says
so, they register a fake notifier and read back what the endpoint asked it to
do, they boot a host whose configured limit is 2 and demand the answer changes.

The domain is a library loans desk - five books, three members, five loans
already out - in `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Model.cs`. Read it first: it
holds the seed data, the small stores, and the one `IServiceRegistrar` that
registers everything. Everything is under `/d22/...` and each exercise owns one
file. Timestamps are always printed with `D22Library.Stamp`, which yields
`2026-03-04T09:30:00Z`.

## Exercise 1 - state belongs to the host, not to the process

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex1.cs`.

- `POST /d22/holds` with `{"code": "...", "cardId": "..."}` - **201**, a
  `Location` of `/d22/holds/{id}`, and the new `Hold` as the body. Ids start at
  1 on each host. The body is always well formed; no validation is needed.
- `GET /d22/holds` - 200 with every hold placed on **this** host, id ascending.

The shipped version keeps the holds in a `static List<>`, so every host in the
process shares one desk. `HoldDesk` is already registered as a singleton in
`Model.cs` - take it as a parameter.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - the clock is a dependency

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d22/desk/due` answers 200
with `{"issuedAt": ..., "dueAt": ..., "loanDays": 14}`, where `issuedAt` is now
and `dueAt` is `D22Library.DefaultLoanDays` later, both through
`D22Library.Stamp`.

The shipped version calls `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow`. Take a `TimeProvider`
parameter instead - it is registered in `Model.cs`, and the gate replaces it
with one that is stuck at a fixed instant.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - an identifier a test can predict

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex3.cs`. `POST /d22/receipts` with
`{"cardId": "m-014"}` answers **201** with a `Location` of
`/d22/receipts/{reference}` and the body
`{"reference": "LOAN-M-014-0001", "sequence": 1}`.

- `reference` is `LOAN-`, the card id in capitals, `-`, then the sequence
  padded to four digits
- `sequence` comes from the injected `ReferenceDesk`, which hands out 1, 2, 3,
  ... per host - never `Guid.NewGuid` and never `Random`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - a seam for the outbound call

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex4.cs`. `POST /d22/reminders` answers 200
with `{"notified": n}` and calls `IOverdueNotifier.Notify(cardId, code,
daysOverdue)` once for every seeded loan whose `DaysOverdue` is above 0, in
**loan id order**.

The shipped version builds a `new DeskLogNotifier()` inside the handler, so the
count is right and the seam is dead. Take the interface as a parameter.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - a limit a test can change

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex5.cs`.
`GET /d22/members/{cardId}/allowance`:

- **404** when `cardId` names no member
- otherwise 200 with
  `{"cardId", "name", "onLoan", "maxLoans", "canBorrow"}`, where `onLoan`
  counts that member's seeded loans, `maxLoans` is
  `LoanPolicyOptions.MaxPerMember` and `canBorrow` is `onLoan < maxLoans`

`MaxPerMember` defaults to 3 and is bound to `Dojo:D22:Loans` in `Model.cs`.
The shipped version hard-codes the 3, which is right until a test says 2.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - order-independent, and safe to call twice

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex6.cs`.

- `POST /d22/returns/{loanId}` - **404** when `loanId` names no seeded loan;
  otherwise 200 with `{"loanId", "alreadyReturned", "returnedCount"}`.
  `alreadyReturned` is true when this host had already recorded that id, and a
  repeat must not change `returnedCount`.
- `GET /d22/returns` - 200 with `{"returned": [ids ASCENDING], "count": n}`.

`ReturnsLog.Add` returns false for a repeat, and `Snapshot` returns the ids in
no particular order.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - three seams on one endpoint

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex7.cs`.
`POST /d22/renewals/{loanId}`, in this order:

- **404** when `loanId` names no seeded loan
- **409** with `{"loanId", "daysOverdue", "graceDays"}` when the loan's
  `DaysOverdue` is **greater than** `LoanPolicyOptions.GraceDays` - and before
  answering, `Notify(cardId, code, daysOverdue)` on the injected notifier
- otherwise 200 with
  `{"loanId", "cardId", "code", "renewedAt", "dueAt"}`, where `renewedAt` is
  now and `dueAt` is `LoanPolicyOptions.LoanDays` later, both stamped

Nothing is notified on the 200 path.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - the whole desk, every seam injected

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex8.cs`. `POST /d22/loans` with
`{"cardId": "...", "code": "..."}`, in this order:

- **400** as a validation problem when either field is missing or blank
  (whitespace counts), keyed `"cardId"` and `"code"`
- **404** when `cardId` names no member, or `code` names no book
- **409** with `{"cardId", "open", "maxPerMember"}` when the member's open
  loans - the seeded ones **plus** the ones this host has issued - already
  reach `MaxPerMember`
- otherwise **201** with a `Location` of `/d22/loans/{id}` and an `IssuedLoan`:
  the id from `LoanBook.NextId` (1001 first), the book's `code` and `title`,
  `issuedAt` = now and `dueAt` = `LoanDays` later, both stamped, and `warned`
  true when the member has any overdue seeded loan. When `warned`, notify with
  the member's **most overdue** loan (`cardId`, `code`, `daysOverdue`), not the
  book being borrowed.

`GET /d22/loans/{id}` answers 200 with a loan this host issued, 404 otherwise.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing

## Notes

Nothing in this set asks you to write a test. Every problem asks you to write
application code that a test could pin down, and then a gate proves it by
actually pinning it down. That inversion is the point: **testability is a
property of the production code**, not of the test project. A handler is
testable when everything it depends on arrives through the door rather than
being fetched from behind it.

Four things a handler is tempted to fetch for itself, and the seam that
replaces each:

- **State** - a `static` field belongs to the process, so every host in the
  test run shares it. A singleton resolved from the container belongs to the
  host, and each `new DojoWebFactory()` is its own host with its own container.
- **Time** - `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` is an input the caller cannot choose. A
  `TimeProvider` parameter is an input the caller can.
- **Randomness** - `Guid.NewGuid()` in a response body makes that response
  unassertable forever. Derive the identifier from something injected.
- **The outside world** - a `new`ed concrete class is welded in. An interface
  resolved from DI can be replaced by a recorder that says what was asked for.

And the two rules that decide whether a suite is stable: no test may depend on
another test's writes, and no endpoint may be dangerous to call twice. A retry
that changes the answer is a bug in the endpoint, not in the runner.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that mutable state has an owner, and that the
owner should be the host. Both hosts in the gate run in the same process, so a
`static List<Hold>` is one list shared between them - the second host's first
hold comes back with id 2, and each host sees the other's writes.

The classic mistake is that this looks fine in manual testing, because a
`dotnet run` is one process with one host and the static is indistinguishable
from a singleton. It only breaks under a test suite, where it breaks as
order-dependent flakiness rather than as an error. The model answer's
reasoning: `HoldDesk` is registered singleton in `Model.cs`, so asking for it
as a parameter gives you exactly one per container - and a container is exactly
what a `WebApplicationFactory` builds fresh.

## ex2

What this was really testing: that "now" is a dependency like any other. The
gate installs a `TimeProvider` stuck at 2026-03-04T09:30:00Z and then asserts
the due date to the second, which is only possible because the handler was told
what time it is instead of asking the machine.

The classic mistake is the "just allow a tolerance" workaround - assert the due
date is within a few seconds of `UtcNow.AddDays(14)`. That reproduces the
handler's arithmetic inside the test, so the test agrees with the code by
construction and catches nothing. The model answer's reasoning: take
`TimeProvider` and call `GetUtcNow()`; the second host in the gate, with a 2019
clock, is there to prove the value is read rather than remembered.

## ex3

What this was really testing: determinism. A response containing
`Guid.NewGuid()` can be checked for shape and never for value, which quietly
downgrades every assertion about it to "something came back". The gate demands
that a fresh host given the same request produce the same reference, byte for
byte.

The classic mistake is treating "unique" and "unpredictable" as the same
requirement. They are not: `LOAN-M-014-0001` is unique within the host and
completely predictable. The model answer's reasoning: build the reference out
of the caller's input and an injected counter, so it is a pure function of
things a test controls - and the four-digit padding is in the contract because
`0001` and `1` are different strings and gates compare literally.

## ex4

What this was really testing: that an outbound effect needs a seam, and that
the seam has to be the object the handler actually calls. The shipped stub
returns the right count and performs the right number of notifications - on an
instance it constructed itself, which no test can see. The endpoint is
"correct" and completely unverifiable.

The classic mistake is asserting only the count. `notified: 3` passes against
the broken version; the recorded call list does not. That is why the gate pins
down the arguments and their order - what was asked, of whom, in what sequence.
The model answer's reasoning: take `IOverdueNotifier` as a parameter and use
what you are handed, so production gets `DeskLogNotifier` and the gate gets a
recorder and the handler cannot tell the difference.

## ex5

What this was really testing: that a policy number is configuration, not a
constant. The shipped `const int MaxLoans = 3` gives the right answer on the
default host and cannot be made to give any other answer without an edit and a
rebuild - so no test can ever explore what happens at the boundary.

The classic mistake is thinking the constant is safe because it matches the
documented default. It does match, which is exactly why the bug survives code
review; the gate catches it only because it boots a second host that says the
limit is 2. The model answer's reasoning: read `IOptions<LoanPolicyOptions>`
inside the handler, so the value comes from whatever configuration this host
was built with, and the defaults on the options class stay the fallback.

## ex6

What this was really testing: two independent properties that together decide
whether a suite is stable. First, the collection endpoint must sort, because
`ReturnsLog.Snapshot` hands back a `HashSet` in whatever order it feels like
and enumeration order is not a contract. Second, `POST` twice with the same
loan id must be a report, not a second effect.

The classic mistake is answering 409 to the repeat. It feels rigorous and it
punishes exactly the callers you want to encourage: a client that never saw the
first response, and a test runner retrying a flaky-looking case. The model
answer's reasoning: `HashSet.Add` already returns whether the id was new, so
the handler can say `alreadyReturned` truthfully while the count stays put -
and the 404 for loan 99 keeps "nothing to do" distinct from "no such thing".

## ex7

What this was really testing: three seams on one handler, and evidence that all
three are live. Any one of them can be faked while the other two stay welded
in, and the endpoint will still pass a careless test - so the gate runs the
same loan against two hosts that differ in clock, in `LoanDays` and in
`GraceDays`, and demands a different answer from each.

The classic mistakes are ordering ones. Checking overdue-ness before existence
answers 409 for a loan that was never there. Notifying on the success path as
well as the refusal makes the notifier useless as evidence, because a recorded
call no longer means "this was refused". And `>=` instead of `>` quietly turns
a two-day grace into a one-day one - the gate's loan 5, one day overdue, exists
to catch precisely that.

The model answer's reasoning: 404, then the rule, then the work; the notifier
fires only inside the refusal branch, and both the grace and the loan length
come out of `policy.Value` at the moment of use rather than being captured
anywhere.

## ex8

What this was really testing: the whole discipline at once. Shape before
existence before rules before work - 400 for a blank field, 404 for a name
nothing answers to, 409 for a request that is perfectly valid and still
refused, 201 with a `Location` that can actually be fetched.

Two traps are worth naming. The open-loan count has to include the loans this
endpoint issued on this host, not just the seeded ones; counting only the seed
lets a member borrow forever by retrying, and the gate's second POST for m-007
is exactly that retry. And the warning has to name the member's *most overdue*
loan rather than the book being borrowed now - the two happen to differ for
m-007, which is the only reason a wrong implementation shows up.

The model answer's reasoning: every input is a parameter -
the store, the clock, the options, the notifier - so the second host in the
gate can change all four at once and the handler needs no knowledge that it is
being tested. That is the whole idea the set has been circling: code that takes
its dependencies is code you can put in a harness, and code that reaches for
them is code you can only run.

## Further reading

- [Integration tests in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests) - `WebApplicationFactory`, `WithWebHostBuilder`, and replacing registrations for a test host.
- [Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/dependency-injection) - service lifetimes, and what a singleton is actually scoped to.
- [TimeProvider class](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.timeprovider) - the abstraction over "now", and why it is abstract.
- [Options pattern in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options) - binding a section to a class and reading it through `IOptions<T>`.
- [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses) - `TypedResults.Created`, `ValidationProblem` and custom status codes.
- [RFC 9110 section 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-idempotent-methods) - what idempotent means, and why a retry must be safe.

## Retrieval deck — Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing

Answer these without rereading the notes first. Written or spoken answers both
count, but always check the answer against the gate, runtime, compiler, or
primary documentation afterward.

1. **Pass 1 · now:** What problem does this lesson solve, and what observable result proves it worked?
2. **Pass 2 · 3 days:** Write the core syntax or API shape from memory. Which pieces are required?
3. **Pass 3 · 7 days:** What happens step by step on the smallest representative input?
4. **Pass 4 · 21 days:** Which plausible beginner solution fails, and what evidence reveals the failure?
5. **Pass 5 · 60 days:** What neighboring technique looks similar? State the decision rule between them.
6. **Pass 6 · 120 days:** Which edge case changes the result, type, ordering, lifecycle, or performance?
7. **Pass 7 · 240 days:** How would you test the happy path, boundary case, and failure path independently?
8. **Pass 8 · 1 year:** What assumption in the model solution is safe here but risky in production?
9. **Pass 9 · 18 months:** How does this lesson connect to an earlier skill and prepare a later one?
10. **Pass 10 · 3 years:** Can you solve and explain the hardest exercise cold, without recognition cues?

## 100 retrieval prompts — Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing

This is the expanded practice bank for this reading: ten retrieval lenses at
each of ten spaced stages. Do one stage per scheduled session. Record an
answer before checking notes; recognition is not retrieval.

### Stage 1 — Cold recall (now)

Answer from memory before opening any course file.
1. **Contract · `ex1`:** For Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing, state the exact inputs, outputs, side effects, and success condition.
2. **Mechanism · `ex2`:** For Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing, trace the language or runtime mechanism that produces the result.
3. **Construction · `ex3`:** For Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing, build the smallest correct example and justify every token or operation.
4. **Prediction · `ex4`:** For Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing, predict the result before executing, compiling, or querying.
5. **Failure · `ex5`:** For Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing, invent a plausible wrong answer and identify the evidence that disproves it.
6. **Boundary · `ex6`:** For Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing, test empty, missing, extreme, duplicate, or otherwise awkward input.
7. **Comparison · `ex7`:** For Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing, contrast the approach with its nearest alternative and give a decision rule.
8. **Verification · `ex8`:** For Reading - dotnet/d22_integration_testing, design an independent check that would catch a superficially correct answer.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - state belongs to the host, not to the process

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex1.cs`.

- `POST /d22/holds` with `{"code": "...", "cardId": "..."}` - **201**, a
  `Location` of `/d22/holds/{id}`, and the new `Hold` as the body. Ids start at
  1 on each host. The body is always well formed; no validation is needed.
- `GET /d22/holds` - 200 with every hold placed on **this** host, id ascending.

The shipped version keeps the holds in a `static List<>`, so every host in the
process shares one desk. `HoldDesk` is already registered as a singleton in
`Model.cs` - take it as a parameter.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `static` field lives for as long as the process does. Each gate builds its
own `new DojoWebFactory()`, and every one of those hosts runs inside this one
process - so a static list is one list for all of them, while a singleton
registered in the container is one per host.

## Hint 2

`HoldDesk` is already registered in `Model.cs`, so a handler can simply ask for
it: add a `HoldDesk desk` parameter and let the container hand it over. Delete
both static fields; `desk.Place(...)` already assigns the id and `desk.All()`
already returns a copy.

## Exercise 3 - an identifier a test can predict

```

Unique and unpredictable are two different requirements, and only one of them
was asked for. An identifier that is a function of its inputs can still be
unique within the host - and unlike a `Guid`, a test can state what it should

`ReferenceDesk`. Take a `ReferenceDesk desk` parameter, call `desk.Next()`
once, and build the string. `ToUpperInvariant()` capitalises the card, and the
`:D4` format specifier does the four-digit padding.

## Exercise 5 - a limit a test can change

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex5.cs`.
`GET /d22/members/{cardId}/allowance`:

- **404** when `cardId` names no member
- otherwise 200 with
  `{"cardId", "name", "onLoan", "maxLoans", "canBorrow"}`, where `onLoan`
  counts that member's seeded loans, `maxLoans` is
  `LoanPolicyOptions.MaxPerMember` and `canBorrow` is `onLoan < maxLoans`

`MaxPerMember` defaults to 3 and is bound to `Dojo:D22:Loans` in `Model.cs`.
The shipped version hard-codes the 3, which is right until a test says 2.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex5
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - order-independent, and safe to call twice

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex6.cs`.

- `POST /d22/returns/{loanId}` - **404** when `loanId` names no seeded loan;
  otherwise 200 with `{"loanId", "alreadyReturned", "returnedCount"}`.
  `alreadyReturned` is true when this host had already recorded that id, and a
  repeat must not change `returnedCount`.
- `GET /d22/returns` - 200 with `{"returned": [ids ASCENDING], "count": n}`.

`ReturnsLog.Add` returns false for a repeat, and `Snapshot` returns the ids in
no particular order.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate properties are being drilled here. One is that a collection
endpoint owes the client an order of its own, because the order a set
enumerates in is an implementation detail. The other is idempotence: the second
identical POST must report, not repeat.

## Hint 2

`ReturnsLog.Add` already tells you which case you are in - it returns `true`
the first time an id is seen and `false` for a repeat, so `alreadyReturned` is
that value negated and the count comes from `Snapshot().Length` afterwards
either way. `Shelved` sorts what `Snapshot()` gives it. Check
`D22Library.FindLoan(loanId)` first, before touching the log at all.

## Exercise 8 - the whole desk, every seam injected

Edit `src/Api/D22_IntegrationTesting/Ex8.cs`. `POST /d22/loans` with
`{"cardId": "...", "code": "..."}`, in this order:

- **400** as a validation problem when either field is missing or blank
  (whitespace counts), keyed `"cardId"` and `"code"`
- **404** when `cardId` names no member, or `code` names no book
- **409** with `{"cardId", "open", "maxPerMember"}` when the member's open
  loans - the seeded ones **plus** the ones this host has issued - already
  reach `MaxPerMember`
- otherwise **201** with a `Location` of `/d22/loans/{id}` and an `IssuedLoan`:
  the id from `LoanBook.NextId` (1001 first), the book's `code` and `title`,
  `issuedAt` = now and `dueAt` = `LoanDays` later, both stamped, and `warned`
  true when the member has any overdue seeded loan. When `warned`, notify with
  the member's **most overdue** loan (`cardId`, `code`, `daysOverdue`), not the
  book being borrowed.

`GET /d22/loans/{id}` answers 200 with a loan this host issued, 404 otherwise.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d22_integration_testing ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four failure modes and one success, in a fixed order: is the request
well formed (400), do the things it names exist (404), does the rule allow it
(409), and only then do the work (201). Each of those is a different claim
about whose fault it is, and collapsing any two of them lies to the client.

## Hint 2

Everything the handler needs is already a parameter - the store, the clock, the
options and the notifier - so nothing here should call `new`, `UtcNow` or read
a constant. Build the validation dictionary first with
`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` on both fields, and return
`TypedResults.ValidationProblem(errors)` when it is not empty.

## Hint 3

The open-loan count is `D22Library.LoansFor(cardId).Count` **plus** the loans
this host has already issued (`loans.Issued()` filtered by card) - counting
only the seeded ones lets the same member borrow forever. The warning uses
`D22Library.MostOverdueFor(cardId)`: when it is not null, notify with *that
loan's* card, code and days, set `warned` to true, and only then take
`loans.NextId()` and `TypedResults.Created($"/d22/loans/{id}", issued)`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Four failure modes and one success, in a fixed order: is the request
well formed (400), do the things it names exist (404), does the rule allow it
(409), and only then do the work (201). Each of those is a different claim
about whose fault it is, and collapsing any two of them lies to the client.

## Hint 2

Everything the handler needs is already a parameter - the store, the clock, the
options and the notifier - so nothing here should call `new`, `UtcNow` or read
a constant. Build the validation dictionary first with
`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` on both fields, and return
`TypedResults.ValidationProblem(errors)` when it is not empty.

## Hint 3

The open-loan count is `D22Library.LoansFor(cardId).Count` **plus** the loans
this host has already issued (`loans.Issued()` filtered by card) - counting
only the seeded ones lets the same member borrow forever. The warning uses
`D22Library.MostOverdueFor(cardId)`: when it is not null, notify with *that
loan's* card, code and days, set `warned` to true, and only then take
`loans.NextId()` and `TypedResults.Created($"/d22/loans/{id}", issued)`.

lessons.briefing:
# d23 - pagination and filtering drills

Eight problems on slicing a collection over HTTP: offsets and their off-by-one,
an envelope with a real total, a sort key that is a vocabulary rather than a
column name, filters that AND in the database, navigation links, and the keyset
cursor that survives an insert. They drill lesson **07_rest_crud** - go back to
it if "just add `?page=`" still sounds like a small change.

The data is a job board: twenty-five postings in SQLite, seeded by the gate, in
`src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Model.cs`. Read it first. `PostedDay` is an
integer 1..60, `Tags` is a comma separated list, and `sql` and `nosql` are both
real tags. Everything is under `/d23/...`, each exercise owns one route and one
file, and several gates count SQL commands - a correct body assembled in memory
still fails.

## Exercise 1 - the first page skips nothing

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d23/postings` answers 200
with one page of `PostingCard`s, **id ascending**.

- `?page=` defaults to 1, `?size=` defaults to 10
- `page` below 1 is **400** as a validation problem keyed `"page"`
- `size` outside 1..`D23Board.MaxSize` (50) is **400** keyed `"size"`

The shipped version skips `page * size` rows, so nobody ever sees posting 1.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - an envelope with a real total

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/page` answers
200 with a `PostingPage`: `items`, `page`, `size`, `total`, `totalPages`.

- `items` is the page itself, id ascending; `page` and `size` echo what was used
- `total` is every matching row, **counted in the database**
- `totalPages` is `total / size` rounded **up** (25 rows in tens is 3 pages)
- defaults and 400s are exactly ex1's
- **two SQL commands at most** for the whole answer

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - a sort key is a vocabulary

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex3.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/sorted`
answers 200 with one page of cards ordered by `?sort=`, which must be one of
`D23Board.Sorts`: `postedDay`, `-postedDay`, `salaryMax`, `-salaryMax`, `title`.

- absent means `postedDay`; a leading minus reverses that column
- **every** order ends with `Id` ascending as the tiebreak - including the
  descending ones, where the tiebreak stays ascending
- a value outside the list is **400** keyed `"sort"`
- `?page=` and `?size=` behave exactly as in ex1

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - four optional filters, one query

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex4.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/filter`
answers 200 with every posting matching all of the filters given, id ascending.
Each is optional and an absent one narrows nothing:

- `?remote=` - `true` or `false`, matched against `Remote`
- `?location=` - matched against `Location` exactly, case sensitive
- `?minSalary=` - keeps postings whose `SalaryMax` is **at least** that
- `?tag=` - keeps postings whose `Tags` list has that tag as a **whole
  element**, so `?tag=sql` must not match the `nosql` postings

They are ANDed, never ORed. No matches is **200** with `[]`. The whole answer
costs **one SQL command**.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - the envelope navigates itself

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/linked`
answers 200 with a `LinkedPage`: ex2's envelope plus `next` and `prev`.

- each link is either `null` or exactly
  `/d23/postings/linked?page=N&size=S` - both parameters, in that order, with
  the size the client actually used
- `prev` is `null` on page 1; `next` is `null` on the last page
- a page past the end (page 4 of 3) is **200** with an empty `items`, the real
  `total` and `totalPages`, `next` null and `prev` pointing at the last page -
  not a 404
- `?page=0` is still **400** keyed `"page"`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - a cursor instead of an offset

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex6.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/keyset`
answers 200 with a `CursorPage` over `(PostedDay ascending, Id ascending)`.

- `?after=` is an opaque cursor built by `D23Cursor.Encode` / read by
  `D23Cursor.TryDecode`; it resumes **immediately after** the row it names, so
  a row sharing that `PostedDay` with a larger `Id` is still returned
- no `after` means start at the beginning
- `?size=` defaults to 10 and is **400** keyed `"size"` outside 1..50
- `nextCursor` is the key of the **last row on this page**, or `null` when
  nothing follows it
- **one SQL command** - including deciding whether there is a next page

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - filter, sort and cursor at the same time

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex7.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/feed` answers
200 with a `CursorPage`, combining everything above:

- `?remote=`, `?minSalary=` and `?tag=` filter exactly as in ex4, and are
  reapplied on every call - the cursor carries a position, not a result set
- `?sort=` is one of `D23Board.FeedSorts` (`postedDay`, `-postedDay`) and
  defaults to `postedDay`. Ascending orders by `PostedDay` then `Id` ascending;
  `-postedDay` orders by `PostedDay` **then `Id`** descending, and the cursor
  comparison flips with it
- `?after=` is a `D23Cursor`; one `TryDecode` cannot read is **400** keyed
  `"after"`, never a silent restart
- a `?sort=` outside the feed whitelist is **400** keyed `"sort"`
- `?size=` defaults to **5**, ceiling 50
- **one SQL command**, whatever combination was supplied

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - the whole search contract

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex8.cs`.
`GET /d23/postings/search?page=&size=&sort=&remote=&location=&minSalary=&tag=`:

- **400 collecting every bad parameter at once** in one validation problem:
  `page` below 1, `size` outside 1..50, `sort` outside `D23Board.Sorts`,
  `location` outside `D23Board.Locations`, `minSalary` below 0. Five mistakes
  produce five keys in one response, not five round trips
- otherwise 200 with a `LinkedPage`: ex4's filters, ex3's whitelist sort with
  the `Id` tiebreak (default `postedDay`), `total` and `totalPages` over the
  **filtered** rows, and `items` for the requested page
- `next` and `prev` follow ex5's rules but carry every supplied parameter
  forward, in exactly this order:
  `/d23/postings/search?page=N&size=S&sort=...&remote=...&location=...&minSalary=...&tag=...`
  - only the ones the client actually supplied appear, and `remote` is written
  lowercase `true`/`false`
- an empty result is 200 with `[]`, `total` 0, `totalPages` **0**, both links
  null
- **two SQL commands at most**

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/d23_pagination_filtering

## Notes

Paging is not "return fewer rows". It is a promise that a client walking the
whole collection sees every row exactly once, and the three things that break
that promise are the three things this set drills: an offset that is off by a
page, an order with no tiebreak, and a window that moves while the client is
walking it.

The pattern that unites all eight problems is that **the slice is decided in
the database**. `Skip`, `Take`, `Where`, `OrderBy` and `Count` on an
`IQueryable` are deferred - nothing runs until you enumerate - so composing
them costs one SQL statement and lets SQLite touch only the rows asked for. The
moment a `ToList()` sneaks in early, the same code reads the entire table and
throws most of it away, and the response body looks identical. That is why
several gates count commands: the body cannot tell you which version you wrote.

The other half of the set is the query string as a contract. `page`, `size`,
`sort`, `location` and a cursor are all values the client invented, and each of
them has a legal range. A parameter that is silently ignored, clamped, or
treated as "matches nothing" turns a client bug into a server that lies.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that the first page skips nothing. The offset is
`(page - 1) * size`, and every off-by-one page bug in the world is the moment
someone wrote `page * size` because `page` felt like an index.

The classic mistake is the other half - accepting `page` and `size` unchecked.
Clamping `page=0` up to 1 answers a question nobody asked; passing it straight
through computes a negative `OFFSET`. An unbounded `size` is worse: one client
sending `?size=1000000` turns a paged endpoint back into a full table scan, and
paging existed to prevent exactly that. The model answer validates the two
values against their ranges first and only then builds the query, so the range
check is a decision rather than an accident of arithmetic.

## ex2

What this was really testing: that `total` is a database question. A client
rendering "page 2 of 7" needs the count of the whole result set, and the page
it is holding cannot supply it.

The classic mistake is `db.Postings.ToList()` followed by `.Count` and
`.Skip().Take()` in memory - correct output, whole table read, and the command
counter is the only thing in the room that can see it. The second classic
mistake is `total / size`, which truncates: 25 rows in tens is 3 pages, not 2,
and the last two postings vanish from the UI. The model answer runs one
`CountAsync` and one windowed query over the same `IQueryable`, and computes
the ceiling with `(total + size - 1) / size` so no floating point is involved.

## ex3

What this was really testing: two independent ideas that always show up
together. First, a sort key is a vocabulary - `D23Board.Sorts` - not a column
name the client gets to pass through to your ORM. Second, a paged sort needs a
**total** order.

The tiebreak is the part people skip. Postings 1 and 14 both top out at 120000;
with only `ORDER BY SalaryMax` the database may return them in either order,
and it is free to choose differently for page 1 and page 2 - so a row appears
twice, or never. `ThenBy(x => x.Id)` costs nothing and makes the order total.
The classic mistake on the validation half is a `switch` with a `default` arm
that quietly serves the fallback order: `?sort=salray` then produces a
plausible, wrong report and no error anywhere. The model answer checks
membership first and answers 400 keyed `"sort"`.

## ex4

What this was really testing: composing optional predicates onto one
`IQueryable`. `if (remote is bool r) q = q.Where(...)` builds an expression
tree; nothing has executed yet, so four optional filters become four `AND`
clauses in a single `SELECT`.

The classic mistake is materialising first - `var all = await
db.Postings.ToListAsync();` and then LINQ-to-objects over the list. It passes
every correctness assertion and fails the command budget, which is the point:
the difference is invisible in the response and enormous in production.

The tag filter is the trap. `Tags.Contains("sql")` is a substring test, and
`nosql` contains `sql`, so `?tag=sql` quietly returns two postings that are not
tagged sql at all. Wrapping both sides in the delimiter -
`("," + x.Tags + ",").Contains("," + tag + ",")` - turns it into a whole
element test and still translates to `instr()`. The real lesson underneath is
that a comma separated column is a denormalised list, and every query against
one is a string trick.

## ex5

What this was really testing: that a paged response should tell the client how
to move, and that "out of range" and "out of bounds" are different failures.

`?page=0` is out of range: no such page can exist, the request is malformed,
400. `?page=4` of a three page result is out of bounds: the request is
perfectly well formed, the window simply lands past the end, and the honest
answer is 200 with an empty `items` and a `prev` link back. Answering 404 there
makes a client that over-scrolled look exactly like a client that asked for a
deleted resource.

The classic mistake in the links is hard coding `size=10` into them, so the
first click silently resets the page size the client chose. The model answer
builds both links from the *effective* page and size, and returns `null` rather
than a link whenever there is nothing on that side - because a `next` that
always exists walks a client off the end forever.

## ex6

What this was really testing: keyset pagination, and why an offset is not a
position. `OFFSET 10` means "skip ten rows of whatever this query returns
now". Insert a row that sorts earlier and every later row shifts down one, so
the client's next page repeats a row it already showed; delete one and a row is
skipped entirely. A cursor names a **place in the order** - here the pair
`(PostedDay, Id)` - and rows inserted elsewhere cannot move it.

The classic mistake is comparing only the first column: `WHERE PostedDay > 12`
after a cursor at `(12, 1)` drops posting 4, which also sits on day 12, and it
is gone from the feed forever with no error. The comparison has to be the whole
key: `PostedDay > d OR (PostedDay = d AND Id > id)`.

The model answer's other move is asking for `size + 1` rows. The existence of
that extra row is the answer to "is there a next page", so `nextCursor` is
`null` on the last page without a second `COUNT` - one query for the page and
its own terminator.

## ex7

What this was really testing: that the three slicing mechanisms are all just
operators on the same deferred query, and that a cursor is bound to the order
it was cut for.

Two details do the teaching. The cursor comparison must follow the direction of
travel: descending, "after" means `PostedDay < d OR (PostedDay = d AND Id <
id)`, and keeping `>` hands the client back the rows it has already seen, which
is an infinite loop rather than a wrong answer. And the filters must be
reapplied on every call, because the cursor carries a position and not a result
set - a feed that only honours `?remote=true` on the first page starts leaking
non-remote postings from page 2 onwards.

The classic mistake at the edges is treating an unreadable cursor as "no
cursor". That restarts the feed at the top, so the client loops over page 1
forever and nothing ever reports an error. `TryDecode` returning false is a 400
keyed `"after"`. Refusing `?sort=title` is the same instinct: a cursor over
`(PostedDay, Id)` cannot resume a title ordering, so the endpoint says so
instead of producing nonsense.

## ex8

What this was really testing: everything above on one endpoint, plus one new
idea - validation is a report, not a tripwire. Returning on the first bad
parameter makes a client with five mistakes fix one, resubmit, fail, and repeat
five times. Collecting into a dictionary and answering once tells it everything
in a single round trip, and RFC 9457's `errors` object exists precisely to
carry that shape.

The subtle one is the links. `next` has to carry the filters and the sort
forward, because `/d23/postings/search?page=2` without them is page 2 of a
completely different result set - the client clicks "next" and lands in
unfiltered data with no error anywhere. The model answer rebuilds the whole
query string from what was supplied, in a fixed order, which also means an
absent parameter stays absent instead of being materialised as a default the
client never chose. `remote` is written `true`/`false` by hand because
`bool.ToString()` produces `True`, and the wire has no capital letters in it.

The two remaining literals are stated in the README rather than left to taste:
`total` counts the filtered rows, and an empty result has `totalPages` 0, not
1. Gates compare literally, and "obvious" is where two reasonable people
disagree.

## Further reading

- [Efficient querying (EF Core)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) - buffering versus streaming, projections, and the pagination section on why offsets get slower as they get deeper.
- [Pagination (EF Core)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/pagination) - `Skip`/`Take`, the ordering requirement, and keyset pagination written out in full.
- [Client vs server evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/client-eval) - what happens when a predicate cannot be translated, and why it is worth knowing before the command counter tells you.
- [Parameter binding in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding) - optional query parameters, nullable value types, and binding failures.
