# Reading - dotnet/d23_pagination_filtering

## Notes

Paging is not "return fewer rows". It is a promise that a client walking the
whole collection sees every row exactly once, and the three things that break
that promise are the three things this set drills: an offset that is off by a
page, an order with no tiebreak, and a window that moves while the client is
walking it.

The pattern that unites all eight problems is that **the slice is decided in
the database**. `Skip`, `Take`, `Where`, `OrderBy` and `Count` on an
`IQueryable` are deferred - nothing runs until you enumerate - so composing
them costs one SQL statement and lets SQLite touch only the rows asked for. The
moment a `ToList()` sneaks in early, the same code reads the entire table and
throws most of it away, and the response body looks identical. That is why
several gates count commands: the body cannot tell you which version you wrote.

The other half of the set is the query string as a contract. `page`, `size`,
`sort`, `location` and a cursor are all values the client invented, and each of
them has a legal range. A parameter that is silently ignored, clamped, or
treated as "matches nothing" turns a client bug into a server that lies.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that the first page skips nothing. The offset is
`(page - 1) * size`, and every off-by-one page bug in the world is the moment
someone wrote `page * size` because `page` felt like an index.

The classic mistake is the other half - accepting `page` and `size` unchecked.
Clamping `page=0` up to 1 answers a question nobody asked; passing it straight
through computes a negative `OFFSET`. An unbounded `size` is worse: one client
sending `?size=1000000` turns a paged endpoint back into a full table scan, and
paging existed to prevent exactly that. The model answer validates the two
values against their ranges first and only then builds the query, so the range
check is a decision rather than an accident of arithmetic.

## ex2

What this was really testing: that `total` is a database question. A client
rendering "page 2 of 7" needs the count of the whole result set, and the page
it is holding cannot supply it.

The classic mistake is `db.Postings.ToList()` followed by `.Count` and
`.Skip().Take()` in memory - correct output, whole table read, and the command
counter is the only thing in the room that can see it. The second classic
mistake is `total / size`, which truncates: 25 rows in tens is 3 pages, not 2,
and the last two postings vanish from the UI. The model answer runs one
`CountAsync` and one windowed query over the same `IQueryable`, and computes
the ceiling with `(total + size - 1) / size` so no floating point is involved.

## ex3

What this was really testing: two independent ideas that always show up
together. First, a sort key is a vocabulary - `D23Board.Sorts` - not a column
name the client gets to pass through to your ORM. Second, a paged sort needs a
**total** order.

The tiebreak is the part people skip. Postings 1 and 14 both top out at 120000;
with only `ORDER BY SalaryMax` the database may return them in either order,
and it is free to choose differently for page 1 and page 2 - so a row appears
twice, or never. `ThenBy(x => x.Id)` costs nothing and makes the order total.
The classic mistake on the validation half is a `switch` with a `default` arm
that quietly serves the fallback order: `?sort=salray` then produces a
plausible, wrong report and no error anywhere. The model answer checks
membership first and answers 400 keyed `"sort"`.

## ex4

What this was really testing: composing optional predicates onto one
`IQueryable`. `if (remote is bool r) q = q.Where(...)` builds an expression
tree; nothing has executed yet, so four optional filters become four `AND`
clauses in a single `SELECT`.

The classic mistake is materialising first - `var all = await
db.Postings.ToListAsync();` and then LINQ-to-objects over the list. It passes
every correctness assertion and fails the command budget, which is the point:
the difference is invisible in the response and enormous in production.

The tag filter is the trap. `Tags.Contains("sql")` is a substring test, and
`nosql` contains `sql`, so `?tag=sql` quietly returns two postings that are not
tagged sql at all. Wrapping both sides in the delimiter -
`("," + x.Tags + ",").Contains("," + tag + ",")` - turns it into a whole
element test and still translates to `instr()`. The real lesson underneath is
that a comma separated column is a denormalised list, and every query against
one is a string trick.

## ex5

What this was really testing: that a paged response should tell the client how
to move, and that "out of range" and "out of bounds" are different failures.

`?page=0` is out of range: no such page can exist, the request is malformed,
400. `?page=4` of a three page result is out of bounds: the request is
perfectly well formed, the window simply lands past the end, and the honest
answer is 200 with an empty `items` and a `prev` link back. Answering 404 there
makes a client that over-scrolled look exactly like a client that asked for a
deleted resource.

The classic mistake in the links is hard coding `size=10` into them, so the
first click silently resets the page size the client chose. The model answer
builds both links from the *effective* page and size, and returns `null` rather
than a link whenever there is nothing on that side - because a `next` that
always exists walks a client off the end forever.

## ex6

What this was really testing: keyset pagination, and why an offset is not a
position. `OFFSET 10` means "skip ten rows of whatever this query returns
now". Insert a row that sorts earlier and every later row shifts down one, so
the client's next page repeats a row it already showed; delete one and a row is
skipped entirely. A cursor names a **place in the order** - here the pair
`(PostedDay, Id)` - and rows inserted elsewhere cannot move it.

The classic mistake is comparing only the first column: `WHERE PostedDay > 12`
after a cursor at `(12, 1)` drops posting 4, which also sits on day 12, and it
is gone from the feed forever with no error. The comparison has to be the whole
key: `PostedDay > d OR (PostedDay = d AND Id > id)`.

The model answer's other move is asking for `size + 1` rows. The existence of
that extra row is the answer to "is there a next page", so `nextCursor` is
`null` on the last page without a second `COUNT` - one query for the page and
its own terminator.

## ex7

What this was really testing: that the three slicing mechanisms are all just
operators on the same deferred query, and that a cursor is bound to the order
it was cut for.

Two details do the teaching. The cursor comparison must follow the direction of
travel: descending, "after" means `PostedDay < d OR (PostedDay = d AND Id <
id)`, and keeping `>` hands the client back the rows it has already seen, which
is an infinite loop rather than a wrong answer. And the filters must be
reapplied on every call, because the cursor carries a position and not a result
set - a feed that only honours `?remote=true` on the first page starts leaking
non-remote postings from page 2 onwards.

The classic mistake at the edges is treating an unreadable cursor as "no
cursor". That restarts the feed at the top, so the client loops over page 1
forever and nothing ever reports an error. `TryDecode` returning false is a 400
keyed `"after"`. Refusing `?sort=title` is the same instinct: a cursor over
`(PostedDay, Id)` cannot resume a title ordering, so the endpoint says so
instead of producing nonsense.

## ex8

What this was really testing: everything above on one endpoint, plus one new
idea - validation is a report, not a tripwire. Returning on the first bad
parameter makes a client with five mistakes fix one, resubmit, fail, and repeat
five times. Collecting into a dictionary and answering once tells it everything
in a single round trip, and RFC 9457's `errors` object exists precisely to
carry that shape.

The subtle one is the links. `next` has to carry the filters and the sort
forward, because `/d23/postings/search?page=2` without them is page 2 of a
completely different result set - the client clicks "next" and lands in
unfiltered data with no error anywhere. The model answer rebuilds the whole
query string from what was supplied, in a fixed order, which also means an
absent parameter stays absent instead of being materialised as a default the
client never chose. `remote` is written `true`/`false` by hand because
`bool.ToString()` produces `True`, and the wire has no capital letters in it.

The two remaining literals are stated in the README rather than left to taste:
`total` counts the filtered rows, and an empty result has `totalPages` 0, not
1. Gates compare literally, and "obvious" is where two reasonable people
disagree.

## Further reading

- [Efficient querying (EF Core)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) - buffering versus streaming, projections, and the pagination section on why offsets get slower as they get deeper.
- [Pagination (EF Core)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/pagination) - `Skip`/`Take`, the ordering requirement, and keyset pagination written out in full.
- [Client vs server evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/client-eval) - what happens when a predicate cannot be translated, and why it is worth knowing before the command counter tells you.
- [Parameter binding in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding) - optional query parameters, nullable value types, and binding failures.
- [Handle errors in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/handle-errors) - `TypedResults.ValidationProblem` and the shape of the `errors` dictionary.
- [RFC 9457 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457) - the media type every 400 in this set is speaking.
- [RFC 8288 - Web Linking](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8288) - `next` and `prev` as relation types, and what a `Link` header would look like.

## Exercise 1 - the first page skips nothing

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex1.cs`. `GET /d23/postings` answers 200
with one page of `PostingCard`s, **id ascending**.

- `?page=` defaults to 1, `?size=` defaults to 10
- `page` below 1 is **400** as a validation problem keyed `"page"`
- `size` outside 1..`D23Board.MaxSize` (50) is **400** keyed `"size"`

The shipped version skips `page * size` rows, so nobody ever sees posting 1.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex1
```

page N skip? Page 1 is the *first* page, so the answer for it is zero. The
other is a vocabulary check of the kind you already did for `?status=` in d15 -
`page` and `size` are values the client invented and each has a legal range.

Bind the defaults with `??` first, then range check the values you ended up
with, then build the query. `Skip` takes the number of rows to skip, not the
page number, and the ceiling for `size` is `D23Board.MaxSize`.

[...] })` is the 400 - the dictionary key is what tells the client *which*

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two separate jobs live in this handler. One is arithmetic: how many rows does
page N skip? Page 1 is the *first* page, so the answer for it is zero. The
other is a vocabulary check of the kind you already did for `?status=` in d15 -
`page` and `size` are values the client invented and each has a legal range.

## Hint 2

Bind the defaults with `??` first, then range check the values you ended up
with, then build the query. `Skip` takes the number of rows to skip, not the
page number, and the ceiling for `size` is `D23Board.MaxSize`.

`TypedResults.ValidationProblem(new Dictionary<string, string[]> { ["page"] =
[...] })` is the 400 - the dictionary key is what tells the client *which*
parameter it got wrong.

And `OrderBy` is not decoration: `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` over an unordered set is
undefined, so the ordering has to be in the query, not in the seed.

## Exercise 2 - an envelope with a real total

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex2.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/page` answers
200 with a `PostingPage`: `items`, `page`, `size`, `total`, `totalPages`.

- `items` is the page itself, id ascending; `page` and `size` echo what was used
- `total` is every matching row, **counted in the database**
- `totalPages` is `total / size` rounded **up** (25 rows in tens is 3 pages)

- **two SQL commands at most** for the whole answer

uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex2

## Hint 1

`total` is a question about the whole result set, and the ten rows you are
about to return cannot answer it. It is a second, separate database call -

`await db.Postings.CountAsync()` translates to `SELECT COUNT(*)`: one row comes
back, not twenty-five. Then the page itself, exactly as in ex1.

`totalPages` is a ceiling division. `total / size` truncates and loses the
short last page; `(total + size - 1) / size` rounds up using only integers.

## Exercise 4 - four optional filters, one query

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex4.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/filter`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An `IQueryable` is a description of a query, not a result. Nothing runs until
you enumerate it, so you can keep adding `Where` clauses in ordinary `if`
statements and still pay for exactly one `SELECT` at the end. That is what the
one-command budget is checking.

The tag filter is a different problem: `Tags` is a comma separated list, and a
tag is one whole element of it, not any run of letters inside it.

## Hint 2

Declare the query once and reassign it:

    IQueryable<Posting> q = db.Postings;
    if (remote is bool wantRemote) q = q.Where(x => x.Remote == wantRemote);

Pattern-matching the nullable into a plain local keeps the expression tree free
of `Nullable<T>.Value`.

For the tag, put the delimiter on both sides so the match has to land on
element boundaries: search `"," + x.Tags + ","` for `"," + tag + ","`. Compute
the needle into a local first. It still translates - it becomes `instr()` over
a concatenation, not client evaluation.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

An `IQueryable` is a description of a query, not a result. Nothing runs until
you enumerate it, so you can keep adding `Where` clauses in ordinary `if`
statements and still pay for exactly one `SELECT` at the end. That is what the
one-command budget is checking.

The tag filter is a different problem: `Tags` is a comma separated list, and a
tag is one whole element of it, not any run of letters inside it.

## Hint 2

Declare the query once and reassign it:

    IQueryable<Posting> q = db.Postings;
    if (remote is bool wantRemote) q = q.Where(x => x.Remote == wantRemote);

Pattern-matching the nullable into a plain local keeps the expression tree free
of `Nullable<T>.Value`.

For the tag, put the delimiter on both sides so the match has to land on
element boundaries: search `"," + x.Tags + ","` for `"," + tag + ","`. Compute
the needle into a local first. It still translates - it becomes `instr()` over
a concatenation, not client evaluation.

## Exercise 5 - the envelope navigates itself

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex5.cs`. `GET /d23/postings/linked`
answers 200 with a `LinkedPage`: ex2's envelope plus `next` and `prev`.

- each link is either `null` or exactly
  `/d23/postings/linked?page=N&size=S` - both parameters, in that order, with
  the size the client actually used
- `prev` is `null` on page 1; `next` is `null` on the last page
- a page past the end (page 4 of 3) is **200** with an empty `items`, the real
  `total` and `totalPages`, `next` null and `prev` pointing at the last page -
  not a 404
- `?page=0` is still **400** keyed `"page"`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two different things can be wrong with a page number, and only one of them is
the client's fault. `page=0` is out of *range* - no such page can exist, so
400. `page=4` of a three page result is out of *bounds* - a perfectly legal
request whose window happens to land past the end, so 200 with nothing in it.

## Hint 2

Build the envelope exactly as in ex2, then add the two links last, from the
effective `page` and `size`:

- `prev` when `page > 1`, pointing at `page - 1`
- `next` when `page < totalPages`, pointing at `page + 1`
- `null` otherwise, and `null` means `null`, not `""`

Those two conditions already give you the right answers for page 4 of 3 -
`4 < 3` is false, so `next` is null, and `4 > 1` is true, so `prev` still
exists. Interpolate the size the caller used into both links; a literal
`size=10` resets the page size on the first click.

## Hint 1

Two different things can be wrong with a page number, and only one of them is
the client's fault. `page=0` is out of *range* - no such page can exist, so
400. `page=4` of a three page result is out of *bounds* - a perfectly legal
request whose window happens to land past the end, so 200 with nothing in it.

## Hint 2

Build the envelope exactly as in ex2, then add the two links last, from the
effective `page` and `size`:

- `prev` when `page > 1`, pointing at `page - 1`
- `next` when `page < totalPages`, pointing at `page + 1`
- `null` otherwise, and `null` means `null`, not `""`

Those two conditions already give you the right answers for page 4 of 3 -
`4 < 3` is false, so `next` is null, and `4 > 1` is true, so `prev` still
exists. Interpolate the size the caller used into both links; a literal
`size=10` resets the page size on the first click.

## Hint 1

Nothing here is new: it is ex4's filters, ex3's whitelist and ex6's cursor on
one `IQueryable`. Because all three are deferred operators, stacking them costs
one `SELECT`, and that is what the budget is checking.

Decide `descending` from the sort key once, then use it twice - for the cursor
comparison and for the ordering - so the two can never disagree:

    q = descending
        ? q.Where(x => x.PostedDay < day || (x.PostedDay == day && x.Id < id))
        : q.Where(x => x.PostedDay > day || (x.PostedDay == day && x.Id > id));

The filters have to be applied on *every* call - the cursor is a position in
the ordering, not a handle on a stored result set.

## Hint 3

The two 400s are about refusing to guess. A cursor `D23Cursor.TryDecode` cannot
read is keyed `"after"`; treating it as "no cursor" restarts the feed and the
client loops over page 1 forever with no error to report.

A `?sort=` outside `D23Board.FeedSorts` is keyed `"sort"`. `title` is a legal
key in ex3 and not here, because a cursor over `(PostedDay, Id)` cannot resume
an ordering by title - check `FeedSorts`, not `Sorts`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Nothing here is new: it is ex4's filters, ex3's whitelist and ex6's cursor on
one `IQueryable`. Because all three are deferred operators, stacking them costs
one `SELECT`, and that is what the budget is checking.

The one genuinely new idea is that a cursor has a *direction*.

## Hint 2

Decide `descending` from the sort key once, then use it twice - for the cursor
comparison and for the ordering - so the two can never disagree:

    q = descending
        ? q.Where(x => x.PostedDay < day || (x.PostedDay == day && x.Id < id))
        : q.Where(x => x.PostedDay > day || (x.PostedDay == day && x.Id > id));

Apply the filters before the cursor clause, order last, then `Take(size + 1)`.
The filters have to be applied on *every* call - the cursor is a position in
the ordering, not a handle on a stored result set.

## Hint 3

The two 400s are about refusing to guess. A cursor `D23Cursor.TryDecode` cannot
read is keyed `"after"`; treating it as "no cursor" restarts the feed and the
client loops over page 1 forever with no error to report.

A `?sort=` outside `D23Board.FeedSorts` is keyed `"sort"`. `title` is a legal
key in ex3 and not here, because a cursor over `(PostedDay, Id)` cannot resume
an ordering by title - check `FeedSorts`, not `Sorts`.

## Exercise 8 - the whole search contract

Edit `src/Api/D23_PaginationFiltering/Ex8.cs`.
`GET /d23/postings/search?page=&size=&sort=&remote=&location=&minSalary=&tag=`:

- **400 collecting every bad parameter at once** in one validation problem:
  `page` below 1, `size` outside 1..50, `sort` outside `D23Board.Sorts`,
  `location` outside `D23Board.Locations`, `minSalary` below 0. Five mistakes
  produce five keys in one response, not five round trips
- otherwise 200 with a `LinkedPage`: ex4's filters, ex3's whitelist sort with
  the `Id` tiebreak (default `postedDay`), `total` and `totalPages` over the
  **filtered** rows, and `items` for the requested page
- `next` and `prev` follow ex5's rules but carry every supplied parameter
  forward, in exactly this order:
  `/d23/postings/search?page=N&size=S&sort=...&remote=...&location=...&minSalary=...&tag=...`
  - only the ones the client actually supplied appear, and `remote` is written
  lowercase `true`/`false`
- an empty result is 200 with `[]`, `total` 0, `totalPages` **0**, both links
  null
- **two SQL commands at most**

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d23_pagination_filtering ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three phases, in order: validate everything, build one filtered query, then
answer from it. The new idea is only in the first phase - validation here is a
*report*, not a tripwire. A request with five mistakes should learn about all
five at once.

## Hint 2

Collect into a dictionary instead of returning early:

    var errors = new Dictionary<string, string[]>();
    if (p < 1) errors["page"] = [...];
    ...
    if (errors.Count > 0) return TypedResults.ValidationProblem(errors);

Note which checks are conditional: `location` is only wrong if it was supplied
*and* is outside `D23Board.Locations`, and an absent `minSalary` is not a
negative one.

Then compose the ex4 filters onto one `IQueryable`, `CountAsync` it, apply the
ex3 ordering, and page it - two commands, both over the same filtered query, so
`total` describes the rows the page came out of.

## Hint 3

The links are where this exercise is actually won. A `next` that is only
`?page=2&size=10` points at page 2 of a *different* result set, and the client
lands in unfiltered data with nothing reporting an error.

Write one local function that rebuilds the whole query string for a target page
in the README's order - page, size, sort, remote, location, minSalary, tag -
appending each optional parameter only when the client supplied it. Two details
the gate compares literally: `bool.ToString()` gives `True`, so write
`remote ? "true" : "false"` yourself, and an empty result has `totalPages` 0,
which makes both links null through the same `page < totalPages` test you used
in ex5.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three phases, in order: validate everything, build one filtered query, then
answer from it. The new idea is only in the first phase - validation here is a
*report*, not a tripwire. A request with five mistakes should learn about all
five at once.

## Hint 2

Collect into a dictionary instead of returning early:

    var errors = new Dictionary<string, string[]>();
    if (p < 1) errors["page"] = [...];
    ...
    if (errors.Count > 0) return TypedResults.ValidationProblem(errors);

Note which checks are conditional: `location` is only wrong if it was supplied
*and* is outside `D23Board.Locations`, and an absent `minSalary` is not a
negative one.

Then compose the ex4 filters onto one `IQueryable`, `CountAsync` it, apply the
ex3 ordering, and page it - two commands, both over the same filtered query, so
`total` describes the rows the page came out of.

## Hint 3

The links are where this exercise is actually won. A `next` that is only
`?page=2&size=10` points at page 2 of a *different* result set, and the client
lands in unfiltered data with nothing reporting an error.

Write one local function that rebuilds the whole query string for a target page
in the README's order - page, size, sort, remote, location, minSalary, tag -
appending each optional parameter only when the client supplied it. Two details
the gate compares literally: `bool.ToString()` gives `True`, so write
`remote ? "true" : "false"` yourself, and an empty result has `totalPages` 0,
which makes both links null through the same `page < totalPages` test you used
in ex5.

lessons.briefing:
# d24 - the mixed gauntlet

This set is cumulative: nothing here is a new topic, and every exercise fuses
two or three things the track already taught - routing and results (**d01**,
**d03**), DI lifetimes (**d04**), configuration and options (**d08**, **d09**),
EF Core queries and projections (**d11**, **d14**), REST reads and writes
(**d15**, **d16**), validation and problem details (**d17**, **d18**), logging
(**d19**) and JWT authorization (**d20**, **d21**). If a problem here feels
like guessing, the lesson it draws on is named in its subsection - go back to
that one first.

The domain is a museum (`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Model.cs`): three exhibits
with a fixed `Capacity`, and tickets held against them by `ada`, `bo` and `cy`.
One rule runs through every capacity question in the set:

```
seats left = Capacity - (tickets on that exhibit where Cancelled is false)
```

A cancelled ticket is still a row and no longer holds a seat. The gates seed
Bronze Age (north, capacity 3), Cartography (north, capacity 0) and Deep Time
(south, capacity 5), with four tickets - so exhibit 1 has one seat left,
exhibit 2 has none, and exhibit 3 has four. Everything is under `/d24/...`,
authentication is the named scheme `d24-bearer`, and the two policies are
`D24Policies.Visitor` and `D24Policies.Curator`.

## Exercise 1 - routing plus results

Routing (**d01**) fused with results (**d03**). Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex1.cs`. One catch-all route is doing two jobs and
parsing its way through them. Split it:

- `GET /d24/exhibits/open` - 200 with the `ExhibitDto`s whose `Capacity` is
  above zero, **Name A-Z**
- `GET /d24/exhibits/{id:int}` - 200 with that `ExhibitDto`, 404 when there is
  no such exhibit
- `GET /d24/exhibits/abc` - **404 from routing**, before any handler of yours
  runs

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```

## Exercise 2 - DI lifetimes through one endpoint

Lifetimes (**d04**) fused with a single request. Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex2.cs`, `Ex2Services` only - the handler is given.
`GET /d24/visits` asks the container for `ID24Visit` twice in one request and
reports the turnstile's next number:

- `perRequest` is the **same** id for both injections in one request, and a
  **different** id on the next request
- `total` counts every request the process has ever seen: 1, then 2

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex2
```

## Exercise 3 - options plus validation

Options (**d09**) fused with validation (**d17**). Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex3.cs`. `POST /d24/reservations` takes a
`NewReservation`:

- blank `holder` and a `count` outside 1..max - **400** validation problem
  carrying **both** keys, `type` `D24Problems.Base + "invalid-request"`
- the maximum comes from `IOptions<D24Options>.Value.MaxTicketsPerVisitor`, not
  from a constant - nothing configures it here, so the class default of 4
  holds, and the gate boots a second host that sets
  `Dojo:D24:MaxTicketsPerVisitor` to 2
- unknown exhibit - 404
- otherwise 200 with `HeldDto`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex3
```

## Exercise 4 - projection plus a query budget

EF Core grouping (**d11**) fused with projection (**d14**). Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex4.cs`. `GET /d24/galleries` returns one
`GalleryRow` per gallery, **gallery name A-Z**, where `sold` counts the
**non-cancelled** tickets on that gallery's exhibits - and it must cost **at
most two** database round trips. The gate counts them.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex4
```

## Exercise 5 - a REST write that refuses in problem details

REST writes (**d16**) fused with problem details (**d18**). Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex5.cs`. `POST /d24/exhibits/{id:int}/tickets` takes
a `NewTicket`:

- unknown exhibit - **404** as problem details, `type`
  `D24Problems.Base + "exhibit-not-found"`, a `detail` naming the id, and
  `instance`
- no seats left - **409** as problem details, `type`
  `D24Problems.Base + "sold-out"`, with the extension member **`seatsLeft`**
- otherwise **201**, `Location: /d24/tickets/{newId}`, and the `TicketDto` that
  was really saved

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex5
```

## Exercise 6 - authorization plus structured logging

Authorization (**d20**) fused with logging (**d19**). Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex6.cs`. `GET /d24/tickets` is behind
`D24Policies.Visitor`:

- 200 with the caller's **own** tickets as `TicketDto`s, id ascending - or
  **every** ticket when the caller is in the `curator` role
- exactly **one** `Information` entry per request, written with a message
  template so it carries `Holder` and `Count` as **named properties**

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex6
```

## Exercise 7 - authorization, EF Core, problem details, logging

Four at once: ownership (**d20**), EF Core writes (**d10**), problem details
(**d18**) and log levels (**d19**). Edit `src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex7.cs`.
`POST /d24/tickets/{id:int}/cancel` is behind `D24Policies.Visitor`:

1. no such ticket, **or** somebody else's and the caller is not a curator -
   **404**, and the two must be indistinguishable
2. already cancelled - **409** problem details, `type`
   `D24Problems.Base + "already-cancelled"`
3. otherwise **204**, with `Cancelled` actually written

Exactly one log entry per request: `Information` for the 404 and for the
success, **`Warning`** for the 409, and nothing at `Error`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex7
```

## Exercise 8 - everything this track teaches, on one write

Policy authorization (**d21**), options (**d09**), collected validation
(**d17**), EF Core (**d10**), problem details (**d18**) and logging (**d19**),
in one handler. Edit `src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex8.cs`.
`POST /d24/bookings` is behind `D24Policies.Curator`, so 401 without a token
and 403 without the role. Then, in this order:

1. **400** collecting `exhibitId`, `holder` and `count` **together**, `type`
   `D24Problems.Base + "invalid-request"` - the count limit is the one from
   `IOptions<D24Options>`
2. unknown exhibit - **404**
3. fewer seats left than asked for - **409** problem details with `seatsLeft`,
   and nothing written
4. otherwise **201**, `Location: /d24/bookings/{firstTicketId}`, a
   `BookingDto` listing the new ticket ids ascending, the holder trimmed, day
   1, and all of it in **one** `SaveChangesAsync`

Exactly one log entry per request, carrying `TraceId` and `Count`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex8
```

# Reading - dotnet/d24_mixed_gauntlet

## Notes

This is the gauntlet, so there is no new idea in it. What is new is the
*combination*: real handlers do not practise one topic at a time, and the
mistakes that survive code review are almost always the seam between two of
them - a route that validates, a filter that runs after the query instead of
inside it, a limit that is a constant instead of a setting, a log line that
reads well and cannot be queried.

Three habits carry all eight problems.

**Push the decision as far out as it will go.** Routing can answer "that is not
an id" without a handler. A policy can answer "not a curator" without a
database. A query can answer "not yours" without loading a row. Every decision
made one layer too late is a decision that can be forgotten one refactor later.

**Say the same thing to the machine and to the human.** Problem details do this
with `type` (what a client branches on) and `detail` (what a person reads);
structured logging does it with a message template, which produces the sentence
and the named fields from one line of code. Both fail the same way: an
interpolated string, or a status code with no stable identity behind it.

**Refusals are a design surface.** 400 means the payload is wrong, 404 means
there is nothing there *or* nothing you may know about, 409 means the payload
is fine and the world says no. The difference between 403 and 404 is the
difference between confirming a resource exists and refusing to.

## ex1

What this was really testing: that routing is a matching stage with its own
answers, not a prelude to parsing. A literal segment outranks a parameter
segment regardless of the order they were registered in, and a route constraint
like `:int` removes non-matching requests from consideration entirely.

The classic mistake is the shipped stub: one `{id}` route, `int.TryParse` at the
top of the handler, and a 400 for `abc`. That 400 is a lie - the caller did not
send a malformed exhibit id, they asked for a URL that does not exist - and the
same shape swallows `/open` as an id too.

The model answer registers two routes and lets the router choose, so each
handler receives exactly the shape it declared and can spend its whole body on
the one thing it is for.

## ex2

What this was really testing: that a lifetime is a claim about a boundary, and
that transient has no boundary at all. `ID24Visit` must be the same object
everywhere inside one request and a new object in the next; `ID24Turnstile` must
outlive every request the process handles.

The classic mistake is registering both as transient because it "works" -
nothing throws, the endpoint returns 200, and the two bugs only show up as a
per-request id that changes inside the request and a counter that is always 1.

The model answer is two words: `AddScoped` for the thing whose boundary is the
request, `AddSingleton` for the thing that must survive it - and the reverse
mistake, a scoped counter or a singleton holding request state, is the one that
leaks one user's data into another user's response.

## ex3

What this was really testing: two habits that always travel together - a limit
that lives in configuration, and validation that reports every failure at once.
`IOptions<D24Options>` resolves whether or not anything bound to it, so the
class default is the value in force until an operator sets the key.

The classic mistake is the hard-coded `4`. It passes every test written against
the default, and the day somebody sets `Dojo:D24:MaxTicketsPerVisitor` nothing
changes and nobody can see why. The second mistake is returning on the first
failure, which turns one bad payload into a sequence of round trips.

The model answer reads the limit once into a local, collects failures into a
dictionary, and returns a `ValidationProblem` only when that dictionary is
non-empty - so a well-formed payload against a missing exhibit can be the 404 it
really is.

## ex4

What this was really testing: whether the shape of the answer is being computed
by the database or by a `foreach`. The response body is identical either way,
which is precisely why an N+1 loop survives review; the cost only appears in the
query count and it grows with the data.

The classic mistake has two halves, and the stub commits both: one query per
exhibit, and counting *every* ticket as sold because the `Cancelled` filter was
never written into the query.

The model answer groups in the database twice - exhibits by gallery, live
tickets by their exhibit's gallery - and joins the two small results in memory,
which is a fixed two round trips no matter how many exhibits exist.

## ex5

What this was really testing: that a write has three outcomes and each one owes
the caller a different, machine-readable answer. 201 says a new thing exists and
`Location` says where; 404 and 409 are both refusals and they mean different
things.

The classic mistake is answering 400 for a full exhibit. Nothing the client sent
is malformed - the request was valid and the world changed - and a client that
retries on 409 but gives up on 400 will do the wrong thing. The other classic is
a bare `NotFound()` with no body, which tells an automated caller nothing.

The model answer counts only non-cancelled tickets, returns `seatsLeft` as an
extension member so the client does not have to ask again, and saves before
building the `TicketDto` so the id in the body is the id in the database.

## ex6

What this was really testing: that the token is the only trustworthy answer to
"who is asking", and that a log line is data rather than prose. The scheme sets
`NameClaimType` to `sub`, so `user.Identity.Name` *is* the token subject.

The classic mistake is the pair in the stub: a query with no `Where` (so every
caller reads every ticket) and `logger.LogInformation($"...")`, which renders
the string before the logger ever sees it and produces an entry with no named
properties at all.

The model answer puts `curator || t.Holder == holder` inside the query, so the
rows that are not yours never travel, and logs with a template so `Count` and
`Holder` are indexable fields as well as a readable sentence.

## ex7

What this was really testing: that a refusal can leak. If "somebody else's
ticket" answers 403 and "no such ticket" answers 404, the difference between the
two is an oracle, and an attacker can walk the id space and map the database
using nothing else.

The classic mistake is writing the two checks as two branches with two answers,
which feels more honest and is exactly the leak. The second is treating the log
level as a function of the status code - both the 404 and the 409 are refusals,
and only one of them is worth anybody's attention.

The model answer collapses "missing" and "not yours" into one `if` with one
`NotFound()`, logs it at `Information` because a caller asking for the wrong
ticket is a Tuesday, and reserves `Warning` for the already-cancelled conflict,
which is somebody repeating work that was already done.

## ex8

What this was really testing: ordering. Every check in this handler is cheap or
expensive, and safe or unsafe to reveal, and the order they run in is the whole
design - policy first (no database touched), then payload validation (no
database touched), then existence, then capacity, then the write.

The classic mistakes are all seams: saving inside the loop, so a half-written
booking becomes a possible state with no request that can finish it; checking
capacity before validating the payload, so a garbage `count` reaches the
database; and logging without the trace identifier, which leaves a pile of
sentences nobody can join to the request a support ticket is about.

The model answer builds every `Ticket` in memory, calls `SaveChangesAsync`
exactly once so the booking is all-or-nothing, reads the ids back after the save
because the database assigns them, and emits one entry carrying `Count` and
`TraceId`.

## Further reading

- [Routing in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/routing) - literal against parameter segments, route constraints, and precedence.
- [Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/dependency-injection) - transient, scoped and singleton, and the captive dependency trap.
- [Options pattern in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options) - `IOptions<T>`, binding a section, and defaults that survive.
- [Efficient querying in EF Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) - projections, grouping, and how N+1 happens.
- [Handle errors in ASP.NET Core APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/handle-errors) - problem details, extension members, and `type`.
- [Logging in .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/logging) - message templates, named properties, and choosing a level.
- [Policy-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/policies) - requirements, roles, and 401 against 403.
- [RFC 9457 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457) - the members, and what `type` is for.

tickets by their exhibit's gallery - and joins the two small results in memory,
which is a fixed two round trips no matter how many exhibits exist.

## ex5

What this was really testing: that a write has three outcomes and each one owes
the caller a different, machine-readable answer. 201 says a new thing exists and
`Location` says where; 404 and 409 are both refusals and they mean different
things.

The classic mistake is answering 400 for a full exhibit. Nothing the client sent
is malformed - the request was valid and the world changed - and a client that
retries on 409 but gives up on 400 will do the wrong thing. The other classic is
a bare `NotFound()` with no body, which tells an automated caller nothing.

The model answer counts only non-cancelled tickets, returns `seatsLeft` as an
extension member so the client does not have to ask again, and saves before
building the `TicketDto` so the id in the body is the id in the database.

## ex6

What this was really testing: that the token is the only trustworthy answer to
"who is asking", and that a log line is data rather than prose. The scheme sets
`NameClaimType` to `sub`, so `user.Identity.Name` *is* the token subject.

The classic mistake is the pair in the stub: a query with no `Where` (so every
caller reads every ticket) and `logger.LogInformation($"...")`, which renders
the string before the logger ever sees it and produces an entry with no named
properties at all.

The model answer puts `curator || t.Holder == holder` inside the query, so the
rows that are not yours never travel, and logs with a template so `Count` and
`Holder` are indexable fields as well as a readable sentence.

## ex7

What this was really testing: that a refusal can leak. If "somebody else's
ticket" answers 403 and "no such ticket" answers 404, the difference between the
two is an oracle, and an attacker can walk the id space and map the database
using nothing else.

The classic mistake is writing the two checks as two branches with two answers,
which feels more honest and is exactly the leak. The second is treating the log
level as a function of the status code - both the 404 and the 409 are refusals,
and only one of them is worth anybody's attention.

The model answer collapses "missing" and "not yours" into one `if` with one
`NotFound()`, logs it at `Information` because a caller asking for the wrong
ticket is a Tuesday, and reserves `Warning` for the already-cancelled conflict,
which is somebody repeating work that was already done.

## ex8

What this was really testing: ordering. Every check in this handler is cheap or
expensive, and safe or unsafe to reveal, and the order they run in is the whole
design - policy first (no database touched), then payload validation (no
database touched), then existence, then capacity, then the write.

The classic mistakes are all seams: saving inside the loop, so a half-written
booking becomes a possible state with no request that can finish it; checking
capacity before validating the payload, so a garbage `count` reaches the
database; and logging without the trace identifier, which leaves a pile of
sentences nobody can join to the request a support ticket is about.

The model answer builds every `Ticket` in memory, calls `SaveChangesAsync`
exactly once so the booking is all-or-nothing, reads the ids back after the save
because the database assigns them, and emits one entry carrying `Count` and
`TraceId`.

## Exercise 1 - routing plus results

Routing (**d01**) fused with results (**d03**). Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex1.cs`. One catch-all route is doing two jobs and
parsing its way through them. Split it:

- `GET /d24/exhibits/open` - 200 with the `ExhibitDto`s whose `Capacity` is
  above zero, **Name A-Z**
- `GET /d24/exhibits/{id:int}` - 200 with that `ExhibitDto`, 404 when there is
  no such exhibit
- `GET /d24/exhibits/abc` - **404 from routing**, before any handler of yours
  runs

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two questions are being answered inside one handler that should have been
answered by the router: "is `open` a resource or an id?" and "is `abc` an id at
all?" Routing can answer both on its own - a literal segment and a route
constraint are the two tools.

## Hint 2

Register two routes. One with the literal segment `open`, one with
`{id:int}`. A literal outranks a parameter, so the order you write them in does
not matter, and `:int` means `abc` matches nothing and the framework answers 404
before your code runs - so neither handler needs `int.TryParse`.

The `open` handler filters on `Capacity > 0` and orders by `Name`; the by-id
handler uses `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, not `FirstAsync`.

## Hint 1

Two questions are being answered inside one handler that should have been
answered by the router: "is `open` a resource or an id?" and "is `abc` an id at
all?" Routing can answer both on its own - a literal segment and a route
constraint are the two tools.

## Hint 2

Register two routes. One with the literal segment `open`, one with
`{id:int}`. A literal outranks a parameter, so the order you write them in does
not matter, and `:int` means `abc` matches nothing and the framework answers 404
before your code runs - so neither handler needs `int.TryParse`.

The `open` handler filters on `Capacity > 0` and orders by `Name`; the by-id
handler uses `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, not `FirstAsync`.

Options (**d09**) fused with validation (**d17**). Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex3.cs`. `POST /d24/reservations` takes a
`NewReservation`:

- blank `holder` and a `count` outside 1..max - **400** validation problem
  carrying **both** keys, `type` `D24Problems.Base + "invalid-request"`
- the maximum comes from `IOptions<D24Options>.Value.MaxTicketsPerVisitor`, not
  from a constant - nothing configures it here, so the class default of 4
  holds, and the gate boots a second host that sets
  `Dojo:D24:MaxTicketsPerVisitor` to 2
- unknown exhibit - 404
- otherwise 200 with `HeldDto`

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate bugs. The first is that `4` is written in the handler, so the value
an operator sets under `Dojo:D24:MaxTicketsPerVisitor` can never take effect -
the `IOptions<D24Options>` parameter is already there and unused. The second is
that the method returns as soon as one thing is wrong.

## Hint 2

Read `options.Value.MaxTicketsPerVisitor` into a local at the top. Then build a
`Dictionary<string, string[]>`, add an entry for each field that failed, and
return `TypedResults.ValidationProblem` only when the dictionary is non-empty -
passing `type: D24Problems.Base + "invalid-request"`.

Put the count message in terms of the limit you read, not the number 4. Check
the exhibit exists only after the payload is known to be good.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - projection plus a query budget

EF Core grouping (**d11**) fused with projection (**d14**). Edit
`src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex4.cs`. `GET /d24/galleries` returns one
`GalleryRow` per gallery, **gallery name A-Z**, where `sold` counts the
**non-cancelled** tickets on that gallery's exhibits - and it must cost **at
most two** database round trips. The gate counts them.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Count the round trips the shipped loop makes against this seed, then against a
museum with two hundred exhibits. The answer is right and the cost grows with
the data - that is an N+1. Separately, `sold` is counting rows it should not:
reread the capacity rule at the top of the README.

## Hint 2

Let the database group. Two queries is the budget: one over `Exhibits` grouped
by `Gallery` counting exhibits, one over `Tickets` filtered by `!t.Cancelled`
and grouped by `t.Exhibit!.Gallery` counting tickets.

Bring both small results back, put the second into a dictionary keyed by
gallery, and zip them in memory - ordering by gallery name.

`TypedResults.Created($"/d24/tickets/{ticket.Id}", dto)` - the id does not exist
until the save.

## Hint 1

Two bugs, and they are independent. One is that the query does not mention the
caller at all, so everybody reads everybody's tickets. The other is that
`$"..."` is evaluated before `LogInformation` is called, so the logger receives
one finished string and no fields.

## Hint 2

The scheme sets `NameClaimType` to `sub`, so `user.Identity?.Name` is the token
subject, and `user.IsInRole("curator")` is the widening. Compute both into
locals and put them in the `Where` - not in a filter after `ToListAsync`.

Then log with a template: the placeholders in
`"Listed {Count} tickets for {Holder}"` become named properties, and the values
go in as arguments after the template.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - authorization, EF Core, problem details, logging

Four at once: ownership (**d20**), EF Core writes (**d10**), problem details
(**d18**) and log levels (**d19**). Edit `src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex7.cs`.
`POST /d24/tickets/{id:int}/cancel` is behind `D24Policies.Visitor`:

1. no such ticket, **or** somebody else's and the caller is not a curator -
   **404**, and the two must be indistinguishable
2. already cancelled - **409** problem details, `type`
   `D24Problems.Base + "already-cancelled"`
3. otherwise **204**, with `Cancelled` actually written

Exactly one log entry per request: `Information` for the 404 and for the
success, **`Warning`** for the 409, and nothing at `Error`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet d24_mixed_gauntlet ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four outcomes and three of them are refusals. Two of those refusals must be
impossible to tell apart from outside: "there is no such ticket" and "it is not
yours". If a caller can distinguish them, they can enumerate your ids.

## Hint 2

Load the ticket with `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, then write the two misses as one
condition: `ticket is null || (!curator && ticket.Holder != holder)` returning
`TypedResults.NotFound()`.

The already-cancelled case is `TypedResults.Problem` with 409 and
`type: D24Problems.Base + "already-cancelled"`. The success sets `Cancelled`,
awaits `SaveChangesAsync`, and returns `TypedResults.NoContent()`.

## Hint 3

Exactly one log entry per request, so log on each of the three paths and only
there. The level is a claim about whose problem it is: a caller asking for a
ticket that is not available is `Information`, and repeating work that was
already done is `Warning`. Nothing here is `Error`.

## Hint 1

Four outcomes and three of them are refusals. Two of those refusals must be
impossible to tell apart from outside: "there is no such ticket" and "it is not
yours". If a caller can distinguish them, they can enumerate your ids.

## Hint 2

Load the ticket with `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, then write the two misses as one
condition: `ticket is null || (!curator && ticket.Holder != holder)` returning
`TypedResults.NotFound()`.

The already-cancelled case is `TypedResults.Problem` with 409 and
`type: D24Problems.Base + "already-cancelled"`. The success sets `Cancelled`,
awaits `SaveChangesAsync`, and returns `TypedResults.NoContent()`.

## Hint 3

Exactly one log entry per request, so log on each of the three paths and only
there. The level is a claim about whose problem it is: a caller asking for a
ticket that is not available is `Information`, and repeating work that was
already done is `Warning`. Nothing here is `Error`.

(**d17**), EF Core (**d10**), problem details (**d18**) and logging (**d19**),
in one handler. Edit `src/Api/D24_MixedGauntlet/Ex8.cs`.

and 403 without the role. Then, in this order:

   `BookingDto` listing the new ticket ids ascending, the holder trimmed, day
