lessons.briefing:
# i3 — Rapid fire

Four short exercises and a review, on the five ⭐⭐⭐ concepts from the question
bank. Every one of them should take under ten minutes; if one takes twenty, that
is the topic to go back to.

The point of this lesson is not to teach you anything new. It is to be
**scheduled**. Every exercise here, and the review, is review-marked, so once you
have finished them `dojo review` brings them back at 3, 7, 21 and 60 days —
which is the interval structure that turns "I understood that in July" into "I
can say that in an interview in October". These are the answers you want
automatic.

Run them cold. No reading, no hints, no scrolling back. If you cannot do one from
memory, that is the signal.

```
uv run dojo review          # what is due today, across every track
uv run dojo review run      # work through it
```

## Exercise 1 — lifetimes

Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex1.cs`. Three interfaces, three lifetimes,
one each. The endpoint is written for you; only the registrations are wrong.

`GET /i3/lifetimes` resolves each service twice in one request and reports the
values. Make it so that:

- `app` is the same across two separate requests
- `request1` and `request2` are equal within a request, and differ between them
- `call1` and `call2` differ within a single request

The names tell you which lifetime each one wants.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — order

Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex2.cs`, method `Configure`. Both
middlewares are given. `RefuseMiddleware` answers **403** for a path ending
`/nope` and does not call `next`; `SeenMiddleware` adds `X-Seen: yes`.

Right now the rejected response has no `X-Seen` header. Fix it, without editing
either middleware.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — tracking

Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`POST /i3/tasks/{id}/complete?tracked=true|false`: load the task — tracked or
with `AsNoTracking()` according to the flag — set `Done` to `true`, save, and
answer **200** with `{"changes": …, "done": …}`, or **404** for an unknown id.

With `tracked=false`: `done` is `true` and `changes` is **0**, and the row does
not change. That silence is the whole exercise.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — status codes

Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex4.cs`. Six answers across two handlers,
and no logic worth the name:

- `POST /i3/codes` with a blank value → **400**
- `POST /i3/codes` with a value already in the store → **409**
- otherwise → **201** with `Location: /i3/codes/{id}` and the created code
- `DELETE /i3/codes/{id}` that was there → **204** with no body
- the same `DELETE` again → **404**

If you have to stop and think about 400 versus 409, reread the answer to
question 34 in `i1_interview_concepts`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex4
```

## Review

`review1` is the one the scheduler leans on hardest, and it is the 401/403 pair.
Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Review1.cs`: add a policy named
`Review1Services.MembersOnly` that authenticates on `I2Jwt.Scheme` and requires
the `member` role, and apply it to `GET /i3/review/secret`.

- no token → **401**
- a token whose role is `guest` → **403**
- a token whose role is `member` → **200**
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/i3_interview_rapidfire

Short lesson, short reading. Each section is the one-paragraph version of the
answer you should be able to give without thinking, plus the follow-up that
comes after it.

## Notes

Spaced repetition works because forgetting is a schedule, not an event. You lose
most of a new fact within days unless it is recalled, and each successful recall
flattens the curve — which is why the review ladder in this dojo is 3, 7, 21 and
60 days rather than "whenever you feel like it". The important detail is that
*retrieval* is what strengthens the memory, not rereading: pulling an answer out
of an empty head is the exercise, and looking at the answer first skips it
entirely. That is why this lesson's five exercises are all review-marked and why
you should run them cold.

## ex1 - the three lifetimes, in one sentence each

Singleton: one instance for the life of the application, so it must be
thread-safe, and it must never hold anything shorter-lived. Scoped: one instance
per scope, which the framework creates per HTTP request, so it is the home for
anything belonging to "this request" — the `DbContext`, the current user, a
correlation id. Transient: a new instance every time anything resolves it, for
cheap stateless helpers, and never for anything that is supposed to accumulate.

The reason the endpoint resolves each service *twice* is that a lifetime has no
observable meaning inside a single resolution. Ask twice within one request and
across two requests, and the four combinations of same/different answer the
question completely. That two-line experiment is also how you find out what an
unfamiliar registration really is.

**↦ The follow-up:** *what happens if a singleton takes a scoped dependency?*
Captive dependency — the scoped instance outlives its request and every later
request sees stale, possibly someone else's, data. In Development the container
refuses to start; the transient-into-singleton version of the same bug starts
cleanly and is just as wrong.

## ex2 - order, in one sentence

The first middleware added is the outermost, so it sees the request first and
the response last; anything that must touch *every* request or response has to be
outside anything that can short-circuit one.

That single rule explains the canonical `Program.cs` ordering and every "why is
my middleware not running" question. Exception handling, correlation, logging and
metrics go near the top because they observe. CORS goes before authentication, or
a rejected preflight comes back without CORS headers and the browser blames the
wrong thing. Authentication goes before authorization, because you cannot decide
whether someone may do something before you know who they are.

**↦ The follow-up:** *what is the difference between `Use`, `Run` and `Map`?*
`Use` adds a link that may call `next`; `Run` adds a terminal with no `next`, so
anything after it is dead code; `Map` splits into a branch that never rejoins,
while `UseWhen` splits into one that does.

## ex3 - tracking, in one sentence

A tracked query snapshots every property, and `SaveChangesAsync` writes the
differences; `AsNoTracking` skips the snapshot, so any change you make afterwards
is invisible to the save — silently, with no exception and no log.

`changes == 0` is the tell, and it is the only one you get. This is the most
expensive quiet bug in EF Core, and the reason to have produced it deliberately
is that you will recognise "the edit didn't stick" instantly the next time you
hear it.

Use `AsNoTracking` for read-only queries, which is most of them; note that a
projection to a non-entity type is untracked anyway, so the flag matters mainly
when you are pulling back whole entities.

**↦ The follow-up:** *what is the identity map, and what does no-tracking do to
it?* Tracking keeps one object per primary key, so the same row appearing twice
in a result is the same instance; `AsNoTracking` materialises a separate object
each time, which costs memory and can leave you holding two divergent copies of
one row. `AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution` is the middle option.

## ex4 - the status codes, in one sentence each

**201** — I made something, and `Location` says where. **204** — done, and there
is deliberately no body. **400** — your request is wrong on its face; look at it
and try again. **409** — your request is fine and the current state forbids it;
you could not have known. **404** — nothing lives at this URL, which is also the
right answer when telling you it exists would itself be a leak.

The pair that gets confused is 400 and 409, and the test that separates them is
whether the answer depends on server state. A blank value is a 400 whatever is
in the database; a duplicate is a 409 because it is a fact about the collection,
and the same request might succeed tomorrow.

**↦ The follow-up:** *should DELETE be idempotent?* By the spec, DELETE is
idempotent — the end state is the same however many times you send it — which is
an argument for 204 every time. The counter-argument, and the choice this API
makes, is that "there is nothing here" is information the client can use. Either
is defensible; being inconsistent across your own resources is not.

## review1 - 401 versus 403, in one sentence

401 means *I do not know who you are* — authenticate and try again. 403 means
*I know exactly who you are and the answer is no*.

Neither status code is something you write. The authentication handler
challenges with 401 when there is no identity; the authorization middleware
forbids with 403 when there is one that fails the policy. Writing `if`s in the
handler to produce them means re-deriving that distinction per endpoint and
getting it wrong somewhere.

`AddAuthenticationSchemes` on the policy is the detail worth remembering in an
application with more than one scheme — which, once you have a public API and an
internal one, or a migration in progress, is most real applications.

**↦ The follow-up:** *when would you return 404 instead of 403?* When the
existence of the resource is itself privileged information. A 403 on someone
else's record confirms that the record exists, and an attacker can walk the id
space and map your data without reading any of it. GitHub returns 404 for private
repositories you cannot see, for exactly this reason.

## Further reading

- [Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/dependency-injection) — lifetimes, scopes and the request scope.
- [Middleware order](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/#middleware-order) — the canonical pipeline, and why each step sits where it does.
- [Tracking vs. no-tracking queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking) — snapshots, the identity map and when to turn tracking off.
- [RFC 9110 §15 — Status codes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-status-codes) — the definitions of 201, 204, 400, 403, 404 and 409.
- [Introduction to authorization in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/introduction) — policies, roles, and where 401 and 403 come from.

# i3 — Rapid fire

Four short exercises and a review, on the five ⭐⭐⭐ concepts from the question
bank. Every one of them should take under ten minutes; if one takes twenty, that
is the topic to go back to.

The point of this lesson is not to teach you anything new. It is to be
**scheduled**. Every exercise here, and the review, is review-marked, so once you
have finished them `dojo review` brings them back at 3, 7, 21 and 60 days —
which is the interval structure that turns "I understood that in July" into "I
can say that in an interview in October". These are the answers you want
automatic.

Run them cold. No reading, no hints, no scrolling back. If you cannot do one from
memory, that is the signal.

```
uv run dojo review          # what is due today, across every track
uv run dojo review run      # work through it
```

## Exercise 1 — lifetimes

Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex1.cs`. Three interfaces, three lifetimes,
one each. The endpoint is written for you; only the registrations are wrong.

`GET /i3/lifetimes` resolves each service twice in one request and reports the
values. Make it so that:

- `app` is the same across two separate requests
- `request1` and `request2` are equal within a request, and differ between them
- `call1` and `call2` differ within a single request

The names tell you which lifetime each one wants.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — order

Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex2.cs`, method `Configure`. Both
middlewares are given. `RefuseMiddleware` answers **403** for a path ending
`/nope` and does not call `next`; `SeenMiddleware` adds `X-Seen: yes`.

Right now the rejected response has no `X-Seen` header. Fix it, without editing
either middleware.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — tracking

Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`POST /i3/tasks/{id}/complete?tracked=true|false`: load the task — tracked or
with `AsNoTracking()` according to the flag — set `Done` to `true`, save, and
answer **200** with `{"changes": …, "done": …}`, or **404** for an unknown id.

With `tracked=false`: `done` is `true` and `changes` is **0**, and the row does
not change. That silence is the whole exercise.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — status codes

Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Ex4.cs`. Six answers across two handlers,
and no logic worth the name:

- `POST /i3/codes` with a blank value → **400**
- `POST /i3/codes` with a value already in the store → **409**
- otherwise → **201** with `Location: /i3/codes/{id}` and the created code
- `DELETE /i3/codes/{id}` that was there → **204** with no body
- the same `DELETE` again → **404**

If you have to stop and think about 400 versus 409, reread the answer to
question 34 in `i1_interview_concepts`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex4
```

## Review

`review1` is the one the scheduler leans on hardest, and it is the 401/403 pair.
Edit `src/Api/I3_InterviewRapidfire/Review1.cs`: add a policy named
`Review1Services.MembersOnly` that authenticates on `I2Jwt.Scheme` and requires
the `member` role, and apply it to `GET /i3/review/secret`.

- no token → **401**
- a token whose role is `guest` → **403**
- a token whose role is `member` → **200**

## The gate

This is the entire gate class, `tests/Gates/I3_InterviewRapidfireTests.cs`:

```csharp
using System.Net;
using System.Net.Http.Headers;
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using DotnetDojo.Api.I1_InterviewConcepts;
using DotnetDojo.Api.I2_InterviewDrills;
using DotnetDojo.Api.I3_InterviewRapidfire;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens;
using Microsoft.IdentityModel.Tokens;

namespace DotnetDojo.Gates;

public class I3_InterviewRapidfireTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex1_ThreeLifetimesInOneRequest()
    {
        using var host = new DojoWebFactory();
        using var client = host.CreateClient();

        var first = await client.GetAsync("/i3/lifetimes");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, first,
            "GET /i3/lifetimes must answer 200 - reread README ex1.");

        var a = await first.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<LifetimeDto>();
        var b = await (await client.GetAsync("/i3/lifetimes")).Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<LifetimeDto>();

        Teach.Equal(a!.App, b!.App,
            "IAppWide is one object for the whole application, so both requests see the same "
                + "value. That is a singleton.");

        Teach.Equal(a.Request1, a.Request2,
            "IPerRequest was resolved twice in ONE request and gave two different objects. "
                + "One instance per request is scoped.");
        Teach.True(a.Request1 != b.Request1,
            "…and two different requests must get two different ones, or it is a singleton.");

        Teach.True(a.Call1 != a.Call2,
            "IPerCall was resolved twice in one request and gave the same object. A new one "
                + "every time anyone asks is transient.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex2_TheOutermostMiddlewareStillRuns()
    {
        using var host = new DojoWebFactory();
        using var client = host.CreateClient();

        var refused = await client.GetAsync("/i3/order/nope");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Forbidden, refused,
            "The given middleware refuses this path with 403 - reread README ex2.");
        Teach.Equal("yes", Header(refused, "X-Seen"),
            "The rejected response has no X-Seen header, because the middleware that adds it "
                + "sits downstream of the one that short-circuits. Anything that must touch "
                + "every response has to be added first.");

        var allowed = await client.GetAsync("/i3/order/fine");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, allowed, "Any other path gets through.");
        Teach.Equal("ok", await allowed.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
            "…all the way to the terminal handler.");
        Teach.Equal("yes", Header(allowed, "X-Seen"), "…and it is stamped too.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex3_NoTrackingSavesNothing()
    {
        using var host = NewTracker();
        using var client = host.CreateClient();

        var untracked = await client.PostAsync("/i3/tasks/1/complete?tracked=false", null);
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, untracked,
            "POST /i3/tasks/1/complete?tracked=false must answer 200 - reread README ex3.");

        var untrackedBody = await untracked.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<CompleteDto>();
        Teach.Equal(true, untrackedBody?.Done,
            "The object in memory really was changed - assigning to a property always works.");
        Teach.Equal(0, untrackedBody?.Changes,
            "An AsNoTracking entity is not in the change tracker, so SaveChangesAsync sees "
                + "nothing to write and returns 0.");
        Teach.Equal(false, host.Query(db => db.Tasks.Single(t => t.Id == 1).Done),
            "…and the row is untouched. No exception, no warning, no update.");

        var tracked = await client.PostAsync("/i3/tasks/2/complete?tracked=true", null);
        var trackedBody = await tracked.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<CompleteDto>();
        Teach.Equal(1, trackedBody?.Changes,
            "A tracked entity you changed produces exactly one write.");
        Teach.Equal(true, host.Query(db => db.Tasks.Single(t => t.Id == 2).Done),
            "…and this time the row really changed.");

        var missing = await client.PostAsync("/i3/tasks/99/complete?tracked=true", null);
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, missing, "There is no task 99: 404.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Ex4_SixCodesAndOnlyOneIsRight()
    {
        using var host = new DojoWebFactory();
        using var client = host.CreateClient();

        var created = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/i3/codes", new { value = "beta" });
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Created, created,
            "Creating a resource is 201 - reread README ex4.");
        Teach.Equal("/i3/codes/2", created.Headers.Location?.ToString(),
            "…with a Location. One code is seeded, so the new one is 2.");

        var blank = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/i3/codes", new { value = "  " });
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest, blank,
            "A blank value is malformed input: 400.");

        var duplicate = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/i3/codes", new { value = "alpha" });
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Conflict, duplicate,
            "\"alpha\" is already there. The request is well formed and the current state "
                + "forbids it, which is 409 - not 400.");

        Teach.Equal(2, host.Services.GetRequiredService<ICodeStore>().Count,
            "The two rejected requests must not have added anything.");

        var deleted = await client.DeleteAsync("/i3/codes/1");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.NoContent, deleted,
            "A successful delete is 204 with no body.");
        Teach.Equal("", await deleted.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(), "…no body at all.");

        var again = await client.DeleteAsync("/i3/codes/1");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, again,
            "The second delete finds nothing at that URL: 404.");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Review1_UnauthenticatedIsNotUnauthorized()
    {
        using var host = new DojoWebFactory();
        using var client = host.CreateClient();

        var anonymous = await client.GetAsync("/i3/review/secret");
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, anonymous,
            "No token: 401. A 200 here means the endpoint is still open - reread README "
                + "review.");

        var ordinary = await client.SendAsync(Bearer("/i3/review/secret", Token("ada", "guest")));
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.Forbidden, ordinary,
            "This caller proved who they are and lacks the role: 403. Sending 401 would tell "
                + "them to authenticate, which they already did.");

        var member = await client.SendAsync(Bearer("/i3/review/secret", Token("ada", "member")));
        await Teach.Status(HttpStatusCode.OK, member, "A member gets in.");
        var body = await member.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<SecretDto>();
        Teach.Equal("the dojo is closed", body?.Value, "…and reads the secret.");
    }

    // … a SqliteHost<TrackerDb> factory, a token factory for I2Jwt.Scheme,
    //   a header reader, and three DTO records …
}
```

In plain English: five tests, one per ⭐⭐⭐ concept, each of them making the
smallest number of requests that can tell the right answer from the plausible
one. That is deliberately the same standard the rest of the track uses — a gate
that can only be passed by understanding, not by pattern-matching.

## The teaching point

Fluency is not the same as understanding, and interviews sample fluency. The
concepts in this lesson are ones you have already understood — twice, in some
cases — and the reason to do them again cold, and then again in three days, and
then in three weeks, is that recall decays on a schedule and the fix is to
practise on the same schedule.

That is the whole design of this part of the course. `i1` gives you the language,
`i2` gives you the reps, and `i3` gets scheduled. Let the ladder do the work:

```
uv run dojo review
```

That is the end of the ASP.NET Core track. You have built, in ten lessons: an
API with real routing and result types, a container you understand the lifetimes
of, a pipeline you can order from first principles, configuration that differs
per environment, a data layer whose SQL you can predict, a REST resource that
tells the truth in six status codes, failures that teach the operator without
leaking to the client, and an authorization model with a test to prove it. That
is a mid-level .NET backend engineer's working vocabulary — not the whole
language of it, but every word you need to hold a conversation.

# Reading - dotnet/i3_interview_rapidfire

Short lesson, short reading. Each section is the one-paragraph version of the
answer you should be able to give without thinking, plus the follow-up that
comes after it.

## Notes

Spaced repetition works because forgetting is a schedule, not an event. You lose
most of a new fact within days unless it is recalled, and each successful recall
flattens the curve — which is why the review ladder in this dojo is 3, 7, 21 and
60 days rather than "whenever you feel like it". The important detail is that
*retrieval* is what strengthens the memory, not rereading: pulling an answer out
of an empty head is the exercise, and looking at the answer first skips it
entirely. That is why this lesson's five exercises are all review-marked and why
you should run them cold.

## ex1 - the three lifetimes, in one sentence each

Singleton: one instance for the life of the application, so it must be
thread-safe, and it must never hold anything shorter-lived. Scoped: one instance
per scope, which the framework creates per HTTP request, so it is the home for
anything belonging to "this request" — the `DbContext`, the current user, a
correlation id. Transient: a new instance every time anything resolves it, for
cheap stateless helpers, and never for anything that is supposed to accumulate.

The reason the endpoint resolves each service *twice* is that a lifetime has no
observable meaning inside a single resolution. Ask twice within one request and
across two requests, and the four combinations of same/different answer the
question completely. That two-line experiment is also how you find out what an
unfamiliar registration really is.

**↦ The follow-up:** *what happens if a singleton takes a scoped dependency?*
Captive dependency — the scoped instance outlives its request and every later
request sees stale, possibly someone else's, data. In Development the container
refuses to start; the transient-into-singleton version of the same bug starts
cleanly and is just as wrong.

## ex2 - order, in one sentence

The first middleware added is the outermost, so it sees the request first and
the response last; anything that must touch *every* request or response has to be
outside anything that can short-circuit one.

That single rule explains the canonical `Program.cs` ordering and every "why is
my middleware not running" question. Exception handling, correlation, logging and
metrics go near the top because they observe. CORS goes before authentication, or
a rejected preflight comes back without CORS headers and the browser blames the
wrong thing. Authentication goes before authorization, because you cannot decide
whether someone may do something before you know who they are.

**↦ The follow-up:** *what is the difference between `Use`, `Run` and `Map`?*
`Use` adds a link that may call `next`; `Run` adds a terminal with no `next`, so
anything after it is dead code; `Map` splits into a branch that never rejoins,
while `UseWhen` splits into one that does.

## ex3 - tracking, in one sentence

A tracked query snapshots every property, and `SaveChangesAsync` writes the
differences; `AsNoTracking` skips the snapshot, so any change you make afterwards
is invisible to the save — silently, with no exception and no log.

`changes == 0` is the tell, and it is the only one you get. This is the most
expensive quiet bug in EF Core, and the reason to have produced it deliberately
is that you will recognise "the edit didn't stick" instantly the next time you
hear it.

Use `AsNoTracking` for read-only queries, which is most of them; note that a
projection to a non-entity type is untracked anyway, so the flag matters mainly
when you are pulling back whole entities.

**↦ The follow-up:** *what is the identity map, and what does no-tracking do to
it?* Tracking keeps one object per primary key, so the same row appearing twice
in a result is the same instance; `AsNoTracking` materialises a separate object
each time, which costs memory and can leave you holding two divergent copies of
one row. `AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution` is the middle option.

## ex4 - the status codes, in one sentence each

**201** — I made something, and `Location` says where. **204** — done, and there
is deliberately no body. **400** — your request is wrong on its face; look at it
and try again. **409** — your request is fine and the current state forbids it;
you could not have known. **404** — nothing lives at this URL, which is also the
right answer when telling you it exists would itself be a leak.

The pair that gets confused is 400 and 409, and the test that separates them is
whether the answer depends on server state. A blank value is a 400 whatever is
in the database; a duplicate is a 409 because it is a fact about the collection,
and the same request might succeed tomorrow.

**↦ The follow-up:** *should DELETE be idempotent?* By the spec, DELETE is
idempotent — the end state is the same however many times you send it — which is
an argument for 204 every time. The counter-argument, and the choice this API
makes, is that "there is nothing here" is information the client can use. Either
is defensible; being inconsistent across your own resources is not.

## review1 - 401 versus 403, in one sentence

401 means *I do not know who you are* — authenticate and try again. 403 means
*I know exactly who you are and the answer is no*.

Neither status code is something you write. The authentication handler
challenges with 401 when there is no identity; the authorization middleware
forbids with 403 when there is one that fails the policy. Writing `if`s in the
handler to produce them means re-deriving that distinction per endpoint and
getting it wrong somewhere.

`AddAuthenticationSchemes` on the policy is the detail worth remembering in an
application with more than one scheme — which, once you have a public API and an
internal one, or a migration in progress, is most real applications.

**↦ The follow-up:** *when would you return 404 instead of 403?* When the
existence of the resource is itself privileged information. A 403 on someone
else's record confirms that the record exists, and an attacker can walk the id
space and map your data without reading any of it. GitHub returns 404 for private
repositories you cannot see, for exactly this reason.

## Further reading

- [Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/dependency-injection) — lifetimes, scopes and the request scope.
- [Middleware order](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/#middleware-order) — the canonical pipeline, and why each step sits where it does.
- [Tracking vs. no-tracking queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking) — snapshots, the identity map and when to turn tracking off.
- [RFC 9110 §15 — Status codes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-status-codes) — the definitions of 201, 204, 400, 403, 404 and 409.
- [Introduction to authorization in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/introduction) — policies, roles, and where 401 and 403 come from.

`/nope` and does not call `next`; `SeenMiddleware` adds `X-Seen: yes`.

uv run dojo test dotnet i3_interview_rapidfire ex2

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two lines, and you are swapping them. Do not edit either middleware.

Trace the refused request: `RefuseMiddleware` sees `/nope`, sets 403, and
returns without calling `next`. Now ask what never got a turn.

## Hint 2

The first middleware added is the outermost, and a short-circuit means nothing
downstream runs at all. So the one that must touch every response has to go
first.

## Hint 3

```csharp
pipeline.UseMiddleware<SeenMiddleware>();
pipeline.UseMiddleware<RefuseMiddleware>();
```

`SeenMiddleware` sets its header *before* awaiting `next`, which is also
load-bearing — after the terminal has written a body the response has started and
headers can no longer change.

## Hint 1

Two lines, and you are swapping them. Do not edit either middleware.

Trace the refused request: `RefuseMiddleware` sees `/nope`, sets 403, and
returns without calling `next`. Now ask what never got a turn.

## Hint 2

The first middleware added is the outermost, and a short-circuit means nothing
downstream runs at all. So the one that must touch every response has to go
first.

## Hint 3

```csharp
pipeline.UseMiddleware<SeenMiddleware>();
pipeline.UseMiddleware<RefuseMiddleware>();
```

`SeenMiddleware` sets its header *before* awaiting `next`, which is also
load-bearing — after the terminal has written a body the response has started and
headers can no longer change.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two handlers, six answers, no logic. Write the create as three guards in the
right order and the delete as a single conditional.

The order of the create's guards matters: a blank value is wrong whatever is in
the store, so it is checked first.

## Hint 2

Create: `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` → `TypedResults.BadRequest()`;
`store.Exists(value)` → `TypedResults.Conflict()`; otherwise `store.Add(value)`
and `TypedResults.Created($"/i3/codes/{code.Id}", code)`.

Delete: `store.Remove(id)` returns a `bool` — true is
`TypedResults.NoContent()`, false is `TypedResults.NotFound()`.

## Hint 3

```csharp
private static IResult DeleteCode(int id, ICodeStore store) =>
    store.Remove(id) ? TypedResults.NoContent() : TypedResults.NotFound();
```

Be able to say, out loud, why the duplicate is 409 and the blank is 400: one
depends on the current state of the collection and the other does not.

## Hint 1

One policy, one `RequireAuthorization`. You write neither status code — the
framework produces 401 when there is no identity and 403 when there is one that
fails the policy.

The scheme to authenticate against is on `I2Jwt`; it is already registered.

## Hint 2

```csharp
services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy(MembersOnly, policy => policy
        .AddAuthenticationSchemes(/* … */)
        .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
        .RequireRole(/* … */));
```

`AddAuthenticationSchemes` is not optional here: this application has more than
one bearer scheme, and without naming one the policy falls back to the default,
which belongs to a different lesson.

Then pass the policy name to `RequireAuthorization` where the route is mapped.

## Hint 3

```csharp
app.MapGet("/i3/review/secret", Secret)
    .RequireAuthorization(Review1Services.MembersOnly);
```

Say the difference out loud before you run it: 401 means *authenticate and try
again*; 403 means *credentials will not help*.

## Hint 1

One policy, one `RequireAuthorization`. You write neither status code — the
framework produces 401 when there is no identity and 403 when there is one that
fails the policy.

The scheme to authenticate against is on `I2Jwt`; it is already registered.

## Hint 2

```csharp
services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy(MembersOnly, policy => policy
        .AddAuthenticationSchemes(/* … */)
        .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
        .RequireRole(/* … */));
```

`AddAuthenticationSchemes` is not optional here: this application has more than
one bearer scheme, and without naming one the policy falls back to the default,
which belongs to a different lesson.

Then pass the policy name to `RequireAuthorization` where the route is mapped.

## Hint 3

```csharp
app.MapGet("/i3/review/secret", Secret)
    .RequireAuthorization(Review1Services.MembersOnly);
```
